finding: A late static-test failure at the side-of-body join forced Boeing to postpone 787 first flight in June 2009.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: In April we announced a reduction to our 777 production rates starting in June 2010 and we postponed rate increases planned for the 67 and the 47. Since that time, BCA has accommodated about 70 airplane deferrals in addition to the 60 processed in the first quarter
finding: In the 2009 recession Boeing cut 777 rates, postponed 767/747 increases and processed about 130 deferrals in 1H 2009.
response: 777 rate cut; 767 and 747 increases postponed

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Accordingly, there has been no change in our current thinking about commercial production levels including our assessment that we can hold 737 at its current build rate.
finding: Boeing held the 737 rate through the depth of the 2009 recession.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: During the quarter we did not acquire any of our shares, but we did pay approximately $300 million in dividends.
finding: In 2009 Boeing stopped share repurchases but kept its roughly $300 million quarterly dividend.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Clearly, we do have the ability to get back in the bond markets and we’ll probably do some of that, I don’t know exactly what the optimal number is, but you’ll see it and we’ll let you know as we do that. We are not at a point where we are considering cutting our dividends.
finding: Under 787 cash pressure Boeing chose to borrow in the bond market rather than cut its dividend.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: So clearly it’s going to be higher than what you’ve seen traditionally, but until we finally have to book financials on our P&L statements, we are not going to disclose what that number is.
finding: Boeing planned a larger-than-usual 787 accounting block, spreading costs over more units, and withheld the number until first delivery.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Well, we have sold 850 of these and we know we are way ahead of our competition and the market is still going to be robust over a timeframe that we think we have the ability to estimate
finding: Boeing relied on its 850-order 787 lead over the competition to justify long-run profitability despite cost overruns.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO (answering Doug Harned, Sanford Bernstein)
quote: are you having to provide more favorable terms for some of them to take these slots? ... The answer is no to the last part of your question.
finding: Boeing said it was not offering more favorable terms to customers taking over deferred slots, i.e. no discounting to fill the skyline.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: there is no doubt that the baseline was too ambitious, and it’s hard for me to characterize exactly whether it was marketing ambition, or financial goals, but clearly the initial plan outran our ability to execute it.
finding: Boeing admitted the 787 baseline was too ambitious and that the plan outran its execution capacity, a lesson for setting future program baselines.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have chosen to bring some of it back in house and that’s what I would anticipate as learning as you go, making practical decisions on what you do with partners and what you do yourself. ... we are not going to go back to the days where we do everything in-house.
finding: Boeing moved to partial insourcing on the 787 but ruled out full vertical integration, keeping a partner-based systems-integrator model.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: our decision to reclassify costs on the first three 787 flight-test airplanes to R&D expense was based on our conclusion that those planes have no commercial market value beyond the development effort. The costs through September for those aircraft resulted in adding 2.6 billion of R&D expense
finding: Boeing wrote off about $2.6 billion by moving the first three 787 test aircraft to R&D after deciding they were unsellable.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Earlier this month, we announced a $1 billion charge on our 747-8 program, due to increased production costs, and difficult market conditions.
finding: Boeing took a $1 billion 747-8 reach-forward loss charge in 3Q 2009 for production cost overruns and weak demand.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The engineering on this program was late to mature, and that was compounded by the limited availability of engineering resources.
finding: Boeing traced the 747-8's problems to late engineering maturity compounded by limited engineering resources.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we've been working closely with our customers in what continues to be a very challenging cargo market. These discussions drove our decision to defer a planned increase in the 747-8 production rate, which was prudent, but also contributed to the charge taken this quarter.
finding: Boeing deferred the 747-8 rate increase because of the weak cargo market, even though the deferral added to the charge.
response: Deferred the planned 747-8 rate increase

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: During the quarter, the company paid 592 million in cash for the acquisition of Vought 787 facilities in South Carolina
finding: Boeing paid $592 million to buy Vought's 787 facilities in South Carolina, bringing supplier work in-house.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: work with our partners on gross margin improvements for both of us, and at the same time, reduce R&D significantly since we don't have an imminent new program in front of us.
finding: In 2009 Boeing planned to cut R&D significantly because it had no imminent new program.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: In our case, on top of a very aggressive baseline, there were significant outsourcing of both manufacturing and engineering, at the same time we were dealing with the new material, new design tools. So we experienced a bridge too far leading-edge kind of development
finding: Boeing's CEO diagnosed the 787 failure as a 'bridge too far': aggressive baselines plus heavy outsourcing of engineering and manufacturing plus new materials and tools all at once.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: One is in realistic baselines that don't try to stretch into a sort of market performance that is unrealistic, at the same time remain competitive obviously. Our competitors also had trouble with some overreach.
finding: Lesson Boeing drew for future programs: set realistic baselines and avoid overpromising performance, noting competitors had also overreached.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: when we outsource some of the engineering that compounded the oversight process, we need to bring some more of the engineering, particularly at the systems level back into Boeing.
finding: Boeing moved to bring systems-level engineering back in-house after the 787 outsourcing problems.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: both the 87 [787] and the 47 [747] reaching their engineering peaks at about the same time, even though we had originally planned to have the peaks be complementary rather than overlap.
finding: The 787 delay made its engineering peak overlap with the 747-8's, against Boeing's plan to keep the two peaks apart.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: what we have are the oversolds that are coming down in to fill in for those that are getting deferred out to the right.
finding: Boeing used deliberate overselling of the skyline to absorb deferrals and keep production rates stable.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: diversifying our labor pool and labor relationship has some benefits. I think the union, IAM [International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers] and the company, have had trouble figuring it out between themselves over the last few contract discussions, and I've got to figure out a way to reduce that risk to the company.
finding: Boeing weighed putting the second 787 line in Charleston to diversify its labor base and reduce strike risk from Puget Sound.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Flight test is still expected by the end of the year, and the first delivery remains scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2010.
finding: After the side-of-body delay Boeing targeted first 787 delivery in 4Q 2010; this later slipped to 3Q 2011.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: R&D guidance also includes the operating model adjustment we discussed in August to better balance future 787 R&D efforts between Boeing and our suppliers.
finding: In August 2009 Boeing changed the 787 operating model to take back part of the R&D burden from risk-sharing suppliers.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we will have to make the 73 re-engining decision, I would say probably a little quicker than the final 777 decision. And you're right. I mean, I think understanding the A350-1000 a little bit better, we have a little time to understand that as we consider alternatives.
finding: Boeing ranked a 737 re-engine decision ahead of a 777 response, and continued to wait on the A350-1000.
trigger: Re-engining pressure in narrowbodies; A350-1000 definition
response: 737 re-engine under active consideration; 777 decision after A350-1000 clarity

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: if we achieve half the market that you described, there will be no problem with profitability on this program.
finding: Boeing's 747-8 business case vs the A380 rested on taking about half of a roughly 740-aircraft very-large-aircraft market.
trigger: A380 competition in very large aircraft
response: 747-8 targeted at half the VLA market

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Disciplined cash management across all areas of the company paid off, as we generated $5.6 billion in operating cash flow, while at the same time, made significant 787 investments in both R&D and inventory.
finding: Through tight cash management Boeing generated $5.6 billion of operating cash in the 2009 recession while funding the 787.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: To support that rate buildup, gain tighter control of our supply chain and better diversify our manufacturing base, we took several recent steps focused on the programs operations in South Carolina.
finding: Boeing took steps in South Carolina to gain tighter control of the 787 supply chain and diversify its manufacturing base.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We have been reintroducing rigorous functional disciplines across the company. And as part of those efforts, we recently appointed nine senior engineering leaders to work closely with program teams to help ensure technical integrity
finding: Boeing responded to development failures by restoring functional engineering discipline and appointing nine senior engineering leaders to oversee programs.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: There has been no change in our production rate plans, which include holding the 737 at its current rate into the foreseeable future. We believe the discipline we have exercised in managing both production rates and market opportunities has paid off. We foresee holding to our production plans without having to enter into bad business deals
finding: Through the recession Boeing held the 737 rate steady and said it would not have to accept 'bad business deals' to do so.
response: Held 737 rate flat and did not cut prices to fill slots

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: 2009 EPS was reduced $2.38 due to the reclassification of the first three 787 flight-test airplanes from program inventory to R&D expense. In addition, we took charges totaling $1.20 per share on the 747 program as a result of difficult market conditions and higher cost estimates.
finding: 2009 earnings absorbed large development write-downs: $2.38/share for the 787 test aircraft and $1.20/share of 747-8 charges.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: In addition to the $5.6 billion of operating cash flow we've generated in 2009, we also issued $5 billion of corporate debt at very attractive rates, which solidify a strong liquidity position.
finding: Boeing issued $5 billion of corporate debt in 2009 on top of $5.6 billion of operating cash flow to build liquidity.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: During the fourth quarter, we contributed approximately 29 million Boeing shares valued at $1.5 billion to our pension plans.
finding: Boeing contributed $1.5 billion of its own stock, not cash, to its pension plans.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We expect 2011 R&D expense to decrease by more than $500 million, a substantial reduction but one that retains funds that support the 787 and 747 derivatives and pursue potential investments in the 777 and the 737.
finding: Boeing planned to cut R&D after 2010 but kept a budget wedge for 787/747 derivatives and possible 777 and 737 investments.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: It's prudent, not conservative.
finding: Boeing's CFO described the contingency in guidance as 'prudent, not conservative', i.e. deliberate buffers during development programs.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: At this point, we're not considering going back and repurchase, our share repurchase program, and we won't get back to that or start considering things like that probably until 2011. Once we get through the challenges we have on our books today.
finding: Boeing suspended share buybacks until the 787/747-8 development risk was behind it, putting liquidity for development and ramp-up first.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: one of those is re-engining the 737 [Audio Gap] which is under active consideration, from a product requirement standpoint. And so we're beginning to harden up alternatives, maturing the technologies with the right amount of R&D spending and have a wedge in our budget to quickly move on both as the market requires.
finding: By January 2010 re-engining the 737 was under active consideration, with R&D budgeted to move quickly on the 737 or 777 when the market required.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: it's that customer base that is pushing us to consider re-engining or in some cases a completely new airplane. So I think in this era of high fuel prices and productivity requirements, I think, airlines are focused less on the obsolescence issue
finding: Customers, driven by fuel prices, were pushing Boeing toward a re-engine or new airplane, and Boeing judged that this reduced the risk of 737 deferrals.
trigger: High fuel prices and customer pressure for a more efficient narrowbody
response: Actively studying a 737 re-engine or new airplane

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO (answering analyst's premise)
quote: You're expecting about 740 sales over the next 20 years for a large aircraft between the -8 and the A380 and I believe you expect to take about half of that market. ... if we achieve half the market that you described, there will be no problem with profitability on this program.
finding: Boeing's 747-8 break-even depended on winning about half of a roughly 740-aircraft very-large-aircraft market shared with the A380.

quote: Our total research and development expense amounted to $6.5 billion, $3.8 billion and $3.9 billion in 2009, 2008 and 2007, respectively. ... Research and development expense in 2009 includes $2.7 billion of production costs related to the first three flight test 787 aircraft that cannot be sold
finding: R&D jumped to $6.5B in 2009 mainly because $2.7B of unsellable 787 flight-test aircraft were written into R&D.

quote: We face aggressive international competitors, including Airbus, who are intent on increasing their market share. We are focused on improving our processes and continuing cost reduction efforts. We continue to leverage our extensive customer support services network
finding: In 2009 Boeing's stated response to Airbus's share push was process improvement, cost cutting and its customer-support network, a formula it repeated through FY2022.
trigger: Airbus intent on increasing market share
response: Cost reduction; leverage support network

quote: A number of our suppliers have made assertions for higher prices or other contractual compensation relief which could affect program/contract profitability.
finding: During the 787 delays suppliers pressed Boeing for higher prices and compensation, showing their leverage over the program.

quote: Production rate reductions could cause us to incur disruption and other costs and result in infrastructure costs being allocated to a smaller quantity of airplanes, all of which could reduce our profitability.
finding: Boeing treats rate cuts as costly because fixed infrastructure is spread over fewer airplanes, which makes it reluctant to cut rates.

quote: We delivered 104 fewer airplanes than expected during 2008 due to the strike. This reduced revenue by approximately $6.4 billion for the twelve months ended December 31, 2008.
finding: The 2008 IAM strike cost Boeing 104 deliveries and about $6.4B of revenue, showing its exposure to labor disruption.

quote: Cash dividends have been paid on common stock every year since 1942.
finding: In 2009, in the middle of the 787 crisis, Boeing kept its unbroken dividend record (since 1942, $1.68/share); it suspended the dividend only in 2020.

quote: Taken together, these core businesses have historically generated substantial earnings and cash flow that permit us to invest in new products and services that open new frontiers in aerospace. We focus on producing the airplanes the market demands and we price our products to provide a fair return for our shareholders
finding: Boeing says it funds new products from core cash flow and prices for a 'fair return' to shareholders, not for share at any price.

quote: Commercial Airplanes earnings decreased by $1,769 million primarily due to $2,693 million of costs related to the first three 787 flight test aircraft included in research and development expense ... The earnings decrease is also attributable to reach-forward losses on the 747 program which grew by $1,352 million in 2009
finding: BCA swung to a loss in 2009 (-1.7% margin) on $2.7B of 787 test-aircraft costs and $1.35B of 747-8 reach-forward losses.

quote: Our 20-year forecast is for a long-term average growth rate of 5% per year for passenger and cargo traffic based on a projected average annual worldwide real economic growth rate of 3%. ... we project a $3.2 trillion market for 29,000 new airplanes over the next 20 years.
finding: In 2009 Boeing projected 29,000 new airplanes ($3.2T) over 20 years, and kept a bullish long-term view through the recession.

quote: These airlines have increased the downward pressure on airfares. This results in continued cost pressures for all airlines and price pressure on our products. Major productivity gains are essential to ensure a favorable market position at acceptable profit margins.
finding: Boeing sees low-cost-carrier fare pressure passing through to airplane prices, and makes productivity its lever for keeping both margin and position.

quote: We are focused on improving our processes and continuing cost-reduction efforts. ... These efforts enhance our ability to pursue pricing strategies that enable us to price competitively.
finding: Boeing links its cost reduction explicitly to room to price competitively against Airbus.
response: Cost reduction to enable competitive pricing

quote: The remaining $362 million was primarily due to challenging cargo market conditions and our related decision to defer a planned increase in the 747-8 production rate, which drove higher allocations of fixed costs and caused us to incur volume-based penalties to suppliers.
finding: Boeing deferred a 747-8 rate increase in the weak 2009 cargo market, accepting higher fixed-cost allocation and paying suppliers volume penalties.
response: Deferred 747-8 rate increase

quote: Of this amount, $643 million was caused by higher estimated production costs, including both additional internal production costs and higher supplier expenses, attributable to greater than expected re-work and disruption in manufacturing due to late maturity of engineering designs as well as the limited availability of engineering resources.
finding: Boeing blamed part of the 747-8 overrun on limited engineering resources while the 787 was absorbing talent, showing that engineering capacity is a binding constraint.

quote: we recorded $347 million of a reach-forward loss due to a reduction in projected delivery price increases associated with escalation and an increase in estimated costs due to our decisions to reduce twin-aisle production rates which impact production rates beginning in 2010.
finding: Boeing cut twin-aisle rates in the 2008-09 recession and took a $347M 747 loss partly because of those cuts.
response: Reduced twin-aisle production rates from 2010

quote: In April 2009, we announced a delay in previous plans to increase the production rate. ... In April 2009, we announced that we will lower the production rate on our 777 airplane program, affecting deliveries beginning in June 2010.
finding: In April 2009 Boeing responded to the downturn by delaying a planned 767 rate increase and cutting the 777 rate (7 to 5 per month from June 2010).
response: 767 rate increase delayed; 777 rate cut
lag: announced about a year before taking effect

quote: The accounting quantity for the 737 program increased by 400 units during 2009 due to the program’s normal progression of obtaining additional orders and delivering aircraft. Production rates remained unchanged in 2009.
finding: Boeing held the 737 rate steady through the 2009 recession and made all its rate cuts on widebodies.

quote: First flight of the 787 occurred on December 15, 2009. ... First delivery is also expected to occur in the fourth quarter of 2010. We continue to work toward our planned increases in 787 production rates as well as the timely introduction of the 787-9 derivative.
finding: Even while the 787 was more than two years late, Boeing kept pushing planned rate increases and the 787-9 derivative in parallel.

quote: On July 30, 2009, we acquired the business, assets and operations of Vought Aircraft Industries, Inc.’s (Vought) 787 business conducted at North Charleston, South Carolina. ... On December 22, 2009, we acquired Alenia North America’s 50% ownership interest in Global Aeronautica.
finding: Faced with 787 supplier failures, Boeing bought its struggling fuselage suppliers (Vought's Charleston plant and full control of Global Aeronautica).
response: Acquired Vought 787 operations and Global Aeronautica

quote: On October 28, 2009 we announced the North Charleston facility as the location for a second final assembly site for the 787 Dreamliner program. ... Until the additional 787 assembly line is fully operational, we will establish transitional surge capability at our Everett, Washington, location
finding: Boeing committed capital to a second 787 final-assembly line (Charleston) plus a temporary Everett surge line to raise rates.

quote: We expect operating cash flows to be lower in 2010 as we continue to build inventories prior to deliveries of the 787 and 747-8 airplanes. We contributed 29,211,295 shares of our common stock with an aggregate value of $1.5 billion to our pension plans in November 2009.
finding: In 2009, as in 2020, Boeing funded its pension with $1.5B of stock to save cash while building 787/747-8 inventory, a repeated liquidity tactic.

quote: Cash provided by financing activities totaled $4,094 million during 2009 compared with $5,202 million used during 2008, primarily due to proceeds from borrowings of $5,961 million in 2009 and reductions in share repurchases in 2009.
finding: In 2009 Boeing borrowed about $6B and cut buybacks to fund the 787 build-up.

quote: During 2009, we repurchased 1,173,152 shares at an average price of $42.94 in our open market share repurchase program ... During 2008, we repurchased 42,073,885 shares at an average price of $69.79 in our open market share repurchase program ... Share repurchase activity is expected to remain at a minimal level in 2010.
finding: Boeing cut buybacks from about 42M shares (2008) to about 1.2M (2009) during the 787 crisis, while keeping the dividend.

quote: We believe our ability to access external capital resources should be sufficient to satisfy existing short-term and long-term commitments and plans, and also to provide adequate financial flexibility to take advantage of potential strategic business opportunities should they arise within the next year.
finding: Boeing kept debt capacity in reserve to take up strategic opportunities, an opportunistic balance-sheet stance.

quote: In 2010, we will begin matching employee contributions to the company-sponsored 401(k) plan with common stock instead of cash for nonunion employees.
finding: Paying the 401(k) match in stock to save cash was first used in 2010 and repeated in 2020.

quote: We do not commit to industrial participation agreements unless a contract for sale of our products or services is signed. ... As of December 31, 2009, we have outstanding industrial participation agreements totaling $11 billion that extend through 2024.
finding: Boeing uses industrial-participation offsets ($11B outstanding) to win foreign sales, but commits only once a sale is signed.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: before the end of this year, Heidi, on the narrow body, we'll have charted a course of either re-engining or moving onto the new airplane.
finding: Faced with a likely Airbus geared-turbofan re-engine, Boeing committed to choose re-engine or new airplane within 2010.
trigger: Prospect of Airbus announcing a GTF-powered A320 re-engine in 2010
response: Decide narrowbody course (re-engine vs new airplane) by end of 2010

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The improving market conditions and the disciplined approach we have taken in managing production rates are paying off. As we announced last month, we have accelerated plans to increase production rates on both the 777 and the 747-8.
finding: Early in the recovery Boeing brought forward planned 777 and 747-8 rate increases, crediting its disciplined rate management through the downturn.
trigger: Recovering air traffic and customer accelerations in early 2010
response: Accelerated 777 and 747-8 rate increases

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we expect to be at a total production rate of 10 787s per month by the end of 2013. Anticipating three per month will be assembled at our expanded Boeing Charleston Facility
finding: Boeing planned a 10/month 787 rate by end-2013, with a second final assembly line in Charleston producing 3/month.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: First of all, we wouldn't increase the rate unless we had a pretty visible look at demand.
finding: Boeing raises rates only with clear demand visibility.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the kind of improvements we think we can make in the 777, both the smaller and larger versions, may be enough to handle the old -10 mission between the two of them. We're not sure yet but that question is something that we're debating and modeling right now.
finding: Boeing weighed whether an upgraded 777 plus the 787-9 could make the 787-10 unnecessary, trading off widebody derivatives.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think before the end of this year, Heidi, on the narrow body, we'll have charted a course of either re-engining or moving onto the new airplane.
finding: Asked how it would answer an Airbus GTF re-engine, Boeing promised a re-engine-or-new-airplane decision by end-2010; by January 2011 it was still leaning new and studying through 2011.
trigger: Prospect of Airbus launching a geared-turbofan re-engined A320
response: Committed to decide re-engine vs new airplane by end-2010

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we try to make these decisions in way where the current demand for current products is supported as we move into derivatives or all new airplanes. And we got a process in place that we don't think is going to cannibalize the demand we see now.
finding: Boeing times new-product decisions so they do not cannibalize demand for current products.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We wouldn't do it if they weren't ready. That's a big mistake in our business. So obviously, before we change the rate on the 777, we had in-depth discussions with our suppliers.
finding: Boeing makes supplier readiness a hard precondition before any rate change.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: As we have experienced in past cycles, the single-aisle market is leading the passenger recovery. This segment is showing the strongest growth, led by emerging markets and low-cost carriers. This growth, combined with our disciplined production and sales strategies, prompted our recently announced 737 production rate increase to 35 airplanes per month beginning in early 2012.
finding: Single-aisle demand from emerging markets and low-cost carriers led the recovery and prompted the 737 rate increase to 35/month in early 2012.
response: 737 rate increase to 35/month from early 2012

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we will continue to assess the demand requirements in this growing market segment along with importantly, the ability of our supply chain to move to higher rates if warranted.
finding: Boeing tied any further 737 rate increase to two tests: market demand and supply-chain ability.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: This decision by the World's ruling body on trade matters is important for both Airbus and Boeing because it sets the precedent for emerging competitors from Canada, Brazil, China, Russia and others, who want to enter the market.
finding: Boeing used trade litigation against Airbus to set rules that would also constrain new entrants from Canada, Brazil, China and Russia.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: With the higher deliveries and our current spending plans for R&D investment, we continue to forecast 2011 operating cash flow at greater than $5 billion.
finding: In mid-2010 Boeing forecast 2011 operating cash flow above $5 billion, later cut to over $4 billion (Oct 2010) and then over $2.5 billion (Jan 2011) as delays mounted.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: particularly with the new order traffic we are starting to see. We're going to be pricing those reasonably and trying to keep them stable. But obviously, we have some room so that we can really be competitive as necessary.
finding: Boeing's pricing stance: keep prices stable on new orders but keep room to discount to compete.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: moving from where we've been, low 30s to something north of 35, puts a -- while your competitor is also looking at moves and while also other airplanes are also moving up in rate, can put pressure on suppliers.
finding: Boeing saw Airbus's parallel rate increases as competing for the same suppliers, making supplier capacity the binding limit on going above 35/month.
trigger: Airbus also raising narrowbody production rates
response: Methodical supplier-by-supplier readiness review before going above 35/month

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: we're going to be building up a lot of inventory on both of those programs, 15 airplanes on the 47 side and 30 on the 87.
finding: Boeing kept building 747-8s (15) and 787s (30) ahead of certification, holding contingency in case retrofits were needed.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: If that is sometime this decade, then the case for re-engining weakens dramatically. If you did re-engine, you'd be doing two major developments in the course of four or five years, which makes no sense.
finding: Boeing's re-engine framework depended on when an all-new airplane became feasible; a new airplane this decade would make a 737 re-engine a wasteful second development.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think on balance, the customer feedback, which was your specific question, is sort of pushing us toward a newer airplane on balance. But there are those that also make the case for re-engining.
finding: In July 2010 Boeing read customer feedback as favoring a new airplane, while acknowledging a pro-re-engine camp.
trigger: Customer discussions at Farnborough 2010 on the 737 re-engine
response: Leaned toward a new airplane; decision due by year-end

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think the 24-day pause was associated with allowing our suppliers to sort of heal up their configurations, in some cases some new engineering as well as their supply chain.
finding: Boeing paused 787 final assembly for 24 days to let suppliers catch up on incomplete work and configuration changes.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: understanding with clarity what the capabilities of the A350-1000 is or isn't is an important input to the 777 decision, and I think that is going to take some time. I mean I wouldn't totally characterize it as a paper airplane at this stage, but it's pretty close to that.
finding: Boeing tied its 777 upgrade decision to how the A350-1000's capabilities firmed up, which it treated as close to a paper airplane.
response: Wait roughly a year for the A350-1000 configuration to firm before deciding on the 777

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: As you know, we have invested in additional capacity of our own in Charleston and some other places. So we do have some options to do some work ourselves if we can't reach the proper accommodation in some cases.
finding: Boeing kept its own capacity (such as Charleston) as a fallback for work it could not reach terms on with suppliers.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Our plan remains to deliver the first airplane by the end of the year, although it could move a few weeks into next year, depending on when we wrap up our remaining flight test and certification activities.
finding: In July 2010 Boeing still targeted first 787 delivery by end-2010 but warned it could slip; it then slipped repeatedly (to mid-1Q 2011, then 3Q 2011).

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We have tremendous customer acceptance for what it does. We have plans to continue to upgrade them. And so the question would be, why re-engine? And the answer, in my view, is you would consider re-engineering if you weren't going to have an airplane available for another 10 to 15 years
finding: Boeing's default was to keep upgrading the accepted 737; it would re-engine only if a new airplane was 10-15 years away.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO (answering Doug Cameron, Dow Jones)
quote: is your overbooking rate right now, given we've seen a splurge of orders, basically, level with what we saw in '05, '06, '07? ... I would characterize it as maybe modestly less but still significant.
finding: Boeing kept significant overbooking in its production skyline, modestly less than in 2005-2007, as a buffer against deferrals.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we recently announced our third 737 production rate increase this year to 38 airplanes per month beginning in the second quarter of 2013. This decision was supported by our current backlog of over 2,000 737s, existing options we expect customers to exercise and ongoing sales campaigns.
finding: Boeing justified its third 737 rate increase of 2010 (to 38/month) by a backlog of over 2,000 737s, expected option exercises and live sales campaigns.
trigger: Resurgence in air travel growth and strong customer demand
response: Third 737 rate increase of the year, to 38/month in 2Q 2013

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we see a new airplane opportunity out in the 220 range. And therefore, are continuing to question the necessity of a re-engine in the meantime, although we're studying it hard. And it is conceivable we would conclude that re-engining makes sense. But with the new airplane in the 2020 timeframe, it's not clear that it would.
finding: In October 2010 Boeing questioned whether a 737 re-engine was needed, given a possible new airplane around 2020, while studying it hard and not ruling it out.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we are continuing to improve the 737. I mean, we've gotten 5% on fuel from the engines since we introduced the NG [ph], there's another 2% out ahead of us that we're introducing now. There's a new interior. So there's no reason to think that we wouldn't keep improving that, which also bears on the re-engine question.
finding: Instead of an immediate re-engine, Boeing defended the 737NG with incremental upgrades (5% fuel gain so far, 2% more coming, new interior), which it said bore on the re-engine decision.
trigger: Pressure to re-engine the 737 (Airbus A320 re-engine under study)
response: Incremental 737NG performance improvements while deferring the re-engine decision

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: On the development side, we are entering the final stages of flight test on the 787-8, with first delivery expected to be in mid-quarter of 2011.
finding: In October 2010 Boeing still guided 787 first delivery to around mid-first quarter 2011; three months later it had slipped to 3Q 2011.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The Rolls [Rolls-Royce] engine is something that we're working on. Rolls is confident that they can support our schedule with a hardware and a software fix.
finding: An engine-supplier problem (Rolls-Royce) posed a risk to the 787 schedule, and Boeing relied on the supplier's hardware and software fix.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: if we do a new 737, roughly on 2020 timing, and as we're studying the market, that seems to be a timing that our customers might require. If we did a new narrow-body then we would probably have to address changes to the 777 before that.
finding: Boeing's sequencing: 777 changes first, then a new 737 around 2020, the timing it believed customers required.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We're studying everything from a completely new airplane to modifications to the weighing in the engines. We're studying a wide range of options, and we're trying to figure out what our customers need.
finding: For the 777 Boeing kept options open, from an all-new airplane to re-engining and new-wing modifications, driven by customer needs.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: if we come up with the right airplane in roughly the 2019, 2020, somewhere in there, I personally feel that there's a strong argument that the market will wait for us, notwithstanding the re-engineering.
finding: Boeing's first answer to the A320neo was to bet that customers would wait for an all-new Boeing airplane around 2019-2020.
trigger: A320neo re-engine launch and its market traction
response: Lean to an all-new narrowbody around 2020 instead of a re-engine
lag: first call after NEO traction; decision deferred through 2011

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: putting our backlog at risk twice, once for the re-engineering, not to mention the cost of two development efforts, and then again, with the new airplane, only makes sense if the new airplane wants to be developed in 2025 or beyond.
finding: Boeing's rule was to re-engine only if an all-new airplane would come in 2025 or later, to avoid two development costs and two backlog transitions.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: In response to this broad-based market strength, Commercial Airplanes made a series of decisions in 2010 to increase production rates across its product line. The most recent was in December, when we announced a 777 rate increase to more than eight per month in the first quarter of 2013.
finding: Boeing responded to the 2010 traffic rebound by raising production rates across all commercial programs, including 777 to more than 8/month by 1Q 2013.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we announced our plans to increase the 737 production rate from 31.5 airplanes per month to 35 in the beginning of 2012, and then to 38 per month in the second quarter of 2013.
finding: Boeing staged 737 rate increases in steps (31.5 to 35 to 38/month) spread over 2012-2013 rather than one jump.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have had discoveries during flight test, the most notable being the in-flight electrical incident this past November that resulted in the move of first delivery to the third quarter of this year.
finding: An in-flight electrical incident during flight test pushed 787 first delivery to 3Q 2011, another schedule slip.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We are currently operating at two per month production rate in final, and despite the delay in first delivery, we are continuing our efforts to reduce auto-sequence work and expect to ramp up to 10 per month by the end of 2013.
finding: Despite the delivery delay Boeing held its 787 ramp target of 10/month by end-2013 from a current 2/month.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Gross inventory for the company now includes $12.9 billion related to the 787 work-in-process, supplier advances, tooling and other non-recurring costs, an increase of approximately $6 billion during 2010. Gross inventory for the 787 is expected to increase by a similar amount during 2011
finding: Boeing was carrying the 787's cost overhang on its balance sheet, with inventory growing about $6 billion a year to $12.9 billion.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: As of fourth quarter, we have determined that the program is not in a loss position, including the additional costs associated with the recently revised schedule. The cumulative impact of the 787 schedule revisions has put pressure on program profitability
finding: Boeing kept the 787 out of a forward-loss (reach-forward) position despite repeated delays, while admitting profitability was under pressure.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: For the year, Commercial Airplanes delivered $31.8 billion of revenue on 462 airplane deliveries. Operating margins were 9.4%.
finding: BCA earned a 9.4% operating margin in 2010 on $31.8 billion of revenue, carried by the 737, 777 and services.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We ended the year with $10.5 billion of cash and marketable securities. Debt levels remained flat during the quarter and decreased $500 million from 2009 due to Boeing Capital debt maturities. Our cash position provides strong liquidity, as we continue investing in our development program
finding: Boeing kept a large cash buffer ($10.5 billion) to fund development programs.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We're forecasting capital expenditures to be $2.3 billion in 2011. Now this represents continued investment as the 787 final assembly line in Charleston, as well as investments to ramp up commercial production rates
finding: Boeing planned 2011 capex of $2.3 billion to fund the Charleston 787 line and production-rate increases.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: The early 787 and 747-8 deliveries will be dilutive to Commercial Airplane margins, as our guidance assumes essentially zero margins on these initial delivery.
finding: Boeing guided to zero margins on early 787 and 747-8 deliveries, accepting margin dilution to get the programs into service.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think we're leaning toward the development in the 2020 timeframe, but we're going to confirm that as we go through with this year. Preserving the option, if we're wrong as we go through the analysis to re-engine, but I don't think it's going to turn out that way.
finding: In January 2011 Boeing leaned toward a 2020 new airplane but explicitly kept a re-engine option open while it studied the market through the year.
response: Kept the re-engine option open while leaning toward a new airplane; decision to be confirmed during 2011

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think what I would look for though is R&D down in the medium term.
finding: Boeing's plan was to let R&D fall after the 787 and 747-8, with derivatives later in the decade and new airplanes at its end.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We're going to make sure they don't come together, okay? Yes, I think that's one of the independent variables in the equation.
finding: Boeing would deliberately stagger the new 737 replacement and a 777 replacement so the two all-new developments did not overlap.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we had a very conservative view and a significant amount of margin in our production ramp up plans. A lot of that margin is now eaten up by this latest delay.
finding: Boeing absorbed the latest 787 delay by using up the schedule margin in its ramp plan rather than lowering the ramp target.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: when you take everything into account, demand, backlog, supplier readiness, investment, and take that all into account, there's more bias to move up than there is to move down from the announcements we've already made.
finding: Boeing weighs demand, backlog, supplier readiness and investment in rate decisions and in early 2011 leaned toward further rate increases.
response: Bias toward further rate increases beyond those announced

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we're mindful of the readiness of our supply base, very mindful of that. As Heidi pointed out earlier, lived through an experienced what we don't want to live through again back in 1997.
finding: Supplier readiness, and the memory of 1997, limit how fast Boeing will accelerate rate increases.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: On the 787-9, we're keeping a little more close control and doing it more typically how we've done it in the past where we would outline what the development effort is and contract with the supply chain for their particular piece, which means we would pay them as we go.
finding: After the 787-8 outsourcing problems Boeing took back design control on the 787-9 and paid suppliers for development as it went, raising near-term R&D.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: this team in Renton has done a wonderful job in freeing up capacity with lean and productivity, so we're moved to one of the big bottlenecks, which was the wing operations
finding: Boeing funded 737 rate increases largely through lean productivity at Renton, clearing the wing-operations bottleneck without big capex.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: the way the model works, we get about 40% of the cash before we deliver at about 60% at delivery.
finding: Boeing's delivery cash model collects about 40% of cash before delivery and 60% at delivery.

quote: on January 18, 2011, we announced that the expected date of first delivery of our 787 Dreamliner had been moved to the third quarter of 2011 due to a combination of flight testing delays, supplier challenges and other issues common to commercial aircraft development programs.
finding: Flight-test and supplier problems pushed 787 first delivery again, to Q3 2011.

quote: we are increasing production capacity in Everett and Charleston and working closely with our suppliers to support 787 production rate increases. If assembly line ramp-up efforts are delayed or if our suppliers cannot timely deliver components to us at the rates necessary to achieve our planned rate increases, we may be unable to meet delivery targets
finding: Boeing was adding 787 capacity before certification, and named supplier component rates as the limit on its ramp.

quote: Commercial Airplanes revenues decreased by $2,217 million due to lower 777 deliveries primarily resulting from a production rate change from 7 to 5 per month beginning in June 2010 and no deliveries on the 747 program due to the transition from the 747-400 to the 747-8.
finding: The 2009 decision to cut the 777 rate from 7 to 5 per month reduced 2010 BCA revenue, and there were no 747 deliveries during the 747-8 transition.

quote: Our 20-year forecast is for a long-term average growth rate of 5% per year for passenger and cargo traffic based on a projected average annual worldwide real economic growth rate of 3%. ... we project a $3.6 trillion market for 30,900 new airplanes over the next 20 years.
finding: Boeing raised its 20-year forecast to 30,900 airplanes ($3.6T) as traffic recovered in 2010.

quote: During 2010, we announced plans to increase monthly production of the 737 from 31.5 to 35 airplanes per month beginning in the first quarter of 2012 and a further increase to 38 airplanes per month beginning in the second quarter of 2013.
finding: Coming out of the recession Boeing announced a two-step 737 ramp (31.5 to 35 to 38 per month) about 1.5-3 years ahead.
trigger: Traffic and airline profit recovery in 2010
response: 737 rate increases to 35 (2012) and 38 (2013)

quote: On March 19, 2010, we announced that we will accelerate, from mid-2013 to mid-2012, a planned production rate increase from 1.5 to 2 airplanes per month.
finding: Boeing brought a 747-8 rate increase forward by a year even while the program was in flight test and losing money.

quote: In March 2010, we announced that we will accelerate by approximately six months, from early 2012 to mid-2011, a planned production rate increase to 7 airplanes per month. In December 2010, we announced that monthly production of the 777 will increase from 7 to 8.3 airplanes per month in the first quarter 2013.
finding: Within a year of cutting the 777 to 5 per month, Boeing reversed course: it pulled the return to 7 forward and then announced 8.3 per month.
response: 777 back to 7/month by mid-2011, then 8.3/month in 2013
lag: about 11 months after the April 2009 cut

quote: On August 27, 2010, we announced that the expected date of first delivery of the 787 had been moved to mid-first quarter 2011 from the fourth quarter of 2010. ... including supplier workmanship issues related to the horizontal stabilizer, instrumentation delays and the expected availability date of an engine needed to support the final phases of flight test.
finding: 787 delays in 2010 came from supplier workmanship and a late engine, so the engine maker and suppliers set the pace of Boeing's schedule.

quote: During 2010, we continued to produce 787 airplanes and until completion of our flight test program, there is risk that additional items will be identified that require further modifications or other changes to those aircraft we have produced.
finding: Boeing built 787s concurrently with flight test, knowingly accepting rework risk to protect the ramp.

quote: during the second quarter of 2010 we delayed some 787 component deliveries to reduce out of sequence work moving into final assembly at our Everett factory and improve supply chain efficiency.
finding: Boeing slowed supplier component deliveries in 2010 to cut out-of-sequence 787 work in final assembly.

quote: On July 1, 2010, we completed firm configuration of the 787-9 airplane with first delivery scheduled for late 2013.
finding: Boeing pressed on with the stretched 787-9 derivative (late-2013 target) before the 787-8 had delivered.

quote: Our current assessment is that the program is not in a reach-forward loss position, however the cumulative impacts of the production challenges, schedule delays and customer and supplier impacts have created significant pressure on program profitability and we expect to record zero margin on our initial deliveries.
finding: Boeing avoided a 787 reach-forward loss by relying on the long accounting quantity, but expected zero margin on early deliveries.

quote: Net cash provided by operating activities decreased by $2,651 million to $2,952 million during 2010 compared with 2009 primarily due to higher net working capital in 2010, driven by growth in inventory as we continue to build inventories prior to the anticipated delivery and production ramp-up of the 787 and 747-8 programs.
finding: In 2010 Boeing let operating cash fall to $3.0B to build 787 and 747-8 inventory ahead of deliveries.

quote: We expect capital spending in 2011 to be higher than 2010 due to the ongoing construction of a 787 final assembly line in North Charleston, South Carolina and higher spending to support commercial airplane production rate increases.
finding: Boeing raised capex for 2011 to support the Charleston line and rate increases (2010 capex: $1,125M).

quote: In 2010, we had 494,939 shares transferred to us from employees for tax withholding and did not repurchase any shares through our open market share repurchase program. During 2009 and 2008, cash used in our open market share repurchase program totaled $50 million and $2,937 million.
finding: Boeing stopped buybacks entirely in 2010 (from $2.9B in 2008) while the 787 drained cash, but kept paying the dividend.

quote: As of December 31, 2010 and 2009 commercial aircraft programs inventory included the following amounts related to the 787 program: $9,461 and $3,885 of work in process (including deferred production costs)
finding: 787 work in process more than doubled to $9.5B in 2010 as Boeing kept building ahead of certification.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Re-engining option is still being looked at, but I'd be less than candid if I didn't say the leader in the clubhouse is the all-new airplane.
finding: In April 2011 Boeing still favoured an all-new narrowbody over a re-engine in response to the NEO.
response: All-new airplane favoured; re-engine still an option
lag: ~3 months after the Jan 2011 call on NEO traction

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the NEO will not seriously erode our customer base if there's a new airplane out there, three or four years after they introduce a re-engine.
finding: Boeing's response rested on the judgment that a new airplane three or four years after the NEO would hold its customers.
response: Bet on a new airplane 3-4 years after NEO

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: But we agree that we have a significant take-share opportunity with the 777 over the intermediate-term, and we won't let that opportunity go.
finding: Boeing moved its 777 stance from building backlog for security toward taking share from Airbus through rate increases.
response: Bias toward taking 777 share and raising rates beyond 8.3/month

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: if you're offering a new plane just a few years after your competitor is offering a re-engined plane and you're already continually improving what you've got, that step does not need to be taken.
finding: In April 2011 Boeing called a stopgap 737 re-engine improbable, a position it reversed later that year.
response: Re-engine stopgap judged unlikely; all options on table

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: These events in Japan have not had a significant impact on our operations. Our major partners there are managing challenges with electric power availability and stressed infrastructure and transportation systems, but they are generally performing well.
finding: Boeing's Japanese 787 partners were exposed to the 2011 earthquake, a supply-chain concentration risk that did not disrupt deliveries.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: Revenue for the quarter was $14.9 billion, down slightly from last year ... Operating margins of 6.7% reflect strong performance across our core businesses on the expected lower volume and higher pension expense.
finding: Q1 2011 was a trough quarter (6.7% margin) with low 777 deliveries and 787/747-8 R&D still high.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: we extended the accounting quantities on the 737 by 600 units and on the 777 by 50 units. The financial impact of these extensions in the quarter was not significant as volume benefits are balanced with an anticipated competitive pricing environment.
finding: Boeing extended the 737 block by 600 units but held margins flat, expecting competitive pricing (A320neo era) to offset volume gains.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: We continue to make progress with our 787 suppliers, reaching fair and equitable settlements on their assertions. We anticipate being substantially complete with supplier negotiations by the end of this year.
finding: Boeing was still settling 787 supplier claims for delay costs in 2011, a lasting financial cost of the outsourced model.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: During the quarter, we used $1 billion of operating cash flow ... We ended the quarter with $7.8 billion in cash and marketable securities. Our cash and debt balances reflect the first quarter repayment of $786 million of Boeing capital debt.
finding: Boeing burned cash in Q1 2011 during the 787 inventory build but kept a large cash buffer and paid down debt.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO (as labelled)
quote: By the end of this year, we should have a sharper view of new airplane versus re-engine. As you know, most of the data and customer feedback is suggesting to us that the new airplane option is the most favorable. ... We're at 2019-2020, that's the timeframe that the market seems to want this new airplane
finding: In April 2011 Boeing said customer feedback favoured a 2019-2020 new airplane; within three months that view was overturned.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: part of the judgment we have to make, Doug, is that the NEO will not seriously erode our customer base if there's a new airplane out there, three or four years after they introduce a re-engine. ... my personal view is that we're not going to lose customers for a few years
finding: Boeing's clean-sheet bet rested on the judgment that the A320neo would not win Boeing customers if a better Boeing airplane came 3-4 years later; American Airlines disproved this in July 2011.
response: bet that customers would wait for a new Boeing airplane

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: it relates to model mix pricing, model introduction down the line. We're looking at a new model or two as alternatives beyond where we are now ... the quantum leap in productivity that these customers will be able to get with these airplanes are going to make the pricing environment, once this plane’s in service proving it so, more robust
finding: Boeing planned to raise 787 profitability through productivity, supplier work, model mix and new derivatives, expecting pricing to firm once the aircraft proved itself in service.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: I think the heart of the market, and that tends to be in the 145-to-175, 185 range in there is -- and we haven't sorted it out totally, is in all likelihood, where we'll start.
finding: Boeing's next narrowbody would target the 145-185 seat core first, leaving the 757 segment for later.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: the R&D spend at the height would be lower even on a new program whether it be re-engined or whether it be a new airplane, because we're only going to do one of those programs one at a time.
finding: After running the 787 and 747-8 at the same time, Boeing committed to one major development at a time to cap peak R&D.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: I think we will take a balanced view of the grab market share versus build a backlog for security. It'll be probably a little more bias toward taking share than backlog for security. ... perhaps, we're a little bias toward worshipping backlog, historically.
finding: With Airbus lacking a 777 competitor, Boeing shifted from protecting backlog to taking market share, admitting it had historically over-valued backlog.
response: bias to take share on 777 via higher rates

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: accelerating it significantly would create risk, okay? It's not as if we're not asking the question. But right now, we’re about we're about where we want to be. ... we’re looking hard at going beyond the 8.3
finding: Even with a share opportunity, Boeing declined to speed up the 777 ramp because of supply-chain risk, while studying rates above 8.3.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: I don't think we see a world where pricing is going to head the way it did in the late '90s, early 2000s where just massive competition on every deal and price deterioration ... On the other hand, we don't see this wonderful world where we're going to be able to raise price everywhere either.
finding: In April 2011 Boeing expected steady pricing, neither a late-1990s-style price war nor broad price increases.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: timing, to meet Airbus' timing if we decide to do that, or meet the 2019, 2020 with a new airplane. So I'm not trying to signal any change in our decision making.
finding: Boeing explicitly tied any re-engine to matching Airbus's A320neo timing, and the clean-sheet alternative to 2019-2020.
response: re-engine timed to match Airbus or new airplane 2019-2020

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: These are integrated decisions where you need to confirm technical readiness, you need to confirm market demand and make sure that your major customers are with you as you make this decision. ... You need to make sure that your supply base can handle it.
finding: Boeing's launch criteria for a new airplane were technical readiness, confirmed demand, key customer buy-in and supply-base capacity.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: I think you have to run a business assuming that they're going to remain high. If you make another assumption, you have an opportunity to make a big mistake.
finding: Boeing planned on sustained high oil prices, which favoured fuel-efficiency upgrades and supported demand for new airplanes.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: the program has been plagued over the last few years with these major subsections coming in and not being completed, and which has driven the rework we've had to do in Everett
finding: The 787's main operational problem was suppliers delivering incomplete major sections, which forced costly rework in Everett.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, BCA CEO
quote: our strategic intent is to be the market leader by all measures. And what does that mean? Well, what it means is you have the most revenues, the most airplanes delivered, the most earnings
finding: In 2011 Boeing's stated goal was to lead Airbus on every measure, including deliveries.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, BCA CEO
quote: what we will do on the 777 is continue to improve the airplane we have. But we also have some major upgrades we could do in the event that we have to respond to a move by the competition.
finding: Boeing held major 777 upgrades in reserve, to use only if Airbus made a firm move with the A350-1000.
trigger: A350-1000 seen as late-decade if real
response: Incremental 777 improvement; major upgrade held in reserve

speaker: Jim Albaugh, BCA CEO
quote: it's one where we're not going to be driven by a date to make an announcement. If you're holding your breath on the Paris air show, well, I'm not going to say we're not going to make that announcement, I would be very surprised if we did.
finding: In May 2011 Boeing refused to let the NEO's momentum force a quick narrowbody announcement. It launched the MAX about three months later.
trigger: A320neo orders ahead of Paris Air Show 2011
response: No announcement at Paris; deliberate process

speaker: Jim Albaugh, BCA CEO
quote: that would preserve the 8% cost of ownership improvement or margin that we have over the competition. And we could offer this airplane over the next couple of years and deliver it sometime 2016-2017 time frame.
finding: Boeing's re-engine option was designed to keep an 8% cost-of-ownership lead over the NEO, with delivery in 2016-17.
response: Re-engine option to preserve 8% cost-of-ownership gap

speaker: Jim Albaugh, BCA CEO
quote: They build a good airplane. They have 52% of the marketplace. And what we have to do is be able to match them ... but always have the most competitive airplane
finding: With Airbus at 52% share, Boeing committed to match Airbus deal by deal on price while keeping a product advantage.
response: Match Airbus deal-per-deal on price

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We ended the year with $3.3 billion of net earnings, $3 billion in positive cash flow during a tough cash year and a strong $10.5 billion in liquidity, all while making significant investments in our development programs.
finding: Boeing kept strong liquidity ($10.5B) and positive cash flow in 2010 while funding 787 and 747-8 development.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Over the past 14 months, we've announced a series of rate increases on existing production lines to help burn down our commercial backlog faster and open new delivery slots for customers who want airplanes sooner ... will increase our commercial airplane output by more than 40%.
finding: Boeing planned to raise commercial output by more than 40%, with rate increases meant partly to open slots so customers need not turn to rivals.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: In the Single-Aisle segment, this year, we are evaluating the market opportunities, product requirements and technology options that will best meet the future needs of our customers. ... We are also evaluating the potential for a 787 derivative to follow the -9 [787-9]. And we will eventually ask the question of how to improve the 777
finding: In May 2011 Boeing was still evaluating its narrowbody response and had queued the 787-10 and a 777 improvement.
response: still evaluating

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we installed a back-to-basics approach for managing all new programs. This includes a disciplined 11-step technical review process for identifying and mitigating risk from the very outset.
finding: After the 787, Boeing added a formal 11-step technical risk review before committing to new programs.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we have increased productivity by approximately 4% annually over the past 4 years, which has provided the cash and earnings to fund our investment in innovative new products and services.
finding: Boeing funded development from about 4% annual productivity gains rather than new capital.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: this company went to hell and back on rate increases in the late '90s ... You just got to have metrics around rate increases. For example, we have to have very clear visibility on at least 2 years of stability in BCA before we will pull the trigger
finding: Boeing's rule for raising rates required clear visibility of at least 2 years of stable demand and supply chain, a lesson from the late-1990s production collapse.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We figure if we can take a rate up or down for 2 years, for sure, 95% certainty, we have time to adjust after that. Now obviously in our minds, we're taking up rates, we're taking them up for 5 or 6 or 7 years.
finding: Boeing required 95% confidence in holding a new rate for 2 years before committing, while planning to keep it 5-7 years.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We delegated too much, we didn't insist on enough commonality of both systems and technical approaches, so we ended up with a wildebeest, okay, that we had to fix.
finding: The CEO admitted Boeing over-delegated 787 design and supply to partners, producing an incoherent system it had to fix.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: you need more cost to supervise outside factories, you need more insistence on commonality of IT tools and you need more insistence on MRP integration. And we just booted it. ... we paid billions upon billions in the learning process there.
finding: Boeing concluded its 787 outsourcing model cost billions and that suppliers need more oversight, not less.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: I think if we had executed on our plan over the last 7 years, you would see phenomenal results ... So the leverage in this company in BCA is execution. ... we've booted 2 developments in terms of cost and schedule, and we are not going to do that again.
finding: Boeing's CEO blamed weak commercial returns on execution failures on two developments (787, 747-8), which made the company averse to development risk.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we're generally within what we anticipated, generally within the business plan that we projected, okay. So we're not in some huge dogfight that we didn't anticipate
finding: In May 2011 Boeing described commercial pricing as normal and within plan despite the A320neo launch.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we know that technologies are going to come together, our best estimate is at the end of the decade, toward the end of the decade, '19, '20-ish
finding: In May 2011 Boeing's best estimate was that the technologies for a much-improved new narrowbody would come together around 2019-2020, which set the clean-sheet timing.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Now our competitor has re-engined current technology. We have a project going. We're going to retain the ability to re-engine if this new airplane doesn't come together over the next 9 months or so as we think it will, okay. So as a betting man, I think that's where we're going to end up
finding: In May 2011 the CEO leaned toward a clean-sheet answer to the re-engined A320neo, keeping re-engine as a fallback; within about 2 months Boeing chose the re-engine.
response: favoured new airplane in May 2011; switched to re-engine by July 2011

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: it may be modestly bigger, we don't see a step-function change in the airplane ... First order business is to replace the heart of the market, which may be slightly bigger than it is now, but not a huge step function bigger.
finding: Boeing's planned new narrowbody would replace the core 737 segment at slightly larger size, with the segment above left to later.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: Our guidance also reflects the dilutive impact from the initial deliveries of 787s and 747-8s, deliveries which we recorded at essentially 0 gross margins
finding: Boeing expected to book the first 787 and 747-8 deliveries at about zero gross margin.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: Our cash and liquidity position remains strong, and we are well positioned to support the ramp up of current development programs and future product development decisions. As we progress along these efforts, we will look more broadly at our cash deployment plans, including dividend increases and share repurchases.
finding: Boeing ranked funding programs and future products ahead of dividends and buybacks, deferring shareholder returns until the ramp succeeded.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: As we prepare for first deliveries on the 787 and the 747-8, we expect to have about 60 of those airplanes in inventory at the end of the third quarter.
finding: Boeing built about 60 787 and 747-8 airplanes ahead of certification, a large working-capital bet on concurrent development and production.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: At the end of the first quarter, gross inventory included $14.5 billion for 787 work-in-process, supplier advances, tooling
finding: 787 inventory reached $14.5B by Q1 2011, then $16.2B in Q2 and $18B in Q3, growing about $1.7B a quarter.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: we will take a much more disciplined approach in developing and executing those programs. We will continue to leverage things that have worked for us, such as risk-sharing arrangements with our partners.
finding: Despite the 787 problems, Boeing intended to keep risk-sharing supplier partnerships on future programs.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: Historically, R&D spending on a new airplane has started about 5 to 6 years in advance of first delivery, and for a new derivative, about 3 to 4 years before delivery. Now typically, R&D peaks about 1 to 2 years in advance of that first delivery.
finding: Boeing's R&D timing rule: new airplanes need 5-6 years of R&D before first delivery, derivatives 3-4 years, peaking 1-2 years before delivery.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: Boeing Capital continues to play an integral role in supporting our businesses. They are an active part of our sales campaigns ... BCC's successful market integration and outreach is evident by the minimal amount of financing we've done on our own books over the last few years.
finding: Boeing used Boeing Capital as a sales tool while keeping little customer financing on its own balance sheet.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: we've negotiated life-of-contract or life-of-program contract with fixed-priced contracts with our supply chain, so we can also estimate the cost pretty well. ... I think we could absorb some slips in terms of the schedule and in the ramp up and still hold pretty much to what our profit assumptions are.
finding: Fixed-price, life-of-program supplier contracts gave Boeing confidence the 787 could absorb schedule slips without a forward loss.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: all the cash associated with the inventory balance and the deferred production are behind us. So as we start delivering these airplanes, we'll get the additional 60% cash on the nose of every one of those aircraft.
finding: Boeing expected a sharp cash rebound as 787s delivered, since about 60% of the price is paid at delivery.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: Well, it would be 7%. But getting there has proved difficult because obviously, you got to get the Commercial business up to a pretty high level and you need the Defense business at double digits.
finding: Boeing kept a long-term 7% net margin target while admitting that reaching it had proved difficult and depended on both commercial leverage and double-digit defense margins.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: we were running at $1.5 billion, $1.7 billion, somewhere in that range. ... So again, we won't be running $4 billion a year as we have the last couple, but we're not going to go down to $1.5 billion.
finding: Boeing set R&D between its $1.5-1.7B pre-787 baseline and its $4B peak, keeping money for technology work ahead of the next program.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: at the end of this year, we're going to understand more what we want to do going forward, whether it be a re-engine or a new airplane, and then we're going to make -- we're going to have the financial strength to make the investment necessary
finding: In May 2011 Boeing's CFO expected the re-engine versus new airplane decision by late 2011; it came about 3 months earlier because of the American Airlines campaign.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: I don't think you're going to see a lot of large things. I don't think you're going to see much more consolidation of primes in the aerospace industry. But there'll be small acquisitions
finding: Boeing favoured organic growth and small bolt-on acquisitions over large M&A in 2011.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: 462 airplanes were delivered. We had orders of 530, what's remarkable about that is that our projection, going into the year, was about for half as many airplanes
finding: Boeing's 2010 orders (530) were about double its plan, showing it under-forecasts demand in recoveries.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: The 61 orders in the first quarter, and we were able to maintain the rates. We didn't give any of those airplanes away.
finding: Boeing held 777 pricing even while booking a large Q1 2011 order volume (61), treating widebody pricing discipline as a priority.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: On rate changes, 737 are going from 31.5 up to 38 a month. And we're taking a very hard look at going to 42, and we'll make that decision probably sometime this summer.
finding: In May 2011 the 737 plan was 38 per month, with 42 under study; Boeing announced 42 in June, about one month later.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we have very well-defined rules on how often you can make a rate break on a program. What you do is you break rate and you stabilize, break rate, stabilize again. The other thing we try to stay away from is having rate breaks on 2 different programs at the same time
finding: Boeing's rate rules: stabilise between rate breaks and avoid breaking rate on two programs at once, to limit operational risk.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I think the days are over when we could arrive with an order book and our terms of conditions and say, how many jets do you want? We got to earn our orders each and every day
finding: Boeing acknowledged it could no longer dictate terms to airlines and had to compete for each order.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we need to put a wall around those technologies, to make sure that nobody else has access to them. ... when you put work outside, I think you do it for really 3 reasons. You do it to get access to capital, you do it to get access to technology and you do it to get access to low cost.
finding: Boeing reset its outsourcing logic: outsource for capital, technology or low cost, but wall off critical technologies.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: My speech to the team is we need to build something of everything. ... we need to build enough of everything, so we can go and help our suppliers when they get in trouble or we can bring the work back, if they really have an issue.
finding: After the 787, Boeing kept in-house capability in every major part so it could rescue or replace failing suppliers.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: right now, if you look at how many active airplane design teams there are in this country, now that F-35 is done, the only active design teams are here. And if you're an Aerodynamicist, if you're interested in airplanes, people do want to come here.
finding: Boeing saw itself as the main US employer for airplane designers, a talent-pool advantage it could use.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: On the 737 program, they've reduced the flow from 22 days down to 11 days. ... On the 777 program, again, we came up from 5 to 7 a month, and we did it in a pretty seamless fashion. And they've reduced the flow days from 67 days down to 47.
finding: Lean flow cuts (737 from 22 to 11 days, 777 from 67 to 47) let Boeing raise rates on existing lines without big capital.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: For people, half of our engineers can retire within the next 5 years, if they choose to do so.
finding: Half of Boeing's engineers could retire within five years, a workforce risk it weighed in its program choices.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: The next option is to re-engine. And certainly, it's technically feasible. ... and that would preserve the 8% cost of ownership improvement or margin that we have over the competition. And we could offer this airplane over the next couple of years and deliver it sometime 2016-2017 time frame.
finding: In May 2011 Boeing costed the re-engine as preserving an 8% ownership-cost edge, with delivery in 2016-2017.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: what they're telling us is they want us to do something transformation. They want us to provide them with a step-function improvement in economics. ... we can deliver an airplane that's 20% more fuel-efficient.
finding: In May 2011 Boeing said customers wanted a step-change clean sheet 20% more fuel-efficient; by July it concluded they valued near-term gains more.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: Now I'll say this, we're going to do one of those last 2. We're going to do a re-engine or we're going to do a new airplane. ... we're probably leaning towards a new airplane, but we'll bring the re-engine along with us.
finding: In May 2011 Boeing was leaning toward a new small airplane while keeping the re-engine option alive; it reversed within about 2 months.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
