quote: probably composite and how do we ramp it from zero airplanes a month up to 40, 50 or 60, and how do you do that in a short period of time? ... In the past, we've adapted airplanes to the production system. This time, we need to design an airplane and a production system together
finding: Production-system scalability to 40-60 per month for a composite narrowbody was the key open question for a clean sheet.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: We're sold out on the 737 through 2015. We're sold out on the 787 through 2019. And one of the biggest challenges that we have is having the slots for our customers.
finding: Boeing's binding constraint in 2011 was delivery slots, not demand.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: If we had slots we could sell a lot of airplanes this year, but we just don't have them near term. And again I think in the last downturn, we probably should have thought long and hard about going up in the rates then, rather than waiting until the market gets better.
finding: Boeing concluded it should have raised rates during the downturn instead of waiting, a lesson favouring earlier capacity moves.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: What you don't want to do is be in a situation where you go up and you have to come down. ... given the option of going higher which would require a capital investment, I’d opt for pushing the 8.3% rate out for a couple of more years and bypassing the capital expenditure
finding: Boeing preferred to hold the 777 at 8.3 per month for longer rather than spend capital on higher rates, avoiding the risk of cutting back later.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: take the time required to mature the technology and only then do we into detail, design and development. And then we'll follow a very disciplined gated process ... when we make a commitment to a date, you're going to see that we have a much higher probability of achieving that date.
finding: For any new airplane Boeing committed to mature technology first and use a gated process, trading speed for schedule reliability.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we're not satisfied with the zero-margin airplane, we've investment too much and we're going to make some money with this airplane. ... if we can get to 10, we can probably get to 11, and if we can get to 11, we get to 12.
finding: Boeing planned to lift 787 margins from near zero through supplier cost-sharing, the -9/-10 mix and rates possibly above 10 per month.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: they also have competed on price, as we've competed on value and, certainly, we have to compete on both price and value. ... They have 52% of the marketplace. And what we have to do is be able to match them deal ... but always have the most competitive airplane, and we will do that.
finding: Facing Airbus at 52% share, Boeing shifted from value-only selling to matching Airbus deal by deal on price as well.
response: match Airbus deal-per-deal on price and value

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: if you look at where most of the newcomers are positioning themselves, it's at the low end and that's becoming a commodity ... I don't think all of those competitors are going to survive, I really don't, but a couple of them probably will.
finding: Boeing expected new entrants to commoditise the low end of the narrowbody market and aimed to keep its own low-end offer differentiated.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: But I think what we're telling our customers is look, if you buy NEO, you're going to buy an airplane that's about as good as what we're producing today. And there's a cost to switching ... we're going to be either the re-engine, which would give us another 8% advantage or we're going to do the new airplane
finding: In May 2011 Boeing tried to freeze customers by promising either an 8%-better re-engine or a better clean sheet, and by stressing switching costs.
trigger: A320neo sales push to Boeing customers
response: promise future product; stress switching costs

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we have set up a team under Ray Conner, and we're bringing in people that have worked at high-rate production in other industries to help us figure out what this business, this manufacturing system would look like.
finding: Boeing recruited high-rate manufacturing talent from other industries to solve the new narrowbody production-system problem.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: On the -8, I think we did about 50% of engineering and in-house. ... And now, we're doing about 70% in-house. We want to control the critical IP.
finding: Boeing raised in-house engineering from about 50% on the 787-8 to about 70% on the -9 to control critical IP.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I think one of the unintended consequences of all the outsourcing we did is we paid people to develop IP that they now own. And we need to be very careful going forward of whether or not we're giving away things that's important to our success over the long haul.
finding: Boeing concluded that 787 outsourcing had handed IP to suppliers and planned a middle path between the 787 and 777 models.

speaker: James F. Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: When we made the decision to go from 31.5 737 to 35, that took us 6 months to get comfortable ... It means second sourcing in a number of areas to make sure that you're not overly dependent on any one supplier
finding: Boeing's rate-increase process took about 6 months of work-cell analysis and included second-sourcing to avoid single-supplier bottlenecks.

speaker: Scott A. Fancher, VP & GM 787 Program
quote: This process has been in place for over 2.5 years, and it's yielded really outstanding results and very balanced results as well. In fact, over that 2.5-year period, we've improved as much on the revenue side as we have on the cost side.
finding: Boeing ran a structured 787 profitability programme that raised revenue (pricing, mix) as much as it cut cost.

speaker: Scott A. Fancher, VP & GM 787 Program
quote: it involves using independent sourcing where it's cost effective. It includes safety stock in the production system, where it's cost effective, and using those 2 techniques and others to decouple the sensitivity.
finding: Boeing used dual sourcing and safety stock to shield the 787 system from disruptions such as strikes or supplier failures.

speaker: analyst (Investor Conference)
quote: originally, this aircraft was supposed to, I don't know, take about 5 years to develop. We're a little over 3 years late to delivery.
finding: The 787 was about 3 years late against a roughly 5-year development plan, the context for Boeing's later caution on clean sheets.

speaker: Scott A. Fancher, VP & GM 787 Program
quote: we've actually got a standard process at BCA called value engineering, where we will work with our partners to actually implement design changes that will allow the product to be produced less expensively and, in fact, have arrangements so that we can share evenly those cost savings.
finding: Boeing cut 787 unit costs by sharing value-engineering savings evenly with suppliers rather than only squeezing prices.

speaker: Scott A. Fancher, VP & GM 787 Program
quote: typically, that minimum duration is about 6 months. ... it's about maturity of the production system and its ability to consume the work that's flowing through the production system, because the last thing you want to do, and it's the big takeaway from '97, is make a rate step with the production system unable to complete that work.
finding: Boeing's industrial rules set about 6 months minimum between rate steps and required proven work absorption, based on the 1997 rate-increase meltdown.

speaker: Dennis A. Muilenburg, CEO Boeing Defense, Space & Security
quote: We are ramping production down from 15 a year to 10 a year. This year we'll be at the midpoint in that ramp down. Next year, we will be at the 10 a year. We think that is the long-term sustainable rate
finding: With C-17 demand fading, Boeing cut the rate to a sustainable floor and kept the line alive with export orders rather than closing it.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: our view of the marketplace changed over the last 3 months, I would say. And as I said in my -- in answer to the last question, I think the significant economics that we can deliver with re-engine are more highly valued over the next 5 to 7 years than even better economics after that point.
finding: Boeing reversed from an all-new airplane to a 737 re-engine within about three months, as NEO demand and the American Airlines campaign showed customers valued near-term economics.
trigger: A320neo traction, including the American Airlines campaign
response: Switched to 737 re-engine (MAX) instead of new small airplane

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Obviously, we provided some lease back-stop financing for this transaction.
finding: Boeing answered Airbus's balance-sheet offer at American with lease back-stop financing of its own.
response: Lease back-stop financing to keep part of American order

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we believe our re-engined airplane will be -- have roughly the same margin of capability over the NEO as our current airplane has over the current A330, which is sort of a 2%, 3%, 4% depending on the mission
finding: Boeing sized the MAX to keep its existing cash-operating-cost lead over the A320 family rather than to leapfrog it.
response: MAX configured to retain 2-4% cash-cost gap

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: In June, we announced plans to further increase the 737 production rate to 42 airplanes per month beginning in the first half of 2014 in order to meet the unprecedented single-aisle demand.
finding: In June 2011, citing unprecedented single-aisle demand, Boeing added a step to 42 per month in its 737 ramp.
trigger: unprecedented single-aisle demand; A320neo order surge
response: 737 rate to 42/month H1 2014

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: With over 2,100 737 airplanes on order, this rate increase allows us to increase -- to meet our customers' requirements and opens new delivery slots for customers who want these airplanes sooner than we could otherwise provide them.
finding: Boeing used rate increases to open earlier delivery slots, treating slot availability as a sales weapon.
response: rate increase to free slots

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: intend to maintain this lead as we evaluate the potential for our 787-10 to follow the 787-9 and eventually take steps to further improve the 777, the leading wide-body operating in the marketplace today.
finding: Boeing aimed to keep its widebody lead through derivatives, a 787-10 stretch and later 777 improvements, not a new widebody.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: the big order announcement last week by American Airlines, which included 100 737NGs and a commitment by the airline for an additional 100 re-engined NGs pending launch approval of that program by our Board of Directors.
finding: Boeing committed to a re-engined 737 through the American Airlines order (100 NG plus 100 re-engined) before the board had approved the program.
trigger: American Airlines campaign with Airbus A320neo
response: commit to 737 re-engine to secure AA

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we have evaluated in rigorous detail 2 potential options for our next narrowbody airplane ... with an entry into service around the middle of the decade or an all ... new airplane if we could get it to market in the 2019 to 2020 time frame.
finding: Boeing framed its narrowbody choice as a mid-decade re-engine versus an all-new airplane only if it could enter service in 2019-2020.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Our primary challenge became that we do not yet have a clear answer on the architecture of a production system that would incorporate new product technologies available to us and could ramp up quickly with acceptable cost and risk profiles to 50 or 60 airplanes per month by the end of the decade
finding: The new small airplane failed on production: Boeing could not define a system to ramp new technologies to 50-60 per month at acceptable cost and risk.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: It has always been our view that if it looked like we are putting meaningful market share at risk by waiting to do a new airplane, we would re-engine instead.
finding: Boeing's stated decision rule: re-engine rather than wait for a clean sheet if waiting would put meaningful market share at risk.
response: re-engine 737

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: a broader customer view has emerged in support of the greater certainty of gaining significant incremental improvement in a re-engined 737 in the near to midterm over the more perfect solution which may be available further down the road.
finding: Customers preferred certain near-term gains from a re-engined 737 over a better airplane later, which moved Boeing to re-engine.
response: re-engine

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: That combined with our new engine technical production assessment against lead time for new engine decision led us to the judgment that we have made. ... Over the next several weeks, we will continue our work to finalize the configuration and other details in anticipation of a launch this fall pending board approval.
finding: Engine lead times forced an early narrowbody decision; Boeing planned formal re-engine launch in fall 2011 pending board approval.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: Revenue for the quarter was $16.5 billion, up 6% from a year ago due to higher delivery volumes and mix. Net earnings were $1.25 per share, up 18% from last year, while operating margins were 9.3%.
finding: Boeing's Q2 2011 earnings grew on mature-program volume: $16.5B revenue, EPS $1.25, 9.3% margin.

speaker: James A. Bell, CFO
quote: The benefits of volume leverage and continued productivity improvements are balanced with the competitive pricing environment and investments in tooling and production systems necessary to achieve the higher production rates.

response: Re-engine the 737 (MAX) instead of a clean-sheet design

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: And on both those programs, again, we're working the details right now. If we can figure out what the NRE is and we can satisfy ourselves that the risk is acceptable, we could be taking these programs to the board sometime later in the year.
finding: Boeing's launch criteria for the 787-10 and 777X were a known non-recurring cost and acceptable risk before seeking board approval.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we've looked at doing a brand-new airplane, and that's something that I don't think we will do. It's a huge investment, time and money. And I think that we can make the 777 that we have much more efficient than it is by putting this generation of engines on the airplane
finding: Boeing ruled out a clean-sheet 777 replacement in favor of re-engining and re-winging the existing 777, again choosing a derivative over new development.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: going up in rate is something that you do with a lot of conservatism. The work cells can only handle so many jobs. We want to make sure that we don't overload the work cells... we will sneak up on these rate changes as opposed to trying to force them.
finding: Boeing makes rate increases conservatively, sizing each to what work cells can absorb rather than forcing output.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: if you see the market slow down, we just look at that as an opportunity to burn down backlog. We should have done it last time when the market softened. We didn't. We cut rates. And then when the market came back, we were in a position that we couldn't support all the demands from our customers.
finding: Boeing said that in a future slowdown it would hold rates and burn down backlog, because cutting rates in the last downturn left it unable to meet demand in the recovery.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: You always see melt-away during good times and bad times... Will things move around? They will. They always do. We don't significantly overbook.
finding: In March 2012 Boeing said it did not significantly overbook; by September it described raising over-quote levels to protect rates, a shift toward more aggressive slot management.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: Well, I'd love to go to 13 because we could sell them all. Our plan all along has been 10. We have the capacity between Charleston and Everett to do 17. I think the big question is can the supply chain do more than 10 without a significant investment?
finding: Supplier capacity and investment, not its own floor space or demand, capped Boeing's 787 rate at 10.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: our view of how you manage the supply chain is you manage it just like you do your internal factories... And just to understand that, you got to understand what they're doing to support some of the other competitors that are out there.
finding: Boeing manages suppliers like its own factories and tracks the capacity they commit to competitors such as Airbus, a lever for supplier-bottleneck competition.
trigger: Airbus, new entrants and F-35 raising load on shared aerospace suppliers
response: A 400-500 person team monitors supplier work centers, including their commitments to rivals

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: Ultimately, the C-17 line will go down though. If there's not an anchor tenant contract with the U.S. Air Force, it's pretty difficult to keep that going.
finding: Boeing accepts closing a program once its anchor customer stops buying and export orders cannot sustain the line.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I wanted to do a new small airplane... But we had 3 issues... how do you build 60 composite airplanes a month? We had a hard time defining what the NRE on the program was going to be, and we also had a real issue guaranteeing to customers when we deliver the first airplane.
finding: Boeing rejected a new composite narrowbody because of three unknowns: making composites at 60 a month, uncertain non-recurring cost, and an entry-into-service date it could not guarantee.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: there's a lot of money we didn't invest, which we would have invested if we'd gone with the new airplane. And with the money we didn't use for the new small airplane, we can do, we think, a derivative of the 787-9... and then still have money left over to refresh the 777 program.
finding: Boeing reallocated capital saved by re-engining the 737 to fund widebody derivatives (787-10 and the 777 refresh).

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: at some point in time, the 777 is going to come under some pressure as a result of the A350-1000... The timing of it really depends on... an understanding of when the A350-1000 is going to be in the marketplace. But we don't want to be disadvantaged on the 777 and won't be.
finding: Boeing timed its 777 upgrade to the A350-1000's entry into service, responding to the rival's schedule rather than moving pre-emptively.
response: 777X upgrade timed to the A350-1000's arrival

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: there are some competitive environments where the price, like it often does in these introductory environments, where the price was pretty aggressive, even more aggressive than an immediate productivity plan to offset the margin we have today.
finding: Boeing matched aggressive NEO launch pricing on some MAX deals beyond what near-term productivity covered, relying on long-run productivity to protect margins.
response: Priced MAX aggressively in some campaigns; offset with productivity

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: job 1 is to get the MAX in the marketplace. And as you point out, the MAX-9 and the A321 do fill a lot of that mission.
finding: In 2012 Boeing had no dedicated answer to the A321's lead in the 757-replacement segment, and put the MAX-9 ahead of a new product.
trigger: Customers leaning to A321 over 737-900ER for 757 replacement
response: Rely on MAX-9; further product planning deferred

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I will say we were aggressive, as I have said, and we worked our supply chain very, very hard and got the same kind of commitments from them that we, in turn, were making to the Air Force, which is a fixed-price development environment.
finding: After losing the 2008 tanker award to EADS, Boeing won the re-competition with an aggressive fixed-price bid backed by matching supplier commitments.
response: Aggressive fixed-price KC-46 bid

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Delivering our record backlog faster to speed the flow of new airplanes to customers and open additional positions for sale remains a priority. Production rate increases planned over the next 3 years will increase our output by more than 40% in support of these objectives.
finding: Boeing's rate increases aim to open sellable delivery slots as well as deliver backlog faster; in April 2012 it put the output gain at more than 40% over three years.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Yes. Well, our philosophy is that we don't let pricing get in the way of margins. And the answer to that is productivity. So that's the plan.
finding: Boeing's stated rule is to protect margins against pricing pressure through productivity.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: there are some competitive environments where the price... was pretty aggressive, even more aggressive than an immediate productivity plan to offset the margin we have today. But our judgment is that over the long term... productivity in the long run, on a program basis, can offset the pricing
finding: Boeing matched some neo prices that its near-term productivity plans could not offset, betting that long-run productivity would recover the margin.
trigger: Reports of A320neo priced at or below current A320 prices
response: Matched aggressive pricing in some campaigns and relied on long-run program productivity

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we work very closely with our customers, understand the financeability of what they want to do, understand their fleet plans... Is this a bubble? Is this -- can you support the growth? Are you going to be in business? And if we get to the point of seeing it differently, we'll adjust our plans.
finding: Boeing screens orders for financeability and fleet plans to avoid double-booked demand, and said it would change rates only if that evidence changed.
trigger: Industry commentary that Boeing and Airbus may be oversupplying the market
response: Kept rate plans; screened customers and financing; would adjust if the data changed

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the Spirit operation supports a number of our programs. The -- where they have the most content is the 737. And they've been back to work full-time starting this Monday after roughly a week's delay.
finding: Boeing's dependence on Spirit AeroSystems for 737 fuselages makes a single supplier site a bottleneck risk, as the Wichita storm showed.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: right now, as I think we've announced many, many times, we are working exclusively with CFM on the MAX, and we're very happy with the development there. We're confident that we can meet the targets that our customers need
finding: Boeing rejected a Pratt & Whitney geared turbofan option and kept CFM as sole MAX engine supplier.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: So when you say Embraer, you're talking about some localization efforts we've got in Brazil.
finding: Boeing's 2012 agreement with Embraer was a localization effort tied to Brazil campaigns, not a commercial joint venture.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, BCA CEO
quote: We do not want them to get to 60% and us, 40%. Just think about that. If they get to 60%, we're at 40%, they come down the learning curve faster than we do, they have pricing power in the marketplace. It's a slippery slope for us to be on.
finding: Boeing's red line was a 60/40 share split, because the leader would gain learning-curve cost advantage and pricing power.
response: Defend ~50% share

speaker: Jim Albaugh, BCA CEO
quote: But we're not going to let Airbus position themselves where they have a disproportionate amount of the market share. If you think about where we want to position Boeing, we want to have half of the small airplane market.
finding: Boeing committed to hold half the narrowbody market against the NEO and expected order parity by 2013.
response: Target half of narrowbody market; parity in orders by end-2012/mid-2013

speaker: Jim Albaugh, BCA CEO
quote: Well, it hasn't been lost on us. We need to go play in their sandbox, too. And we've targeted a few of those airlines.
finding: After losing share at American, Garuda and SAS to the NEO, Boeing began targeting Airbus's own customers.
trigger: Losses at AMR, Garuda, SAS to NEO
response: Target Airbus-loyal airlines

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Proceeding with the MAX allows us to maintain our performance and value advantages in the single-aisle market at lower development costs and risk -- substantially lower development costs and risk than all new airplane. This combination of virtues will enable investment in other growth projects
finding: Boeing chose to re-engine the 737 rather than launch a new single-aisle, citing much lower development cost and risk and freeing capital for other projects.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The 737 MAX will be 13% more fuel-efficient than today's 737 depending on flight length, of course, and it will cost less to operate than its competitors.
finding: Boeing sized the MAX's efficiency step at 13% over the NG and claimed lower operating cost than its competitors.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: what we have in mind is opening up capacity because we do see a big growth opportunity; diversifying risk and there are many elements of risk, there's financial risk, there's geographic risk, there's risk in other kinds of interruptions
finding: Boeing adds production capacity in new, open-shop locations both to grow and to spread labor and geographic risk.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we want to move from worshiping backlog to managing backlog. And I think what that comment implies -- and I think our company came out of the late '90s where we screwed up the NG supply chain ramp-up and so we were probably a little gun-shy
finding: Boeing's past caution on rate increases came from the failed late-1990s NG ramp, and in 2012 it chose to work down backlog more actively.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: if you knew the costs as I do of taking up rate and then taking it down again, you would be very cautious about that decision, and we are. Yet I think, on balance, we're going to be a little more aggressive this decade than we were last decade
finding: Boeing weighed the high cost of raising and then cutting rates but decided to be somewhat more aggressive on production rates in the 2010s than in the 2000s.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think it stands in the way when you're trying to decide between 8.3 and 8.6. I think there it becomes a factor. But if the market, for some reason, tells us they want 10 or 11 777s a month... I don't think the capital would stand in our way for a nanosecond.
finding: Capital cost limits small rate increases, but Boeing would fund a large rate step if demand was sustained.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think the world's adjusted to it pumping back and forth between $90 and $110. And so I am confident that in that level, it both spurs replacement demand, the paybacks are quick, and it doesn't dampen overall economic demand.
finding: Boeing's demand case assumed oil at $90-110, high enough to drive replacement but not to hurt the economy.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: There's a breakeven calculation the airlines do that say, at $50, the payback on a MAX versus an NG has stretched from X to Y... I think when you're down in that range, I think that payback obviously changes significantly.
finding: Boeing acknowledged that low oil prices around $50 would weaken the business case for new-engine narrowbodies over current models.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: for me, the deciding item is the depth and length of their technical maturation program that they've had on this program, starting from the mid-'90s, that didn't exist to the same degree on the GEnx and the Trent offerings.
finding: Boeing chose CFM's LEAP as sole MAX engine on the strength of its long technology maturation, a lesson from the late 787 engines.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the engine that will go on the MAX will be the third version of the assembling of these technologies, okay? China and then the NEO, which is not a bad place to be with new engine technology.
finding: Boeing saw entering service after the A320neo and COMAC's aircraft with the same engine family as a maturity advantage rather than a disadvantage.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Carefully managed production rate increases from 2012 through 2014 will raise our commercial airplane output by more than 30%... contract extension we reached with our machinists' union in Puget Sound late last year will help ensure delivery of this growth plan.
finding: Boeing planned to raise commercial output by more than 30% in three years and secured a labor contract first to protect the ramp.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Very minimal, Cliff. We don't see a need to do that. I think there is plenty of capacity out there, as Jim talked about, between XM, capital markets.
finding: Boeing planned only minimal direct customer financing, relying on Ex-Im Bank and capital markets instead.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: the percentage of those blocks that are sold, which is one of the indicators that we utilize before we make a rate or make a block extension.
finding: Boeing bases rate increases and accounting-block extensions on how much of the future block is already sold.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: It really all depends on how much incremental investment you have in those programs. So if you don't do them today, you continue to make minor modifications or improvements on the 777.
finding: Boeing's fallback if it did not launch the 777X or 787-10 was incremental upgrades to the current 777, with commercial R&D in the low $2 billions.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Certainly, with a dilution impact on the 87 and 47 makes that even more challenging, but it's something we have kind of refreshed and we're trying to figure out how we want to utilize that, if at all, going forward.
finding: Boeing's 7% net margin goal, set in 2005, was still out of reach because of 787 and 747-8 dilution, and a 5% near-term net margin was accepted as reasonable.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: Supplier capacity and quality. Obviously, with us going up in rate, Airbus, with other people entering the marketplace, with F-35 and other programs, we have to manage our supply chain very carefully and very diligently
finding: Boeing sees its own rate increases competing with Airbus, new entrants and defense programs for the same supplier capacity.
trigger: Airbus and new entrants raising output on shared suppliers
response: Tighter supply-chain monitoring and management

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I think most of the discussion about that is really coming from the leasors, or the leasers, and there is certainly something to be gained on their part by talking about a bubble. They would like to see the supply go down, so prices will go up.
finding: Boeing dismissed lessor warnings of a production bubble as self-interested and kept its rate increases, a stance it repeated through 2012.
trigger: Lessors warning of a production bubble
response: Kept rate increases; cited traffic and low deferrals

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we're going up in rate on every program. We want to match our capacity with the demand that's out there. And 7 years of backlog is just too much. It drives our good customers to go and look at other alternatives, which we don't want them to do.
finding: Boeing raises rates partly so that long lead times do not push its customers to the rival.
trigger: Seven-year backlog making customers consider alternatives (Airbus)
response: Rate increases on every program

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: We want our airplanes to get a premium in the marketplace because they provide what the customers want... whenever we have a competition, we have an airplane in there that provides greater value than the competitor, and that means that we'll get a premium
finding: Boeing's pricing strategy is to earn a premium over the rival through better product value, not to win on price.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: We did make some bad decisions on the 787. We did outsource too much. And I think we did it because we were looking to maximize RONA... we have brought a number of things back inside the Boeing company. We're not going to totally vertically integrate
finding: Boeing admitted that chasing return on net assets led it to over-outsource the 787, and it reversed course by insourcing critical work short of full vertical integration.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: there aren't any active airplane design teams in the United States of America other than the Boeing company. And if you're a new freshly degreed aero engineer or any kind of engineer that wants to work in airplanes, work with airplanes, they're going to come and work with us.
finding: Boeing saw itself as the only U.S. employer for commercial aircraft design talent, an advantage in the talent market.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: To go to 10, I really believe that the real issues are going to be in our control, and that's good. It's going to be the aft and also the midbody assembly that we do down in Charleston.
finding: Boeing identified its own Charleston fuselage work, not suppliers, as the main bottleneck to 787 rate 10.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: Most of the contracts we have with our suppliers expire at airplane 100, so we'll have an opportunity to work with them to take costs out of what they do. And our commitment... is, that over the next 5 years, we're going to make this program more profitable each and every year.
finding: Boeing planned to use supplier contract renewals at airplane 100 to cut 787 cost and committed to improving 787 profitability every year.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: And we need some orders on this program. I think our backlog right now is about 90 airplanes, something in that order.
finding: Boeing raised the 747-8 rate to 2 per month on a thin backlog of about 90, a program exposed to weak demand.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: That is about all we're planning on doing. And if anybody wants to do anything more, they've got to earn their way onto the airplane, and they got to get by Delaney first and then me next. So our plan is to keep this very simple in terms of what the scope of work is.
finding: Boeing strictly limited MAX scope (new engine, taller gear, fly-by-wire spoilers, winglet) to contain development risk and cost.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: On this program, one thing we want to do is we do want to underpromise and overdeliver. On the 787 and 747, we fell a little bit short.
finding: After missing guarantees on the 787 and 747-8, Boeing set conservative performance promises for the MAX.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: We start looking at a rate increase 24 months before we make the change... there are about 1,200 suppliers that we monitor religiously and there are about 500 of those, that could possibly shut our facility down... about 12 of those right now.
finding: Boeing plans each rate increase two years ahead and monitors the suppliers that could stop its lines.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: It's seat-mile costs are going to be about 7% less than the -9... On the timing, that's a good question. We got to finish the -9 first. After we have to finish the -9, we'll take a hard look at rolling in to the -10.
finding: Boeing sequenced the 787-10X behind the 787-9, launching one derivative at a time.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: what we're looking at is a composite wing with a new engine... It would be more efficient than whatever the A350-1000 winds up being. And right now, we really got 3 things we're working on. One, understanding what the A350-1000 is; understanding what the non-recurring cost
finding: Boeing sized its 777X decision against the A350-1000, waiting to see the rival's final definition and weighing non-recurring cost before committing.
response: 777X study of a composite wing and new engine, designed to beat the A350-1000; decision deferred until the rival and costs are understood

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: at some point in time, we will do something to the airplane, and we'll do it because we need to continue to have the most efficient airplane out there in every category. And I think we will do that with both the 787-10 and the 777X.
finding: Boeing aims to have the most efficient airplane in every size category and will upgrade widebodies to keep that position.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: Health of the core production programs. In the 777 and 37, they pay a lot of bills, and we've got to continue to execute on those.
finding: Boeing treats the 777 and 737 as the cash generators funding the rest of the portfolio.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: the real issue that we had, as we tried to go from 2.5 to 3.5, to get to 2.5 was the design instability that we had. All the change traffic that was coming at us as a result of simultaneous building of airplanes, the flight test program
finding: Building 787s while design and flight test were still changing (concurrency) was the main obstacle to Boeing's early 787 rate increases.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I think Jim talked about looking at the 777 above 8.3. We're looking at could we go higher on the 737?... if the demand is there, we've got to match the capacity with the demand. We're giving up market share if we don't.
finding: Boeing links rate increases directly to market share and considers going beyond announced 737 and 777 rates to avoid ceding share.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: We're 48%, they're 52%. Pretty darn close to 50-50. We get paid a premium for our airplane. We like that. We do not want them to get to 60% and us, 40%... they come down the learning curve faster than we do, they have pricing power in the marketplace. It's a slippery slope
finding: Boeing's narrowbody red line is about 40% share: below it Airbus would gain learning-curve and pricing advantages, so Boeing will fight to stay near 50%.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we're not going to let Airbus position themselves where they have a disproportionate amount of the market share. If you think about where we want to position Boeing, we want to have half of the small airplane market.
finding: Boeing's narrowbody share target is 50% versus Airbus.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I fully expect by the end of this year, or sometime in the middle of next year, that if you look at the number of MAX airplanes on order versus the number of neos on order, you're going to see the kind of parity that we've had in years past.
finding: Boeing expected the MAX to catch up with the A320neo's earlier order lead within about 12-18 months.
trigger: A320neo order lead after its earlier launch
response: MAX order push targeting parity
lag: expected parity by end-2012 to mid-2013

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: you don't tell me you need to have more capital to go up in rate... Two years ago, when we talked about going above 7 on the 777, it was going to be a significant capital bill. And we're going to 8.3 now, and we're going to spend very, very little capital
finding: Boeing funds rate increases through lean and flow gains rather than new capital wherever it can.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: We don’t talk much about 767, a couple of airplanes a month, couple of airplanes a month for the next 20 years. We're standing here 15 months ago thinking we're going to shut that line down. We didn't.
finding: Boeing had planned to close the 767 line but kept it open once the tanker win provided long-run volume, reversing a near-cancellation.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: That airplane, it's a little short on the guarantees, and we said that in the past. But we've got a number of performance improvement packages that we're going to be getting from GE, and I think we'll get the engine's specific fuel consumption where it needs to be.
finding: The 747-8 missed performance guarantees, and Boeing relied on GE engine improvement packages over one to two years to close the gap.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I think we also are not overselling on the front end. We're also trying to limit what the liquidated damages would be. We're also, as we always do, where the supply chain doesn't perform, the impact is on them.
finding: After the 787, Boeing wrote MAX contracts to cap its liquidated-damages exposure to customers and pass the cost of supplier failures back to suppliers.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO Boeing Defense, Space & Security
quote: The large majority of those people have been moved over to our Commercial Airplane unit... Now the advantage is, that allows us to keep the talent and experience inside the company. We also avoid severance costs and other things that might come with layoffs.
finding: Boeing moved defense staff into commercial to keep talent and avoid severance, a practice it repeated in November 2012.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO Boeing Defense, Space & Security
quote: We're also continuing to build selective presence, leveraging Boeing Defense Australia, Boeing Defense U.K. and our Alsalam operation in Saudi Arabia, as well as the partnerships like those signed during the last year with Mubadala in UAE and with Embraer in Brazil.
finding: Boeing had formed a partnership with Embraer in Brazil by 2011-12 as part of its international strategy, an early link to a later joint-venture option.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO Boeing Defense, Space & Security
quote: our position is to assume that sequester will happen in terms of a $1 trillion cut to size our cost structure to accommodate that so we can meet our margin commitments in the face of a sequester but continue to invest in prototyping assuming that some of the major new programs go forward
finding: Boeing hedges both ways, sizing cost for the worst case while investing for the upside, and held this stance from May to November 2012.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO Boeing Defense, Space & Security
quote: at some time, we will have to shut down the C-17 line some time out in the future. That's a well-defined process. That's included in our Air Force contract, including the shutdown cost, so that's not a financial risk to us.
finding: Boeing contracts for line-shutdown costs up front so that ending a program carries no financial risk to it.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: With stability now achieved at 3.5 airplanes per month, we expect to increase the rate of 787 production to 5 per month by the end of this year, tracking to our plan to reach a rate of 10 per month across our final assembly lines by late 2013.
finding: Boeing raised the 787 rate only after demonstrating stability at the previous rate.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We recently firmed up our maximum takeoff weight projections, extending the airplane's existing range advantage significantly to allow our customers the flexibility to open up new markets. We are on schedule to reach firm configuration in 2013 and to enter service in 2017.
finding: Boeing raised the 737 MAX takeoff weight to widen its range advantage while holding the 2013 firm-configuration and 2017 service-entry dates.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: it’s any time you're ramping down a program and then ramping up a new one, certainly, there's pricing considerations taken in that. Customer by customer, it's different.
finding: Boeing accepts pricing concessions on both the outgoing NG and the incoming MAX during the product transition, deciding them customer by customer.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Certainly, investing in the business, and we've obviously talked about the MAX and some of the other potential investments going forward, proactively managing the pension fund... But expect to kind of restart share repurchase, in particular, in the 2013 timeframe and then, of course, pay down our debt.
finding: Boeing ranked capital uses as investing in products such as the MAX, then pension, then restarting buybacks in 2013 and paying down debt.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the small tactical deals are kind of the flow deals that we're implementing in areas that you're well aware of... the big major deal is one that is -- would not be done without a great deal of thought. And that's really not on our radar screen
finding: Boeing preferred small bolt-on acquisitions and ruled out large transformational M&A in 2012.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: there is always some launch pricing that is -- tends to be a little more aggressive for a while. And as the older models wind down, there's some fill-the-gap pressure. But our view is, we're not going to change that. And so our issue is driving productivity to offset it.
finding: Boeing treats aggressive narrowbody launch pricing as structural and answers it with factory productivity rather than price discipline.
trigger: Competitive narrowbody pricing during the NEO/MAX transition
response: Accept launch pricing and offset it with productivity in factories and development

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I agree that orders will probably be less next year than this year. I think it will be driven more by a massive introduction being converted this year. Recall that we still see a 5% growth rate, about half replacement, about half fleet.
finding: Boeing saw the post-MAX-launch order decline as a return to steady state rather than a cyclical trough, so it kept its rate increases.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: it's end of this year, beginning of next year could be timing. It's not timing we have baked into any plans yet... So we'll make the judgment the last half of this year on exactly when we'd begin some conditional offerability.
finding: Boeing approached the 787-10X in stages, deciding on conditional offerability to airlines before any formal launch.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA CEO
quote: SilkAir was a great example of we won down there and actually flipped an all Airbus customer to an all Boeing customer now. ... because of the range of the MAX over the NEO, they felt like they could go in and open new markets
finding: Boeing converted an all-Airbus operator (SilkAir) to the MAX, citing the MAX's range over the NEO.
trigger: NEO campaign; need to take Airbus customers
response: Won SilkAir from Airbus

speaker: Ray Conner, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we're going to have widebody orders as well. And I wish I had more position to sell on the 87, but we don't just yet.
finding: 787 sales were capped by a sold-out production skyline, so capacity rather than demand limited widebody orders.

speaker: Ray Conner, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I think it's better to be steady, and we really manage our skyline well now. I think what -- if you go back in 2008 and 2009, we managed ourselves through that cycle, and we did not take – in the single aisles, we did not take the rate down.
finding: Boeing prefers to hold production rates steady through the cycle, and it did not cut narrowbody rates in 2008-09.
response: Held single-aisle rates; cut 777 briefly

speaker: Ray Conner, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we over-quote when we feel like it's necessary. We raise the over-quote percentages if we think it's necessary so we can maintain whatever rate we are at.
finding: Boeing deliberately sells more delivery slots than it builds (over-quoting) to protect production rates against deferrals.

speaker: Ray Conner, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I would prefer to, once we get to a 42 a month to maintain that as we go forward, once we get to 8.3 on the 777, maintain that as we go forward.
finding: Boeing planned to hold rates at each new plateau (737 at 42, 777 at 8.3) rather than keep chasing demand.

speaker: Ray Conner, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I've been getting called all the time about trying to get to those positions now. So I mean, we could sell them if we chose to do that. We're using that kind of an opportunity to de-risk a little bit into our rate ramp
finding: Boeing used slots freed by a large cancellation as schedule margin for the 787 ramp rather than reselling them at once.
response: Did not change 787 rate plans; used freed slots to de-risk the ramp and deferred resale to outer years

speaker: Ray Conner, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: that's why we put in the temporary surge line was to better deal with that and de-risk that whole scenario, bringing in the Dash 9 while you're in this pretty fast rate on the Dash 8
finding: Boeing added temporary capacity (a surge line) to protect the 787 rate ramp while introducing the 787-9 derivative.

speaker: Ray Conner, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: So we'll get ourselves through the MAX, get ourselves through the 9, get the production stable, look at where we're at. And then as we speak right now, we are defining the airplanes with our customer
finding: Boeing sequences new programs: it finishes current developments and stabilizes production before committing to the next launch, while defining the next airplanes with customers in parallel.

speaker: Ray Conner, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: the 10X, that's a very straightforward derivative. I mean, it's a couple of donuts... The 777X, that's a bigger work statement, wing, those kinds of things, that's building off of what -- of the success that we've had with the 777. Those are kind of out later on in the decade.
finding: Boeing framed both widebody responses as derivatives: a simple 787-10 stretch and a new wing for the 777, timed for later in the decade.

speaker: Ray Conner, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we are still driving a great premium on the MAX over the NEO, and we're driving a great premium on the MAX over the classic, the current NG. So our pricing, I'm very comfortable with our pricing as it is today
finding: Boeing claimed it priced the MAX above both the A320neo and the 737NG despite reports of heavy discounting.
trigger: Reports of heavy discounting on both MAX and A320neo
response: Asserted a price premium over the NEO; declined to give breakeven

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: customer demand for the 737 MAX remains high with 858 orders to date, including 119 orders booked in just the last couple of weeks. Development of the airplane is tracking to plan for firm configuration in 2013 and entry into service in 2017.
finding: The re-engined 737 MAX gathered 858 orders about a year after launch, with firm configuration planned for 2013 and service entry in 2017.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we are facing more aggressive competition from both existing and emerging OEMs. To get out in front of these dynamics now rather than fall victim to them later, we have reached out to key supply chain partners and asked them to join us in driving major improvements in product quality, reliability, cost
finding: Boeing reacts to rising competition by pushing cost reduction into its supply chain before the pressure arrives.
trigger: More aggressive competition from existing and emerging OEMs; customers wanting more for less
response: Launched a supply-chain competitiveness initiative (Partnering for Success) on cost, quality and efficiency

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: It's also a way to perform our best -- to reward our best performing partners, give them more work if they signed up for this kind of an approach... its objective at the end of the day is to improve the operating margins of our business and to offset inflationary and pricing pressures
finding: Boeing uses future work share as leverage to get suppliers to cut costs, aiming to protect its own margins against pricing pressure.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: The deferred production balance for the program was $14.3 billion at the end of the third quarter... This will peak at slightly over $20 billion and then decline after the program achieves the planned rate of 10 per month and stabilizes at that level.
finding: Boeing accepted a 787 deferred-production balance heading above $20 billion, expecting to recover it only after reaching and holding rate 10.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we have extended the accounting quantity on the 737 program by 200 units this quarter. While the majority of the incremental units are NGs, we also incorporated an additional MAX aircraft and the associated nonrecurring MAX investments, initial production costs and pricing.
finding: Boeing folds MAX development cost and introductory pricing into the 737 program accounting block, relying on NG productivity to hold margin.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: this company has absorbed a lot of development risk over the last decade but now that we're coming out of it, we have a suite of technologies that we can harvest in a de-risked environment for the next decade or 2.
finding: After the 787, Boeing chose to harvest existing technology through lower-risk derivatives (787-10, 777 successor, MAX) rather than new clean-sheet programs.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: one of the options, for example, with that airplane, and we're discussing this with our customers as we speak is to put a composite wing and a new engine on the current airframe. The kind of performance improvements that can be generated by the composite wing and new engines are pretty eye watering
finding: For the 777 successor, Boeing favoured a new composite wing and new engine on the existing fuselage over a clean-sheet design.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: there is some price pressure during an introductory period. We're seeing some of that ease off. In any case, we are getting a margin; we are getting paid for the new technology that we're putting into the airplanes. So there's a margin versus the NG.
finding: Boeing accepted introductory price pressure to launch the MAX but said it still captured a price premium over the NG.
trigger: Introductory-period price pressure in 737 MAX campaigns
response: Accepted launch discounts, said the pressure was easing and a premium over the NG remained

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: first and foremost, priority is returning cash to shareholders. So we're looking at share repurchase... From a dividend perspective, similar to what we've talked before, kind of a 20% to 40% payout of earnings looking at the yield.
finding: Boeing ranked returning cash to shareholders first, with a dividend payout target of 20-40% of earnings.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we are looking at the end of the decade, beginning of the next decade, kind of EIS but that's the assumption we're working with. Our customers would like it then or sooner. That gives us plenty of time to develop it. What we're really trying to do is choose the right configuration
finding: Asked about the A350, Boeing did not accelerate the 777 successor; it kept an end-of-decade entry into service and put getting the configuration right ahead of speed.
response: Kept 777X entry into service at end of decade or start of the next; focused on configuration

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: as we take the 37 up from 35 to 38 to 42, 87 up to 10, 777 at 8.3, clearly, there's a solid cash generation that goes with those production rate increases.
finding: Boeing's cash and deployment plan is explicitly tied to stepping up production rates on all three main commercial lines.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we go through that discipline process before we'll make the final decision to make the rate break. So if there's metrics that are outside the control limits, there'll be a pause, and you've seen us do this before.
finding: Boeing gates each production-rate increase on stability metrics and will pause a rate break if they are out of control limits.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: 50% of our backlog is really linked to replacement versus growth... you can close a business case when you're 20-plus percent more efficient.
finding: Boeing sees replacement demand, triggered by a 20%-plus efficiency gain, as the driver of half its backlog.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: I see R&D at this point about flat to this year with the -9 -- 787-9 kind of ramping down but the MAX picking up, and that will probably peak in about 2015 time frame.
finding: Boeing kept commercial R&D flat by substituting MAX development spending for the declining 787-9 spend, with MAX R&D peaking around 2015.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we're building 35 a month in the same footprint we were building 21... we've cut about 20%, 25% of our footprint and double-digit improvement in flow time there.
finding: Boeing raises output on mature lines through productivity in existing floor space rather than new capacity.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Certainly, we were in a development phase. Recently now, we're in the production phase. It's all about delivery... And cash deployment, obviously, was not something we were talking about going through development. Now we are.
finding: Boeing's financial posture shifts with the product cycle: cash is conserved in development and returned once production ramps.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO Boeing Defense, Space & Security
quote: those investments would likely be slowed down to align with whatever kind of schedule changes would happen due to sequester. So I think it gets more to the question of somewhat stretching out our investments with the idea that we have to provide a fundamentally healthy business.
finding: Under top-line pressure Boeing would stretch out investments to protect margin and shareholder expectations rather than accept lower profitability.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: In 2012, Boeing restored our market share leadership, as Commercial Airplane deliveries was 601 delivered, the most since 1999 and the second most in commercial aviation history...we also led the industry in net new orders, with 1,203
finding: Boeing regained market share leadership in 2012 by ramping production to 601 deliveries and leading the industry with 1,203 net orders, driven by the new 737 MAX.
trigger: Loss of market share leadership in prior years
response: Rate increases to 601 deliveries; 1,203 net orders

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: These achievements, combined with the strength of our balance sheet, enabled us to announce in December a dividend increase of 10% and the resumption of our share repurchase program this quarter.
finding: Boeing raised its dividend 10% and resumed buybacks once higher rates and new-program execution had been demonstrated.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We were also successful last year in more than doubling 787 production, increasing the rate from 2 airplanes per month to 5 per month. The program remains on track to further increase the final assembly build rate to 7 per month in mid-2013 and then 10 per month by late 2013
finding: Boeing followed a stepped 787 rate plan (2, 5, 7, 10 a month) across 2012-13.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: consistent with previous introductions of new minor models, we have planned a period of longer production flow times across the extended supply chain for the first few 787-9 airplanes. This will accommodate learning and ensure that we minimize disruption while still achieving our planned rate increases.
finding: Boeing builds in longer flow times for the first units of a new derivative to protect rate increases.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Operating cash flow was very strong, at $9.1 billion before $1.6 billion in discretionary pension contributions made in the year.
finding: Boeing generated strong cash in 2012 and used part of it for discretionary pension funding.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We expect Commercial Airplane operating margins to be approximately 9.5% in 2013, resulting from higher deliveries and continued strong core operating performance, while considering for some dilution on 87 and 747 deliveries
finding: Boeing guided BCA margins to about 9.5% for 2013, held down by dilution from 787 and 747-8 deliveries.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: And so our plan, as you know, is to continue production of the 787. And to continue the development of the widebody airplanes that we've told you about and we're continuing to do that.
finding: During the grounding Boeing refused to consider cutting the 787 rate or pausing its widebody development plans.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we've been conditionally offering the airplane in the marketplace and the response has been very strong...So I don't want to prejudge when we might reach a final launch decision
finding: Boeing offers new derivatives such as the 787-10 conditionally to customers before a formal launch decision, testing demand first.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we are focused on a tactical solution that offers significant performance advantages to an already market-leading airplane. I think it's been widely discussed that the most likely design is some increased capacity and a composite wing with new engines
finding: Boeing's answer to growing A350 orders was a limited-scope 777 upgrade (more capacity, composite wing, new engines) rather than a new aircraft.
response: 777X 'tactical' derivative

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: as derivatives go, will be a significant amount of work...You're right, it's at a scale that's different than we've done before, so it's not without challenges. But the advantage we have in using composites for airfoils and other aerospace applications is something I don't want to give up on.
finding: Boeing accepted the risk of a large new composite wing on the 777X to keep its composites lead, a bigger step than a pure re-engine.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: moving in every real way that you can think of towards a successful launch on the MAX, getting very close on the -10, and getting close to operability on the 777X. And all of those airplanes have the...kinds of performance capabilities that I think is going to keep us in the market share lead
finding: Boeing's plan to keep the market-share lead over Airbus rested on three concurrent derivatives: MAX, 787-10 and 777X.
response: Three-derivative product plan

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: notwithstanding a difficult market situation, as we sit here today we have confidence that we're going to be able to hold rate. But we're going to be taking a look at it every quarter.
finding: In January 2013 Boeing tried to hold the 747-8 rate by selling hard, but cut it twice in 2013 as cargo demand stayed weak.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: No instructions to slow down. Business as usual. Let's keep building airplanes and then let's ramp-up as we'd planned.
finding: Boeing told its 787 supply chain not to slow down during the delivery halt and kept the ramp plan intact.

quote: We face aggressive international competitors who are intent on increasing their market share, such as Airbus, Embraer and Bombardier, and other entrants from Russia, China and Japan. We are focused on improving our processes and continuing cost reduction efforts. We intend to continue to compete with other airplane manufacturers by providing customers with greater value products, services, and support.
finding: Boeing frames its competitive answer to Airbus and other entrants as cost reduction plus value-based products and support rather than price leadership.

quote: We must meet planned production rate targets in order to satisfy customer demand and maintain our profitability. We continue to increase production rates for the 737, 777 and 787 programs, while at the same time engaging in significant ongoing development of the 787-9 and 737 MAX derivative aircraft.
finding: In 2012 Boeing chose to raise rates on three programs simultaneously while developing two derivatives, accepting concurrent ramp and development risk.

quote: Further, if we cannot efficiently and cost-effectively incorporate design changes into already-completed 787 and 747-8 production aircraft, we may face further profitability pressures on these programs.
finding: Boeing built 787 and 747-8 aircraft before designs were final and then had to rework them, a concurrency practice that pressured program profitability.

quote: Although alternative sources generally exist for these raw materials, qualification of the sources could take one year or more. Many major components and product equipment items are procured or subcontracted on a sole-source basis with a number of companies.
finding: Boeing depends on sole-source suppliers for many major components and needs a year or more to qualify alternatives, making supplier bottlenecks a structural vulnerability.

quote: We focus on producing the products and providing the services that the market demands and we price our products and services to provide a fair return for our shareholders while continuing to find new ways to improve efficiency and quality.
finding: Boeing states that its pricing is set to deliver a fair shareholder return, signalling margin discipline over share-at-any-price.

quote: Total $3,298 $3,918 $4,121 Our Research and development expense decreased by $620 million and $203 million in 2012 and 2011. These decreases were primarily due to lower spending at BCA on the 747-8 and 787-8 programs.
finding: Boeing let total R&D fall from $4.1bn (2010) to $3.3bn (2012) as 747-8 and 787-8 development wound down rather than immediately funding a new clean-sheet program.

quote: Our 20-year forecast is for a long-term average growth rate of 5% per year for passenger and cargo traffic, based on a projected average annual worldwide real economic growth rate of 3%. ... we project a $4.5 trillion market for 34,000 new airplanes over the next 20 years.
finding: Boeing anchors its capacity and product decisions on a 5% annual traffic growth outlook and a 34,000-airplane, $4.5tn 20-year market.

quote: has resulted in intense pressures on pricing and other competitive factors, and we expect these pressures to continue or intensify in the coming years. ... We are focused on improving our processes and continuing cost-reduction efforts. ... These efforts enhance our ability to pursue pricing strategies that enable us to price competitively.
finding: Boeing responds to rival-driven pricing pressure by cutting costs so it can price competitively, rather than by exiting segments.
trigger: Aggressive, government-supported competitors (Airbus, Embraer, Bombardier) intensifying price pressure
response: Process improvement and cost reduction to enable competitive pricing

quote: Revenues $49,127 $36,171 $31,834 % of total company revenues 60% 53% 50% Earnings/(loss) from operations $4,711 $3,495 $3,006 Operating margins 9.6% 9.7% 9.4% Research and development $2,049 $2,715 $2,975 Contractual backlog $317,287 $293,303 $255,591
finding: In 2012 BCA grew revenue 36% to $49.1bn at a 9.6% margin while cutting its R&D to $2.0bn, and its backlog rose to $317bn.

quote: Deliveries 415 (1) 31 26 83 46 (2) 601 ... The decrease in operating margins from 9.7% in 2011 to 9.6% in 2012 was primarily due to the dilutive effect of the 787 and 747-8 deliveries.
finding: Boeing delivered 601 jets in 2012 (415 737s, 83 777s, 46 787s) and accepted margin dilution from early, low-margin 787 and 747-8 units.

quote: As planned, production increased from 31.5 to 35 airplanes per month during 2012. We continue to expect to increase production from 35 to 38 airplanes per month beginning in 2013 and a further increase to 42 airplanes per month beginning in 2014. The majority of the 737 orders during 2012 related to the 737 MAX
finding: Boeing followed a stepwise 737 rate plan (31.5 to 35 to 38 to 42 per month) while its orders shifted to the re-engined 737 MAX.

quote: The accounting quantity for the 737 program includes NG and MAX units. First delivery of the 737 MAX is expected in 2017.
finding: Boeing treats the re-engined 737 MAX as a continuation of the 737 program in one accounting block, not as a new airplane, with first delivery set for 2017.

quote: The production rate increased from 1.5 to 2 airplanes per month in May 2012. Ongoing weakness in the air cargo market and lower-than-expected demand for large commercial passenger aircraft have resulted in pricing pressures and fewer orders than anticipated in 2012. We have a number of unsold Freighter and Intercontinental production positions beyond 2013.
finding: Boeing raised the 747 rate to 2 per month in 2012 despite weak demand, leaving unsold production slots and pricing pressure.
trigger: Weak air cargo market and low demand for very large passenger aircraft
response: Carried unsold 747 slots; considered rate cuts or building without firm orders

quote: reducing the number of airplanes produced and/or building airplanes for which we have not received firm orders. ... If market and production risks cannot be mitigated, the program could face an additional reach- forward loss that may be material.
finding: Facing weak 747 demand, Boeing's options included building airplanes without firm orders rather than only cutting rate, at the risk of a further reach-forward loss.

quote: As we reconfigure the 767 assembly line to include the USAF KC-46A Tanker, we plan to decrease our production rate from 2 to 1 airplanes per month in late 2013. ... As previously announced, we plan to increase our production rate from 7 per month to 8.3 per month in 2013.
finding: Boeing cut the 767 rate to fit the KC-46A tanker onto the line and raised the 777 rate from 7 to 8.3 per month.

quote: During the second quarter of 2012 we achieved a production rate of 3.5 per month in final assembly and in the fourth quarter of 2012, we achieved a program production rate of 5 airplanes per month in final assembly. We also activated the temporary surge line in Everett in the third quarter.
finding: Boeing pushed 787 output from 3.5 to 5 per month within 2012 and added a temporary surge line to hold its ramp.

quote: We continue to expect to increase the production rate of 787 aircraft to 10 per month in final assembly by the end of 2013 ... Our efforts to achieve planned production rate targets include improving the production system, coordinating rate increases with suppliers and increasing production rates in both Everett and North Charleston final assembly.
finding: Boeing targeted a doubling of the 787 rate to 10 per month within a year, using two final assembly sites and coordinated supplier ramps.

quote: The accounting quantity of 1,100 units remains unchanged and represents approximately 10 years of production at planned production rates. The cumulative impacts of production challenges, change incorporation, schedule delays from prior periods and customer and supplier impacts have created significant pressure on program profitability.
finding: Boeing admits that 787 delays, rework and customer and supplier claims squeezed program profitability, yet it kept a 1,100-unit block covering about 10 years.

quote: While production continues on the 787, we have suspended deliveries until appropriate clearance is granted by the regulatory agencies. We are unable to reasonably estimate a loss or a range of loss at this time
finding: When the 787 was grounded in January 2013, Boeing kept production running and paused only deliveries, building inventory instead of cutting rate.
trigger: January 2013 787 battery incidents and FAA suspension of 787 operations
response: Kept 787 production running; suspended deliveries
lag: immediate (within days of the January 16, 2013 directive)

quote: (excluding the 747 and 787 programs which have gross margins that are breakeven or near breakeven at December 31, 2012) ... If we are unable to mitigate risks associated with the 747 and 787 programs ... we could be required to record reach forward losses
finding: By end-2012 both of Boeing's newest widebodies, the 747-8 and 787, sat at or near breakeven gross margin, one step from reach-forward losses.

quote: $21,289 and $16,098 of work in process (including deferred production costs at December 31, 2012 of $15,929 and $10,753) ... $5,458 is expected to be recovered from units included in the program accounting quantity that represent expected future orders.
finding: Boeing let 787 deferred production costs grow by about $5bn in a year to $15.9bn, betting on future orders to recover part of them.

quote: Net cash provided by operating activities was $7.5 billion during 2012, an increase of $3.5 billion compared with 2011 primarily due to lower inventory growth in 2012, which was partially offset by $1.6 billion of contributions to our pension plans in 2012 compared with $0.5 billion in 2011
finding: Operating cash flow rose to $7.5bn in 2012 as 787 inventory growth slowed, even after Boeing put $1.6bn into its pension plans.

quote: Our investment in gross inventories increased by $6.2 billion in 2012, and by $9.8 billion in 2011, driven by higher investments in commercial airplane program inventory, primarily 787 inventory.
finding: Boeing funded a 787 inventory build of about $16bn over 2011-2012 from its own cash flow.

quote: In 2012, capital expenditures totaled $1.7 billion, consistent with the prior year. We expect capital expenditures to be higher in 2013 due to continued investment to support growth.
finding: Boeing kept capex around $1.7bn a year and planned to raise it in 2013 to support its rate increases.

quote: In February 2009, repurchases were suspended and in December 2012 we announced the resumption of this program with repurchases expected to total between $1.5 and $2.0 billion in 2013.
finding: Boeing suspended buybacks from 2009 through the 787 delays and resumed them only once 787 deliveries and cash flow recovered in late 2012.

quote: In 2012, we repaid $2.1 billion of debt, including repayments of $0.9 billion of debt held at BCC. At December 31, 2012 and 2011, the recorded balance of debt was $10.4 billion and $12.4 billion
finding: Boeing used 2012 cash to cut debt from $12.4bn to $10.4bn before it restarted buybacks.

quote: In the event we require additional funding to support strategic business opportunities, our commercial aircraft financing commitments, unfavorable resolution of litigation or other loss contingencies, or other business requirements, we expect to meet increased funding requirements by issuing commercial paper or term debt.
finding: Boeing says it would fund strategic opportunities or shocks with commercial paper or term debt, showing it is willing to lever up when needed.

quote: Financing commitments totaled $18.1 billion and $15.9 billion as of December 31, 2012 and 2011. We anticipate that we will not be required to fund a significant portion of our financing commitments as we continue to work with third party financiers to provide alternative financing to customers.
finding: Boeing offers large customer-financing commitments ($18.1bn) to win sales but expects third-party financiers to fund most of them.

quote: This contract is a fixed-price incentive firm contract valued at $4.9 billion and involves highly complex designs. Changes to our estimated cost to perform the work could result in a material charge.
finding: Boeing took the KC-46A tanker development, a 767 derivative, on a fixed-price basis and accepted the risk of a material charge to win the contract.

quote: Cash dividends have been paid on common stock every year since 1942.
finding: Boeing presents its unbroken dividend record since 1942 as a fixture of its capital allocation.
Boeing held or raised its dividend every year from 2008 to 2012 ($1.62 to $1.81 a share), even through the 787 delay years.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, BDS President & CEO
quote: So kind of a, call it, 1/2 a sequester. And we're investing for that kind of an outcome. So we want to protect our growth opportunities while we also take affordability actions for worst-case bottom line.
finding: Boeing plans costs for the worst case but invests for the most likely case, a dual-scenario approach to uncertainty.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, BDS President & CEO

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, BDS President & CEO
quote: we've ramped down our production rate from 15 a year to 10 a year. That was done purposely to try to extend that line farther...I think it's also important we keep that line hot for the U.S. in case there is a need for strategic lift production capacity
finding: In February 2013 Boeing was slowing the C-17 line to stretch it; within months it reversed and chose to close the line in 2015.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, BDS President & CEO
quote: this a process we go through every quarter where we look at the prospects, what are the long lead investments necessary to keep that line hot, and we like to have that line planned out in detail, about 2 years ahead of us.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA CEO
quote: Well, I think there was a -- we were a little late getting into the marketplace, so that played a little bit of that in that respect.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: we were about a year late. And so there were some head-to-heads that we were involved with that we had to be a little bit more aggressive on. But more aggressive than what we would have probably been had we not been.
finding: Being about a year late against the A320neo forced Boeing to price more aggressively on the MAX in head-to-head campaigns.
response: Aggressive MAX launch pricing

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: the initial launch deals can get a little bit more aggressive than what you see as you start to stabilize out, and I think what we're seeing now is a stabilization that's occurring in the marketplace.
