speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: one of the reasons why we do go down a sole source scenario is that we end up optimizing the engine, airplane -- airframe combination, and that's what gives us the performance that we do
finding: Boeing chooses a sole-source engine (here CFM on the 737 MAX) so it can optimise the engine and airframe together.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: we've got an engine that's built -- that kind of comes off of the NEO CFM. But it's optimized for the 737.
finding: The 737 MAX used a CFM engine derived from the one offered on the NEO but optimised for the 737.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: A little -- just a little bit longer than that.
finding: Boeing needs a little more than 12 months' lead time for a 747 rate decision, similar to the 777.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: we couldn't see any reason to make the switch back...there was no reason for us to make that switch. It's much faster for us to get back into the air that way.
finding: Boeing kept lithium-ion batteries rather than follow Airbus's switch to nickel-cadmium, putting speed of return to service ahead of a design change.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: we want to maintain our market position with the -- in that sized market. And I think we've got the airplane in the 777X that will do that...And I think it only benefits the 777 for us to be there with the 777X, much like with the MAX.
finding: Boeing upgraded the 777 into the 777X to defend its share of the large twin market, accepting cannibalisation of the current 777 as it had with the MAX.
response: Launch 777X as a defensive derivative

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: because we potentially could have 5 development programs going on at any one time with the MAX, the Tanker, the Dash 9, Dash 10 and the 777X. We separated production and development.
finding: Boeing reorganised BCA to separate development from production so it could run five development programs at once and move teams between them.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: In some cases, we are doing -- aggregating the demand from across some of these common commodities and doing the buying for their...And then there are other instances where we are utilizing some competitive situations to drive cost down too...So we've qualified some of the people, and now we have some new competition out there.
finding: Boeing qualified new second-source suppliers and pooled commodity purchasing to push supplier costs down.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: We stepped into some of that risk knowingly, and we're not doing that again. And I think the MAX is a great example of how we've approached this thing. And you're going to see that on the 10X as well
finding: Boeing explicitly renounced 787-style knowing risk-taking on new programs and pointed to the MAX and 787-10X as the lower-risk model.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: And despite the 3-month delivery suspension, our forecast remains to deliver greater than 60 787s during 2013.
finding: Boeing held its 2013 787 delivery target despite a three-month delivery halt, planning to catch up with higher rates.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Softness in this segment contributed to the decision announced last week to adjust the 747 program build rate down to 1.75 airplanes a month from 2 a month beginning in early 2014.
finding: Boeing cut the 747-8 rate from 2 to 1.75 a month in April 2013 and to 1.5 in October 2013 as cargo demand stayed weak.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We also received a commitment from Ryanair to order 175 737NGs. As a result, we now effectively have bridged production from the NG to the MAX, allowing us to smoothly transition our production system later this decade.
finding: Boeing sold late-model 737NGs in bulk (Ryanair 175) to bridge production until the MAX.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We remain focused on balancing production schedules with this strong demand in order to minimize long-term volatility in build rates and maximize productivity and profitability.
finding: Boeing aims to keep build rates stable over the long term rather than chase short-term demand.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: During the quarter, we selected GE as the sole-source engine manufacturer for the 777X program. New engines and an all-new composite wing that leverages the design and technologies of the 787 wing
finding: Boeing chose GE as sole-source engine supplier for the 777X, keeping the 777's single-engine-supplier model.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: timing of the 787 events limited our ability to repurchase shares in the first quarter. However, we expect to begin our repurchase plan in the second quarter and remain committed to our $1.5 billion to $2 billion of share repurchase planned for 2013.
finding: Boeing paused buybacks during the 787 grounding and resumed them once the fix was approved.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Gross inventory for the company included $28.8 billion related to the 787 program, an increase in the first quarter of approximately $3.3 billion, driven by the planned increase in production rate on the program and fewer 787 deliveries in the quarter.
finding: During the grounding Boeing kept building 787s and absorbed a $3.3 billion inventory increase in one quarter.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: these are derivative programs that tend to leverage more efficiently what we know. There is not a lot of invention going on. There is a lot of creative application and use of the technological lead that we have.
finding: Boeing's post-787 development strategy relied on derivatives (777X, 787-10X, MAX) with little new invention, to keep R&D and risk low.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: At certain points in time, we had to spend a lot of money. The 47-8 costs us a little bit more than we assumed it would.
finding: Boeing's shift to cheaper derivatives followed costly overruns on the 787 and 747-8.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: once we get to 10 and stabilize and feel good about where we are and all the operational metrics are in the -- all within the right bandwidth, that's the timeframe where we'd be making a decision
finding: Boeing's criteria for a further 787 rate increase were stability at 10, operating metrics within tolerance, capital needs and continued demand.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the one thing that we don't lack for with the Dash 10 is demand. Customers want this airplane. And so, we're being pushed to get this airplane out. This is more us being disciplined about feeling comfortable with the business case, about the stability of the manufacturing environment
finding: Boeing delayed the 787-10 launch despite customer pull until the production system was stable, putting discipline ahead of speed.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: as you phase out NG, ramping up MAX at the same time, so there's some capital that we've invested there to really do that seamlessly and have the MAX running down, being proved out on a -- on 1 line as the NG line continues to be at peak rate
finding: Boeing invested capital to run the MAX on a separate line while the NG stayed at peak rate, avoiding a production dip at the transition.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: more attractive pricing in that regard. But overall, I think it's coming in within our expectations.
finding: Boeing accepted lower prices on launch-customer MAXs and end-of-line NGs and said overall pricing was in line with plan.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the composite wing, a modified fuselage new engines, okay? And so, the question there is -- the question then becomes and we're sort of in the middle of the assessment now, where to assemble it and where to build the major components.
finding: By April 2013 the 777X configuration was settled (composite wing, modified fuselage, new engines) and Boeing was running a site competition for assembly and major components.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We should have been -- that's not an excuse. We should have been more disciplined about the way we went about that...I think we may be in an era where we can absorb somewhat less risk and still deliver a lot of performance.
finding: Boeing's CEO admitted the 787 was not run with enough discipline and set a lower-risk posture that reuses matured 787 technology in derivatives.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: whether it's the 737, 787 or the 777 new derivatives, are all going to be step function improvements much more than a normal derivative even though the cost and work will be roughly the same as the new derivative.
finding: Boeing believed its post-787 derivatives would deliver near new-aircraft gains at derivative cost, which supported choosing derivatives over clean-sheet designs.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: there are no contractual obligations there. But having said that, there are a few places where we'll work with our customers to ensure -- and there's a variety of ways we can work with them to ensure that the disruption doesn't hurt
finding: Boeing had no contractual obligation to compensate airlines for the grounding but negotiated case-by-case concessions to protect relationships.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: when we peak on our deferred production and basically peak at rate in about 1 year, 1.5 year from that time period is when we -- on a unit basis, we will break the curve versus program accounting.
finding: Boeing expected 787 unit cost to fall below unit revenue about 1-1.5 years after reaching rate 10, roughly two years from April 2013.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: there'll be a splitting of value between us and our customers that works for both of us...We have a lot of confidence that the -- about the executability of this plane and the pricing we think we can get
finding: Boeing priced the 777X by splitting the efficiency value between itself and airlines, expecting strong pricing.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Composite wings are incredibly efficient as compared to aluminum wings...And that, plus the engines, are producing over 90% of the value of this airplane.
finding: Boeing attributed more than 90% of the 777X's value to the new wing and engines, so a re-wing and re-engine captures most of the gain of a new aircraft.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we don't see the 777X introduction cannibalizing significantly the 47-8...And I think the timing is up to the approval of the Board of Directors, but it wouldn't be a shock if this was settled before the end of the year.
finding: Boeing expected to launch the 777X in 2013 (subject to board approval) and judged it would not significantly cannibalise the 747-8.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We're about 5 years ahead of them, and we're going to bracket them. We're going to have 777, 360 to 410 pax. We're going to have 87, 350 down to 250 pax. They're trying to respond with something in the middle because they know we got them.
finding: Boeing's wide-body plan was to bracket the A350 with the 787 family below and the 777X above.
trigger: A350 aimed at the middle of Boeing's wide-body line
response: Bracket A350 with 787-10 and 777X

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA CEO
quote: if we hadn't had the battery situation on the 10X, we would have probably gotten there a lot sooner in terms of the launch.
finding: The 787 battery grounding delayed the 787-10 launch that Boeing was aiming at the A350.
response: 787-10 launch delayed by battery grounding

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA CEO
quote: we were early. We weren't completely defined at the timing that they were making their decision.
finding: Boeing lost British Airways' wide-body decision to the A350-1000 because the 777X was not yet defined in time.
response: 777X still undefined; game 'not over yet'
lag: Boeing late relative to customer decision

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Success in standing up Boeing South Carolina along with other recent steps to expand our production capacity and the geographic diversity of our manufacturing and engineering footprint will help ensure continuity for our business
finding: Boeing built a second 787 site in South Carolina partly to diversify its footprint away from Puget Sound and protect continuity of production.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Our objective in the single aisle market is to maintain our strong historical market share position and healthy margin performance with airplanes that continue to provide customers an efficiency and value advantage over the competition.
finding: Boeing's narrowbody goal was defensive: keep its historical share and healthy margins through the 737 MAX derivative rather than a new airplane.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have no fly lists across the company. So if a certain group is not working with us on Program A, they will feel the pain on every other program, and they'll be on a corporate no fly list for next programs. They'll not be allowed to bid on new programs with Boeing.
finding: Boeing uses company-wide supplier 'no fly lists', barring suppliers that resist its cost demands from bidding on new programs.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: aren't there some places where you're held hostage. And yes, there are. And if we can't move the work or if we can take it in house, and you've seen this come in house a little bit, Charleston is one big in house vertical integration effort.
finding: Boeing admits it is captive to some sole-source suppliers and uses vertical integration, such as bringing Charleston 787 work in-house, to reduce that dependence.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Now some of the choices we made on the MAX were as a result of this program already...And we have sent out a lot of letters to folks that we've told not to bother to bid on these programs. We've never done that before.
finding: Boeing used supplier selection on the 737 MAX, 777X and 787-10 as leverage, excluding uncooperative suppliers from bidding for the first time.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We will not hit the high watermark that we hit on R&D out of BCA. We won't come close to that high watermark, as we see the flow out on the 10, on the MAX and the 777. As a matter of fact, those development efforts fit together pretty well at a lower level.
finding: Boeing sequenced its derivative programs (787-10, MAX, 777X) to keep commercial R&D well below its 787-era peak.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: And we have a plan to return significantly more cash to shareholders, okay? Now as we -- burps can happen along the way, okay, in our business, and so we'll be more conservative than you'll want us to be.
finding: Boeing planned much larger shareholder returns funded by lower R&D and 787 cash, while keeping a conservative buffer for program setbacks.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think if you look at our historical behavior, you will see more of a bias to production increases, a little less worshiping of the backlog, a little more converting it.
finding: Boeing signalled a shift toward raising production rates to work down its backlog rather than protecting a long backlog.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: It's because it's 30% operating cost and 20% fuel...until we came across the 787, it was mostly a 5% to 7% proposition with a new airplane. That's a much longer payback year as a result, easier to defer planes if you're buying. Hard to defer a 30% airplane
finding: Boeing's view is that a step-change aircraft (roughly 20% fuel, 30% operating cost) protects demand from deferrals, whereas 5-7% improvements are easily deferred.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the next possible rate up decision that we haven't talked about out loud is 787, okay? And there is a bias on the 37 to go above 42, but we're being -- there's no more capital involved there, so we're being a little more cautious.
finding: Boeing leaned toward further rate increases on the 787 and the 737 above 42, but was more cautious on the 737 because going higher required new capital.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: What that airplane is, compared with the 300ER, is 40 more -- 35, 40 more -- where's Ray -- passengers. Yes, 45, 40, 50 new pax, heavier airplane, composite wing, flies farther and has a smaller engine.
finding: Boeing defined the 777X as a 777-300ER derivative: a composite wing, new smaller engines, and 35-50 more seats.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We're now taking, what is it, Ray, about 2,000 folks out of both production and 3,000 folks out of production and engineering just because we don't have the disruption anymore
finding: Once 787 disruption eased, Boeing cut several thousand production and engineering jobs at BCA to take out cost.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: there is a scenario where some of the work would be in Everett within the context of other kinds of arrangements we make with the people who work for us...And now that we have internal competition, we're going to get much better deals, much better deals.
finding: Boeing uses competition between its own sites (Charleston vs Everett) to win concessions from its workforce and suppliers.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Our Commercial Airplane business successfully executed 8 production rate increases over the past 17 months, including 5 alone on the 787 program.
finding: Boeing ran an aggressive cadence of rate increases in 2012-13: eight in 17 months.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Our target going forward is a payout of approximately 80% of our free cash flow in the form of dividend and share repurchase...remain committed to the $1.5 billion to $2 billion of repurchase for 2013.
finding: Boeing formalised a policy of returning about 80% of free cash flow, with $1.5-2 billion of buybacks in 2013.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we continue to expect dividends to increase in line with our core earnings growth.
finding: Boeing's dividend policy was to grow the dividend in line with core earnings.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, BDS President & CEO
quote: We think 10 a year is about the right long-term sustained production rate. Much below that begins to create undue pressure in our supply chain.
finding: Boeing treats a minimum production rate (10 a year for the C-17) as a floor below which the supply chain becomes unsustainable.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: Clearly, you have the battery situation on the 787, posed a significant challenge for us. But I would say that our team responded in a way that was really phenomenal. Some people would say we did 3 years of work in 3 months.
finding: Boeing threw large resources at the 787 battery grounding to compress the fix into about three months.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: We executed on all of the rate increases including the 787s. So while the battery issue was going on, we were still increasing rate across the 787 as well.
finding: Boeing kept raising 787 production during the battery grounding rather than pausing the ramp.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: We have carefully managed this backlog for size and breadth and diversity, particularly after 2001, where we ended up taking the production lines down because we were so concentrated in North America.
finding: After the post-2001 production cuts, Boeing deliberately diversified its backlog by region and customer to make rate plans more resilient.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: If we're deferring or pushing things out, it's primarily because we are trying to do that because we've overbooked or something like that, and we're working with the customers to move them out.
finding: Boeing overbooks production slots and actively moves customers out when needed to manage the skyline.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: our strategy, from a product standpoint, is always to provide a full array of passengers. We go from 137 seats all the way up to 460 seats, and our plan is to go with 15% -- 10% to 15% seating increments between them.
finding: Boeing's product-line rule is full seat coverage from 137 to 460 seats in 10-15% increments.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: we talked a lot about the A350 1000 and the A350 900, the 8X really is the one that matches up with the A350 1000.
finding: Boeing sized the 777-8X specifically to counter the A350-1000.
response: 777-8X sized against the A350-1000; 777-9X uncontested above it

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: we're going to be 20% better on fuel efficiency, and we're going to be 15% better on a per seat operating cost basis than the 300ER. The 9X is going to be 40 to 50 seats more than a current 300 ER
finding: Boeing set 777X re-wing/re-engine targets of 20% better fuel efficiency and 15% lower seat cost than the 777-300ER.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: It is 25% better than -- on the operating cost basis per seat than a A330 300, 25% better. It does all the missions of an A330. It does all the missions of an A340 300.
finding: Boeing positioned the 787-10 as a replacement for Airbus's A330-300 and A340-300 fleets, claiming 25% lower seat cost.
response: 787-10 targeted at the A330/A340 replacement market

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: I think if we hadn't had the battery situation on the 10X, we would have probably gotten there a lot sooner in terms of the launch. But it's difficult for somebody to go forward and want to say, "Hey, I want to go buy a 10X when the airplanes on the ground."
finding: The 787 battery grounding delayed the 787-10X launch because customers would not commit while the fleet was grounded.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: 1999, we did 24 airplanes per month. In 2006, we did it -- we did 28. Today, we're at 38 737s...and we're going to ramp to 42 in mid 2014. And we're going to do it all the same footprint as we were back in 1999
finding: Boeing's 737 rate history (24 in 1999, 28 in 2006, 38 in 2013, 42 in 2014) shows steady increases through productivity in a fixed footprint.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: I ran a 777 program in 2003, and I thought for sure we'd be capped at 7 per month max...drove the 777 to 8.3 a month
finding: Boeing pushed 777 output past its assumed ceiling of 7 to 8.3 a month with a moving line.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: we carry more passengers, we fly further than that airplane, and I think our operating cost are at least on par with what we think they could do, against the 300ER.
finding: Boeing countered Airbus's A350-1000 efficiency claims by stressing the 777X's larger capacity and longer range.
trigger: Airbus claims of large A350-1000 efficiency gains over the 777-300ER
response: Argued 777X capacity/range superiority and cost parity

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: If they get more efficient, Howard, and it benefits us in general, I think that's okay. We work with everybody. We've just made sure that we're getting the benefit and they're not getting more.
finding: Boeing accepts that shared suppliers may pass savings to Airbus but insists Boeing gets at least equal benefit.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: We weren't completely defined at the timing that they were making their decision...My only point is, that game is not over yet. That's yet to be defined and yet to be won and our intention is to win it.
finding: Boeing attributed the British Airways A350-1000 order to the 777X not yet being defined, and treated the campaign as still open.
trigger: British Airways ordered the A350-1000 before the 777X was defined
response: Kept campaigning for the 777X at BA/IAG

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: the NEO data argument defined the NEO, okay? We were still thinking about going with a new small airplane up to that point, but it was clear that our customers, they didn't want to wait that long for the new efficiency. So we always had a re engine as part of the option
finding: Boeing switched from a clean-sheet small airplane to re-engining the 737 because customers would not wait for new efficiency after the A320neo launch.
response: Dropped the new small airplane in favour of the 737 MAX re-engine

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: the airplanes that we're rolling off the factory today are almost 3% better than the airplane that rolled off 10 years ago. So we have continually improved this product as we move forward, and now we're going to be 13% better than that airplane.
finding: Boeing extends incumbent products through continuous incremental upgrades, about 3% over 10 years on the NG, before re-engining.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: it is primarily upstream to us. I think everybody would have to make a capital investment to do that, nobody has bought the idea of doing that. So we're still in the study phase
finding: The constraint on raising the 787 above 10 a month was supplier capital investment, which suppliers had not yet committed to.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: That's something that we're looking at, George. We'll get -- let's get the Dash 10 launched, and then we can talk about that.
finding: Boeing sequenced its decisions: launch the 787-10 first, then decide on a higher 787 rate to provide delivery slots.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: it gives us time to go look at this new small airplane, it give us time to go think about where do you start in terms of the right size...but we need to go address the widebodies first
finding: Boeing kept a new small airplane on the table but explicitly put widebody launches first, using the MAX's long life to buy time.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA President & CEO
quote: then we brought that forward with the American deal as an option...Well, would I have loved to have taken all the share? Absolutely. But we got half of it...And the NEO, I think got a little bit of a jump on us, frankly, and we're still playing a little bit of catch up
finding: Boeing brought the 737 MAX re-engine forward during the American Airlines campaign and settled for half the order, admitting the NEO had a head start it was still catching up on.
trigger: American Airlines fleet order contested by the A320neo
response: Accelerated the MAX re-engine offer; accepted a split order

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: They introduced their -- the NEO about 1.5 years before we did. I think if you look at relative orders along a similar point in time, you'd see that we're at or slightly ahead of where they were as we penetrate our customer base. We're both producing at roughly the same rate.
finding: Boeing put its lag behind the NEO at about 1.5 years, and argued MAX orders matched the NEO's at the same point in its life, with both firms at similar rates.
trigger: NEO launched ~1.5 years before MAX; Airbus ahead in re-engine share
response: Expect ~50/50 narrowbody split once penetration equalises; ready to raise rate

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the difference maker overall will be in widebodies, where we've got 5 relatively new offerings to their 3 when they get the A350 variance introduced.
finding: With narrowbodies heading to parity, Boeing looked to widebodies for overall share leadership over Airbus.
response: Win share in widebodies (5 new offerings vs Airbus's 3)

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: In anticipation of planned action by the FAA and other regulators in response to the AAIB's recommendations, we have provided customers instructions for the proper inspection and/or temporary removal of the fixed ELTs.
finding: After the Heathrow 787 fire, Boeing moved ahead of regulators with precautionary inspection or removal instructions to protect confidence in the program.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we launched the 787-10 with 102 orders and commitments, including 50 firm orders from 5 of the most prominent customers in the industry. The -10 further strengthens our unmatched twin-aisle lineup and leverages prior technology investments.
finding: Boeing launched the 787-10 stretch in June 2013 only once it held more than 100 orders and commitments, including 50 firm, as a low-risk derivative built on earlier technology investment.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The business case for the 777X is maturing as planned, as we gain further insights from our customers and develop our design and production system strategies. We continue to target the launch for later this year and entry into service for the 777X around the end of the decade.
finding: Boeing matured the 777X business case with customers before launch, targeting a 2013 launch and entry into service around the end of the decade.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: During the quarter, we completed all of the 787 battery system enhancements on previously delivered airplanes and returned the full fleet to service. 787 production is progressing smoothly at a rate of 7 per month, and we remain on track to increase the rate to 10 per month by yearend.
finding: Boeing completed the 787 battery fix and returned the grounded fleet to service in Q2 2013 without changing its plan for rate 10 by year end.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: The deferred production balance is still expected to peak at slightly over $20 billion, and then decline as the program achieved the planned rate of 10 per month and stabilizes at that level.
finding: In July 2013 Boeing expected 787 deferred production to peak just over $20 billion, a view it raised to about $25 billion three months later.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: if you kind of just go back to unit 8 to around unit 100, we've seen anywhere from 55% to 60% reduction.
finding: Boeing reported a 55-60% cut in 787-8 unit cost from roughly unit 8 to unit 100, reflecting learning-curve progress.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: number 1 priority is to get to 10 a month and do it well...But there is pressure beyond that to raise production rates. And it is led by demand for -9s and -10s...we'll make the call on going beyond 10 once we've settled in at 10 and have a very firm foundation.
finding: Boeing deferred any 787 rate increase beyond 10 until rate 10 was stable, despite demand for the -9 and -10; it repeated this stabilise-first rule on every 2013 call.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We're both producing at roughly the same rate. As I said in my remarks, we're ready to go higher if the market demand is there. So I fully anticipate about a 50-50 when it all sorts out
finding: Boeing's narrowbody objective against Airbus was roughly 50-50 share, backed by matching production rates and readiness to go higher.
response: Target 50-50 narrowbody share; ready to raise 737 rate

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: you either can take too much risk if you're reaching too high or if you go too low, you can get off a learning curve relative to your competition. So the way to think about market share is there's a corridor you want to be in...After that, it's all about operating performance.
finding: Boeing manages market share within a corridor: it avoids chasing too much share, which is risky, or falling too low, which hurts the learning curve, and otherwise optimises margins and cash.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: one of the reasons we've managed Boeing Capital Corporation down significantly over the last number of years is so if we ever do get to that point, we'll have some room to help.
finding: Boeing shrank its captive finance arm to keep balance-sheet room for customer financing if market financing tightens.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: at the normal timing for deciding on production placement would be if we did introduce, launch in the back half of the year would be anywhere from 2 to 6 months after that.
finding: Boeing normally decides where to build a new program 2-6 months after launch.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the reliability of this airplane is about the same as the reliability that we've had introducing new models, including the most successful widebody we've ever introduced, the 777, we're about at the same kind of dispatch for liability levels that we had then
finding: Boeing rebutted Airbus's attack on 787 reliability by comparing it with the 777's reliability at entry into service, rather than conceding a problem.
trigger: Airbus's John Leahy called the 787 'not reliable'
response: Brushed off the remark and compared the 787 with the 777's early record

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: which is not to say that they don't compare and ask for better pricing in every campaign, they do. But in the sense that you asked the question, I think, which is pricing to the place where it destroys or significantly impairs our economics, I don't see that.
finding: Boeing said it would pursue 50-50 narrowbody share against the A320neo without a price war that impairs its economics.
trigger: A320neo share lead and the risk of a price war
response: Rejected price war; relied on MAX value to hold pricing

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We will take a disciplined approach to any 787 production increases by first stabilizing at the 10-per-month rate, not an insignificant achievement in and of itself, as many of you know. This will minimize the required investment and reduce production risk going forward.
finding: Boeing's rule for rate increases is to stabilise at the current rate before stepping up, to limit investment and production risk.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: With nearly 1,500 firm orders and counting, the 737 MAX continues to capture a premium for its compelling economic advantages. Development remains on track, with firm configuration achieved in July. And through our disciplined gated development process, we were recently able to accelerate entry into service to the third quarter of 2017.
finding: Boeing pulled the 737 MAX entry into service forward to Q3 2017, crediting its gated development process, and claimed the MAX sells at a premium.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: De-risking the decade is a theme that a number of you have heard from me before on previous occasions...Spiral technology development that leverages previous investments is a vital element to our strategy to materially reduce risk
finding: After the 787 problems, Boeing adopted 'de-risking the decade': spiral, incremental technology reuse instead of big leaps.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: You mentioned the landing gear, that decision is a big contract, landing gear on the 777X. And the winner has shown a strong willingness to be part of the Partnering for Success program.
finding: Boeing awarded new-program work such as the 777X landing gear to suppliers who signed up to its Partnering for Success cost terms.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I'm convinced the demand is real and there is financing for it...The bigger question is on the readiness of the supply chain to do it.
finding: Boeing saw supply chain readiness, not demand, as the binding constraint on rate increases.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we tend to think about a small, bolt-on capability improvements in services, particularly on the defense side...nothing so big that it will prevent us from doing the right thing with dividends and buybacks.
finding: Boeing limits M&A to small bolt-ons so that it never constrains dividends and buybacks.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Softness in this market contributed to steps we took last week to adjust the 747 production rate to 1.5 per month from 1.75 per month beginning in early 2014 and continuing at that rate through 2015.
finding: Boeing cuts production rates on a weak-demand program (747-8 freighter) rather than building to stock.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: reduce supply chain risks, capture productivity and learning, improve profitability and help minimize the investment required to meet the high customer demand for the 787.
finding: Boeing paces its 787 rate increases to reduce supply chain risk, capture learning and minimise the capital needed.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We continue to anticipate market launch of the 777-8X and 777-9X this year. The latter of which will be the only twin-aisle, twin-engine airplane available in the 400-seat market.
finding: Boeing positioned the 777-9X as the only twin-aisle, twin-engine aircraft in the 400-seat market, a segment where it would have no twin-engine rival.
trigger: Competition in the large twin-aisle market
response: 777-8X/9X launch planned for 2013

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: partnering for success is a long-term effort designed to achieve double-digit improvement in total costs across our supply chain.
finding: Boeing targeted a double-digit cut in total supply chain costs through Partnering for Success.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: the 2 design pillars of the remaining part of the decade, we're avoiding major pileups of engineering with concurrent work being done, and the second pillar was not absorbing as much risk in each development. ... our plans do not have big pileups in R&D along the way.
finding: Boeing staggered its development programs to avoid R&D spikes and limited technology risk in each one.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: we've got, in the widebody space, 5 new airplanes, all of which exceed the competitive performance of what we've seen from our competitor. ... And I think with the Emirates cancellation, that our competitor may even be negative for the year.
finding: Boeing answered the A330neo by pointing to its five new widebodies and to Airbus's weak widebody orders after the Emirates cancellation, not by changing its products.
trigger: A330neo launch and Farnborough 2014 order activity
response: Stood by its lineup of five new widebodies; noted 150 777X orders the week before Farnborough

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: our strategy is to produce the most-capable airplane and then share the value with our customers ... big advantage -10 compared to the A330 NEO in the neighborhood of mid-double-digits ... we feel very comfortable even under scenarios where, as your question implies, they'd have to accept less price for a less-capable airplane.
finding: Boeing modelled A330neo price undercutting and concluded 787-10 returns hold up, so it would not follow Airbus into a price war.
response: Kept value-based pricing; modelled Airbus discounting and judged 787 returns acceptable

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: on the Partnering for Success efforts, 787 is the big -- our #1 priority. So we started to see some of that come together with our suppliers and reach an agreement and we booked it.
finding: Boeing's first increase in 787 program margin came from supplier price agreements, which were its top supplier-negotiation priority.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: losing some campaigns out there where that is important if we didn't have the Ex-Im Bank scrambling, using our balance sheet somewhat more. And we've worked the net-earning assets in BCC down significantly over the last few years, so there's some room there.
finding: Boeing would use its own balance sheet for customer financing if export credit disappeared, having left room by shrinking Boeing Capital.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: starting with a 787, and it's now flowing through the rest of our widebody product line, promises to flow into our narrowbody product line sometime in the next decade, end of next decade, we don't know yet.
finding: In 2014 Boeing placed a new-technology narrowbody somewhere in the 2020s, possibly late in that decade, with timing undecided.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: we tend to have lumpy earnings when we take too much risk in development. ... enough to capture enough of this technology advantage but not more than people are willing to pay for or more than would drive risk that we're not willing to absorb
finding: After the 787, Boeing caps technology content at what customers will pay for and what risk it can absorb.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: we are starting with a 777 fuselage. ... And yes, I think it is fair to say that over time, we would anticipate expanding that capability.
finding: Boeing began automating 777 fuselage build ahead of the 777X and planned to extend automation to other lines for cost and quality.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA CEO
quote: when we did the new airplane that we just announced, it was just playing to that strength of the 8 and putting more seats into it for the low-cost carriers, which is a much lower-risk solution than trying to go all the way up to a 321.
finding: In 2014 Boeing chose not to chase the A321neo, arguing 70% of demand sat in the 737-8/A320 size, and launched a higher-density MAX 8 variant instead.
trigger: A321neo gaining favour with customers and lessors
response: Higher-density MAX 8 variant; no A321-sized response

speaker: Ray Conner, President and CEO, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we're at 42 a month right now. Today, we're going to 47 in 2017. But we see a lot of pressure to go higher than that. And as we look at it today, we're kind of narrowing in on a 52 a month production rate.
finding: A month before announcing it, Boeing signalled that 737 demand was pushing it beyond 47 toward 52/month.

speaker: Ray Conner, President and CEO, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: We've gone through these production rate increases, particularly on the 737, really well. ... when we went to 47, we were preparing for the possibility of something higher, too.
finding: Boeing prepared its supply chain for rates above the announced one, so later increases could follow quickly.

speaker: Ray Conner, President and CEO, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: It's primarily the propulsion change and then some of the things around that. ... GE, because they're going to be producing both Dash 7, CFM Dash 7s and then they'll -- moving into the LEAPs.
finding: Boeing framed the MAX as mainly a propulsion change, with CFM building both current engines and LEAPs through the transition.

speaker: Ray Conner, President and CEO, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: 70% of the demand sits in the 737-8, A320 ... when we did the new airplane that we just announced, it was just playing to that strength of the 8 and putting more seats into it for the low-cost carriers, which is a much lower-risk solution than trying to go all the way up to a 321.
finding: Against A321neo momentum, Boeing chose not to build an A321-sized airplane and instead added seats to the 737-8 (the MAX 200), betting the core market is 737-8/A320 size.
trigger: Customer and lessor enthusiasm for the A321neo
response: Launched the higher-density 737-8 variant (MAX 200) rather than stretching to A321 size

speaker: Ray Conner, President and CEO, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we don't have anything in play right now. We're pretty focused on getting the 737 MAX into the marketplace and those kinds of things. I think we'd be looking more into the next decade for that one.
finding: In 2014 Boeing pushed a new narrowbody into the 2020s and focused on the MAX.

speaker: Ray Conner, President and CEO, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: But we'll sell you a 777. ... Well, we had quite a bit of surge there, I mean, 300 firm orders today.
finding: Boeing steers customers who cannot get early 777X slots to the current 777, using the bridge to protect the franchise.
trigger: 777X delivery slots not available until about 2022
response: Offers current 777s to customers who need aircraft sooner

speaker: Ray Conner, President and CEO, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we always want to be the most efficient in every particular market segment, and that's what we are today, whether it's 787 family against the A330 ... against the A350 with the 787-9 or even then moving into the 777X, 8X against the A350-1000; and of course, the 777-9X is kind of sitting by itself.
finding: Boeing's widebody strategy is to be the most efficient airplane in every size segment, mapping each Boeing model against an Airbus rival.

speaker: Ray Conner, President and CEO, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: since we came into the market with the MAX, we've split pretty much 50-50. ... you can't go chase market share and start to destroy your margins either, and we're playing -- we want to play for our margin
finding: Boeing puts margin ahead of market share and accepts a roughly 50-50 narrowbody split rather than buying share with price.

speaker: Ray Conner, President and CEO, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we brought that in while we were increasing rate 40% ... And then we'll increase the rate again as we stabilize and then bring the Dash 10 in there after that.
finding: Boeing sequences 787 changes: stabilize the -8/-9 mix at rate 10, then raise the rate, then add the -10.

speaker: Ray Conner, President and CEO, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: our ability to continue to be highly productive and continue to offset any pricing pressure that we may see with great productivity ... we're getting a premium for the MAX over the NG because it's a much better machine in that respect, and we continue to get a premium over our competitor
finding: Boeing absorbs pricing pressure through productivity, and says it gets a MAX premium over the NG and over Airbus.
response: Offset price pressure with productivity; claims a price premium

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: Given the 737's robust backlog of more than 4,000 orders, we plan to increase production from the current rate of 42 per month to 47 in 2017 and then increase production again to 52 per month in 2018.
finding: In Oct 2014 Boeing announced the 737 increase to 52/month, justified by a backlog of over 4,000.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: the compelling value proposition of the 787 and its sizable backlog of more than 850 orders are driving production rate increases from today's 10 per month to the previously announced rate of 12 per month in
finding: Boeing reaffirmed the 787 increase to 12 (2016) and added 14 by decade end, plus 767 from 1 to 2 per month.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: delivering the fifth 787-9 as well as the first -9 with GE-powered engines. Both the GE and Rolls-Royce engine types are now certified on the -9.
finding: Boeing offers two engine suppliers (GE and Rolls-Royce) on the 787-9.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: on the 787-10, we'll continue to look for opportunities to accelerate our build plan in early 2015 to mitigate early introduction risk while preparing to increase the overall 787 production rate to 12 per month in 2016.
finding: Boeing brought forward 787-10 builds to reduce early-introduction risk before the rate increase to 12.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We expect to complete the remaining $5.8 billion repurchase authorization over approximately the next 1 to 2 years.
finding: In Oct 2014 Boeing was buying back about $1B a quarter and planned to use the remaining $5.8B authorization within 1-2 years.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we're lowering our outlook for capital spending by $200 million to now be approximately $2.3 billion for the year. This performance allowed us to further return cash to shareholders as we continue to aggressively repurchase shares and pay dividends.
finding: Boeing cut 2014 capex guidance and presented the savings as funding more shareholder returns.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: On the overall deferred, there's really no change. I said it would be approximately $25 billion. We're at $25.2 billion, but again, keep in mind, in the last 2 or 3 quarters, we pulled forward -9 and that wasn't in the original plan.
finding: Boeing let 787 deferred production pass its ~$25B guide with an unplanned -9 inventory pull-forward, calling the risk reduction worth the near-term cost.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we also had a block extension of 200 units that included the investment to go up to 52, but also, most of that, those 200 units, were MAX airplanes.
finding: Boeing folded the cost of going to 52/month and 200 mostly-MAX units into the 737 accounting block in Q3 2014, and repeated a 200-unit MAX extension in Q4.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Latter. I'll save you, the latter. Absolutely. ... over $16 billion of cash generation coming from the core operation. ... The risk profile obviously has changed dramatically
finding: Boeing said its fast buybacks reflected confidence in execution and a lower risk profile, not a view that the stock was mispriced.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: I think we've got maybe 3 or 4 production rate increases going forward that we need to execute. We've already been through almost 17 to date.
finding: Boeing had completed about 17 rate increases and pointed to that record as the basis for its confidence in further increases and buybacks.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: once we get to peak rate, it's really where you should see the real potential, our peak potential, from the company.
finding: Boeing expects cash flow to peak once production reaches peak rates, which ties cash strategy to rate increases.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we've already made the investments or accounted for the investments that go into 52 a month on the 37. ... I wouldn't call it moving investments or moving rate to the right, it's more moving rates up.
finding: Boeing had already committed or accounted for the investment in 737 rate 52, and repeatedly raised its peak-rate targets.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: this generation of new planes that we're introducing anywhere from 16% to 24% more efficient than the planes they're replacing ... we do sensitivities on both interest rates and price of oil, and you've got to go a long way from where we are now before you begin to see even incremental impact.
finding: Boeing stress-tests demand against oil and interest rates and concluded that falling oil would not undermine its rate plans.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: this all gives us more flexibility on either taking it in margin or using it in price in the marketplace when we face those situations. And if we hadn't had this program, we wouldn't be able to respond properly.
finding: Boeing uses supplier cost savings (Partnering for Success) as a war chest either to raise margin or to cut prices when competition requires.
response: Uses supplier-cost savings to fund lower prices or keep as margin

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: history is sort of 75% growth, 20% to 25% replacement. And starting with, really, the 787, it's -- the replacement has been double that ... I think that's going to continue probably for another decade or so
finding: Boeing expects its technology to keep replacement at about half of demand for a decade, which it says decouples it from GDP.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: Our best analysis as we sit here today says that the marketplace will support the rates that we have in place. The macro picture is improving. We'll just have to look at it every quarter
finding: Boeing kept the 747-8 at its current rate despite a shrinking backlog, reviewing it quarterly instead of cutting pre-emptively.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: we started 1.5 years behind the other guys. If you look at the trajectory of where we are at a similar point in time where they were, we're right -- we're in a similar place. So the market share will be what market share will be, but our view hasn't changed on that at all.
finding: Faced with the A320neo's order lead (including IndiGo) and a longer-range A321, Boeing kept its roughly 50-50 narrowbody share expectation and did not change course.
trigger: A320neo sales not tapering (large IndiGo order), 737 at about 40% share, possible longer-range A321
response: Reaffirmed its share view, citing the MAX's 1.5-year later start; no product change
lag: MAX launched about 1.5 years after the neo

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Vice Chairman, President and COO
quote: Many of our suppliers are gaining volume advantage as a result, which turns into pricing advantage for Boeing ... We've reached, I would say, mature agreements with about 40% of our global supply chain. The next 30% are pretty much done
finding: By Dec 2014 Partnering for Success had closed about 40% of supplier agreements, with another 30% near done, worth billions in value.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Vice Chairman, President and COO
quote: the composite wing that we're building for the 777X, right? That is an item that we have decided as a company to strategically pull back inside of Boeing as a make because we believe complex composites manufacturing, for the long run is a capability that we need to have internally.
finding: Boeing insourced the 777X composite wing to keep a core technology in-house, and says make-or-buy calls are strategic.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Vice Chairman, President and COO
quote: generally, higher volumes are going to be beneficial. ... But the opportunity for margin generation improves as we increase volume.
finding: Boeing links higher production rates directly to higher margins, which drives its appetite for rate increases.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Vice Chairman, President and COO
quote: We're rating up to 12 a month on 787 in 2016, 14 a month before the end of the decade, ramping to 47 a month on 737 by 2017, now going to 52 in 2018. That should give you a sense of our confidence that this is not some kind of a short-term cycle.
finding: Boeing committed to rate increases (787 to 12 then 14; 737 to 47 then 52) on the view that demand is a long-term cycle, not a spike.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Vice Chairman, President and COO
quote: We have about 7 years of production backlog today, $430 billion, about 5,500 aircraft in backlog ... More than 3/4 of that backlog is outside of the U.S. and Europe.
finding: Boeing reads a geographically spread, seven-year backlog as protection against a cyclical downturn.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Vice Chairman, President and COO
quote: the bridge that we need to build between now and then is about 600 airplanes in total, including the feathering at the edges. 300 of those are in firm backlog today, so that leaves 300 to go. ... We need to sell them at about 40 to 60 a year
finding: Boeing sized the 777 to 777X bridge at about 600 aircraft to 2020 EIS, half already sold, and managed it with an annual order target.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Vice Chairman, President and COO
quote: we had a customer who needed airplanes sooner than we had slots available. And so as part of our disciplined production system ... we're also not going to do things that would create iterations or anomalies in our production system for single campaigns
finding: In the Delta widebody campaign, where the customer needed slots earlier than Boeing had, Boeing refused to disrupt its production system to win a single campaign.
trigger: Lost the Delta widebody campaign because the customer needed earlier delivery slots
response: Kept production and financial discipline instead of creating extra slots

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Vice Chairman, President and COO
quote: While we're doing that, we're going from 42 to 47 to 52, so the rate-ups are certainly cash generators. ... And the rate-ups will more than compensate for the fact that we'll be introducing a new model.
finding: Boeing timed 737 rate increases to overlap the MAX introduction so higher volume offsets transition costs.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Vice Chairman, President and COO
quote: we can't depend on it changing. So we've assumed that sequestration will play out in full. ... $4 billion of cost structure taken out already, another $2 billion planned.
finding: Boeing planned defense on the worst-case budget and cut costs pre-emptively rather than betting on relief.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: we completed a comprehensive refresh of our Commercial Airplane product line with the highly successful launches of the twin-aisle 787-10 and the 777X on a combined 400 orders and commitments and the launch of the single-
finding: Boeing renewed its widebody line with derivatives, launching the 787-10 and 777X on a combined 400 orders and commitments.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: To meet customer demand for our market-leading Commercial Airplanes, we have 5 more rate increases ahead of us over the remainder of the decade.
finding: After six rate increases, Boeing committed to five more before 2020 and treated them as chances to cut costs with suppliers.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: our December announcement of the new share repurchase authorization totaling $12 billion and a 25% increase in the quarterly dividend.
finding: Boeing escalated shareholder returns with a $12B buyback authorization and a 25% dividend increase in December 2014.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: repurchased 7.8 million shares for $1 billion in the fourth quarter, bringing our total 2014 repurchase activity to 47 million shares or $6 billion. ... increased the dividend 25%, up 88% in the last 2 years. We expect to complete the repurchase authorization over approximately the next 2 to 3 years.
finding: Boeing bought back $6B of stock in 2014 and planned to use the full $12B authorization within 2-3 years, having raised the dividend 88% in two years.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: this transition will leverage new manufacturing processes and technologies being proven on the current 777 to optimize the 777X production system.
finding: Boeing de-risks the 777X production system by proving new manufacturing processes on the current 777 first.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: demand for our new fuel-efficient 737 MAX also remains high with cumulative orders totaling more than 2,660 airplanes from 57 customers. Development of the MAX remains on track for first delivery in 2017.
finding: The 737 MAX re-engine had over 2,660 orders and a 2017 first delivery target.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: On the 787-8, we've seen a decline in unit costs of approximately 30% over the last 175 deliveries. And on 787-9, we've seen declines of 20% since the first delivery.
finding: Boeing tracked 787 learning-curve cost cuts to support its plan for positive program cash flow in 2015.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: the 787 deferred production increased $960 million to $26.1 billion, and we now anticipate 787 deferred production to grow at moderate levels for the next several quarters as productivity improvements on both models offset timing of supplier negotiations
finding: Boeing let 787 deferred production keep growing, accepting higher staffing and delayed supplier deals, while keeping its 2015 cash-positive and post-12/month decline milestones.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we expect research and development spending for 2015 to be approximately $3.5 billion ... Capital spending guidance for 2015 is approximately $2.8 billion, driven by the new 777X facilities and equipment, Charleston expansion to support the 787 rate increase
finding: Boeing's 2015 plan funded 777X/787-10 development and capacity at about $3.5B R&D and $2.8B capex alongside the buybacks.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: one of the strategies we had in place was to derisk the decade, and we've certainly done that. The risk profile going forward is very different than it was in the past. ... With regards to deployment ... It's in place to utilize it, and we plan to do that.
finding: Boeing linked its lower program risk to a commitment to spend the full buyback authorization.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: there is no competition for the airplane, so I feel very good about the long- ... I think, on the 787, I think what you're going to see is a mix from Dash 8s to Dash 9s to Dash 10s.
finding: Boeing sees no competitor for the 777 and expects 787 buyers to shift to larger models, which it says means selling more capability at a higher price.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: we're a little bit hampered by the number of orders we have. I mean, it's -- we're out to 20, 21-ish.
finding: The 787 was sold out to about 2020-21, which held back new orders; Boeing expected orders to pick up again in 2015-16.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: On the supply chain side, we've talked about the timing of some of our discussions and negotiations. And some of those have moved out to the right, and I think I've mentioned before that we've seen a benefit in doing that.
finding: Boeing deliberately delayed some 787 supplier price negotiations until suppliers had moved further down their learning curves.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: This year will be increased because of preparing for the entry into service of those aircraft, and we'll probably have a similar year next year, and then it will start to decline from there.
finding: Boeing expected capex to peak in 2015-16 for the 777X, 787-10 and rate increases, then fall.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: very similar to what you've seen on the 787, you'll have some additional flow time associated with those early introductory units, and that will get feathered in to the current 777s
finding: Boeing planned to phase the 777X into the 777 line gradually, reusing the 787-9 introduction approach, to protect deliveries.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: there is not much competition for this capability. So versus any alternative, both the old and the new make sense ... And so we're in a fortunate position here, and it's one that we will shamelessly take advantage of.
finding: Boeing plans to exploit the lack of an Airbus rival at the 777's size to sell both 777 and 777X, bundled together.
trigger: Airbus has no product competing at the 777/777X capacity point
response: Sold mixed 777/777X orders (ANA, Qatar) and pressed its pricing advantage

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: there is no question that seat supply did impact some deliveries and some fall in our production system. ... I think the supply base is adjusting to these higher volumes in both 787 and anticipated higher volumes in other programs
finding: Supplier bottlenecks (seats) delayed some 787 deliveries during the ramp; Boeing treated it as within plan and expected suppliers to catch up.

quote: In November 2013, we launched the 777X, which features a new composite wing, new engines and folding wing-tips all designed to deliver greater efficiency and significant fuel savings.
finding: Boeing chose to upgrade its large widebody (777X: new wing plus new engines) rather than do nothing, framing the move around fuel efficiency.

quote: We face aggressive international competitors who are intent on increasing their market share, such as Airbus, Embraer and Bombardier, and other entrants from Russia, China and Japan. We are focused on improving our processes and continuing cost reduction efforts.
finding: Boeing's stated competitive answer to Airbus and new entrants in 2014 was process improvement and cost reduction rather than price or new products.

quote: We must meet planned production rate and productivity improvement targets in order to satisfy customer demand and maintain our profitability. We continue to increase production rates for the 737 and 787 programs, while at the same time engaging in significant ongoing development of the 787-10, 737 MAX and 777X aircraft.
finding: In 2014 Boeing was simultaneously raising 737 and 787 rates and developing three derivatives, accepting concurrent ramp and development risk.

quote: during the second quarter of 2014, we recorded a reach-forward loss of $425 million on the USAF KC-46A Tanker contract, primarily due to initial engineering and design issues.
finding: Boeing took a reach-forward loss on the fixed-price 767-derived KC-46A development contract, showing willingness to bid fixed-price development work and absorb overruns.

quote: For example, we are monitoring political unrest involving Russia and Ukraine, where we and some of our suppliers source titanium products and/or have operations.

quote: We focus on producing the products and providing the services that the market demands and we price our products and services to provide a fair return for our shareholders while continuing to find new ways to improve efficiency and quality.
finding: Boeing's stated strategy ties pricing to shareholder return and market demand rather than market-share maximisation.

quote: This market environment has resulted in intense pressures on pricing and other competitive factors, and we expect these pressures to continue or intensify in the coming years.

quote: Major productivity gains are essential to ensure a favorable market position at acceptable profit margins.
finding: Boeing ties its market position to productivity gains, implying it will not buy share at unacceptable margins.

quote: These efforts enhance our ability to pursue pricing strategies that enable us to price competitively.
finding: Boeing uses cost reduction and services to fund competitive pricing.

finding: Boeing pursued stepwise 737 rate increases (38 to 42 to 47 to 52) announced years ahead, overlapping the MAX transition.

quote: 747 Program Lower-than-expected demand for large commercial passenger and freighter aircraft has resulted in ongoing pricing pressures and fewer orders than anticipated. We are currently producing at a rate of 1.5 per month with plans to reduce the rate to 1.3 per month in September 2015.

quote: In October 2014 we increased our combined tanker and commercial production rate from 1 to 1.5 per month and plan to increase to 2 per month in 2016.
finding: Boeing used the 767 line's tanker demand to raise rates on an old widebody.

quote: We are producing at a rate of 10 per month and the first delivery at this rate occurred in March 2014. We remain focused on stabilizing 787 production rates at 10 per month while improving aircraft reliability and satisfying customer mission and performance requirements.
finding: Boeing reached 787 rate 10 in 2014 and prioritized stabilization before further increases.

quote: The accounting quantity of 1,300 units remains unchanged and reflects the incorporation of revenue and cost estimates associated with the 787-10 and planned production rate increases to 12 and 14 per month in future years.
finding: Boeing's 787 program economics assumed rate increases to 12 and then 14 per month.

quote: The combination of production challenges, change incorporation, schedule delays and customer and supplier impacts has created significant pressure on program profitability.
finding: Boeing acknowledged the 787 program's profitability was under significant pressure in 2014.

quote: the 787 program: $33,163 and $27,576 of work in process (including deferred production costs of $26,149 and $21,620)
finding: 787 deferred production costs grew from $21.6bn to $26.1bn in 2014, showing Boeing financed the 787 learning curve on its balance sheet.

quote: At December 31, 2014, $20,982 of 787 deferred production costs, unamortized tooling and other non-recurring costs are expected to be recovered from units included in the program accounting quantity that have firm orders and $8,968 is expected to be recovered from units included in the program accounting quantity that represent expected future orders.
finding: About $9bn of 787 balances depended on orders not yet won, a bet on future sales.

quote: Our investment in gross inventories increased by $7.6 billion in 2014, $5.7 billion in 2013 and $6.2 billion in 2012, driven by continued investment in commercial airplane program inventory, primarily 787 inventory.
finding: Boeing put $5-8bn a year into inventory, mainly for the 787, in 2012-2014.

finding: Boeing more than doubled buybacks in 2014 ($6.0bn, from $2.8bn) and authorised a new $12bn plan.
