quote: We're already at an all-time high, 10 a month. A widebody airplane has never been produced 10 a month before, and so we have plans to go to 12 and possibly higher.
finding: Boeing kept pushing 787 rate beyond an industry-record 10/month, planning 12 and possibly more.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: derivative programs flowing technology as opposed to another major 787 kind of development, and that's done by design. ... we're very cognizant of another 787. We don't want that in terms of the risk profile. We love the airplane. And customers like it. But the financial characteristics were not fun.
finding: After the 787, Boeing deliberately chose derivatives (737 MAX, 777X) over clean-sheet programs to avoid another 787-style financial risk.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: we were trading volume for margin in deals that we cut with them and giving them more visibility to a future and at the same time giving -- paying us for what -- the risk we're taking. So that's a program, Partnering for Success
finding: Boeing uses its volume as leverage to extract supplier price concessions (Partnering for Success), trading volume visibility for margin.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: you remember the 787 program was approved at $40 oil. People forget that.
finding: Boeing argues its fuel-efficient products pay back at any plausible oil price, so it does not adjust plans for oil price swings.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: we can get pricing commensurate with value because there is not an immediately ready competitive offering. ... 63 orders last year. As I think you know, we're trying to get between 40 and 60 a year to get the bridge done.
finding: Boeing prices the 777 on value where Airbus has no ready competitor and targets 40-60 bridge orders a year to hold rate into the 777X transition.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: manning, in particular, coming down more slowly than we'd anticipated, as we ramped this program up so fast that we had to keep manning on a little bit longer than we'd anticipated
finding: The fast 787 ramp left staffing higher for longer than planned, pushing up deferred production cost, which Boeing treated as quarterly timing rather than a structural problem.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: we have some prudence in our guidance only because -- not because we're trying to be sandbaggers but because we just live in a world where things move around a little bit.
finding: Boeing builds prudence into its cash flow guidance because progress payments and deliveries are lumpy.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: our guidance on 80% return to shareholders ... I see that as very doable and consistent with R&D levels to get the new airplanes out, consistent with the CapEx required to facilitize 777 and Charleston in support of the 87.
finding: Boeing judged returning about 80% of free cash flow to shareholders compatible with funding 777X/787 R&D and capex.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: I don't want to buy things as a -- to replace my inability to grow organically. And so organic growth is going to be our first, second and third priorities.
finding: Boeing put organic growth ahead of M&A and limited acquisitions to small bolt-ons.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: the A330neo, the example you used, is a 1970s design with new engines. And our analysis shows many tens of millions of dollars of value of difference between that airplane and a model of a 787 that they may sell against it.
finding: Boeing answered the A330neo and weak-euro price threat by stressing the 787's value advantage rather than signalling price cuts.
trigger: Airbus A330neo priced well below the 787, helped by a weaker euro
response: Relied on the 787's value proposition and said it was not deeply concerned

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: We don't think it's needed short or medium term based on discussions with our customers. ... 80% of that mission now is handled by the bigger, longer-range narrow-bodies.
finding: Boeing held off on a 757 replacement, arguing larger 737s already cover most of the mission.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: no business case would close today as we look at it, which doesn't mean pretty far into the future it might not.
finding: Boeing will not launch a middle-of-market airplane until the business case closes, and said in 2015 that it did not.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman and CEO
quote: our productivity number, each year, is slightly bigger than our R&D number. And I want to make sure it stays that way.
finding: Boeing aims to self-fund R&D from productivity gains, keeping annual productivity savings above R&D spend.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: when we make a rate break, we really try to look at that -- at maintaining that rate at a 2 to 3-year period ... very detailed analysis by airline, how many are firm? How many are options? What do we think the probability of those options are? We look at the operating performance of that airline.
finding: Boeing's rate-break rule is to raise rates only when it expects to hold the new rate for 2-3 years, based on airline-by-airline analysis of firm orders, option probabilities and airline health.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: there's really no correlation between oil and demand for airplanes. I think some people forget that when we launched the 787, we were $40 a barrel and you saw the success of that launch.
finding: Boeing does not treat low oil prices as a reason to delay launches or cut rates; it notes it launched the 787 at $40 oil.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: We've got very aggressive productivity targets that are deployed, not only inside, but obviously, outside within the supply chain. So we're not asking the supply chain to do anything different that we're doing ourselves.
finding: Boeing imposes the same aggressive productivity targets on suppliers as on itself.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: So we pretty much -- 3% to 4% productivity is what we target everybody, whether you're a function or whether you're a program on an annual basis, and that has gone unchanged. ... Some of that's going to go back in price as it has, but ultimately, we want to make sure we're driving value for all the stakeholders
finding: Boeing targets 3-4% annual productivity everywhere and expects part of it to be passed on to customers as lower prices in competitive campaigns.
response: Pass part of the 3-4% annual productivity gain into price

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: they're also getting ahead of the 12 a month and getting ahead of the 52 a month, and we're doing that together, we're doing it now. And looking at how do we optimize current infrastructure and the tools and the capital to really try to minimize investment, overall
finding: Boeing prepares suppliers early for rate increases (787 at 12, 737 at 52) while pressing them to reuse existing capacity and minimise new investment.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We've announced 52. They count a little bit differently. 60 is not -- is roughly the same as 52, 54.
finding: Boeing claimed its announced 737 rate of 52 was roughly equal to Airbus's 60, keeping rate parity.
response: Hold 52/month plan; claim equivalence

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: We continue to anticipate completing the remaining $9.5 billion repurchase authorization over the next 2 to 3 years. Returning cash to shareholders, along with continued investment to support future growth, remains top priority for us.
finding: The buyback-as-top-priority language was repeated every quarter from April 2015 to April 2016, showing a steady commitment.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: I'd say, roughly, Doug, it's about 1/3, 1/3, 1/3 ... some of the supplier negotiations that we talked about, moving some of those to the right as we get more mature on the learning curve within those suppliers; and then some of the productivity initiatives
finding: Boeing attributed 787 deferred growth roughly equally to reliability and readiness staffing, early 787-9 costs and delayed supplier price step-downs, and was willing to spend up front for long-term cost.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: proving it out, making it rate capable and then a smooth implementation as you're continuing to build 8.3 a month. ... And if we see any issues along the way, we have a plan B or, I'll say, an offramp to continue with the current production system.
finding: Boeing introduces new manufacturing technology off-line first, with a fallback to the existing system, to avoid disrupting a running line.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: Well, I mean some of that, Sam, is just the fact that we're going up in rate, so there's some of that. The disruption, we've talked about, again, the team has done a fantastic job managing through that disruption, reaching back into the supply chain and helping wherever we can help out.
finding: Faced with seat and GE engine delivery shortfalls, Boeing sent its own staff into suppliers and carried extra inventory ($2B gross increase) rather than cut deliveries.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: so I think the team made the right call on when to curtail the program. You always want to curtail these things where you end up having a little more demand than you've got airplanes at the end, so hold pricing and production.
finding: Boeing's rule for ending a program (C-17) is to stop while demand still slightly exceeds remaining airplanes, protecting pricing on the last units.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: We're in a technology cycle now. We're not tied to GDP growth. We are tied to a very favorable replacement economics. And so half our growth is replacement.
finding: Boeing believed new-technology replacement demand decoupled its orders from GDP, which supported its rate increases.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: one group has a union, one doesn't. We prefer to have a direct relationship with our employees, but when they choose to have a union, we want to work with them. So it's not either/ or. Our task is to work with both environments and to grow them to their potential.
finding: Boeing prefers non-union sites (South Carolina) but runs a dual-site model, giving it labor leverage when placing work.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: I didn't see Airbus' comments today, but it's the -- I think our supply chain has anticipated robust growths, probably from both of us. ... We've announced 52. They count a little bit differently. 60 is not -- is roughly the same as 52, 54.
finding: When Airbus said it was studying A320 rates beyond 60 a month, Boeing called its own 52/month roughly equivalent and said the supply chain was ready; it did not match immediately but announced 57 about nine months later.
trigger: Airbus announced it was studying A320 production above 60 per month (Apr 22, 2015)
response: Called Airbus 60 roughly equal to Boeing 52-54; kept 52 plan; announced 57/month in Jan 2016

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: I think that all of the problems are not resolved. We do have a high confidence in the plan to resolve them. We have -- and it's because our people are deeply involved with them in the resolution.
finding: Boeing put its own people into a struggling supplier (Zodiac seats) to protect delivery plans rather than switch suppliers immediately.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: "Hey, isn't it about time we started pricing down on the 777?" I mean, we're entering -- we're transitioning to a new thing and Ray Connor goes, "Are you kidding me?" I mean, this is a totally unique airplane yet today. It's outsold the A350-1000 5:1
finding: Boeing refused to cut 777 prices during the 777X transition, arguing the 777-300ER was outselling the A350-1000 five to one.
response: Hold 777 pricing

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: Second theme, commercial airplane pricing, and whether we're seeing deterioration, the answer is no. Every sale is highly competitive for sure, but pricing is holding up well due to the value of our airplanes and what they bring to the marketplace even in model transition environments, 737 to MAX, 777 and 777X.
finding: At the 2015 Investor Day Boeing denied that pricing was deteriorating against Airbus, while admitting every sale was highly competitive, including during model transitions.
trigger: Investor concern about pricing deterioration in competitive campaigns and model transitions
response: Held pricing on product value; no price deterioration accepted

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: in 2011, we selected the 737 MAX derivative as our next entry in the single-aisle market rather than pursue a higher risk, higher cost clean sheet design with an entry in the service date that will have placed years of near-term market share strength at risk
finding: Boeing's 2011 choice to re-engine the 737 (MAX) instead of launching a clean-sheet narrowbody was driven by lower risk and cost and by the risk that a later entry-into-service date would cost years of market share.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: the record launch of the 777X, both of which smartly adapt the hard-fought technology gains of the original 787 to further extend our lead in this high-value segment of the market
finding: Boeing's widebody strategy is to reuse 787 technology in derivatives (787-10, 777X) to extend its twin-aisle lead rather than launch new clean sheets.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: Through these contracts, as well as changes announced for 6,000 nonunion employees, we also reduced the threat to our balance sheet from defined benefit pensions. Beginning next year, around 90% of our workforce will be covered by defined contribution plans
finding: Boeing systematically de-risked its balance sheet by moving about 90% of its workforce to defined-contribution pensions through long-term labor deals.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: our efforts to derisk the decade also go hand-in-hand with our work to break the upward cost spiral of development programs. ... it includes working aggressively within and across individual product families ... to increase design, parts, consistent commonality, eliminate duplication of effort and share resources
finding: Boeing's development policy seeks to break rising development costs through commonality and shared resources across programs, favouring derivatives.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: Our team successfully raised production rates 15x over the past 4 years by following disciplined processes that enable us to assess and ensure readiness in our factories and throughout our supply chain. In 2014, we stabilized our 787 production system at our planned 10 per month rate, the highest ever for a twin-aisle airplane
finding: Boeing made 15 rate increases in four years (2011-2015), gated by factory and supply-chain readiness, and ran the 787 at a record 10/month.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg
quote: What is the market telling us in terms of unit cost requirements? What are we seeing in terms of pricing pressures in the marketplace? What do we need to do to be competitive? That outside-in view, market-based view is driving a different level of aggressive step function target.
finding: Boeing sets its cost targets from market pricing pressure (outside-in), turning competitive price pressure into internal step-change cost targets.
trigger: Market pricing pressures and competitor unit costs
response: Market-based, step-function cost reduction targets

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg
quote: We have now reached agreement, long-term agreements, with 40% to 50% of our supply base. ... As I've said, we've now expanded this to more than 500 suppliers. ... Now more than 1,900 ideas have been implemented and the pipeline is still full at a little over 1,000 projects.
finding: Through Partnering for Success Boeing secured long-term cost agreements with 40-50% of its supply base, a structural way of squeezing supplier cost.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg
quote: In the lower right quadrant, this idea of competitiveness and bringing in new supply base where we need it, 737 MAX displays, 777 landing gear, a couple of good examples there.
finding: Boeing re-sources components to new suppliers (MAX displays, 777 landing gear) to create supplier competition and leverage.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg
quote: We need to make sure that we not only break the ever-increasing cost of development programs, but also provide stability, repeatability, predictability in our R&D profile, and that allows us to do a good job of planning our long-term R&D streams
finding: Boeing commits to a stable, predictable R&D profile and to staggering development programs so engineers can move from program to program.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: Our commercial airplane production plans include 5 more rate increases over the remainder of the decade, with the 787 going to 12 per month in 2016, and then 14 per month by the end of the decade. The 737, moving to 47 per month in 2017, and then 52 per month in 2018
finding: As of May 2015 Boeing's rate plan had the 787 at 12 then 14 and the 737 at 47 then 52 a month (plus the 767 at 2); 737 57/month was added in January 2016.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: we also revised our long-term management compensation structure to more closely align to shareholder returns, which, once again, reinforces the culture of financial discipline
finding: Boeing tied long-term executive pay more closely to shareholder returns, which reinforces its bias toward buybacks and near-term financial discipline.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: between 2012 and 2015, we've made investments of approximately $22 billion in research and development capital expenditures. This spending supports the next generation of products, allows for those higher production rates
finding: Boeing spent about $22B on R&D and capex over 2012-2015 for the MAX, 787 and 777X and for rate capacity.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: Since we restarted that repurchase program in 2013, we've spent more than $11 billion buying back approximately 90 million shares and remain committed to continuing to reduce our share count going forward. In addition, we paid more than $4 billion in dividends to our shareholders, an increase of per share basis over 90%.
finding: Between 2013 and early 2015 Boeing returned over $15B ($11B buybacks, $4B dividends), about two-thirds of what it invested in R&D and capex over a similar period.

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: We are delivering the most efficient, comprehensive set of world-class products and services to our customers while continuing to pursue single- and twin-aisle market share while expanding our service business.
finding: BCA's stated strategy was to pursue market share in both single- and twin-aisle segments and to grow services.

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: we announced that we were going to retire the temporary surge line up in Everett at the end of the year. ... Seats are recovering, the engines are recovering, those are 2 things that were driving a lot of disruption into our production system.
finding: Seats and engines were the main supplier bottlenecks disrupting 787 production in 2014-15, and Boeing consolidated to single lines once the system stabilised.

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: We launched that last year with Ryanair. ... 30% of those new airplanes are going to be coming out of the low-cost market. ... Now that our product strategy is largely set for the foreseeable future, we're very focused on execution and meeting our existing commitments.
finding: In May 2015 Boeing considered its product strategy set (MAX variants including the MAX 200 for low-cost carriers, 787-10, 777X) and put execution ahead of new launches.

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: yes, I know that the other guy has talked about going to 60 month, we can go to 60 a month. We could do that. We got to just make sure that we've got the kind of demand necessary to take it up there. ... We do have the capability to go higher if we need to.
finding: Responding to Airbus talk of 60 a month, Boeing claimed it could also build 60 737s a month but would do so only if demand justified it; it chose 57 eight months later.
trigger: Airbus signalling a narrowbody rate of 60 per month
response: Claimed capability for 60/month but tied any increase to demand; announced 57/month in Jan 2016

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: it was in 75% to 80% difference in part numbers. ... What was the number when we first started? About 70%. ... So through the development organization with the intense focus on commonality, reuse all those kinds of things. Producibility and still maintaining an airplane that could do what we sold, we went from 70% to 95%.
finding: After the 787-9 changed 75-80% of part numbers, Boeing's development organization pushed 787-10 commonality from 70% to 95% to cut production disruption.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: if you went back and looked at the transition from the classic to the NG, you would see margin degradation through just end-of-line sales and early introduction. And you've seen on the MAX or the NG to the MAX that not taking place. That was a very clear objective, partnering for success, playing into that
finding: Boeing set out to avoid the margin collapse of the Classic-to-NG transition in the NG-to-MAX changeover, using supplier cost-downs and productivity.

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: You also can't separate the fact that in both the 73 MAX and the 777X, we're bringing in a new engine program on track there, too. ... I mean, when you look at all the engine development that's going on concurrently, I mean, those -- it's a combined schedule between ourselves and the engine companies too.
finding: Boeing's derivative schedules (about 72 months for MAX and 777X) are set jointly with the engine makers' new-engine programs, which lengthens development.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg
quote: traditionally, we've had cases where we're doing upfront engineering where we might launch a lot of concurrent activity ... And so now, we're thinking about how do you, in a lean way, sequence engineering work, do clean handoffs.
finding: Boeing moved from concurrent engineering to sequenced development work to cut rework and hold R&D plans.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: looking at the size of the company today kind of high, mid -- high single-digit balance is what I think is probably prudent ... Yes, I don't think there's a need to do that. If we didn't have the backlog and the growth profile associated with that, then we may be in a different place.
finding: Boeing targeted a cash buffer in the high single-digit billions and declined to add leverage for buybacks, instead funding returns from backlog-driven cash flow.

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: It's the fact that you don't take these massive technology jumps in one single fell swoop to create -- you take a jump that you know you can deliver, that you don't have to have multiple innovation processes going on at one particular point in time.
finding: Boeing's 'no moonshots' rule does not rule out new airplanes but limits each program to technology jumps it knows it can deliver.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg
quote: also being mindful about what verticals are we going to rebuild, in some cases, internally, the fact that we're building a 777X composite wing in-house. That is another way to de-risk our supply chain.
finding: Boeing selectively insources critical items (the 777X composite wing) to reduce supply-chain risk and dependence.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: And so if there is a plateau, there is going to be a whack. And we are very, very careful about rate increases, which gives us the ability to adjust along the way if conditions change.
finding: Boeing's leadership knew a demand plateau would hurt after rate increases, and says it raises rates cautiously so it can adjust if conditions change.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: I think at that point, end of the decade, let's just pick that, then I think the growth in production will return to the growth of the market which is characterized by 2 things. It's growth in seat mile consumption by consumers on airliners, that's about 5%; and then replacement
finding: Boeing expected production growth after about 2020 to slow to market growth (about 5% traffic plus replacement) after a catch-up super-cycle with about 50% production growth.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: Well, like I said, the commitment to the buyback is unchanged. ... So we'll certainly look for opportunities to capture more value in buying back shares. ... typically, our progress payments at the commercial side, about 40% of that comes in flow and about 18 to 24 months out from delivery. And then about 60% on delivery.
finding: Boeing kept buying back stock and bought more when the price dipped; about 40% of commercial cash arrives 18-24 months before delivery, so rate increases boost cash early.

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: we're -- obviously the Dash 9 brings a little more value because it's more seats, more range than the Dash 8. So we're going to price the value into the product. Similar story on the Dash 10
finding: Boeing prices derivatives on value to the customer (seats, range, cost per seat) while pushing their cost down to that of the base model.

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: But we took the rates to 1.3, we feel -- the airplane program remains profitable even at a 1 per month, so I feel okay about 747 right now.
finding: In May 2015 Boeing judged the 747 still profitable at 1 a month; the break-even floor it cites guides its step-down rather than a cancellation.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: if the 5 and 40 are the numbers, if you had 2 or 3 years of 4, 4.5, which you wouldn't need a global recession to have... ... Shouldn't impact our production rates.
finding: Boeing said two or three years of traffic growth at 4-4.5% instead of about 5% would not change its production rates.

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: The replacement demand was still pretty high. I mean, and it fluctuates between 40 and 50. ... But also China, they're going to start going into a replacement cycle as well, and that's a pretty big fleet.
finding: Boeing sees replacement demand at 40-50% of deliveries, which it treats as a floor under its rate plans.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: in the narrowbody space is where it will most likely happen first, and who knows precisely when. But I would imagine somewhere out there, there will be a requirement for a new smaller airplane that, in all likelihood ... will be a thicker route kind of upgrade, just like we've done with the MAX.
finding: In 2015 Boeing expected its next all-new airplane to be a narrowbody (757-class, for thickening routes) some time in the 2020s, after stabilising its development system, not before.

speaker: Ray Conner, Vice Chairman
quote: we're doing that in exactly the same footprint as we did when we were doing 21. ... you create a lot of flexibility to respond to the market in a way without throwing your cost line off and being able to maintain your margins. Your revenue line may change a bit, but the margin line won't.
finding: Boeing argues its lean, footprint-constant production lets it move rates up or down without hurting margins, which lowers the perceived risk of rate increases.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: During the quarter, we purchased $2 billion of Boeing stock and paid $625 million in dividends. Year-to-date, we have returned nearly $6 billion to our shareholders, which remains the top priority for us under our balanced cash deployment strategy.
finding: In his first call as CEO, Muilenburg called shareholder returns 'the top priority' after returning nearly $6B in the first half of 2015.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: our very strong second quarter operating performance was impacted by a $536 million after-tax charge to complete development and hold to the delivery schedule on our KC-46 Tanker program for the U.S. Air Force. That program, as you know, is being developed on a fixed-price contract.
finding: Boeing accepts fixed-price development risk and pays to hold schedule, here a $536M after-tax KC-46 charge.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: our #1 priority remains that disciplined investment in innovation for the future; secondly, returning cash to shareholders, as you've seen through both the stock repurchase and through dividends; and then thirdly, where it makes sense, bolt-on acquisitions.
finding: Boeing ranked cash uses as innovation investment, then shareholder returns, then bolt-on acquisitions, although the same call's opening remarks called shareholder returns 'the top priority'.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: So the theme you'll be hearing from me and the rest of the team is one of strategic consistency. We like the path we're on, the direction we're headed. ... I think Tanker is a good reminder to us to continue to hone that effort.
finding: The new CEO promised strategic consistency and named development-program execution, highlighted by the KC-46, as the main risk.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: we've already planned to up -- to go up from 1.5 a month to 2 a month next year. ... that 50 plus 50 is the largest single order in the history of the 767 program. ... And any changes that we might consider beyond 2 a month, again, will go through that normal, very financially disciplined assessment.
finding: Boeing raises rates on mature lines only step by step after a disciplined review, even after a record order (FedEx 50+50 767Fs); the 767 went to 2.5/month three months later.
trigger: FedEx order for 50 767 freighters plus 50 options
response: Keep planned 1.5 to 2/month; later raised to 2.5/month (Oct 2015)

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: And that's part of how we're continuing to pay for the implementation, if you will, is by driving productivity on the base programs to fuel our future innovation and allows automation into the production lines.
finding: Boeing funds new-program investment from productivity gains on existing programs.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: We have about 15% of our customers that use Ex-Im financing as backstop financing, but in the current financing market, that doesn't create risk for us. This is about long-term global competitiveness. And that's why we're so forceful on this topic that it's important Ex-Im be reauthorized.
finding: Boeing lobbied hard for export-credit support as a long-term competitive tool against foreign rivals, though only about 15% of customers used Ex-Im backstop financing.
trigger: Lapse of US Ex-Im Bank authorization
response: Forceful lobbying for reauthorization

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: Given the strong market demand, we continued to see upward pressure on narrowbody production rates, beyond the announced 52 per month in 2018. However, we remained steadfast in our financial discipline as we assess the market demand for further production rate changes.
finding: In October 2015 Boeing acknowledged demand pressure above 52/month but held off deciding, citing financial discipline; it announced 57/month three months later (January 2016).
response: Deferred decision; announced 57/month in Jan 2016

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: Frankly, with about 5,700 aircraft in backlog, annual book-to-bill ratios are not that important to us ... that included an announcement around 300 aircraft, 250 narrowbodies and 50 widebodies.
finding: Boeing downplays annual book-to-bill because of its large backlog, and used a head-of-state visit (President Xi) to secure a 300-aircraft China commitment.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: Well, we think that the stock is still undervalued. ... So we see -- obviously see a lot of value still left in that stock. That's why we bought back $20 billion in the last 3 years and remained committed to that.
finding: Boeing kept buying back stock near all-time highs, spending about $20B in three years because it judged the shares undervalued.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: We remain very confident that our supply chain can meet our ramp up to 52 a month on the MAX. If we were to go beyond that, factoring in supply chain capability is a key component of that decision.
finding: Supplier capacity is an explicit gating factor in Boeing's decisions to raise rates beyond committed levels.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: top priority remains organic investment. And this is delivering on our development programs like the 777X, the MAX and the 787-10. ... Second priority, as we said, is returning strong value to our shareholders, both in the form of dividends and share repurchase.
finding: Boeing's stated cash-deployment order was organic program investment first, shareholder returns second and M&A third.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: we announced taking the rate down from 1.3 to 1 a month early in '16. So we continue to monitor that marketplace. It is challenging. ... And we'll likely take another look at the rate here early next year and see where we are on orders and backlog
finding: Boeing cuts 747 rate step by step (1.3 to 1/month, then to 6 a year) as orders fail to appear, reviewing it each year instead of cancelling.
response: Cut 747 rate from 1.3 to 1 per month for early 2016, with further review
lag: reviewed again about 3 months later (cut to 6/year in Jan 2016)

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: some uncertainty around Ex-Im Bank reauthorization, those are factors that could cause some customers to delay decisions around widebodies, so we're being mindful of that. We want to make sure we maintain a highly profitable line through the transition. ... we don't see any scenarios where we've come down below a 7 a month production rate during the transition.
finding: Facing widebody order hesitancy, Boeing planned a 777 rate cut but set 7/month as the floor, prioritising line profitability through the 777X transition.
trigger: Widebody order hesitancy from the cargo slump and Ex-Im Bank lapse
response: Plan 777 rate cut with a 7/month floor; pull automation forward

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: We continue to do studies on possibilities of ramping up beyond that. ... we're going to maintain very strict financial discipline as we do those studies ... We are still in a slightly overbooked position in terms of our order profile for the 737, and all of that just creates general upward pressure to production rates.
finding: Boeing studies rate increases while keeping the 737 slightly overbooked, and uses that overbooking as a signal for further increases.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: The depth of that bridge is most significant in the 2018, 2019 time frame. So we're very focused on filling that out. And we need about 40 to 60 aircraft per year over that 5 years to fill that bridge.
finding: Boeing sized the 777 bridge as about five years, needing 40-60 orders a year, with 2018-19 the deepest gap.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: we see our current product line as being the right answer for that segment. ... if we need to respond with a new airplane in that marketplace, that would be something that would be more towards the middle of the next decade. It's not something that would dramatically affect our R&D profiles over the next 4 to 5 years.
finding: In October 2015 Boeing's default was to do nothing in the middle of the market (MAX-9 and 787 cover it), with any new airplane pushed to about 2025 and no R&D spike before 2020.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: since we launched the MAX, it's actually been about 50-50 in terms of orders. ... we don't simply make decisions based on market share desires. We make decisions for the long-term perspective of what's going to be valuable to our shareholders.
finding: Under Muilenburg, Boeing stopped treating market share as a decision driver even though the NEO led the MAX in backlog (about 4,400 to 3,100).
response: Raise 737 to 57/month on profitability grounds, not share

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: For the full year, we repurchased 47 million shares for $6.75 billion, and paid $2.5 billion in dividends. In December, our Board of Directors approved a new $14 billion share repurchase authorization and a 20% increase in our quarterly dividend.
finding: In 2015 Boeing returned about $9.25B to shareholders and then authorized $14B more in buybacks plus a 20% dividend increase.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: Boeing Commercial Airplanes reported record revenue of $66 billion, thanks in large part to an industry record 762 deliveries last year, which extended our market share leadership in airplane deliveries to a fourth consecutive year. Airplane order activity was healthy as we captured 768 net orders.
finding: Boeing measures itself against Airbus on deliveries and highlighted a fourth straight year of delivery leadership in 2015, with book-to-bill about 1.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: Given the 737s robust backlog of nearly 4,400 firm orders and continued healthy global demand, we have decided to move ahead with an additional production rate increase in 2019 to 57 aircraft per month. ... We have long maintained a disciplined and conservative approach in assessing future production rate increases
finding: In January 2016 Boeing raised the 737 rate plan to 57/month in 2019, citing a 4,400-order backlog and describing its rate approach as disciplined and conservative.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: On the 787 program, we captured 71 net orders for the year, which further shows the healthy market demand for this compelling wide-body airplane. The 787's backlog of nearly 800 orders fully supports our planned production rate increases to 12 per month in 2016 and 14 per month later this decade.
finding: Boeing kept the 787 rate plan (12 then 14/month) on a backlog of nearly 800, even though 2015 net orders were only 71.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: Core operating margins were 5.3%, reflecting solid productivity gains in both businesses, which were offset by the previously announced $885 million pretax charge on the 747 program. The charge reflects the slow recovery in the cargo market that required us to account for the market impact and lower production rates going forward.
finding: Boeing took an $885M charge to reflect lower 747 rates and market pricing rather than exit the program.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: Revenue for 2016 is forecast to be between $93 billion and $95 billion, reflecting the planned transition to the 737 MAX, lower F/A-18 and C-17 volume and reduced 747 production and timing of deliveries. We continue to see revenue growth over the remainder of the decade, with 7 more Commercial production rate increases planned
finding: Boeing accepted a 2016 revenue dip for the MAX transition and 747 cut while planning seven more commercial rate increases through 2020.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: we expect research and development spending for 2016 to be approximately $3.6 billion, with about 75% related to BCA, primarily driven by the planned increases in 777X development ... Capital spending guidance for 2016 is set to be approximately $2.8 billion, driven by the new 777X facilities and equipment, the expansion of our Boeing South Carolina
finding: Boeing's 2016 investment envelope was $3.6B R&D (75% BCA, mainly 777X) and $2.8B capex for 777X facilities and 787 capacity in South Carolina.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: that approach we've used on the -8 to -9 transition on the 87, using that same approach now on the MAX, we'll apply that same approach as we get to 777, 777X transition.
finding: Boeing reuses one model-transition playbook (787-8 to -9, NG to MAX, 777 to 777X): extra flow time and build-ahead while holding the line rate.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: But given that you're also -- your pricing looks pretty much set for most everything in '16 and '17. And if you put escalation aside for a moment, are you looking at any pressure on pricing in those next 2 years? ... No, nothing material.
finding: Boeing's 2016-17 pricing was largely locked in and it expected no material price pressure on those deliveries, apart from escalation.

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: the 747 just is not as profitable. I mean, it's that simple. And where the 777 is a pretty significant contributor to us and operates at a higher margin
finding: Rate cuts produce charges only on low-margin programs: the 747 cut triggered a reach-forward loss while the more profitable 777 cut did not.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: that is a sustainable rate position for that line to our bridges to the 2019 replacement cycle. ... And while the 747 is a niche market, it's an important niche market, and one that we think is sustainable.
finding: Boeing chose to keep the 747 at 6 a year instead of cancelling, bridging to an expected 2019 freighter replacement cycle.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: since we launched the MAX, it's actually been about 50-50 in terms of orders. ... And so as we think about rate ramp-ups, we don't simply make decisions based on market share desires. We make decisions for the long-term perspective of what's going to be valuable to our shareholders.
finding: Faced with Airbus's lead in the single-aisle backlog (about 4,400 vs 3,100 per the analyst), Boeing refused to chase share and pointed to 50-50 orders since the MAX launch and its delivery leadership.
trigger: Airbus A320neo family backlog lead over the MAX (about 4,400 vs 3,100 per analyst)
response: No share-chasing; stick to profitable rate ramp to 57/month and MAX value proposition

quote: Our BDS strategy is to leverage our core businesses to capture key next-generation programs while expanding our presence in adjacent and international markets
finding: Change in wording: the 'capture key next-generation programs' strategy, stated company-wide in FY2008 and FY2011 (pp. 843, 1209), is attributed only to BDS in FY2015.

quote: We launched the 787-10 in June 2013 and the 777X in November 2013.
finding: Boeing's widebody response in 2013 was two derivatives, a 787 stretch and a re-winged, re-engined 777, not a new airplane.

quote: In the fourth quarter of 2013, we launched the 777X, which features a new composite wing, new engines and folding wing-tips. The 777X will have a separate program accounting quantity, which will be determined in the year of first airplane delivery, targeted for 2020.
finding: The 777X upgrade combines a new wing, new engines and folding wingtips, with first delivery targeted about seven years after launch.

quote: We must meet planned production rate and productivity improvement targets in order to satisfy customer demand and maintain our profitability. We continue to increase production rates for the 737, 767 and 787 programs, while at the same time engaging in significant ongoing development of the 787-10, 737 MAX and 777X aircraft.
finding: In FY2015 Boeing tied profitability to hitting rate targets and was running three ramps alongside three derivative developments.

quote: In addition, we continue to seek opportunities to reduce the costs of building our aircraft, including working with our suppliers to reduce supplier costs, identifying and implementing productivity improvements, and optimizing how we manage inventory.
finding: New relative to the FY2011 risk factors (p. 1197): Boeing names squeezing supplier costs as an explicit part of its profitability plan.

quote: We are currently producing at a rate of 42 per month and plan an additional increase to 47 per month in 2017. We plan to further increase the rate to 52 per month in 2018 and to 57 per month in 2019. First delivery of the 737 MAX is expected in 2017.
finding: Boeing committed to a multi-year 737 ladder (42 to 47 to 52 to 57/month) that overlaps with the MAX entry into service.

quote: During the second half of 2015, the cargo market recovery slowed, and in January 2016, we announced a plan to further reduce the production rate to 0.5 per month
finding: Boeing responded to weak large-aircraft and cargo demand by cutting 747 output again, to 0.5/month.
trigger: Lower-than-expected demand for large passenger/freighter aircraft; cargo recovery slowed in H2 2015
response: Further cut 747 rate to 0.5/month (from 1.3 via 1.0)

quote: forward loss of $885 million on the program. The charge, which was recorded during the fourth quarter of 2015, is primarily related to lower anticipated revenues reflecting ongoing pricing and market pressures, as well as higher estimated costs due to the reduced production rate.
finding: The 747 rate cut came with an $885M charge: lower rates raise unit cost under program accounting, and pricing pressure cut expected revenue.

quote: We are currently producing at a rate of 8.3 per month and plan to reduce the rate to 7 per month in 2017.
finding: Boeing planned to step the 777 down from 8.3 to 7/month in 2017 as the 777X transition approached.

quote: We continue to produce at a rate of 10 per month and plan for rate increases to 12 per month in 2016 and 14 per month by the end of the decade. First delivery of the 787-10 derivative aircraft is targeted for 2018. The accounting quantity of 1,300 units remains unchanged.
finding: Boeing hit the 10/month 787 target and planned 12 and then 14/month, keeping the ramp going while margins were near breakeven.

quote: The combination of production challenges, change incorporation on early build aircraft, schedule delays, customer and supplier impacts and changes to price escalation factors has created significant pressure on program profitability and we continue to have near breakeven gross margins.
finding: Four years after entry into service the 787 was still at near-breakeven gross margin; the same wording recurs in FY2016 (p. 1000).

quote: $34,656 and $33,163 of work in process (including deferred production costs of $28,510 and $26,149) ... $8,679 is expected to be recovered from units included in the program accounting quantity that represent expected future orders.
finding: 787 deferred production costs reached $28.5B by end-2015 (up from $10.8B in 2011), and $8.7B of recovery depends on future orders.

quote: Earnings from operations in 2015 decreased by $1,254 million or 20% compared with 2014 primarily due to higher reach-forward losses of $1,160 million and higher research and development spending of $459 million, largely on the 777X ... the dilutive impact of 787 volume and mix.
finding: Commercial Airplanes' margin fell from 10.7% to 7.8% in 2015 because of reach-forward losses, 777X R&D and the dilutive 787 ramp.

quote: In second quarter 2014, we recorded a reach-forward loss of $425 million on the EMD contract. In second quarter 2015, we recorded an additional reach-forward loss of $835 million. ... The reach-forward loss on the EMD contract was driven primarily by design changes required in the aircraft fuels and aerial refueling systems
finding: The fixed-price KC-46A (767 derivative) bid produced $1.26B of losses by 2015 from design changes, the cost of Boeing's 2011 decision to take fixed-price development risk.

quote: However, until the U.S. Senate confirms members sufficient to reconstitute a quorum of the bank’s board of directors, the bank will not be able to approve any transaction totaling more than $10 million. As a result, we may fund additional commitments and/or enter into new financing arrangements with customers.
finding: When Ex-Im Bank financing stalled, Boeing was prepared to finance customers from its own balance sheet to protect sales.
trigger: Ex-Im Bank charter lapse (30 Jun 2015) and lack of a board quorum
response: Boeing may fund additional customer financing commitments itself and help customers find third-party financing

quote: We continue to monitor political unrest involving Russia and Ukraine, where we and some of our suppliers source titanium products and/or have operations. A number of our commercial customers also have operations in Russia and Ukraine. To date, we have not experienced any significant disruptions to production or deliveries.
finding: Boeing depends on Russian and Ukrainian titanium supply and treats it as a monitored geopolitical supply risk rather than one it has acted on.

quote: Net cash provided by operating activities was $9.4 billion during 2015, compared with $8.9 billion during 2014 and $8.2 billion in 2013. ... Our investment in gross inventories increased $7.6 billion in 2014 and $5.7 billion in 2013, largely driven by continued investment in commercial airplane program inventory, primarily 787 inventory.
finding: Operating cash flow rose to $9.4B as 787 inventory growth slowed after absorbing $5.7-7.6B a year in 2013-2014.

quote: In 2015, capital expenditures totaled $2.5 billion, up from $2.2 billion in 2014 and $2.1 billion in 2013. We expect capital expenditures in 2016 to be consistent with 2015 due to continued investment to support growth.
finding: Boeing held capex at about $2.5B a year and guided it flat for 2016, a modest level of spending to support growth.

quote: During 2015 and 2014 we repurchased 46.7 million and 46.6 million shares totaling $6.8 billion and $6.0 billion through our open market share repurchase program. ... At December 31, 2015, the amount available under the share repurchase plan, announced on December 14, 2015, totaled $14 billion.
finding: Reversal of the 2009-2011 pause: by 2014-2015 Boeing returned $6-7B a year through buybacks and authorized another $14B.

quote: Cash dividends declared $2,575 $2,210 $1,642 $1,360 $1,263
finding: Dividends declared roughly doubled between 2011 and 2015 ($1.26B to $2.58B), part of a sharp increase in shareholder payouts.

quote: At December 31, 2015 and 2014 , our pension plans were $17.9 billion and $17.3 billion underfunded as measured under GAAP. On an Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) basis our plans are more than 100% funded at December 31, 2015 with minimal required contributions in 2016.
finding: Although the GAAP pension deficit was about $18B, the plans were over 100% funded on an ERISA basis, so Boeing planned only minimal contributions (about $0.1B in 2016, same page).

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: It will not be based on market share. We are not in business just to chase market share. We are going to run a disciplined, profitable growing business.
finding: Boeing declined to launch a dedicated A321neo competitor for share reasons. It put any middle-of-the-market airplane after the 777X, a change from its 2012 insistence on half the market.
response: No new plane solely to match A321neo; MOM after 777X

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: while we're in a competitive marketplace and we're continually dealing with pricing pressures, we haven't seen that roll into our booking rates. Our booking rates hold up well. ... And we recognize if pricing pressure is going to be a threat, so our job is to continue to drive cost competitiveness.
finding: Boeing's stated response to pricing pressure (reported after Ray Conner's internal comments) is to cut its own cost, not to concede margin.
trigger: Pricing pressure in the market; press reports of Ray Conner comments
response: Drive cost competitiveness to protect booking rates

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: As you mentioned, we also do selectively overbook, oversell, to protect backlog.
finding: Boeing deliberately oversells production slots to protect against deferrals and cancellations.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: the fact that we've got 7 years of backlog, it doesn't mean we have to be precisely right. We have to be directionally right. And when you have 7 years of backlog, it gives us the flexibility to adjust the back end of that backlog if we see the market starting to change.
finding: Boeing sees a 7-year backlog as a buffer that lets it commit to rate increases and adjust later, which supports high rate-risk appetite.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: We've got to sell about 40 a year to finish filling out the bridge. And as we announced, we're going to take the 777 line from the current 8.3 a month this year and we're completely sold out at 8.3 a month this year. We're going to drop to 7 a month next year
finding: Boeing cut 777 rate from 8.3 to 7/month for 2017 to match the bridge to the 777X, with a sales target of about 40 a year.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: we have a plan in place now to execute this 7-year backlog that introduces all of these new models concurrently with production ramp-up. So not only are we going to deliver more cash over that time period, we're going to exit that time period with an all-new fleet of new airplanes
finding: Boeing chose to introduce the MAX, 787-10 and 777X concurrently with production ramp-ups, betting it could grow cash while renewing the whole lineup.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: as you get to the end of the NG line and transition to MAXs, you see some pricing pressure on NGs ... the pricing pressure we see is roughly in line with our plan. As I've mentioned before in this forum, we're not satisfied with the margins of our commercial airplane business today. And we've guided to 9% margins
finding: Boeing accepted end-of-line price pressure on the NG and 777 as planned, while saying it was not satisfied with BCA margins guided at 9% for 2016.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: You could come to the conclusion ultimately that the current product set is satisfactory. You could come to the conclusion that some kind of a modified version of the 737, the so-called stretch that was in the news, that could be an answer. It could be an all-new middle-of-the-market airplane.
finding: For the middle of the market, Boeing kept three options open: do nothing, stretch the 737, or launch an all-new airplane, with a decision targeted in 1-1.5 years.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: whatever the solution space might be, will be on the backside of 777X. ... We and you can't stand a spiky R&D profile. We need a predictable time-phased R&D profile.
finding: Boeing sequences new programs so R&D stays smooth: any MOM or new airplane would follow the 777X rather than overlap it.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: if we see a real market demand evolve that leads to a business case for a modified or a new airplane, we'll make that based on business case analysis. It will not be based on market share. We are not in business just to chase market share.
finding: Asked whether it needed a new plane to beat the A321neo, Boeing said a new or modified narrowbody would be launched only on business-case returns, not to defend share.
trigger: Airbus A321neo success in the upper narrowbody segment
response: No immediate new airplane; study options and decide on business case, not market share

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: Now all 5 of those were the right things to do, but the fact we did them all at once was difficult, and that's why it shows in deferred balance. ... incremental innovation that still leads to big step improvements for our customers but in a risk-managed way.
finding: The 787 lesson made Boeing favour incremental, risk-managed innovation and stable R&D over doing many big technical steps at once.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: That is the market. I mean, you look at 787 volume going to 12 and 14, that is demand. ... But just as we're working on cost reductions and lean implementation in our own factories, we're doing that hand in hand with our suppliers. That's all part of this Partnering for Success umbrella.
finding: Boeing says 787 rate increases to 12 and 14 are demand-driven, not driven by the deferred balance, and it pushes cost reduction into suppliers through Partnering for Success.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: The 787, ultimately, will perform like the 777 in terms of profitability. ... If I look at 787-8 deliveries over the last, roughly, 240 units, it's about a 40% cost reduction, right? If I take a look at 787-9, just over the first 70, 80 units, it's a 30% cost reduction.
finding: Boeing relies on steep learning curves (40% cost cut over ~240 787-8s, 30% over the first ~75 787-9s) to argue the 787 will eventually earn 777-like margins.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, President & CEO
quote: the deferred production inventory a little north of $28 billion, right, that tells you that we've made a substantial investment. But that is investment that's now behind us, right? ... a product that is clearly differentiated in the marketplace, that offers 15% to 20% operating cost advantage to our customers.
finding: Boeing treats the $28B 787 deferred production balance as a sunk investment justified by a 15-20% operating cost advantage.

speaker: Randy Tinseth, VP Marketing
quote: last year, we delivered a record 762 aircraft. That's not just a record for Boeing, but it's an industry record. And we've seen our backlog now grow to 5,800 aircraft valued at about USD 430 billion. ... we continue to be on track to deliver somewhere between 740 and 745 aircraft this year.
finding: Boeing delivered a record 762 aircraft in 2015 and planned a slight dip to 740-745 in 2016 (the 777/747 bridge and MAX transition), against a 5,800-aircraft backlog.

speaker: Randy Tinseth, VP Marketing
quote: What we see as a healthy market moving forward is one that will take somewhere between 6.5% to, say, 7.5% of its deliveries in terms of the installed base. At those types of levels, you see a healthy replacement demand of somewhere between 2.5% and 3% of the installed fleet, plus growth ranging between 3.5% and 4% of the fleet.
finding: Boeing's supply-demand test for industry rates is annual deliveries of 6.5-7.5% of the installed fleet (2.5-3% replacement plus 3.5-4% growth).

speaker: Randy Tinseth, VP Marketing
quote: we are creating a number of improvements to today's 777 that will roll out in the third quarter of this year, improvements that will improve the fuel consumption of the airplane by about 2% per trip and also give our customers the ability to add up to 14 more seats.
finding: To support the 777 bridge to the 777X, Boeing invested in incremental performance upgrades to the current 777.
trigger: Need to fill 777 bridge to 777X amid competition
response: 2% fuel-burn improvement and up to 14 more seats on current 777

speaker: Randy Tinseth, VP Marketing
quote: is it an all-new engine, which is expensive and challenging for us all, but it might be the right step forward as we look at not only at this airplane, but future applications? Or is it a derivative of things that we have on the table today?
finding: For a new mid-market airplane, Boeing weighed a costly all-new engine that could serve future platforms against a derivative engine.

speaker: Randy Tinseth, VP Marketing
quote: it has to have a business case that works for us and has to have a business case that works for our customers. ... a business case where the development of the program makes sense, where the unit cost to produce it makes sense ... When the business case comes together, we move forward. We're not there yet.
finding: Boeing gates a new airplane launch (MOM) on a two-sided business case covering development cost and unit cost, and had not launched as of March 2016.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: I mean, certainly, it's a factor as we think about competing. ... We don't rely on exchange rates.
finding: A strong dollar that favoured Airbus was one input into Boeing's 2016 cost-cutting and headcount reductions.
trigger: Strong dollar giving Airbus cost edge
response: Productivity and headcount reduction

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: In the first quarter, we've repurchased $3.5 billion of Boeing stock and increased our dividend per share 20% for a payout of $717 million.
finding: Boeing front-loaded shareholder returns in early 2016, buying back $3.5B in a single quarter and raising the dividend 20%.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: in the past year, deferrals, accelerations, debookings and cancellations combined for about 1% of our backlog. That is well below the 6% average over the last 15 years.
finding: Boeing tracks backlog churn against a 15-year historical norm (6%) as a key input to rate decisions; 2015-16 churn was only ~1%.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we remain on track to raise 737 production from the current 42 a month to 47 in 2017, followed by 52 a month in 2018 and then 57 a month in 2019. The production bridge between the current 737NG and the MAX remains in an oversold position.
finding: Boeing committed to a stepped 737 ramp (42 to 47 to 52 to 57/month over 2017-2019) and describes the NG-to-MAX transition bridge as oversold.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We are sold out of production slots in 2016 and more than 80% sold out in 2017. ... we've added 11 new 777 orders, a solid first step towards our target of 40 to 50 orders a year to finish filling the 777 production bridge.
finding: Boeing manages the 777 classic-to-777X bridge with an explicit sales target of 40-50 orders a year, with 2018 slots the priority.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we cannot stand still and sustain our industry leadership in the face of intense competition. For Boeing to continue winning in our second century of business, it is imperative that we seize the initiative to get on and stay on a steep and steady glide path to lower cost performance. We intend to play offense
finding: Under the new CEO, Boeing framed competition as requiring an aggressive, continuous cost-reduction push ('play offense').

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: 787 deferred production was better than planned and increased $141 million to $28.7 billion in the first quarter, reflecting the favorable mix towards more -9s as well as continued unit cost reductions. ... for the full year, the deferred production balance should be flat year-over-year.
finding: Boeing carried a $28.7B 787 deferred production balance and targeted it to stop growing in 2016 via -9 mix and unit cost cuts.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: So if we were to see deferrals and cancellations begin to creep up, we wouldn't change our plans. We've, in fact, designed our plans to envelope those historical averages.
finding: Boeing sizes production-rate decisions to withstand historical-average cancellation and deferral levels, so it says it would not cut rates if churn rose back toward the 6% norm.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we are pushing towards returning to double-digit margins in our Commercial Airplane business next year. And when we look at that mid-teens margin, the more aspirational target, this is something that we intend to focus on here over the next several years as we head towards the end of the decade.
finding: Boeing set a margin trajectory for BCA: back to double digits in 2017 and mid-teens by about 2020, driven by productivity rather than price.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: As we take a look at the MAX 7, sort of the lower seat end of that family of aircraft, that is an area where we're having active discussions with our customers. It's too early to give any specific details or decisions ... And we also have the flexibility to design it to meet their needs.
finding: Asked about a new 737 derivative to counter the Bombardier C Series, Boeing signalled it would reshape the existing MAX 7 rather than launch a new small aircraft.
trigger: Bombardier C Series competition at the low-seat end (analyst question about a new 737 derivative)
response: Customer discussions on redesigning the MAX 7; no decision yet

speaker: Gregory Smith, CFO
quote: But exchange rates are going to move around over time. We don't rely on exchange rates. But the fact is, they're sometimes where there's an advantage, there's sometimes to a disadvantage, and we have to have the flexibility in our own enterprise to be able to compete, no matter what that exchange rate is
finding: Boeing responds to a strong dollar favouring Airbus by cutting its own costs, not by relying on currency moves.
trigger: Strong US dollar potentially giving Airbus a competitive cost edge
response: Cost containment and productivity to compete regardless of exchange rates

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: this is about the fact that we are concurrently finishing up development and ramping up production. We've got the first 7 production aircraft flowing through our Everett factory now in our supply chain. ... So you can see there's some concurrency cost. That is an intentional investment we're making to keep the program on schedule.
finding: Boeing deliberately pays concurrency costs to hold schedule rather than slow production during development.

speaker: Ray Conner, BCA CEO
quote: They've got a seat advantage on us at the 9, and -- but we still believe the heart of the market still sits in the 8 size. ... potentially, we're thinking through how do we want to address the very top of that market with the MAX.
finding: By May 2016 Boeing admitted the A321 had a seat advantage over the MAX 9 and began studying a larger MAX.
trigger: A321 success at top of the narrowbody market
response: Study MAX stretch (MAX 10)

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Now we're going to continue to invest our R&D wisely, but do it a more stable and feathered approach in terms of our R&D profile and how we invest in new programs in a complementary fashion with time sequencing, so disciplined innovation
finding: Boeing's 2016 Investor Day introduced the policy of time-sequencing new programs to keep R&D spending flat.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Partnering for Success, I want to stress that this is not a temporary program. This is a new way of doing business that we will continue for as long as we can see... This is singular negotiations with our supply chain instead of 100 different negotiations across programs.
finding: Boeing made supplier price pressure permanent, negotiating company-wide with each supplier instead of program by program.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we've successfully achieved 17 rate increases in the last 6 years... We expect growth in Commercial Airplane is driven by 5 more production rate increases that we've talked about.
finding: Boeing had completed 17 rate increases in six years and planned 5 more.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: remain focused on profitably filling the 777 production bridge. As you know, we need 40 to 50 airplanes a year to fill that bridge. We've got 12 so far... continuing at the 7 per month rate, but at the same time, closely monitoring industry trends
finding: In May 2016 Boeing needed 40-50 777 orders a year to hold 7/month and had 12.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: over the long term, we do have an aspirational goal of a mid-teen margin. And when you step back and assess the segment margins, we do see an imbalance between risk and reward, and we want to fix that.
finding: Boeing justified its mid-teens margin goal by arguing that its margins had been too low for the risks it takes.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we have stability now through 2022 and, at the same time, converting nearly all of our employees to a defined contribution plan. That makes us more competitive and more agile in the marketplace
finding: Boeing locked in labor agreements to 2022 and moved nearly all employees to defined-contribution pensions to cut cost and risk.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: early on in the program, early pricing disruption, customer settlements clearly impacting on profitability and cash all in that deferred production. That will not be the case going forward... These 2 elements of mix and pricing will account for approximately 70% of the 787 deferred production recovery.
finding: Boeing admitted that early 787 discounts and delay settlements drove deferred production, and said mix and pricing would deliver about 70% of the recovery.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
