quote: $32,501 and $34,656 of work in process (including deferred production costs of $27,308 and $28,510) ... $7,115 is expected to be recovered from units included in the program accounting quantity that represent expected future orders.
finding: 787 deferred production fell for the first time in 2016 ($28.5B to $27.3B), meaning unit costs had dropped below the program average.

quote: We increased the combined tanker and commercial production rate from 1.5 per month to 2 per month in April 2016. We plan to further increase the rate to 2.5 per month in the fourth quarter of 2017.
finding: The combined 767 commercial and tanker line was ramping (1.5 to 2 to 2.5/month), so the tanker derivative adds volume to the older 767 line.

quote: The decrease in earnings and operating margins is primarily due to higher research and development costs of $1,415 million, delivery mix and higher reach-forward losses on the 747 program of $1,258 million compared with $885 million in 2015.
finding: Commercial Airplanes' margin fell to 4.8% in 2016 (from 10.7% in 2014) because of 777X R&D, the 787 flight-test write-off and 747 losses.

quote: Through 2015, we recorded reach-forward losses of $1,260 million related to the EMD contract and LRIP aircraft. During 2016 we recorded reach-forward losses of $1,128 million.
finding: KC-46A losses kept coming ($2.39B cumulative by 2016), a repeated cost of the fixed-price derivative bid.

quote: Net cash provided by operating activities was $10.5 billion during 2016, compared with $9.4 billion during 2015 and $8.9 billion in 2014.
finding: Operating cash flow reached $10.5B in 2016 even as reported earnings fell, helped by lower 787 inventory spending (p. 1010).

quote: In 2016, capital expenditures totaled $2.6 billion, up from $2.5 billion in 2015 and $2.2 billion in 2014. We expect capital expenditures in 2017 to be lower than 2016.
finding: Change: after years of rising capex, Boeing guided capex down for 2017.

quote: During 2016 and 2015 we repurchased 55.1 million and 46.7 million shares totaling $7.0 billion and $6.8 billion through our open market share repurchase program. ... At December 31, 2016, the amount available under the share repurchase plan, announced on December 12, 2016, totaled $14 billion.
finding: In a year of falling earnings and large 747, 787 and KC-46A charges, Boeing still bought back $7.0B of stock and renewed a $14B authorization, putting shareholder returns ahead of balance-sheet cushion.

quote: During 2016, we issued $1.3 billion and repaid $1.4 billion of debt. At December 31, 2016 and 2015 the recorded balance of debt was $10.0 billion and $10.0 billion
finding: Boeing held debt flat at about $10B and funded record buybacks and dividends from operating cash and cash balances (cash fell from $11.3B to $8.8B).

quote: The lower service costs reflect the changes to our retirement plans whereby certain employees transitioned in 2016 to a company-funded defined contribution retirement savings plan.
finding: Boeing moved some employees from defined-benefit to company-funded defined-contribution plans, which lowered service cost and contributed to a $2.26B drop in net pension cost in 2016 (same page).
Headcount fell by about 11,000 in 2016 and by about 24,000 since 2012, while deliveries held near 750 a year (p. 998), a sustained productivity and cost-cutting push.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We continue to see, I'll say, more moderate demand signals in widebody, so we're paying close attention to that... It just reminds us we're going to have to continue to be very focused on taking costs out and driving productivity in our widebody lines. It'll help us sell airplanes
finding: Boeing answered soft widebody demand by cutting widebody production costs so it could sell more aircraft.
trigger: moderate widebody demand and muted cargo market
response: cut cost and raise productivity on widebody lines to win sales

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Now that does include the Iran deal, and those Iranian deliveries, as currently planned, would start in 2018 and spread out over several years. So they're not concentrated in any 1 year, and I think that's an important part of how we calibrate the risk around that order.
finding: Boeing counted Iran orders in the 777 bridge but spread the deliveries over several years to calibrate the risk.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: One is the option, in essence, using the current MAX family and the 787 family to address that space. Another has been to look at a stretched -- additional stretched version of the MAX, our so-called MAX 10... And we're also taking a look at a -- potentially an all-new airplane
finding: For the middle of the market, Boeing weighed three options: do nothing (cover it with the MAX and 787), a MAX 10 stretch, or an all-new airplane.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: the MAX 10 is a straightforward thing for us to do, not a technology stretch at all and something that we can bring to the market quickly and effectively... when and if they're ready, we're very prepared to move out on that
finding: Boeing treated the MAX 10 as a low-risk, quick stretch it would launch once customers committed.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We don't see doing anything here that would somehow step on our 787 family, which is in a very strong position for the long run.
finding: Boeing would not design an NMA that cannibalized the 787.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we've proactively made the right decisions on the 777 production line and that includes stepping down to the 5 a month later this year. It gets us well aligned on supply versus demand in widebodies.
finding: Boeing presented the 777 cut to 5/month as a proactive move to align widebody supply with demand.
response: step 777 down to 5/month

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: How do we minimize the risk? How do we have a gated process in that we don't push risk and then push requirement, things like that?
finding: Boeing adopted gated development reviews so risk and requirements are not pushed downstream.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: some of those programs don't have a lot of margin. But the business case on those programs over the long term is very strong. And Tanker's a great example. I mean, that's about a 400-airplane marketplace plus
finding: Boeing accepts thin early margins on development programs when the long-term franchise is large.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: a very, I'll say, clear understanding of the competitive landscape and no dismissal of it. We're assuming people are going to be successful, and they want share. And we're obviously going to do everything we can to not only maintain share, we want more share.
finding: Boeing assumed rivals will succeed and want share, and said it would compete to gain market share, not just hold it.
response: drive productivity and cost to maintain and gain share

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Some of that has made its way to the bottom line, some of that's made its way into pricing and so on. But if you think about transition of the 737 going from the NG to the MAX, from a bottom-line perspective, you didn't see any disruption there
finding: Boeing passed part of its productivity gains into sharper pricing and managed the NG-to-MAX changeover without hurting earnings.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: as you look at 57 and look at percentage sold at 57, you look at options that we think have high probability of being exercised, book's really good... It's taken over 3,000 MAX airplanes that we sold before we even flew the airplane
finding: Boeing based rate decisions on the share of slots sold plus options likely to be exercised; the 57/month decision had no near deadline.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: In the first quarter, we generated $2.1 billion of operating cash, repurchased $2.5 billion of Boeing stock and increased our dividend per share 30% for a payout of $868 million.
finding: Boeing kept returning cash heavily, with Q1 2017 buybacks exceeding operating cash flow and a 30% dividend increase.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we have a concerted effort in place to secure additional 787 orders to support the 14 per month production rate plan through the end of the decade. We will remain disciplined... with a focus, as always, on ensuring supply and demand are kept in balance
finding: Boeing made the 787 step to 14/month depend on first selling enough new orders.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We're looking at a range of scenarios between the current 12 a month and 14 a month and the specific timing around that... and we're not looking at scenarios that would drop us down from 12 a month.
finding: Boeing treated 12/month as a firm 787 floor and considered only upward moves.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: where 50% of our comp now will be free cash, 25% on core EPS, 25% on revenue and then, of course, the long term reflecting the same, plus the TSR element.
finding: Boeing tied half of 2017 incentive pay to free cash flow, reinforcing a cash-first management focus.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: selectively rebuilding some vertical capabilities. As you've noted, we've selectively brought in some capability, things like building the all-composite wing for the 777X, the propulsion center that we stood up in Charleston, where we're building nacelles, the actuation capability
finding: Boeing was selectively bringing components in-house (777X composite wing, nacelles, actuation).

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Where we need to, we will build selective vertical capability so that we can further drive costs down and value up for our customers. And in some cases, we may decide to create additional new sources of competition if we need to.
finding: Boeing said it would build in-house capability selectively and could create new sources of competition to drive supplier costs down.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: it's not unusual for us to have some shifts in our customers, in some cases, deferrals and in some cases, accelerations. But across the whole profile every year, we're oversold against that profile... MAX will represent about 15% to 20% of the deliveries from that line this year.
finding: Boeing kept the 737 ramp unchanged despite customer deferrals, relying on an oversold skyline to backfill slots.
trigger: 737 delivery deferrals by major customers (United, Ryanair cited by analyst)
response: hold the 47/52/57 ramp; backfill from oversold skyline

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: some of the tough affordability actions we've had to take have been necessary so we can continue to fuel our R&D and our innovation machine for the future... So we've largely been able to leverage voluntary layoffs and take advantage of natural attrition rather than massive steps.
finding: Boeing cut headcount steadily, mostly through voluntary layoffs and attrition, as part of affordability actions to fund R&D.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we're doing our due diligence on business case opportunities that gets into reducing development cost. This is all the work we're doing on step-function reduction in development cost... our decisions on whether or not we launch will be dependent on that vigorous business case.
finding: Boeing tied an NMA launch to a business case built on step-function cuts in development cost.
trigger: customer pressure for a low NMA price (a reporter cited $70-75 million)
response: pursue step-function cuts in development and production cost before any launch

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: A MAX 10, as we've been able to configure the airplane and talk with our customers, would be basically the same size as the A321, have about 5% lower operating cost per seat ... It's not a big R&D expenditure. It's an airplane that would enter into service in the 2020 time frame.
finding: Boeing's answer to the A321neo was a low-cost MAX 10 stretch rather than a new airplane, about a year after first studying it.
response: MAX 10 stretch, EIS ~2020

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: notionally an airplane that's a little larger and longer-ranged than the 757. ... Entry into service would be 2024, 2025 kind of time frame.
finding: Boeing framed a possible middle-of-the-market airplane above the A321 as unhurried, with entry into service in 2024-25.
response: NMA study, EIS 2024-25

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We have a backlog that's 7 years, instead of 2 years, a backlog that's geographically diversified... And this is how we manage our production rates, keeping supply and demand in balance, the freeze on our pension, long-term labor agreements, a phased R&D plan, so we have stable R&D
finding: Boeing frames its management system as de-cyclicalizing the business: rates held in supply/demand balance, pension freeze, long-term labor deals and phased, stable R&D.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We're at 42 a month production rate right now. We're stepping into 47 a month in the third quarter. We're going to 52 a month next year, 57 a month the year after. Even against that production profile, we are strongly oversold.
finding: Boeing committed to a stepped 737 rate ramp 42-47-52-57 per month over 2017-2019 while saying demand exceeded even that.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: market demand signals are telling us, "You could go even higher." So as part of our effort to keep supply and demand in balance, have a long-term growth plan, we've settled in at that 57 a month rate structure.
finding: Boeing deliberately capped the 737 rate at 57/month below perceived demand to keep supply and demand in balance.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: If you take a look at 787, right now, we're running at 12 a month. We've got almost 700 airplanes in backlog... We're currently evaluating timing of stepping up to 14 a month... but we want to be very diligent about keeping supply and demand in balance.
finding: Boeing held the 787 at 12/month and deferred the timing of a step to 14/month despite a ~700-aircraft backlog, citing supply/demand discipline.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: On the 777, we've made the decision to cut back on the production rate as we go through the bridge. We'll be stepping down to 5 a month this fall... that is in effect delivering airplanes at 3.5 a month as we ramp over to 777X. At that rate, we're about 90% sold-out in 2018 and 2019.
finding: Boeing cut 777 output to 5/month (about 3.5 deliveries/month) through the bridge to the 777X and said it was about 90% sold for 2018-19.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: 777X development is right on track... We still see that airplane entering into final assembly in 2018, entry into service on 2020. So we're about midway through the development program, right on track.
finding: In mid-2017 Boeing described the 777X as midway through development and on schedule for 2018 final assembly and 2020 EIS.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: It's not a big R&D expenditure. It's an airplane that would enter into service in the 2020 time frame. And it's one, if we were to make that investment, would fit within our existing investment profile overall
finding: Boeing preferred a low-cost derivative (MAX 10) that fits the existing R&D envelope over new spending to answer the A321neo.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: it could eventually be 20%, maybe 25% of the sales of the MAX profile and one that would be highly common with the MAX 9 in our production system.
finding: Boeing expected a MAX 10 to take 20-25% of MAX sales with high commonality to the MAX 9.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Pricing of the airplanes is holding up very well in the marketplace. So it's not as if we have to rush to make a rate decision... It's not a big capital investment.
finding: Boeing ties rate increases to protecting pricing and sees no urgency when the step costs little capital.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: something that would be positioned between the 737 family and the 787 family, notionally an airplane that's a little larger and longer-ranged than the 757... this isn't something we need to rush to do. Entry into service would be 2024, 2025 kind of time frame.
finding: Boeing described the middle-of-market airplane as a 757-plus between 737 and 787, with EIS 2024-25 and no rush to launch.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: If we were to do this airplane, it would be on the backside of 777X and it would be the next thing that would fit within that phased R&D profile that I talked about.
finding: Boeing times a new program launch to begin only as the prior one (777X) rolls off, keeping R&D level.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: On the deferred production inventory, about 70% of that will be transitioned into cash because of favorable mix and pricing going forward... we haven't given up any pricing on those future airplanes for early settlement for late airplanes.
finding: Boeing counted on the 787 mix shift to -9/-10 and held pricing to unwind 70% of deferred production.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: on Spirit, obviously one of our big investment partners, we're not all the way to the finish line on our agreement... We need to have a good long-term deal and one that generates value.
finding: Boeing kept negotiating with Spirit, one of its big partners, and would not rush a deal.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: In the past, what has happened is if you change production rates, you had big expenditures to go with that. In these new digitized manufacturing facilities, low tooling facilities, the capital expenditure to go up and down is muted. That gives us more flexibility.
finding: Boeing's downturn playbook relies on lower-capital, flexible production so rates can move up or down cheaply.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We see 3 priorities on cash deployment. First priority continues to be organic investment... Second priority is returning value to shareholders. And we're committed to returning roughly 100% free cash flow to our shareholders.
finding: Boeing ranked organic investment first but committed to return roughly all free cash flow to shareholders.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: our third priority is M&A. And again, we're looking primarily at targeted acquisitions that fill out our strategy. We still see our primary growth mechanism is organic investment, complemented with selective acquisitions.
finding: Boeing ranked M&A third, limited to targeted acquisitions, with organic investment as the main growth route.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we will make another $3.5 billion of discretionary pension contribution using Boeing common shares. We will utilize our strong cash position to increase share repurchase by the $3.5 billion above our prior plan for 2017, and we now expect to repurchase approximately $10 billion
finding: Boeing pre-funded pensions with $3.5 billion of its own stock (removing mandatory contributions through 2021) and offset the dilution by lifting 2017 buybacks to about $10 billion.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Recall that 60% to 70% of our cost base in the Commercial Airplane business is in our supply chain, so the work we're doing through our Partnering for Success initiative.
finding: With 60-70% of BCA costs in the supply chain, supplier cost pressure is Boeing's main margin lever, along with mix and block extensions.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We continue to see a potential market there for 2,000 to 4,000 aircraft. We're continuing to work our way through the details of what that airplane might look like, potentially a family of 2 airplanes
finding: In July 2017 Boeing sized the NMA market at 2,000-4,000 aircraft as a possible two-model family; by May 2018 its estimate had risen to 4,000-5,000 (p. 1223).

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: That said, with the backlog of over 5,700 aircraft, we don't have a great sense of urgency to have to build overall backlog.
finding: With a backlog above 5,700 aircraft, Boeing felt no need to chase orders (expecting book-to-bill of about 1) and focused sales on filling the 777 bridge.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: But I think as far as general capital structure, what you see today is what you should expect to see going forward.
finding: Boeing accepted a move to a net debt position of about $4 billion after the pension funding and signalled that this leverage was its intended capital structure.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Now are there going to be some places where we're going to have to make some hard decisions, where we're going to have to develop alternatives, where we're going to have to build additional supply chain capacity? Yes, there will be some hard things that we'll have to do
finding: Faced with supplier distress and pushback over its services push, Boeing said it would develop alternative suppliers or capacity where needed.
trigger: Supplier profit warning after a Partnering for Success deal, and a supplier threat to change pricing because of Boeing's services push
response: Kept up supplier pressure and said it would develop alternative suppliers or capacity where needed

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: And we don't see a need to change that strategy. We're going to continue to look for bolt-on opportunities, things that complement our organic investment, but our best, most efficient use of capital is our organic investment machine.
finding: In July 2017 Boeing ruled out larger strategic acquisitions in favour of bolt-ons; within months it pursued KLX ($4.25 billion) and an Embraer combination (change of position).

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: So I think you will see an evolution that's more towards additional vertical content with a clear focus on life cycle value addition as an evaluation criteria around that. And if we decide to proceed with a middle-of-the-market airplane, that philosophy, that strategy will be reflected in the airplane.
finding: Boeing reversed its long shift toward outsourcing, bringing engineering and composite work back in-house on the 777X, and planned more vertical content on any NMA.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Again, all of this is being governed by U.S. government policy, and we're staying completely within that licensing process, stepping our way through the gates. That is moving forward on track, and we still expect to begin delivering airplanes next year.
finding: In July 2017 Boeing expected to start Iran deliveries in 2018; by April 2018 it had removed them from the skyline (p. 1264), showing it follows US policy over its own order book.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we have a focused effort underway to secure additional 787 orders to support the 14-per-month production rate planned for the end of the decade.
finding: In July 2017 Boeing had planned but not confirmed 787 at 14/month and was selling to fill it; it confirmed the rate in September 2017 after further orders (sequence: plan, sell, confirm).

speaker: analyst (Jefferies)
quote: you started almost 2 years behind Airbus with respect to where you were in terms of entry into service. And if we look out 18 months, that difference between your market share almost narrows to a de minimis amount.
finding: The MAX entered service almost two years after the NEO, and the analyst expected the share gap to close within 18 months.
trigger: NEO entry into service before MAX
response: MAX ramp

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we got to have competition in places where we don't have a competition. ... And so with that, we're looking for people that compete in that, and we're making investments in those areas where we can have more competition.
finding: Under Partnering for Success, Boeing invests to create competition in single-source supply areas as a lever over suppliers.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: how do you fulfill that need in a manner in the timeframe and a price point that works. And that was the challenge for the team and minimizing the development cost is key part of that obviously in getting that airplane into market.
finding: Boeing launched the 737 MAX 10 as a low-development-cost derivative aimed at the right price and timing; the analyst said it created strong pent-up demand.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We expect competition from COMAC while they're also partners for us in China and supporting us in our supply chain. We expect other countries and companies to be investing. We know Airbus will continue to be a strong and aggressive competitor. All of that tells us we can't stop.
finding: Boeing treats COMAC as both a competitor and a supply-chain partner, expects Airbus to stay aggressive, and responds by pushing productivity to fund innovation.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: In some places, we won't and we'll develop alternative supply chain opportunities or build our own vertical capabilities.
finding: Where suppliers will not cooperate, Boeing develops second sources or brings work in-house; it added Heroux-Devtek as a second 777X landing gear supplier.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: So this is not the idea of pulling demand forward or somehow accelerating production, this is filling skyline into the future.
finding: Boeing justified the 787 move to 14/month (confirmed September 2017) by a backlog of 700 aircraft and skyline sales into 2022, not by pulling demand forward.

speaker: John Langford, Aurora founder & CEO
quote: I look at us a very much as a people may have been wondering what Boeing was going to do in response to A³, I think you just found out.
finding: Aurora's CEO framed Boeing's acquisition of Aurora as its answer to Airbus's A³.
trigger: Airbus A³ Silicon Valley innovation outpost
response: Acquired Aurora Flight Sciences and aligned it with HorizonX

speaker: Greg Hyslop, Boeing CTO
quote: we want Aurora to stay Aurora, but be part of Boeing. So John and his team will report to me and that's a little different model than we've done in prior acquisitions
finding: Boeing acquired innovative talent (Aurora had beaten Boeing in early research competitions) and kept it semi-independent under the CTO.

speaker: Greg Hyslop, Boeing CTO
quote: we have every intention of having them maintain those relationships and continuing that work, so there should not be any change or concern there.
finding: When it bought a supplier to rival programs, Boeing publicly committed to keep supplying competitors rather than cut them off.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: recent changes in the marketplace, the discussions between Airbus and Bombardier don't change our plans. We have a strong strategy in place. We'll continue to look at our strategic alternatives, but we don't need to change the path that we're on.
finding: Boeing said the Airbus-Bombardier deal did not change its plans, but kept strategic alternatives open.
response: Keep MAX strategy; evaluate alternatives

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: And we don't see the recent announcements around the partnership plan or new production lines changing that process or changing our position on the fact that the trade matter needs to be addressed.
finding: Boeing kept its CSeries trade case going after Airbus announced an Alabama CSeries line that could avoid tariffs.
trigger: Airbus-Bombardier plan for a US (Alabama) CSeries line
response: Continue anti-dumping/subsidy case

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: BCA operating margins increased to 9.9% on higher 787 margins and strong execution on production programs, again, partially offset by the $256 million pretax charge on the KC-46 Tanker program.
finding: The KC-46 tanker took another $256 million charge in BCA in Q3 2017 (plus $73 million in BDS), holding BCA margin to 9.9% (11.6% excluding it).

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we extended the 787 accounting block by 100 units. This resulted in higher margins on the program and moderates the decline of deferred production balance
finding: Boeing extended the 787 accounting block by 100 units, raising reported program margin (it says cash is unaffected).

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: In that 100- to 150-seat category that you mentioned, the MAX 7 is performing strongly. And again, as most of our customers look at family of narrowbody products, the MAX family is the strongest family in the marketplace.
finding: Boeing's product answer to Airbus taking over the CSeries was the existing MAX 7 and MAX family, not a new small aircraft.
trigger: Airbus-Bombardier CSeries partnership targeting the 100-150 seat market
response: Relied on the MAX 7 within the MAX family; no new 100-150 seat program

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Some of the recent developments in the marketplace are not surprising to us. As we've said before, it's an attractive market with a lot of global competitors. We like competition. It makes us better. We're confident we can win, but it's important that everybody plays by the same rules.
finding: Boeing's first public response to the Airbus-CSeries tie-up played down the threat and repeated its fair-trade argument.
response: Downplayed the move and stressed its level-playing-field message

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: On your first question, relatively stable from a dollar basis. That's the best way to think about it for 2018.
finding: In October 2017 Boeing guided 2018 R&D as flat in dollars; by January 2018 it guided an increase to about $3.7 billion, citing timing shifts and tax reform (change of position).

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we don't see the 767 line as a sunsetting production line. It's a strong long-term production line, and it does have some growth opportunities for us.
finding: Boeing kept the 767 line (2.5/month, shared with the tanker) as a long-term product for the small-widebody segment rather than letting it run down.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: And we do have tools related to contractual obligations and regulatory matters, and if necessary, we're able to leverage those tools and make use of them.
finding: Boeing threatened to use contractual and regulatory levers against supplier consolidation (UTC-Rockwell Collins) it saw as not adding value.
trigger: UTC's proposed acquisition of Rockwell Collins
response: Remained skeptical and signalled readiness to use contractual rights and regulatory review

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: recent actions that you see that Airbus and Bombardier have announced are not actions that change our game plan. And while we execute our strategy, we're going to continue to evaluate all of our alternatives. ... We evaluate different opportunities for inorganic or partnership models as well. And we're going to continue to keep those options open.
finding: Boeing said the Airbus-Bombardier deal did not change its plan but kept partnership and inorganic options open; Embraer talks were announced about two months later (p. 1317).
response: No change to plan; kept inorganic and partnership options open

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we don't see the recent announcements around the partnership plan or new production lines changing that process or changing our position on the fact that the trade matter needs to be addressed.
finding: Boeing kept its trade case against the CSeries even after Airbus and Bombardier proposed a US (Alabama) assembly line to sidestep duties.
trigger: Airbus-Bombardier plan to assemble CSeries in Alabama
response: Maintained the Department of Commerce trade case against the CSeries

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: So when we make a decision like this, it's based on the fact that, for the long term, we have to have a fair and equal playing field. And we're mindful of how we're taking our actions on the trade case so that we respect our customers while we do that.
finding: Boeing accepted strain with customers and governments (UK, Canada) to pursue the trade case against a rival, putting a long-term level playing field first.
trigger: Airbus-Bombardier CSeries tie-up; concern over UK and Canadian defense orders
response: Kept the trade case while trying to limit damage to customer relationships

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We are evaluating production rates beyond the 57 a month. It's always part of our due diligence around production rate plans for the future.
finding: Boeing was studying 737 rates above 57/month, relying on productivity to fit higher rates in the existing Renton footprint.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We do see that as a market segment that is complementary to our 737 market segment, so we don't see those as overlapping segments. So this is really a separate decision
finding: In October 2017 Boeing treated the NMA as separate from, not overlapping, the 737; by March 2018 it acknowledged some cannibalization of single-aisle demand (p. 1275).

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we are sold out, more than sold out. In fact, we're quoting positions for the 737 MAX now out in 2023
finding: The 737 was sold out beyond the planned 57/month rate, with new MAX delivery positions being quoted in 2023.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we have to nail the transition to 52 a month this year while we bring the MAX fully up to speed, go to 57 a month next year, and then we'll continue to evaluate our options beyond that. But all of the market pressures are clearly upward.
finding: Despite acknowledged upward demand pressure, Boeing sequences rate increases one step at a time and defers any decision beyond 57/month until execution is proven.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we've had some challenges, as you said, on LEAP engine ramp-up with GE; those have been handled effectively. Spirit, working with us on the fuselages, we've handled those effectively.
finding: Boeing acknowledged LEAP engine ramp-up and Spirit fuselage supply problems during the 737 ramp, while claiming they were mitigated.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: So as we think about new airplanes, when we think about ramping up production rates, supply chain health is a fundamental requirement.
finding: Boeing treats supply-chain health as a gating condition for both new airplane launches and rate increases.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we just made the decision to go to 14 a month based on some deep analysis, long-term analysis. So we feel very strong that, that is a level we can hold for the longer run.
finding: Boeing decided to raise the 787 to 14 per month, justifying it by long-run demand analysis and an intent to sustain the rate.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: it's very clear to us that the 5 a month production rate or 3.5 month delivery rate that we've already moved to is the floor for the program
finding: Boeing cut the 777 to 5/month production (3.5 delivery) during the 777X transition and declared that the floor.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We have no committed production slots for Iranian jets, and that's been purposeful on our part. Now if, for some reason, that deal were to come back or to occur, it creates upside opportunity for us. But we're not going to be dependent on it.
finding: Boeing deliberately kept politically uncertain orders (Iran) out of its production skyline, treating them only as upside.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we see a significant widebody replacement wave coming early in the next decade. So between 787 and 777X coming online in 2020, both of those airplanes are going to be very well-positioned for that widebody replacement wave.
finding: Boeing times its widebody portfolio (787 plus 777X from 2020) to catch an expected early-2020s replacement wave.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We still see that as a marketplace that's 4,000 to 5,000 airplanes. We see it as an airplane that's 220 to 270 seats and about a 5,000 nautical mile range airplane.
finding: Boeing sized the NMA market at 4,000-5,000 aircraft and defined the concept as 220-270 seats with about 5,000 nm range.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: This is now all about closing the business case. So we haven't made a decision yet to launch or not. That is a decision we'll get to during the next year here.
finding: In May 2018 Boeing had not decided to launch the NMA and framed the decision as contingent on closing the business case within about a year.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: It's an airplane that would enter the market 2025 time frame. Not a technology push, it's going to be more about the production system of the future to hit a price point
finding: Boeing's NMA thinking targets 2025 entry and relies on production-system cost rather than new airframe technology to hit a price point.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: closing the business case will be dependent on our confidence in that production system.
finding: Boeing makes its NMA launch decision explicitly conditional on confidence in a new, lower-cost production system.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We don't see this as a technology push on engines or avionics or any of the internal systems in the airplane. Again, in large case, the ability to reuse or modify 787 systems or 737 systems or use existing engine technology packaged in a new way.
finding: For the NMA, Boeing planned to reuse 787/737 systems and existing engine technology rather than require a new-technology engine.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We'll build our fourth-generation composite wing now for 777X. That's a technology that we've decided to bring inside that would be ready and available for NMA.
finding: Boeing brought composite wing manufacturing in-house on the 777X partly to make it available for a future NMA.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we've already stated that whatever challenges may arise, that we're going to be in compliance with WTO rules, right? It's important that we all play by the same rules. Boeing is committed to that. We expect our global competitors to play by the same rules.
finding: Boeing used the WTO ruling against Airbus subsidies to press a level-playing-field message while pledging to comply with any ruling against itself.
trigger: Final WTO ruling in Boeing's case against Airbus launch aid
response: Publicly welcomed the ruling, left remedies to governments, pledged its own WTO compliance

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: I don't see it as a deal that we must do from Boeing's standpoint, but it clearly adds strategic value if we can get to the finish line.
finding: Boeing described the Embraer combination as strategically valuable but optional, signalling it would walk away rather than overpay.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: it also gives us more resources and, I'll say, an engineering talent set that's complementary to Boeing's, aligned from a culture and engineering discipline standpoint. So it gives us some team and talent synergies.
finding: Access to Embraer's engineering talent was an explicit rationale for the Boeing-Embraer tie-up.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: When I think about cash deployment, organic investment remains #1. Returning value to our shareholders, 100% free cash flow remains #2. And then targeted acquisitions that complement our organic strategy is #3.
finding: Boeing's stated cash-deployment order is organic investment first, 100% FCF return second, targeted acquisitions third.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: rebuilding some vertical capacity inside of our company. And we don't need to be vertical everywhere, but there are some key areas where we want to be vertical for the future
finding: Boeing was selectively re-verticalizing (avionics, actuation, composite wings, parts distribution) rather than relying fully on suppliers.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: And we found a way where we can take cost out to the benefit of our customers and create intellectual property value that differentiates our products, creates better performance in the field compared to our competitors. And targeted areas of propulsion integration, nacelle integration fit in that category.
finding: Boeing took MAX nacelle inlet work in-house, framing propulsion and nacelle integration as a cost and IP lever against competitors.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: really, this time through as we evaluate the business case, looking at it through that life cycle lens.
finding: Boeing evaluates the NMA business case including aftermarket and lifecycle services revenue, not just aircraft sales.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we recently increased our year-end guidance for this year to $15 billion to $15.5 billion of cash.
finding: Boeing raised 2018 operating cash flow guidance to $15.0-15.5 billion, driven by production rate growth and 787 profitability.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We said it before the KLX acquisition that we're going to return 100% free cash flow, and I'm saying it again, after the KLX acquisition, we're returning 100% free cash flow.
finding: Boeing kept its 100% FCF return pledge unchanged after the KLX acquisition, showing M&A was not allowed to crowd out shareholder returns (persistence).

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we've got more than 460 orders for the MAX 10. So the customer interest has been very high. And if you just look at the MAX 10 versus the competing A321 family, we create 5% to 10% operating cost advantage for our customers.
finding: Boeing answered the A321neo LR transatlantic threat by pointing to the MAX 10 and a claimed operating-cost edge, not by launching a new aircraft.
trigger: A321neo LR range targeting transatlantic routes
response: Relied on the MAX 10 derivative (460+ orders) and claimed 5-10% operating cost advantage

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: And while I can't comment on our competitor's approach, what I can comment on is our disciplined approach. We're going to maintain that approach.
finding: Boeing refused to follow Airbus's rate 70-75 talk, pointing to 20 successful rate breaks and supply-chain limits.
response: Hold disciplined 737 ramp (52->57)

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: However, the program did see additional cost growth in the quarter of $334 million after tax primarily due to higher estimated cost of incorporating changes into 6 flight tests and 2 early build aircraft
finding: The fixed-price KC-46 tanker, a commercial derivative, kept overrunning, with another $334 million after-tax charge in Q2 2018.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Commercial Airplanes generated revenue of $14.5 billion, reflecting 194 deliveries with operating margins of 11.4%. Continued healthy sales activity contributed to 239 net new airplane orders worth $16 billion during the quarter, including 91 widebody orders
finding: In mid-2018 Boeing's order intake (239 net) outpaced deliveries (194), adding to a backlog of nearly 5,900.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: As we transition production to the 777X, we expect 777 deliveries of approximately 3.5 per month in 2018 and 2019... we continue to believe the rate plan we've put in place establishes a floor for the program and supports our production bridge from the current 777 to the 777X.
finding: Boeing cut the legacy 777 to a 3.5/month floor and used freighter orders to bridge to the 777X.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: earlier this month, we signed an MOU with Embraer for formation of a joint venture comprising the commercial aircraft and services business of Embraer... Additionally, we will create another joint venture to promote and develop new markets and applications for defense products and services, especially the KC-390
finding: Boeing chose a JV structure to take in Embraer's commercial aircraft and services business, plus a second JV for the KC-390.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We continue to anticipate completing the remaining $12 billion repurchase authorization over the next 18 to 24 months. And since the end of 2012, we returned more than $48 billion to our shareholders through dividend and share repurchase. At the same time, we've invested more than $30 billion
finding: Since 2012 Boeing had returned $48 billion to shareholders, well above the $30 billion it invested strategically, and planned $12 billion more of buybacks.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we extended the 787 accounting block by 100 units. This resulted in higher margins on the program and, therefore, moderated the decline of deferred production balance this quarter.
finding: Boeing used program-accounting block extensions (100 more 787s) to lift reported 787 margins.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: several lessons learned. One includes digitizing our engineering at a more detailed level upfront. This is the model-based engineering initiatives that we have underway, as an example. Also, more significant investments in system integration labs upfront to de-risk development
finding: After the tanker overruns, Boeing front-loaded de-risking through model-based engineering and system integration labs on 777X and planned the same for the NMA.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: what we're hearing from customers is we need something that has the comfort and twin-aisle benefit of widebodies but has narrowbody economics, and that's, frankly, the challenge of closing the business case... And if we don't, we'll continue down the path with our current product lines.
finding: Boeing named twin-aisle comfort at narrowbody economics as the hurdle for the NMA and said that if the case did not close it would keep its current products.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: it's important to note that pricing is holding up. It's driven by a number of different parameters, including supply versus demand that you're pointing out, but it's also value... in many cases, we think about pricing, and we're looking at it holistically across airplanes and services
finding: Boeing did not echo Airbus's scarcity pricing message; it said pricing was holding up and priced airplanes and services together.
trigger: Airbus comments on pricing power from slot scarcity (Farnborough 2018)
response: Said pricing was holding up and priced airplanes and services together

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we figured that into our overall organic investment profile and that phased R&D plan that I mentioned earlier... We don't need to be vertical everywhere... The work on APUs with Safran is one of those areas. You mentioned avionics. It's another area.
finding: Boeing folded selected vertical investments (APUs with Safran, avionics, interiors) into its phased R&D plan alongside new-platform spending.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we'll make great decisions not only informed by market pressures, but informed by our ability to execute them successfully... And while I can't comment on our competitor's approach, what I can comment on is our disciplined approach. We're going to maintain that approach.
finding: Asked whether it must match Airbus's 70-75/month talk, Boeing declined to follow and kept 57 as its next step, tied to execution capability.
response: Kept disciplined plan of 52 now and 57 in 2019; no commitment to match

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We've seen constraints with what we talked about, with our fuselages in Spirit as well as with CFM... So we're working with them, putting resources into -- and particularly into Spirit, additional resources into our factory and out in our ramp to really burn off the open jobs
finding: When Spirit and CFM fell behind at 52/month, Boeing surged its own people into Spirit and finished incomplete aircraft out of sequence on the ramp.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: how we can hold a particular rate increase for a period of time to really optimize the efficiency... capital, tooling, people... can they be ready in time? But equally important, looking at all the other scope that they have within the supply chain that is also potentially going up in rate
finding: Boeing's rate-readiness gate checked whether a new rate could be held long enough to pay back, and whether shared suppliers could cope with other customers' ramps at the same time.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: How long can you maintain that rate?... Everything needs to work. And if it doesn't work, you shouldn't go up in rate, obviously... if your supply chain or yourself can't meet that demand, there's no upside for you or your customer or your supplier to put yourself into that risk profile
finding: Asked about Airbus's talk of 70/month on the A320, Boeing said it would not raise rates beyond what capital, sustainability and its supply chain could support.
response: No matching commitment; rate decisions stay gated on capital, sustainability and supply-chain readiness

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we're also going through a very disciplined gated process to ensure the business case is very solid, to ensure that we're transferring technology. No big leaps here. It's really leveraging that $60 billion of investment I mentioned over the last 10 years. Leveraging that, derisking the program, getting the nonrecurring effort down to a manageable state
finding: Boeing designed the NMA to avoid technology leaps and hold nonrecurring cost down by reusing prior investment, putting business-case discipline ahead of the 2025 date customers wanted.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we stepped back, obviously, after the 787 and really kind of assessed overall risk profile and as well as IP and so on and where we want to have critical points in the airplane as well as through the life cycle lens... Do you buy it? Do you partner it? Do you develop it? Everything's open for discussion.
finding: After the heavily outsourced 787, Boeing reassessed which critical content to keep in-house for risk and IP, choosing buy, partner or build case by case.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: First priority, organic... and then the partnerships potentially or inorganic... On Embraer, it's much broader... It's not only a complementary product line offering, whether it's the KC-390 or the E2 or the E1, it's also capability and it is also services... a company that we've been collaborating with for over 30 years.
finding: Boeing chose a JV with a long-time partner, Embraer, to fill product, engineering-capability and services gaps that organic investment would not.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we spent a lot of time derisking this portfolio over the last number of years... doesn't mean you don't take risk, but how do you make sure you don't have concurrent risk on top of risk and how you're thinking about the risk mitigation plans
finding: Boeing's risk appetite allowed risk but avoided stacking concurrent risks, such as overlapping development programs or model changes during rate breaks.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We've done 20 production rate ramp-ups in our commercial lines since 2010... when we stepped from 42 to 47 a month, at that point, about 10% to 15% of the 737s were the new MAX model... This year, about 40% to 45% of the airplanes are MAXs. So we're mid-stride on the model transition while we're doing our rate ramp-up.
finding: Boeing had made about 20 rate increases since 2010 and stacked the 52/month step on top of the NG-to-MAX changeover, which added complexity.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Seats have been a supply chain challenge for us for some time period, and that's been quite visible. Frankly, that's one of the reasons we recently launched our new seat joint venture with Adient. It's to create some more supply chain flexibility
finding: Boeing answered a chronic seat-supplier bottleneck by forming a JV (Adient) to create an alternative source.
response: Launched seat JV with Adient

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: aircraft a month to 52 a month on our 737 line, and that's been a bit of a challenge with some of our supply chain. We've seen some of the public challenges around the Spirit delivery of fuselages, CFM with delivery of engines... in July, we delivered 29 737s, which was below our 52 a month production rate.
finding: Boeing's 2018 step to 52/month broke its supply chain (Spirit fuselages, CFM engines), and July 737 deliveries fell to 29.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: in some cases, creating new sources of supply; in some cases, bringing resources to bear, putting them into our supplier plants to help them be successful... What I do see is general supply chain pressure as we raise up rates. And to me, that's a great problem to have, right?
finding: Boeing treated supplier strain from rate increases as normal and handled it with dual sourcing and its own staff inside supplier plants, not slower ramps.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: roughly 1/3 of our 737s are being delivered to China... We're building a 737 finishing center in China. That's part of that equation, too. It's really a win-win as it adds jobs and capacity in China. And it's also helping us ramp up our U.S. production manufacturing in Renton.
finding: Boeing used a China 737 completion center to add capacity and to support its Renton ramp, with China taking about a third of 737s.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we use that system, pulled it ahead, onto our current 777 to de-risk it. So as 777X moves into the production system, we already have a mature automation system.
finding: Boeing reduced new-model risk by proving new automation on the current 777 before the 777X entered production.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we brought about 600 additional people into our 737 line to help with the recovery actions. They're going to stay... All of the market signals are telling us we could support a production rate higher than 57 a month. So we're taking a close look at that. We're well within our decision windows.
finding: In September 2018 Boeing was actively considering a 737 rate above 57/month for 2020 and kept 600 extra workers to support further ramps.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: it's winning, more than 500 orders since we've announced... It's got about a 5% to 10% operating seat cost advantage over our competition. It's got a 5% trip cost advantage over our competition.
finding: Boeing marketed the MAX 10 derivative against the rival's narrowbody on claimed 5-10% seat-cost and 5% trip-cost advantages, with more than 500 orders.
trigger: Competition in the large single-aisle segment
response: MAX 10 stretch derivative (launched 2017) marketed on seat and trip cost

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: This again, I think, is the advantage of our revised approach to how we do development programs, feathering them in, in succession rather than doing them all concurrently... We learned some tough lessons there... It's one of the reasons we decided to bring the composite wing manufacturing in-house
finding: After the 787's troubles Boeing sequenced development programs one at a time and brought 777X composite wing manufacturing in-house.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: with 340 orders in backlog, at a similar point in time on the original 777 program, we had about 70 to 80 orders in backlog... We still have some work to do on filling the bridge, particularly out for 2020 slots.
finding: Boeing judged the 777X upgrade successful on orders (340 vs 70-80 for the original 777 at a similar stage) but still had gaps in 2020 bridge slots.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Not only are we looking at the net present value of the airplane itself in our traditional business case analysis, but also with the investments we're making in services and verticals. How does that create lifecycle value that could be factored into the business case?
finding: Boeing tried to close the NMA business case by counting services and vertical-integration lifecycle value on top of the airplane's own NPV.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Boeing will recognize the investments through an after-tax charge of $541 million in the quarter. This strategy reflects a commercial investment mindset, a deliberate and purposeful decision to position ourselves to capture significant future market opportunity
finding: Boeing accepted up-front losses ($541 million after tax) to win long-duration franchises, a commercial-style investment approach applied to T-X and MQ-25 bids.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we continue to anticipate completing the remaining $9.6 billion of repurchase authorization over the next 12 to 18 months... we remain committed to returning approximately 100% of our free cash flow to shareholders while continuing to invest in future growth opportunities.
finding: In October 2018 Boeing committed to finishing $9.6 billion of buybacks within 12-18 months and to returning about 100% of free cash flow to shareholders.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We are taking some lessons learned from our recent 52-a-month step and applying those. That includes ramping up staffing earlier... This year was especially challenging as we stepped to 52 a month and we also had major model mix changes. Roughly half of the airplanes this year are NGs and half are MAXs.
finding: Boeing blamed the troubled 2018 ramp on raising the rate to 52 while switching half of output from NG to MAX, and planned earlier staffing for 57.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: it's not something that changes our near-term modeling and analysis... our decision drivers around stepping to 57 a month will be health of the production system, the supply chain, our ability to execute that in a way that's smooth for our customers and profitable for our company.
finding: Boeing kept 737 rate decisions separate from US-China trade risk, driven by backlog and production readiness.
response: No change to the planned step to 57/month

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: NPV, return on invested capital, I'd say a very traditional way to look at a business case. But as Dennis said, not just looking at the contract quantity but looking at the broader market opportunities and what it would take to win
finding: Boeing judged new programs on NPV and ROIC over the broader market opportunity and what it would take to win, not just the initial contract quantity.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we got to get the supply chain on all elements fully healthy at 52... That will give us our confidence to continue that rate up to 57... the capital investment and the sustainability and what's fundamentally driving the demand... What's their financial condition? How much of those do we think will be paid in cash?
finding: Boeing's rate-break criteria combined supplier stability at the current rate, required capital, and the quality and financing of the underlying demand.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: As you said, we are in an oversold position because of the way we make those rate increases, and we assume that we will have movement and then try to find that, I'll say, kind of optimum place to -- and production meeting market demands.
finding: Boeing deliberately set rates below demand so the skyline stays oversold and can absorb customer deferrals.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: there's opportunities to shorten it. And we're working every day to try to shorten that lead time as best we can because that gives us more flexibility obviously in the marketplace.
finding: Boeing was working to shorten the roughly 24-month supplier notice needed for a rate break, to gain flexibility in rate decisions.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: since 2012, I think we've taken a share count down by over 200 million shares and the dividend up close to 250%... So we've set approximately 100% of our free cash going back through dividend and repurchase. And again, that's what you should expect from us.
finding: Before the MAX crisis Boeing's policy was to return roughly 100% of free cash flow to shareholders through dividends and buybacks.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we generated record operating cash flow of $15.3 billion. We repurchased 26.1 million shares for $9 billion and made dividend payments totaling $3.9 billion in 2018... our Board of Directors authorized a new $20 billion share repurchase program and a 20% increase in our quarterly dividend.
finding: At peak cash generation in 2018 Boeing returned $12.9 billion to shareholders, then authorized a new $20 billion buyback and a 20% dividend increase in December 2018.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: The combined 777, 777X production rate is 5 per month. As we transition to 777X, we continue to expect the delivery rate to be approximately 3.5 aircraft per month in 2019
finding: Boeing cut combined 777/777X deliveries to about 3.5/month in 2019, below the 5/month production rate, during the 777X transition.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: In 2018, we invested $5 billion in R&D and CapEx, repurchased $9 billion of Boeing stock and paid $3.9 billion in dividends... Over the last 5 years, we've repurchased more than 205 million shares and increased our dividend by more than 180%.
finding: In 2018 Boeing spent $12.9 billion on shareholder returns against $5 billion on R&D and capex, and it had retired more than 205 million shares over five years.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We ended the quarter with $8.6 billion of cash and marketable securities, $13.8 billion of debt and stable credit ratings.
finding: Boeing ended 2018 with $8.6 billion of cash against $13.8 billion of debt after buybacks and the KLX acquisition.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Operating cash flow for 2019 is forecasted to increase by $2 billion to be between $17 billion and $17.5 billion... In all, BCA is expected to deliver between 895 and 905 airplanes... Commercial airplane operating margin guidance is set to be between 14.5% and 15%
finding: Boeing's pre-grounding 2019 plan assumed about 900 deliveries, a 14.5-15% commercial margin and $17-17.5 billion of operating cash flow.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We expect research and development spending to increase to approximately $4.1 billion in 2019 with approximately 60% related to BCA... going forward, we expect our overall R&D spending as a percentage of revenue to be relatively stable.
finding: Boeing budgeted $4.1 billion of R&D for 2019, about 60% for commercial airplanes, and held R&D flat as a share of revenue.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: we've taken our own actions to reduce cyclicality in our business. This includes remaining disciplined in our production rate decisions, derisking our pension liabilities, strategically phasing our research and development spending, creating labor stability with long-term contracts and expanding our services business
finding: Boeing tried to reduce cyclicality through rate discipline, phased R&D, pension de-risking, long labor contracts and services growth.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We still have some areas that need work, including engines. And we're doing some additional work with CFM, including deploying some additional Boeing personnel to their factories and to their sub-tier suppliers.
finding: Boeing sent its own staff into CFM and CFM's sub-tier suppliers to fix late engines holding back the 737.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: Some elements of the supply chain have already moved to that position. We still have some work to do before we move the entire line to 57 a month... I think we learned some lessons from the 52 a month step that we did last year.
finding: Boeing said it had learned lessons from the 2018 step to 52 and was staging the 57/month ramp by moving parts of the supply chain up first.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: assuming a positive market response or depending on the market response, we'll make the final launch decision next year... maturing the technologies, reducing risk in parallel to protect a 2025 EIS... if we launch NMA, it will feather in on the backside of 777X.
finding: Boeing kept de-risking NMA technology in parallel to protect a 2025 entry into service, with launch depending on customer response and R&D phased after 777X.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: But the competition is only getting tougher, and we're not going to slow down. So the pace of progress you've seen is the pace of progress we aim to sustain. And what we're looking for is continued year-over-year margin and cash flow growth.
finding: Having hit mid-teens commercial margins, Boeing set no ceiling and pointed to tougher competition as the reason to keep pushing margin and cash growth.
response: Continued year-over-year margin and cash-flow growth targets

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: there's also a big benefit from the high level of manufacturing commonality between the -10 and 9... So on the pricing side, it's holding up well there as well just because of the value it's creating for our customers.
finding: Boeing said 787 pricing was holding up and credited the family's manufacturing commonality for margin gains.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: depending on the market response and our ability to build the right kind of group of launch customers, then we get to an official launch or authority to launch decision next year... there are also decisions related to the enterprise transformation objectives that we have in terms of production system for the future.
finding: Boeing made NMA launch depend on securing a group of launch customers and on the program's value as a pilot for a future production system.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: how could we use an NMA investment to think about leverage and creating the production system for the even more distant future, whether that be some future narrowbody airplane or other alternatives that we might invest in. But think of this as a continuum of R&D efforts.
finding: Boeing saw the NMA partly as a stepping stone whose production system could later serve a future narrowbody, placing a new single-aisle after the NMA.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: it's still kind of early introduction, right? So just take that into account. But net-net, you're in a similar margin profile as you are on the NG.
finding: Boeing said the MAX re-engine carried margins similar to the 737NG, so the transition did not dilute narrowbody profitability.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We still have work to go to get CFM to be supporting our 52 a month production rate and having those systems synchronized; and then even more work to go yet to get them ramped up to 57 a month.
finding: In January 2019 CFM could not yet support 52/month, let alone 57, which made the engine supplier the binding limit on 737 rates.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: And in some cases, it's skyline positioning. In some cases, it's services and training support. In some cases, there are other currencies that we can trade with customers... And in some cases, cash may be part of the solution... I don't see this as an additional material event for us
finding: Boeing planned to settle MAX customer compensation case by case, mixing delivery slots, services and training, and cash, and in May 2019 it played down the financial exposure.
trigger: Airline customers publicly seeking compensation for the MAX grounding
response: Customer-by-customer compensation using skyline positions, services and training, and some cash

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: the fundamental nature of traffic has changed so that it's no longer a cyclical environment. It's a much more steady growth kind of environment... it's also how we're thinking about development program phasing and how we make our investments and our production line discipline, rate discipline.
finding: Boeing believed air travel had become non-cyclical and designed rate and investment plans around steady year-over-year cash growth.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: There's demand, right? We got a great skyline, great demand for the airplane. But to get to 57, and I'll say not be healthy and have an optimized production system, isn't the right answer. ... Not a demand issue, right? It's not a backlog issue. It's about production -- stability in production and supply chain health.
finding: From the start of the grounding Boeing said production and supplier stability, not demand, would limit its return to 57 a month.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: a lot of the work that we did upfront on this disciplined gated process, reuse, just prototyping. So -- and money we've spent in labs upfront, I think after 4 airplanes, you start to see the benefit of that investment. ... doing this upfront has derisked the program. That was the intent.
finding: Boeing ran the 777X as a deliberately de-risked derivative, spending on labs, prototyping and reuse up front, and saw its remaining risk as mainly the engine.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Dash 9 entry into service, but looking at the timing also and the demand for the Dash 8 and see if that still makes sense and do we want to push that out and how do we want to manage that.
finding: Boeing reconsidered the timing of the smaller 777-8, prepared to push it out and manage the 777 family mix against demand.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: campaign reviews, it used to be 777 bridge. So that was where company energy was in the 777 bridge. That shifted now. So certainly fill in 777X skyline. That's a big priority ... And now 87 at 14 a month, obviously, a little more energy going into filling that skyline as well.
finding: By mid-2019 Boeing's sales effort had moved from bridging the 777 to filling 777X and 787-at-14 skylines, a sign that widebody demand was softening.
trigger: Widebody skyline gaps at the planned 787 rate of 14 and the 777X ramp
response: Refocused sales campaigns on 777X and 787 slots

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Is there an opportunity to be more efficient? I'd have a hard time sitting up here telling you there isn't. ... Can we bring in a third party or one of our banks to help near term? Can we work something out on payment terms?
finding: Boeing kept pushing suppliers for efficiency during the MAX crisis while offering bank financing and payment-term relief to those under strain.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: In April, we reduced the 737 production rate to 42 per month to accommodate the pause in MAX deliveries. Both within Boeing and our supply chain, we are using this time to improve the production system health and stability.
finding: Boeing responded to the MAX grounding with a partial cut to 42 a month rather than a halt, keeping the line and suppliers running and storing the output.
response: Cut 737 rate to 42/month in April 2019

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: We recorded negative $0.6 billion of operating cash and paid $1.2 billion in dividends, reflecting a 20% increase in dividends per share from last year.
finding: Months into the grounding Boeing was paying a dividend 20% higher than a year earlier, even with negative operating cash.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: aligned with our targeted vertical integration strategy to strengthen internal capabilities, increase innovation and provide greater end-to-end value for our airline customers, we entered into an agreement to acquire EnCore Group, an aerospace interiors company.
finding: Boeing kept pursuing targeted vertical integration through acquisitions during the MAX crisis, bringing supplier capabilities such as interiors in-house.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: as announced at the Paris Air Show, we're excited about Boeing's first off-platform component service program with British Airways for the airline's A320 and A320neo aircraft.
finding: Boeing's services arm began servicing its rival's aircraft, winning its first component contract for British Airways' A320/A320neo fleet.
trigger: Services growth strategy extending to non-Boeing fleets
response: Won component services for Airbus A320/A320neo at British Airways

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: BCA revenue and earnings were reduced by $5.6 billion of pretax charge related to our estimate of potential concessions and other considerations to customers ... We also booked an additional $1.7 billion of program costs on the 737 in the second quarter.
finding: Boeing booked the whole estimated MAX customer-compensation cost up front ($5.6B) plus $1.7B of extra 737 program costs in Q2 2019.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: So I can't comment on our competitors' comments that you mentioned, but I can comment on the fact that our customers see value in the 787 Dreamliner and the 777X. ... with the 787 currently running at 14 a month, we're continuing to gain efficiency on that line, and that's allowing us to be even more competitive in the marketplace.
finding: Accused by competitors of oversupplying widebodies and pricing aggressively, Boeing defended its 787 rate of 14 and said cost efficiency let it compete harder on price.
trigger: Competitors' claims that Boeing was oversupplying widebodies at very aggressive prices
response: Kept 787 at 14/month and used efficiency gains to compete

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: We see a potential market there for 4,000 to 5,000 aircraft ... when and if that business case closes, we would make a launch decision. We still see it as a 2-step decision process ... And we're not going to run to any artificial time line.
finding: Boeing sized the NMA market at 4,000-5,000 aircraft but would launch only if the business case closed, with no fixed timeline.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: Part of that business case is addressing development program risk, as you noted, and we are investing significantly in improving development program performance. ... model-based engineering, our digital transformation, production system of the future. These are all important elements of reducing development cost
finding: After troubled programs, Boeing made proof that digital engineering tools cut development risk and cost a condition for launching the NMA.
trigger: Analyst concern over MAX, 787, 747-8 and KC-46 development troubles

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: Obviously, CFM with the engine, Spirit on the fuselage, as examples there where we've been able to increase -- improve our production's health and stability by having them run at a higher than 42 a month production rate. With CFM, for example, we're also working to sustain that higher production rate to make sure we have sufficient engine spares
finding: During the MAX grounding Boeing kept CFM (engines) and Spirit (fuselages) producing above its own 42 a month to rebuild buffers and engine spares, protecting its bottleneck suppliers.
response: Kept key suppliers above Boeing's rate to catch up to master schedule

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: if regulatory approvals extend significantly and return to service is significantly delayed, then we would consider things like lower production rates or a temporary shutdown to the production line. Those are not decisions we would make lightly. If you think about our production line against 600-some suppliers, hundreds of thousands of jobs
finding: Boeing resisted a MAX production shutdown in 2019 mainly to protect its 600-plus suppliers and their jobs, keeping it as a last resort.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: We're not just applying automation to how we used to build to airplanes, which is the first step of efficiency. But when we design airplanes to take advantage of automation in our factory systems, there's a whole new wave of productivity that we gain.
finding: Boeing saw design-for-automation and digital engineering as the main source of advantage in any future airplane, as much as the product itself.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: We're still working towards a 2025 sort of time line for entry into service. ... we still expect that to be a 2-step decision process where we do authority to offer and then authority to launch. ... If it does, we'll go. If not, we've got other investments we can make.
finding: In August 2019 Boeing still targeted 2025 NMA entry into service through a staged offer-then-launch process, willing to walk away if the business case failed.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: if you look more broadly at our commercial production plans, in particular 787 profitability and where we're at in the production profile of the 787 at 14 a month, that will be another cash tailwind for us next year. ... we expect 2020 to be a cash growth year for us.
finding: In August 2019 Boeing expected 2020 cash to grow on MAX deliveries and 787 at 14 a month; within months both assumptions were reversed.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: we have a bias towards stability. ... if we had to make a change to production rate, in some cases, it might make more sense to temporarily halt production rather than try to change the rate from 42 a month to some lower number. It may actually be more efficient to temporarily halt.
finding: Boeing's rate logic favoured a clean temporary halt over running the line at a very low rate, which foreshadowed the January 2020 MAX suspension.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
