quote: even during this year while we've been largely on the sidelines in terms of MAX orders, with IAG coming forward for 200 MAXes around the Paris Air Show. And that's just a signpost of the demand signals and confidence for the future.
finding: While out of the order market during the grounding, Boeing pointed to IAG's 200-MAX commitment at the Paris Air Show as proof its narrowbody was still competitive.
response: Won a 200-aircraft MAX commitment from IAG at the Paris Air Show

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: in the widebody production system, those tend to be longer lead. We don't have as much skyline flexibility to trade positions because those airplanes tend to be more tailored for individual customers. So that is a risk area for us.
finding: Boeing saw widebody skylines as less flexible than narrowbody ones, so missing orders (e.g. China) translate quickly into rate cuts.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: We have taken some actions to make it more rate-flexible so we can be productive regardless of rate, but our clear preference is to continue operating that production line at 14 a month.
finding: In September 2019 Boeing clearly preferred to keep the 787 at 14 a month; six weeks later it announced a cut to 12.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: I can tell you the pricing on the 787 is holding up in the marketplace, and we're winning in the marketplace because we're creating more value for our customers. ... but largely pricing is being held up in the market because of customer value.
finding: Asked whether Boeing was cutting 787 prices to fill its skyline, the CEO said pricing was holding up and credited product value and cost reduction.
trigger: Market talk of aggressive 787 pricing to fill the skyline
response: Held that 787 pricing was intact

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: We have pulled some resources and people to focus on the MAX. ... But we have a dedicated team that's continuing to work on NMA, making good progress on risk reduction and the business case. We're not ready to make that decision yet ... We're not going to rush to a particular time line on that decision.
finding: The MAX crisis pulled people and resources off new-airplane work, and Boeing refused to commit to an NMA decision date.
response: Diverted resources to MAX; NMA decision deferred

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: we expect to maintain our current production rate of 42 deliveries per month ... This will be followed by incremental rate increases that would bring our production rate to 57 by late 2020. ... we might need to consider possible further rate reductions or other options including a temporary shutdown of the MAX production line.
finding: In October 2019 Boeing still planned to hold 42 a month and ramp to 57 by late 2020, with shutdown only a contingency; three months later it suspended production.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: We remain convinced that both the Commercial Aviation and the KC-390 joint ventures will increase competition in the market and create value for our customers ... We now expect the transaction to close in early 2020.
finding: Under Muilenburg Boeing justified the Embraer JVs as a way to sharpen competition in commercial aviation and defense airlift, expecting closing in early 2020.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: As part of our practice for a significant market such as China, we have forecasted orders from operators based on the country as part of our skyline assumptions. The lack of orders from China in the past couple of years has put pressure on the production rate.
finding: Boeing's 787 rate plan had assumed unsold Chinese orders, so the US-China trade dispute forced a rate cut once those orders failed to come.
trigger: US-China trade tension; no Chinese orders for about two years
response: Cut 787 from 14 to 12 per month from late 2020 for about 2 years

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: The GE9X engine remains the pacing item as we work towards first flight of the 777X. GE, our engine supplier, has made good progress to address the durability challenges. ... we now expect first delivery of the 777-9 to be in early 2021.
finding: Durability problems with the GE9X from GE, Boeing's 777X engine supplier, pushed first delivery to early 2021, showing the schedule risk of relying on one engine supplier.
response: 777-9 first delivery moved to early 2021

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: The delivery rate is expected to be at approximately 3 per month in 2020 as we mitigate some of the impact of the slide in 777X time line by producing more 777 current generation aircraft.
finding: Boeing used extra production of the legacy 777 to bridge the 777X delay.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: In the third quarter, we paid $1.2 billion in dividends. And as I previously mentioned, we have temporarily paused our share repurchase program. Our long-term balanced cash deployment strategy and commitment to returning cash to shareholders remains unchanged.
finding: Seven months into the grounding Boeing still paid a $1.2B quarterly dividend and called the buyback pause temporary, holding to its shareholder-return commitment.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We raised additional debt in the quarter, increasing the balance by $5.5 billion, primarily to fund the Embraer acquisition and also to help shore up liquidity position as we work through the current MAX challenges.
finding: Boeing borrowed $5.5B in Q3 2019 mainly to pre-fund the Embraer acquisition, showing it was still willing to lever up for the JV during the MAX crisis.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: production rate discipline is one of our key management principles, something that will drive stable, long-term growth. Our prospects for the long-term widebody market haven't changed. ... we see a market for roughly 1,000 new small- to medium-sized widebodies over the next decade.
finding: Boeing presented the first-ever 787 rate cut as rate discipline, while still expecting a widebody replacement wave of about 1,000 aircraft.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: don't anticipate share repo until we've got return to service. We're executing on the production rates and reaching the stability that we expect. And once we get to that level, then we'll reassess our cash deployment efforts. And of course, as I mentioned, we've got additional debt on the balance sheet and we plan to address that as well.
finding: Boeing made any buyback restart conditional on the MAX's return to service, stable production rates and debt reduction.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: Our long-term objectives and targets have not changed. We're still driving towards a mid-teen margins business. We haven't altered our plans for that.
finding: In October 2019 Boeing still held to its mid-teens commercial margin target despite the grounding and rate cuts.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: we are continuing to drive forward with our efforts evaluating NMA. We still are not at a decision point nor are we ready to be at a decision point yet. ... So still a project of interest. We're still looking at a middle of the next decade entry-into-service time frame
finding: In October 2019 Boeing kept the NMA alive but undecided, still aiming for mid-2020s entry into service; by January 2020 new leadership had put it under reassessment.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: We have had discussions with customers who, given time lines and fleet needs, may want to move skyline positions. In some cases, model differences or model trades are options. So as we think through customer compensation models ... there is some trade space around delivery profiles in skyline positions.
finding: Boeing compensated MAX customers partly with delivery-slot moves and model swaps rather than only cash, to keep the backlog intact.
response: Offer skyline repositioning and model trades as compensation

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, CEO
quote: in terms of our priorities for capital allocation, those priorities haven't changed. As we've always said, our #1 use of cash is investment in organic growth, and that continues to be the case.
finding: Muilenburg insisted that organic investment remained Boeing's first use of cash despite higher expected certification costs after the MAX.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: getting stability in the factory, which we have done at the 42 a month, and then storing of the airplanes and putting them into preservation and keeping them in that preserved state and operating them.
finding: During the 2019 grounding Boeing kept building MAXs at 42 a month and storing them in preservation, rather than halting output.
response: Cut rate to 42/month and stored undelivered aircraft

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: So we see the -- more and more, I think of the win-win, not just in the go to market but also within the supply chain, within the engineering function and also within the production system side ... there's some great best practices that we'll reverse-integrate in.
finding: Boeing's case for the Embraer JV rested on engineering, supply-chain and first-time-quality synergies as well as market access.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we've also decided to temporarily suspend the 737 production beginning this month. We believe this decision is least disruptive to maintaining long-term production system and supply chain health.
finding: Once the MAX grounding dragged on, Boeing chose to suspend 737 production entirely rather than keep building aircraft it could not deliver.
trigger: MAX grounding extending into 2020 with 400+ aircraft stored
response: Suspended 737 production from January 2020

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We'll take the time to reassess our product development strategy in a fairly methodical way. I think that's a natural course for any new incoming leader to take. We'll return to this topic in future discussions. This is not intended to delay, simply to refresh.
finding: The new CEO paused and reopened Boeing's product development strategy on arrival, while insisting it was a refresh rather than a delay.
trigger: CEO change during the MAX crisis
response: Reassess product development strategy

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: continuing to progress the 777X and the 737 MAX 10 and further growth of our global services business and full implementation of our Embraer partnership.
finding: In January 2020 Boeing still committed to fully implementing the Embraer partnership, a position it reversed three months later by terminating the deal.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Clearly, our narrowbody delivery market share has been and will continue to be impacted by the MAX. Although we've not seen a direct impact on the value proposition of the 737 MAX in the marketplace, we will continue to monitor the market dynamics this creates.
finding: Boeing conceded narrowbody delivery share to the rival during the MAX grounding but maintained the MAX's value proposition was intact.
response: Accept near-term delivery share loss; defend MAX value proposition

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: With regards to the middle of the market aircraft, as Dave noted, we are reprioritizing and streamline some of our investments. We've asked the team to step back and reassess our commercial product development strategy to determine what family of airplanes will be needed in the future.
finding: Boeing formally stepped back from the middle-of-the-market airplane (NMA) in January 2020 and reopened the question of its next airplane family.
response: NMA put on hold; product strategy reassessed

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we will transition the 787 production rate from 14 per month to 12 per month in late '20. As we're in the planning window of a rate decision and to reduce risk in the '21 and 2022 skyline, we've decided to further reduce the rate to 10 per month in early '21 before returning to 12 per month in 2023.
finding: Before COVID, a weak widebody and China trade environment already drove Boeing to cut the 787 twice, from 14 to 12 and then to 10 a month.
trigger: US-China trade tensions and weak widebody orders
response: 787 rate to 10/month in early 2021, back to 12 in 2023

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we are in the process of starting to transition the 767 production rate from 2.5 to 3 per month.
finding: Boeing was still raising 767 output (freighter and tanker) while cutting 787 and pausing the 737.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Some of the suppliers have had challenges with production rate changes in the past. And therefore, we are extremely engaged ... Suppliers' health and rate readiness will be critical as we assess production rates going forward.
finding: Boeing made supplier health and readiness an explicit gate on its future rate decisions after earlier rate changes strained suppliers.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: In the fourth quarter, we added $2.6 billion of program costs to the 737 program. ... accounting block of approximately 3,100 units ... Adding these to the program costs brings the total cumulative program impact to $6.3 billion.
finding: By end-2019 the MAX grounding had added $6.3B of cumulative program costs across a 3,100-unit accounting block.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: This includes costs related to our decision to maintain the 737 production infrastructure, including labor during the suspension and low rate production. As you may recall, this decision is part of our efforts to sustain the gains in the production system and supply chain quality and health
finding: Boeing chose to keep its 737 workforce and infrastructure through the suspension, accepting about $4B of abnormal costs to protect production-system gains.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: No, I don't. I know that in airplane type by type, sometimes you got to lead, sometimes you don't. But in the family and ultimately the performance of this MAX and the feedback I get from our customers, I'm not actually worried about that.
finding: Asked whether Boeing's narrowbody lineup was deficient against the rival, the new CEO denied it and accepted trailing in some sub-segments rather than launching a response.
trigger: Analyst question on narrowbody competitiveness during the MAX grounding
response: Defend the MAX family; no new narrowbody launch

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: me not immediately signing up to the NMA is not -- is me not wanting to do new airplanes. We'll do one. And I don't want to even suggest or convey to you that it's anywhere near the narrowbody fleet we have today. I don't see big deficiencies there.
finding: Calhoun committed to a new airplane eventually but signalled it would not replace the current narrowbody (MAX) family.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We are on a very long cycle world. Getting decisions right is way more important than getting them fast.
finding: Calhoun's rule for new-airplane decisions put getting them right ahead of speed, which explains Boeing's slow next-airplane timing.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: I just want to get exactly the right airplane for the market that's out there. And I want to refresh our view as to what it is. The last 2.5 years have been tumultuous. ... But I will not hesitate to move forward on it.
finding: Asked how Boeing would compete with Airbus later in the decade, the CEO deferred the next-airplane choice to refresh the demand view while promising not to hesitate once decided.
trigger: Analyst concern that Boeing must decide soon how to compete with Airbus in the second half of the decade
response: Defer the new-airplane decision; MAX recovery first

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: their rate in return in these early months will be ahead of ours, and that's by design simply because we want the protection in our factories so that we never travel work.
finding: Boeing deliberately had suppliers restart ahead of its own line to build a buffer and stop traveled work.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we're going to have to have a confidence level -- a higher confidence level in that exact time frame on return to service because, obviously, we don't want to build more airplanes and store them.
finding: Having stored 400+ MAXs, Boeing refused to restart production at scale until it was confident on return-to-service timing.

quote: We face aggressive international competitors who are intent on increasing their market share, such as Airbus and other entrants from Russia, China and Japan. We are focused on improving our processes and continuing cost reduction efforts. We intend to continue to compete with other airplane manufacturers by providing customers with greater value products.
finding: By its FY2019 10-K Boeing's list of commercial competitors dropped Embraer and Bombardier, both named in 2012 and 2017, while its stated answer (cost reduction and value products) stayed the same.

quote: On March 13, 2019, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an order to suspend operations of all 737 MAX aircraft in the U.S. and by U.S. aircraft operators following two fatal 737 MAX accidents. ... we have developed software updates for the 737 MAX, together with an associated pilot training and supplementary education program.
finding: Boeing's response to the two fatal 737 MAX accidents and the grounding was to fix the existing airplane with software updates and pilot training, not to replace it.
trigger: FAA grounding of the 737 MAX on March 13, 2019 after two fatal accidents
response: Developed software updates and a pilot training program to return the existing 737 MAX to service

quote: During the second quarter of 2019, we announced plans to reduce the 737 production rate from 52 aircraft per month to 42 per month. During the fourth quarter of 2019, we announced plans to temporarily suspend 737 MAX production beginning in January 2020.
finding: Boeing cut the 737 rate only partly after the grounding (52 to 42) and kept building for about nine more months before suspending production.
response: Rate cut 52 to 42/month in Q2 2019; production suspension announced Q4 2019 effective January 2020
lag: rate cut within one quarter; suspension about 9 months after grounding

quote: we recorded an earnings charge of $8,259 million, net of insurance recoveries of $500 million, in 2019, in connection with an estimate of potential concessions and other considerations to customers for disruptions related to the grounding and associated delivery delays.
finding: Boeing compensated airlines for the MAX grounding with concessions, taking an $8.26bn charge in 2019 to keep customers and orders.

quote: In the event of unanticipated additional training requirements in one or more jurisdictions, delays in regulatory approval, and/or delays in our ability to resume deliveries, we may be required to take actions with longer-term impact, such as further changes to our production plans, employment reductions and/or the expenditure of significant resources to support our supply chain and/or customers.
finding: Boeing names its escalation ladder if the MAX crisis drags on: further production changes, job cuts, and spending to prop up suppliers and customers.

quote: In addition, our debt balances increased significantly in 2019, and we expect further increases in 2020, in order to manage liquidity impacts related to the 737 MAX grounding. This has also resulted in downgrades to our credit ratings.
finding: Boeing borrowed heavily to ride out the MAX crisis, expected more borrowing in 2020, and absorbed credit-rating downgrades as a result.
In the grounding year Boeing raised its declared dividend to $8.22 a share even as operating cash flow turned negative ($2.4bn) and total debt doubled to $27.3bn.

quote: BDS earnings from operations decreased by $726 million as earnings growth from higher revenues was more than offset by charges of $691 million related to winning the T-7A Red Hawk and MQ-25 competitions, as well as higher KC-46A Tanker reach-forward losses.
finding: Boeing booked $691m of charges tied to winning the T-7A and MQ-25 competitions, showing it will accept upfront losses to win strategic programs.

quote: Certain aircraft parts and components that Boeing procures are subject to these tariffs. ... Overall global trade tensions and increased market uncertainty have resulted in fewer orders than anticipated for our commercial aircraft.
finding: U.S.-China tariffs covered some parts Boeing procures, and trade tensions left its commercial orders below plan.

quote: The grounding of the 737 MAX and the associated suspension of 737 MAX deliveries have significantly reduced our market share with respect to deliveries of single aisle aircraft in 2019 and may provide competitors with an opportunity to obtain more orders and increase market share. We are continuing to monitor the impact of the 737 MAX grounding on our suppliers
finding: Boeing acknowledged that the grounding handed single-aisle delivery share to competitors, and its stated response was to monitor and protect suppliers ahead of a restart.
trigger: Loss of single-aisle delivery share during the MAX grounding
response: Monitor supplier health so the supply chain can support restart; return the MAX to service

quote: Revenues $32,255 $57,499 $54,612 % of total company revenues 42% 57% 58% (Loss)/earnings from operations ($6,657) $7,830 $5,285 Operating margins (20.6)% 13.6% 9.7% Research and development $1,956 $2,188 $2,247
finding: BCA went from a record 13.6% margin in 2018 to a 20.6% loss margin in 2019, and it kept trimming commercial R&D ($2.25bn to $1.96bn) through the period.
Boeing's deliveries fell from a record 806 in 2018 (580 737s) to 380 in 2019 (127 737s), while 787 deliveries rose to 158.

quote: BCA total backlog of $376,593 million at December 31, 2019 decreased from $408,140 million at December 31, 2018 ... We are experiencing fewer new 737 MAX orders than we were receiving prior to the grounding. ... To date, the 737 MAX grounding has not resulted in significant order cancellations.
finding: The grounding slowed new 737 MAX orders and cut BCA backlog by about $31bn, but customers had not yet cancelled in large numbers.

quote: Program accounting quantities 10,400 1,574 1,195 1,690 ** 1,600 Undelivered units under firm orders 4,398 17 94 68 309 520 (29)
finding: Despite the grounding Boeing kept the 737 accounting block at 10,400 units, with 4,398 still on firm order, and 309 777X firm orders.

quote: 747 Program We are currently producing at a rate of 0.5 aircraft per month. We believe that ending production of the 747 at the end of the current accounting quantity would not have a material impact on our financial position, results of operations or cash flows.
finding: Boeing now said ending 747 production at the end of the current block would be financially immaterial, a change of position from only 'evaluating viability' in its 2017 10-K.

quote: We have experienced issues in engine design and development on the 777X. The first flight of the 777X was completed on January 25, 2020, and first delivery is targeted for 2021. ... We plan to produce more 777 models and fewer 777X models in the near term than previously planned.
finding: Engine development problems pushed 777X first delivery from 2020 (2017 plan) to 2021, and Boeing bridged by building more current 777s.

quote: At the end of the first quarter of 2019, we increased the production rate from 12 per month to 14 per month. As a result of fewer orders than anticipated, we plan to reduce the 787 production rate to 12 per month in late 2020 and to 10 per month in early 2021.
finding: Boeing raised the 787 to 14 per month in 2019 and then reversed within the year, planning a cut to 10 per month because orders fell short.
response: Plan to cut 787 rate from 14 to 12 (late 2020) and 10 (early 2021)

quote: Cash used to fund Inventory was $12.4 billion during 2019 as we continued to produce aircraft while deliveries were suspended. ... In December 2019, we announced plans to temporarily suspend production of the 737 MAX beginning in January 2020. This will enable us to prioritize the delivery of stored aircraft.
finding: Boeing kept building through the MAX grounding, absorbing $12.4bn of inventory, before halting to clear stored jets; this repeats its 2013 practice of producing through the 787 grounding (persistence).

quote: In addition, compensation payments to 737 MAX customers of $1.2 billion for disruption to their operations also reduced 2019 cash from operating activities.
finding: Boeing paid airlines $1.2bn in cash for MAX disruption in 2019, beyond in-kind concessions.

quote: During 2019 and 2018 we repurchased 6.9 million and 26.1 million shares totaling $2.7 billion and $9.0 billion through our open market share repurchase program. ... Share repurchases under this plan are currently suspended. We increased our quarterly dividend from $1.71 to $2.055 in December 2018, which resulted in $684 million of higher dividend payments in 2019
finding: Boeing suspended buybacks after the grounding ($9.0bn in 2018 to $2.7bn in 2019) but kept paying the higher dividend it had raised 20% in December 2018.
response: Suspended share repurchases; kept the raised dividend

quote: Net borrowings were $13.2 billion in 2019, $1.4 billion in 2018 and $1.1 billion in 2017. At December 31, 2019 and 2018 the recorded balance of debt was $27.3 billion and $13.8 billion of which $7.3 billion and $3.2 billion was classified as short-term.
finding: Boeing funded the MAX crisis with $13.2bn of net new borrowing in 2019, doubling debt to $27.3bn, much of it short-term.

quote: The partnership contemplates that the parties enter into a joint venture comprising the commercial aircraft and services operations of Embraer, in which Boeing will acquire an 80 percent ownership stake for $4,200, as well as a joint venture ... C-390 Millennium, in which Boeing will hold a 49 percent ownership stake.
finding: Boeing chose a controlling JV structure (80% for $4.2bn) to gain Embraer's commercial aircraft business, plus a 49% JV on the C-390 military transport.

quote: as it progresses its Phase II investigation of the transaction. Pending timely resolution of the remaining regulatory approvals, the transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2020. If the transaction is not completed due to failure to obtain antitrust approvals, we would be required to pay a termination fee of $100.
finding: Boeing was still pursuing the Embraer JV into 2020 through an EU Phase II antitrust review, with a $100m termination fee if antitrust approvals failed.

quote: As of January 31, 2020, we have received commitments from a syndicate of banks sufficient for us to enter into a $12 billion delayed draw two-year term loan credit facility. This facility may be increased at the Company’s option if the facility is oversubscribed.
finding: Boeing met the MAX liquidity strain with more bank debt, a $12bn two-year term loan that could be upsized.

quote: We have concluded that the suspension of production and the gradual resumption of production at low production rates will result in abnormal production costs which will be expensed when incurred rather than inventoried. Prior to the grounding, we had planned to increase the production rate to 57 per month in 2019.
finding: Before the grounding Boeing had planned to reach 57 737s a month in 2019; the suspension and slow restart now forced it to expense abnormal production costs.

quote: have increased the estimated costs to produce aircraft included in the current accounting quantity by approximately $6.3 billion, which will be recorded in program inventory. In addition, the suspension of 737 MAX production and lower production rates is expected to result in approximately $4.0 billion of abnormal production costs in 2020 and 2021 that will be expensed as incurred.
finding: The MAX grounding and rate disruption added about $10.3bn of production cost ($6.3bn deferred into inventory plus $4.0bn expensed).

quote: We have assumed that regulatory approval of the 737 MAX will enable deliveries to resume during mid-2020. ... we expect to gradually increase to previously planned production rates over the next few years.
finding: Boeing planned to rebuild the MAX to its previously planned rates over several years after a mid-2020 return to service.

quote: We have continued to produce at a rate of 42 per month through December 2019, which has resulted in approximately 400 airplanes in inventory as of December 31, 2019. ... including the 737 MAX grounding continuing longer than expected, our decision to prioritize delivery of stored aircraft
finding: Boeing built about 400 undeliverable 737 MAXs before halting, and halted only when the grounding ran longer than it expected.

quote: $24,772 and $27,852 of work in process (including deferred production costs of $18,716 and $22,967), ... $6,422 is expected to be recovered from units included in the program accounting quantity that represent expected future orders.
finding: 787 deferred production kept falling ($23.0bn to $18.7bn in 2019) as the program generated unit profits, though $6.4bn still relied on future orders.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We will bring the resources back to the first position and then gradually bring the line back up in a very smooth, methodical fashion ... we've got the added element in that delivery now with the FAA being involved in every delivery of every MAX airplane that we've assumed will continue.
finding: Boeing planned a gradual MAX restart from empty lines and assumed the FAA would inspect every MAX delivery, a new regulatory constraint on throughput.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we are collecting PDPs at 52, 57 a month. And now with the brought down in rate and the pause and those airplanes moving to the right, we've got to burn off those PDPs before customers will start to pay
finding: Because pre-delivery payments had been collected for a 52-57/month plan, the MAX pause meant little new PDP cash until rates recovered, amplifying the cash hit.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: if you think about the cost to manufacture the aircraft and the pricing established is unchanged once you get back to that rate. What I talked about in those 3 buckets is a period of time that is financially constrained.
finding: Boeing held that MAX unit pricing and cost were unchanged by the crisis, so it treated the losses as temporary and expected per-unit cash to recover at rate.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: priority one is MAX and has been and needs to be certainly versus the next product. ... we use this as an opportunity to step back from what we were, I'll say, specifically focused on the NMA and relook at the commercial product landscape, near term, long term, competitive dynamics that will inform what our next product will be.
finding: The MAX crisis made Boeing subordinate any new airplane to MAX recovery and reopen the NMA decision against the wider competitive landscape.
response: Stepped back from the NMA; restudied the next product

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: get the MAX safely back up into the air and certainly focus on the balance sheet, get the balance sheet healthy and then don't lose sight of the competitive dynamics and how we would address that.
finding: Boeing set a clear order: fix the MAX, repair the balance sheet, then answer the competition with a new product.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we're not assuming business as usual certify the aircraft, nor should we. ... We're taking some of the learnings off the MAX and trying to get ahead of it and apply them on the 777X.
finding: Boeing expected tougher, longer 777X certification after the MAX and began provisioning for more tests and documentation.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: if you don't have the lead time lining up, we'll have to push that to the right. And that's what we're getting in the -- we're right in that sweet spot on the lead time where we have to make a decision, and we think it's a prudent thing to do.
finding: Supply-chain lead times forced Boeing to commit to 787 rate cuts before order visibility improved, so it cut pre-emptively.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Fixed-price development better than what it was but still not where it needs to be. ... Not only are they fixed-priced, we're dealing with a lot of technology in these products and risk that we've got to manage well in advance.
finding: Boeing admitted its fixed-price development bets (tanker, Starliner) were still underperforming, a sign of costly risk-taking on development contracts.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Certainly, Spirit being a big one, which we are partnering with and helping through this transition. ... How is their production health that will then inform our production health and our decision to go up to the next rate
finding: Boeing made MAX rate increases depend on the health of its key fuselage supplier, Spirit, and supported it through the pause.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: It's going to be a couple of years. ... Look, we've got -- everybody's been at that rate, to your point, not all healthy. And this period of time has allowed a lot of people to get healthy
finding: Boeing admitted the supply chain had not been healthy at the pre-grounding 52-57 rates and expected it to take a couple of years to get back to 57.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: First and foremost, to pay down the debt. ... Long term, as far as a balanced deployment strategy, unchanged. But clearly, this has caused us to re-shift that balanced approach and primarily pay down a significant amount of this debt
finding: Even before COVID, the MAX crisis had moved Boeing's capital deployment from balanced shareholder returns to debt repayment first.
response: Prioritise debt paydown over buybacks and M&A

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: one of the things that we learned is when you're at a rate of 52 and a fuselage is a day late, it makes a big difference. And we don't want work out of position ... So let's relook at the buffer. Let's relook at economic order quantities.
finding: Boeing learned that at 52 a month even a one-day supplier delay disrupted the line, so it planned bigger buffers before ramping again.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Embraer's not going away. They're going to fight tooth and nail to win at that low end of the marketplace, and they'll battle Airbus, the former Bombardier, in doing so. And I don't think that's going to move the market in any significant way
finding: After the Embraer JV collapsed and the NMA was shelved in 2020, Boeing accepted leaving the A220 segment uncontested.
trigger: Airbus covering both ends of the narrowbody market (A220, A321)
response: No response at the low end; NMA off the table

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: A number of our suppliers have suspended or reduced their operations, resulting in some supply shortages for our own operations. In some cases, this contributed to our site suspension decisions.
finding: Supplier shutdowns during COVID directly contributed to Boeing suspending its own final-assembly sites, showing how exposed its production was to supply bottlenecks.
response: Temporarily suspended Boeing production sites

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we believe that government support will be critical to ensuring our industry's access to liquidity. We continue to evaluate options in the capital markets as well as funding options from the U.S. government via the U.S. Treasury and various federal reserve programs.
finding: In April 2020 Boeing kept both US government funding and capital markets open as options while it looked for liquidity.
response: Weighed Treasury/Fed support against capital-markets funding

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: it will take 2 to 3 years for travel to return to 2019 levels ... narrowbody airplanes will lead the way to recovery, trailed by widebody fleets, as airlines progressively bring their networks back online. Therefore, widebody passenger fleets will likely be more significantly impacted than narrowbody airplanes in the near term.
finding: Boeing's COVID demand view (2-3 year recovery, widebodies hit hardest) justified deeper widebody cuts than narrowbody cuts.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We expect to gradually increase the production rate to 31 during 2021, with further gradual increases that correspond with market demand. The slower production rate ramp-up reflects commercial airline industry uncertainty due to the impact of COVID-19.
finding: In April 2020 Boeing targeted a 737 MAX rate of 31 during 2021; by July it had pushed this to early 2022, a progressive slippage.
response: Slowed MAX ramp to 31/month during 2021

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We now plan to reduce the 787 production rate to 10 per month in 2020, and then gradually reduce to 7 per month by 2022. ... we plan to reduce the combined 777, 777X production rate to 3 per month in 2021.
finding: Boeing's first COVID rate action cut widebody output sharply: 787 to 10 then 7 a month, and 777/777X to 3 a month.
response: 787 cut to 10/month in 2020 and 7 by 2022; 777/777X to 3/month in 2021
lag: about 6 weeks after the March shutdowns

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We will be a smaller company for a while. We've worked hard to maintain the stability of our workforce, avoiding layoffs even though -- even through the suspension of MAX production
finding: Boeing kept its workforce through the MAX production halt, and only the COVID shock made it shrink.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we are taking action to reduce our workforce by approximately 10% of our roughly 160,000 employees by end of this year ... more than 15% across commercial airplanes and services businesses, as well as our corporate functions.
finding: Boeing cut about 10% of its 160,000 staff, over 15% in commercial airplanes and services, using defense stability to limit the overall cut.
response: 10% workforce reduction, over 15% in BCA/BGS

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we have terminated the agreement to establish a strategic partnership between our 2 companies, covering both the planned commercial and defense joint ventures. We worked diligently for 2 years to finalize the transaction, but ultimately, we could not come to resolution around critical, unsatisfied conditions
finding: Boeing walked away from the Embraer commercial and defense joint ventures after two years, using its contractual termination rights instead of renegotiating.
trigger: Unsatisfied closing conditions in the Embraer master transaction agreement, amid MAX and COVID cash stress
response: Terminated the Embraer JV agreement
lag: 2 years after the deal work began

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we reduced the number of aircraft in the 737 accounting quantity by 400 units as a result of the reduction to planned production rates due to COVID-19. ... result in around $1 billion of additional abnormal production costs, increasing the total from approximately $4 billion to $5 billion.
finding: COVID-driven rate cuts shrank the 737 accounting block by 400 units and raised MAX abnormal production costs from $4B to $5B.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Operating margins declined to negative 33.3% due to the following: lower delivery volume, $797 million of abnormal costs from the temporary suspension of the MAX program mentioned earlier; a $336 million charge related to the 737 next-generation frame-fitting component, also known as the pickle fork
finding: In Q1 2020 Commercial Airplanes ran at a -33.3% margin, adding a 737NG pickle-fork quality charge to the MAX abnormal costs.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: In March 2020, we suspended payment of our dividend until further notice. Since April 2019, we've suspended our share repurchase program. And in March 2020, our Board of Directors terminated its prior authorization to repurchase shares
finding: Boeing stopped buybacks in April 2019 during the MAX crisis and suspended its dividend only in March 2020 when COVID hit.
response: Buyback suspended April 2019; dividend suspended and buyback authorization terminated March 2020
lag: about 11 months between the buyback stop and the dividend suspension

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: The most important source of liquidity for our suppliers is good credit of the OEM and Tier 1 suppliers.
finding: Boeing saw its own credit standing as the main source of liquidity for its supply chain, tying its balance sheet to supplier survival.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we drew down the $13.8 billion delayed draw term loan early ... bringing the total debt balance now to $38.9 billion. We ended the quarter with $15.5 billion of cash and marketable securities.
finding: By March 2020 Boeing had drawn its $13.8B term loan early, taking debt to $38.9B against $15.5B of cash.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: 777X is a use of cash this year, will peak this year. We expect it to be a use of cash next year. But then, it's cash flow-positive in the following year. So that transition that will take place will be key to 2022 cash flow.
finding: Boeing expected 777X cash burn to peak in 2020 and the program to turn cash positive in 2022, making that transition central to recovery.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: the production rate is the one that we will sort of change based on what happens in the marketplace. Marketplace gets more robust for any reason, we'll increase that rate sooner rather than later. And if it defers and/or gets any worse, we will do the opposite.
finding: Boeing treated the MAX production rate as its adjustment valve, with deliveries of stored jets first and the rate rising or falling with market signals.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: at the end of the day, it's going to be what it's going to be on the investment grade. But certainly, we'd prefer to stay investment grade.
finding: Boeing wanted to keep an investment-grade rating but would not make it a binding constraint on its crisis borrowing.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: The demand for the 87 is pretty strong. And our issue is, in our assumptions, and we think we're right, is that the international route structures are going to come back much slower than the domestic ones. And as a result, the 87 suffers for that.
finding: Boeing cut 787 rates because it expected a slow international recovery, not because it saw weakness in the product.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we do everything in our power to defer when we can, swap where we can, et cetera. And remember, a lot of our customers, all of them are invested with respect to PDPs that, of course, we have retained.
finding: Boeing handled COVID requests by steering customers to deferrals and swaps instead of cancellations, using the pre-delivery payments it held as leverage.
trigger: Airline requests to defer or cancel during COVID
response: Negotiate deferrals and swaps; retain PDPs

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we have stress test the case that we're putting forward in many, many ways that are much more difficult than what we believe we're going to do. And we do get through it. And we do -- ultimately, when we do take on more debt, we also believe strongly that we're going to start paying it down.
finding: Boeing stress-tested its plan against harsher cases before borrowing and committed to repay new debt once rates stabilised.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: with respect to the MAX, I have a lot more confidence in the MAX and its place in the market than maybe the question implies. We have a value prop that actually is still pretty good. In some ways, if airplane loads want to get smaller ... it might actually play to us.
finding: Asked how the MAX could compete when squeezed between Airbus products at both ends of the narrowbody market, Boeing defended the existing MAX instead of committing to a new airplane.
trigger: Airbus has products at both the low and high ends of the narrowbody market; Embraer deal ended; NMA off the table
response: Defend and keep selling the MAX; no near-term new narrowbody

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we're not out of the product development business. We're definitely in it. We are invested in capabilities with respect to manufacturing and engineering that we believe will offer a very differentiated product in whatever strategy we choose. ... It will probably not be applied to an NMA
finding: Boeing kept funding production and engineering capabilities for an unnamed next-generation airplane while signalling that work would probably not go to an NMA.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: on the widebody world, and particularly in the freighter world, we like our strategies. We're going to continue to invest in it. And I believe, at the moment, that's our -- probably our biggest priority.
finding: In April 2020 Boeing made widebody and freighter investment, not a new narrowbody, its top product priority.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: 2019, where we did have some balance, the defense business was 45%. This year, of course, the defense business will probably be bigger than the commercial business.
finding: The MAX crisis and COVID made defense Boeing's larger business in 2020, and it leaned on that ballast through the downturn.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: After an approximately 4-month suspension of production operations, in May, we resumed early stages of our 737 production line. During the suspension, we implemented more than a dozen initiatives focused on workplace safety, product quality
finding: Boeing used the roughly four-month 737 production halt to rework the production system for stability before any rate increase.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we expect to continue to produce the 737 at low rates for the remainder of 2020 and gradually increase the rate to 31 by the beginning of 2022, with further gradual increases that correspond with market demand. ... We have moderated the production rate ramp-up from our prior assumption
finding: Boeing slowed its planned 737 MAX recovery ramp to reach only 31 a month by early 2022, with further increases tied to demand.
trigger: COVID demand shock on top of the MAX grounding
response: Moderated 737 ramp to 31/month by 2022

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We previously planned to reduce the 787 production rate to 10 per month in 2020 and gradually reduce to 7 per month by 2022. ... we now plan to reduce the 787 production rate from the current 10 per month to 6 per month in 2021 to further de-risk our skyline
finding: Boeing cut 787 production a second time, deeper and sooner, to 6 a month in 2021, citing customer finances and geopolitics.
trigger: Pandemic hit to widebody demand and customer finances
response: 787 rate cut from 10 to 6 per month in 2021 (prior plan 7 by 2022)
lag: one quarter after the previous cut

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we will prudently evaluate the most efficient way to produce the 787 to include the studying the feasibility of consolidating our 787 production into one location.
finding: Lower 787 rates led Boeing to consider collapsing its two 787 final-assembly sites into one.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we have adjusted the timing of the first 777-9 delivery to 2022 versus our prior forecast of 2021. This reflects our assessment of the development and test time line, feedback from our customers and projected impacts from COVID-19. We are also incorporating lessons learned from the 737 certification process.
finding: Boeing slipped the 777X first delivery by a year to 2022, citing test schedule, customer feedback, COVID and stricter post-MAX certification.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We will take a measured approach to the 777X rate ramp as we look to minimize the amount of change in corporation work by managing the number of aircraft produced prior to entry into service. ... we now plan to reduce the combined 777/777X production rate to 2 per month in 2021 versus our previous plan of 3
finding: Boeing capped 777X pre-certification production to limit rework and cut the combined 777/777X rate to 2 a month for 2021.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: On the 747, we will continue building 747s at the current rate as we deliver on our commitments to key customers. In light of the current market dynamics and the outlook, we anticipate completing production of the iconic 747 in 2022.
finding: Boeing ended a legacy program, setting 747 production to finish in 2022 after meeting existing commitments.
trigger: COVID market collapse and weak widebody outlook
response: Announced end of 747 production in 2022

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Protecting long-term flexibility, while adjusting capacity in the interim to balance near to medium-term supply and demand will be critical to preserve our long-term prospects.
finding: Boeing's stated rule in the downturn was to cut capacity to near-term demand while keeping the flexibility to ramp back up.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We currently have approximately 450 737 MAX aircraft built and stored in inventory. ... We have also assumed that the majority of the 737 MAX aircraft in storage will be delivered during the first year after resumption of deliveries.
finding: Boeing planned to clear most of its roughly 450 stored MAXs within a year of delivery restart, putting stored-jet deliveries ahead of new production.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Cumulatively, we've accrued a $9.6 billion liability for the estimated potential concessions and other considerations. To date, we've made $2.6 billion of payments to customers in cash and other forms of
finding: The MAX grounding cost Boeing a $9.6B cumulative customer-compensation liability by mid-2020.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: In some cases, we would have liked to bring production rate down sooner to match near-term demand. However, there's a number of key factors that need to take into consideration, including orderly supply chain transition and production system stability. Therefore, we expect production to continue to outpace delivery rate
finding: Boeing accepted building excess inventory rather than cutting rates abruptly, putting supply-chain stability ahead of matching demand.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Operating cash flow for the second quarter was negative $5.3 billion ... Clearly, the additional reductions in our commercial production rates, as well as the updated 777X schedule, have made our cash profile even more challenging. However, based on what we know today and our actions, we still see a path to positive cash flow in 2021.
finding: Boeing burned $5.3B of operating cash in Q2 2020 but still guided to positive cash flow in 2021.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we paid down $2.4 billion of commercial paper, bringing our total debt to $61.4 billion. ... We ended the second quarter with $32.4 billion of cash and marketable securities. We also continue to have access to our $9.6 billion revolving credit facility, which to date has not been drawn upon.
finding: By mid-2020 Boeing carried $61.4B of debt against $32.4B of cash plus an undrawn $9.6B revolver, a much more leveraged balance sheet.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We suspended our dividend and terminated our prior share repurchase authorization. We've proactively drawn down on our $13.8 billion term loan in mid-March and raised $25 billion of new debt, cut discretionary spending and reduced or deferred R&D and capital expenditures.
finding: Boeing reversed its shareholder-return model under stress: it suspended the dividend, ended the buyback authorization, borrowed heavily and cut or deferred R&D and capex.
response: Dividend suspended, buyback terminated, $13.8B term loan drawn, $25B raised, R&D/capex deferred

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: there was about 480-odd cancellations that were noted. About 300 of those were associated with 606.
finding: In Q2 2020 about 480 orders left Boeing's backlog, around 300 of them removed under ASC 606 as unlikely to be delivered.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We don't see a need to raise any additional capital at this time. ... if we see opportunities to pay down that debt sooner or restructure that in any way, we will absolutely be doing that, and we'll be laser focused on bringing that debt down
finding: After the $25B raise Boeing ruled out more capital for now and committed to repay debt early wherever it could.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we're still trying to de-risk the skyline. That has been our motive and to emphasize to everyone, including our own people, that we're going to move the finished goods first. ... We're still going to hold our production rates as conservative as we can so that we can get that inventory on the move.
finding: Even with some airlines wanting to buy countercyclically, the CEO kept rates as conservative as possible until finished inventory was delivered.
trigger: Mixed airline demand, some customers wanting to buy countercyclically
response: Hold rates conservative, deliver finished inventory first

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: I think as much about the recovery and the pace of as I do sort of the retrenchment and to deal with today's liquidity because I think actually that ramp-up is going to be the more important part of this puzzle going forward.
finding: Calhoun saw the post-COVID ramp-up, not the retrenchment, as the harder strategic problem and expected demand to return faster than feared.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: For most of the year next year, the governor on rate is going to be the pace at which we sell that finished goods inventory.
finding: Boeing's CEO made the pace of inventory sales, not demand or supplier capacity, the binding limit on the 2021 MAX rate.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: having detailed discussions with each of them by model and by time horizon around how they plan to take aircraft ... And that's ultimately what has informed our production rates that we outlined last week.
finding: Boeing set its COVID-era production rates bottom-up from customer-by-customer, model-by-model fleet discussions rather than from its own ramp targets.
response: Cut production rates based on airline-by-airline intake discussions

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Last year, about $5 billion in CapEx and R&D and $2 billion year-to-date. And have we sharpened our pencil on all that? Absolutely, in delaying some things and refining some of those investments, again, with a keen eye towards liquidity. But we're continuing to fund the key franchises
finding: Under liquidity stress Boeing delayed and trimmed R&D/capex but ring-fenced funding for its in-development programs (777X, 737-10, Starliner).
response: Delay discretionary investment, protect key development franchises

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: How successful we are with that will ultimately inform our rate ramp. ... it will be how we're doing on depleting the inventory off that ramp. We don't want to put more product on the ramp.
finding: Boeing made the 737 MAX rate increase conditional on burning down its parked inventory, refusing to build more airplanes than customers were absorbing.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We've got roughly 12,000 suppliers. For every dollar we spend, $0.70 goes to the supply chain. And we've continued to fund the supply chain through this pandemic to keep them healthy
finding: Boeing kept paying suppliers through the downturn to preserve supply-chain health for the eventual ramp, since 70% of its spend goes to suppliers.
response: Continued funding suppliers and helping them access financing and government aid

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we've asked the team to back step and reassess our commercial product development strategy and determine a family of airplanes that we think will be needed in the future. And the team is going to -- has been building on the work that through NMA and whole production system
finding: After stepping back from the NMA, Boeing reopened its whole new-airplane strategy to define a family of aircraft rather than one model, building on NMA and production-system work.
response: Step back from NMA and reassess the product family

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: in mid-March, we advanced our bank loan of $13.8 billion, which some would have, at the time, may be viewed early. We viewed it as trying to be prudent and then issuing the $25 billion to ensure that we had appropriate liquidity to get through this period.
finding: Boeing moved early and heavily to add debt, drawing $13.8B of bank loans in March 2020 and then issuing $25B of bonds to build a liquidity buffer.
response: Drew $13.8B term loan and issued $25B of bonds
lag: weeks (mid-March draw, bond issue later in spring)

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: When we come out the other side, as I mentioned, priority one, pay down the debt, and continue to make the investments, pay down the debt. ... We've not certainly lost sight on our long-term objectives around a balanced deployment. But we're a ways away from that.
finding: Boeing put debt repayment ahead of shareholder returns after COVID, deferring its balanced-deployment (dividend/buyback) policy indefinitely.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Market share, without a doubt, we've lost some share. When you don't produce an airplane for a year and the other guy does, by definition, you take a big hit with respect to share.
finding: Boeing conceded that Airbus gained narrowbody share during the MAX grounding, while insisting the 737 still competed against the A320 family.
response: Accept share loss; no new product

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: It only takes one part of our -- one part to delay production of an aircraft or delay service delivery, so we have to work together as an industry to get through these difficult times.
finding: Boeing saw weak suppliers as a single-point risk to production and supported them through the crisis.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: While we continue to drive towards entry into service in 2022, this timing will ultimately be influenced by certification requirements defined by the regulators.
finding: In Oct 2020 Boeing still targeted 777X entry into service in 2022; three months later it slipped to late 2023.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: We still expect to produce the 737 at very low rates for the remainder of 2020 and gradually increase the rate to 31 by the beginning of 2022, and expect further gradual increases to correspond with market demand.
finding: Boeing first set the 31-per-month early-2022 737 target in 2020 and held it through 2021.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we took a proactive step to fully draw down on our $13.8 billion delayed draw term loan.
finding: Boeing fully drew its $13.8B term loan in March 2020 as a pre-emptive liquidity move.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Almost immediately thereafter, we suspended our dividend and terminated our share repurchase authorization.
finding: Boeing suspended its dividend and ended buybacks at the start of COVID.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Shortly thereafter, we went to the bond market and raised $25 billion, which has proven to be instrumental to helping us navigate this crisis.
finding: Boeing funded its 2020 crisis with a $25B bond issue.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: through our 787 study, it became evident that the consolidation to a single production location in South Carolina will make us more efficient and lower production and better positioned for the future. As a result, earlier this month, we made the decision to consolidate the 787 production in South Carolina by mid-'21.
finding: In Oct 2020 Boeing decided to consolidate 787 production in South Carolina to cut cost.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We originally plan to invest over $6 billion this year. Through prioritization, we have pared back these investments by approximately $2 billion.
finding: Boeing cut 2020 investment by about $2B (a third) to conserve cash.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: our production has outpaced our delivery rate. And we expect this to continue in the near term, resulting in higher finished goods inventory.
finding: Boeing kept production above deliveries in 2020, accepting a growing finished-goods inventory.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: While we're still aiming to turn cash positive in late '21, the recovery and the continued elevated virus cases make the path much more challenging. Based on what we know today, it's looking more likely that we will be cash flow-positive in the 2022 time frame.
finding: In Oct 2020 Boeing pushed its target for positive cash flow from late 2021 to 2022.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: what will be hostage to the movement of those airplanes will be our production rate. We're determined not to create a bigger problem than we started with. And so that production rate will stay low until the movement of those airplanes
finding: Boeing tied 737 rate increases to clearing stored inventory, refusing to add to its stock.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: the psychology will lend itself, in my opinion, to a little bit of a run on the bank with respect to narrow-body airplanes. ... I want to make sure we're stable and ready for that.
finding: Boeing anticipated a sudden narrowbody demand surge and prioritized being stable enough to meet it.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: This time -- or I will call it deferral of the NMA or whatever that slot was, this is actually going to advantage us in determining the point design based on what I think are some changing market conditions. But we never let up on the underlying technologies
finding: Boeing framed deferring the NMA as an advantage, letting it redefine the next airplane after COVID while continuing technology spend.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: We attempted quite a while ago to derisk our delivery stream on the inventoried airplanes such that we pushed out the Chinese airplanes for later delivery.
finding: Boeing pushed Chinese MAX deliveries later in its inventory plan to derisk its delivery stream.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we've made a modest adjustment to the 787 production rate from what we had previously announced rate of 6 aircraft a month beginning in mid-'21 to a rate of 5 per month by mid-'21.
finding: Boeing cut its 787 rate plan again (6 to 5 per month) as international traffic stayed about 90% below 2019.
trigger: International traffic ~90% below 2019; weak widebody demand
response: Cut planned 787 rate from 6 to 5 per month by mid-2021

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: I want to thank again, Michael O'Leary and Neil from Ryanair for the recent order of 75 airplanes that we announced yesterday.
finding: Boeing secured a 75-aircraft Ryanair MAX order right after the MAX was ungrounded.
trigger: FAA lifted the 737 MAX grounding order
response: Won a Ryanair order for 75 MAX

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: we've got 450 aircraft parked on the 737. The constraint there won't be our ability to deliver them. It's the pace and ability for the customers to take them.
finding: Boeing's 450 stored MAX gave it capacity to meet a faster recovery, limited by customer uptake rather than production.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: in some cases where we've had cancellations, we've provisioned for the ability to reconfigure those aircraft and remarket them. So we absolutely have that flexibility
finding: Boeing provisioned to reconfigure and remarket MAX aircraft from cancelled orders to new customers.
trigger: MAX order cancellations during grounding and COVID
response: Reconfigure and remarket stored aircraft

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: when we were in pursuit around the NMA, we asked the team to step back and reassess the commercial development strategy and determine what family of aircraft that we needed for the future. And that team continues to work, and they're building off the work that we did on NMA.
finding: After stepping back from the NMA, Boeing reassessed its whole commercial development strategy, building on the NMA work.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: So when it comes to capital deployment, we got -- we want to -- it will be all about paying down that debt. We'll continue, obviously, to invest in the business
finding: Boeing made debt paydown the core of post-crisis capital deployment.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: And we'll look for every opportunity to do that in the most efficient way, including equity. So nothing's off the table.
finding: Boeing kept equity issuance open as a deleveraging option.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Broadly speaking and on balance across the portfolio, we like where our portfolio plays with the MAX at the lower end and the 87 at the higher end and very successful airplanes. So that just said -- all that means is we're going to take our time.
finding: Boeing deliberately did not answer the A321XLR's success, and deferred any new airplane.
response: No product response; 'take our time'

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: we still expect to deliver the vast majority of the 787 aircraft inventory by the end of the year.
finding: In Jan 2021 Boeing expected to deliver the vast majority of stored 787s in 2021; this was cut to 'majority' in April, 'fewer than half' in July, and deliveries stopped entirely later.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: we now anticipate that the first 777X delivery will occur in late 2023. This schedule and the financial impact to the program this quarter reflect a number of factors, including an updated assessment of global certification requirements
finding: Boeing delayed the 777X to late 2023, citing stricter global certification requirements after the MAX.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: we've made the decision to implement certain modifications to the aircraft design. Our decision to make these modifications, which will involve firmware and hardware changes to the actuator control electronics, reflects our current judgment of global regulators' compliance expectations.
finding: Boeing pre-emptively redesigned 777X flight-control electronics to meet expected regulator demands, accepting delay.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: we booked a $6.5 billion pretax charge in the quarter, a significant component of which is driven by a reduction in the program's initial accounting quantity.
finding: Boeing took a $6.5B 777X reach-forward loss, largely from cutting the accounting quantity.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: COVID-19 has had a significant impact on passenger traffic, particularly international long-haul routes serviced by large widebodies such as the 777X, which has shifted the anticipated replacement wave and overall demand for widebody airplanes to the right.
finding: Boeing saw COVID pushing the large-widebody replacement wave later, weakening 777X near-term demand.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: Across the total widebody market of more than 8,000 projected deliveries over the next 2 decades, we see replacement demand for over 1,500 large widebody airplanes, which are well suited for the 777X.
finding: Boeing justified continuing the 777X on long-term large-widebody replacement demand.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Our revenue of $58.2 billion and core earnings per share of negative $23.25 reflected lower commercial delivery and service volume ... Operating cash flow of negative $18.4 billion
finding: In 2020 Boeing burned $18.4B of operating cash on revenue of $58.2B.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: $25.6 billion of cash and marketable securities on our balance sheet ... Our debt balance at the end of the quarter was $63.6 billion, reflecting our $4.9 billion bond issuance
finding: Boeing funded its crisis with heavy borrowing, reaching $63.6B of debt.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We have taken production rates for the 787 and 777 programs down by approximately half due to COVID impact and also moderated the ramp of the 737 production rate.
finding: Boeing halved widebody rates and slowed the 737 ramp in response to COVID.
response: Halve 787/777 rates, slow 737 ramp

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We continue to take steps to reach our previously shared plan to bring our overall staffing levels to approximately 130,000 by the end of '21.
finding: In Jan 2021 Boeing planned to cut staff to about 130,000, a plan revised by July 2021 to hold at about 140,000.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: I see no reason why the competitive dynamics are any different. I really don't. ... We will have demonstrated performance on the MAX that is very good for the applications that it competes for. And their airplane will have advantages on other applications.
finding: Boeing expected the MAX-versus-Airbus competitive balance, and therefore pricing, to be unchanged by the grounding.
trigger: Pricing pressure fears after the MAX grounding
response: Stay disciplined on pricing while liquidating inventory

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: we like where our portfolio plays with the MAX at the lower end and the 87 at the higher end and very successful airplanes. So that just said -- all that means is we're going to take our time.
finding: Boeing chose not to rush a new airplane in response to the A321XLR.
trigger: A321XLR success in the middle of the market
response: Delay new airplane; rely on MAX and 787 portfolio

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: differentiation at the airframe level itself is really, really important in the next run, which means that these technologies that we are working with and trying to demonstrate to ourselves at scale with determinant assembly, those are the things that we'll differentiate.
finding: Boeing made proving determinant assembly at scale the key criterion for launching its next airplane.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: I don't feel in any way, shape or form that 1 year or 2 years more in the market to learn more is going to hold us back
finding: Boeing judged a one-to-two-year delay in launching a new airplane as costless.

quote: We face aggressive international competitors who are intent on increasing their market share, such as Airbus and other entrants from Russia, China and Japan. We are focused on improving our processes and continuing cost reduction efforts. We intend to continue to compete with other airplane manufacturers by providing customers with greater value products.
finding: Boeing's stated answer to Airbus and new entrants seeking share is cost reduction and 'greater value products', not a named new-airplane launch.
trigger: Airbus and Russian/Chinese/Japanese entrants pushing for market share
response: Process improvement, cost reduction, compete on product value

quote: During the year ended December 31, 2020, net cash used by operating activities was $18.4 billion. At December 31, 2020, cash and short-term investments totaled $25.6 billion. Our debt balance totaled $63.6 billion at December 31, 2020, up from $27.3 billion at December 31, 2019.
finding: In 2020 Boeing burned $18.4B of operating cash and more than doubled debt to $63.6B, funding the crisis with borrowing.

quote: During 2019, we announced plans to reduce, and ultimately to suspend 737 production. Impacts related to these actions significantly increased costs to produce aircraft included in the current accounting quantity and have resulted in reduced 737 program and overall BCA segment operating margins.
finding: Boeing reduced and then suspended 737 production during the grounding, accepting higher unit costs and lower BCA margins.
response: Cut, then suspended 737 production

quote: In January 2021, we entered into a Deferred Prosecution Agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice that resolves the Department of Justice’s previously disclosed investigation into us regarding the evaluation of the 737 MAX airplane by the FAA. We expensed $744 in the fourth quarter of 2020 related to this agreement.
finding: Boeing settled the DOJ 737 MAX investigation via a Deferred Prosecution Agreement, expensing $744M in Q4 2020.

quote: we recorded an earnings charge of $8,259 million, net of insurance recoveries of $500 million, in 2019, in connection with an estimate of potential concessions and other considerations to customers for disruptions related to the grounding and associated delivery delays.
finding: Boeing compensated airlines for the MAX grounding with an $8.26B 2019 concessions charge.

quote: We enter into firm fixed-price aircraft sales contracts with indexed price escalation clauses which could subject us to losses if we have cost overruns or if increases in our costs exceed the applicable escalation rate.
finding: Boeing sells airplanes on fixed prices with indexed escalation, so it carries cost-overrun risk itself.

quote: For example, in the fourth quarter of 2020, we expanded the scope of production inspections on the 787 program, and those inspections and associated rework are delaying scheduled deliveries and resulting in additional 787 aircraft in inventory.
finding: 787 quality problems in late 2020 led Boeing to widen inspections, delaying deliveries and building inventory.

quote: If one or more of our suppliers or subcontractors experiences financial difficulties, delivery delays or other performance problems, we may be unable to meet commitments to our customers or incur additional costs. ... In some instances, we depend upon a single source of supply.
finding: Boeing depends on some single-source suppliers, so a supplier bottleneck can block its deliveries.

quote: In October 2020, the WTO authorized the EU to impose approximately $3.99 billion in annual tariffs on U.S. products in connection with a tax incentive used by Boeing in Washington state that has since been repealed. The EU is currently imposing 15% tariffs on Boeing airplanes imported into the EU.
finding: The WTO dispute cut both ways: Boeing aircraft faced 15% EU tariffs over its Washington tax incentive, which has since been repealed.

quote: Generally, we expect domestic travel to recover faster than international travel. As a result, we expect the narrow-body market to recover faster than the wide-body market.
finding: After COVID Boeing expected narrowbodies to recover before widebodies, a view that shaped where it cut rates hardest.

quote: To balance the supply and demand given the COVID-19 shock and to preserve our long-term potential and competitiveness, we have reduced the production rates of several of our BCA programs. These rate decisions are based on our ongoing assessments of the demand environment and availability of aircraft financing.
finding: Boeing cut BCA production rates in response to COVID-19, basing rate decisions on demand and whether aircraft financing is available.
response: Reduced production rates on several BCA programs

quote: We will maintain a disciplined rate management process, and make adjustments as appropriate in the future. Notwithstanding the changes we have made to production rates, risk remains that further reductions will be required.
finding: Boeing described its rate policy as 'disciplined rate management' and kept further cuts on the table.

quote: our Commercial Market Outlook forecast projects a 4% growth rate for passenger and cargo traffic over a 20 year period. Based on long-term global economic growth projections of 2.5% average annual GDP growth, we project demand for approximately 43,000 new airplanes over the next 20 years.
finding: Despite COVID, Boeing still projected long-term demand of about 43,000 new airplanes over 20 years, supporting continued investment.

quote: Through our portfolio and investment prioritization, we reduced research and development and capital expenditures during 2020 by $1.3 billion from the prior year.
finding: In the 2020 crisis Boeing cut R&D and capex by $1.3B together, prioritising investment rather than protecting it.

quote: During 2020, we recorded severance costs for approximately 26,000 employees, of which approximately 18,000 have left the Company as of December 31, 2020 ... These activities are not intended to constrain our capacity, but to enable the Company to emerge stronger and be more resilient when the market recovers.
finding: Boeing cut about 26,000 jobs but said the goal was resilience, not a permanent cut to capacity.

quote: We made the decision during the third quarter of 2020 to consolidate 787 production in South Carolina in 2021, which did not have a significant financial impact on the program.
finding: Boeing chose to consolidate 787 final assembly in South Carolina (leaving Everett) as a footprint cut in the downturn.

quote: The loss in 2020 primarily reflects a reach-forward loss recorded in the fourth quarter of $6,493 million on the 777X program. The reach-forward loss reflects a number of factors, including an updated assessment of global certification requirements ... resulting in a management decision to make modifications to the aircraft’s design, an updated assessment of COVID-19 impacts on market demand
finding: The $6.5B 777X reach-forward loss came from tougher certification requirements (forcing design changes) and weaker COVID-era demand.

quote: Research and development expense decreased by $743 million in 2020 compared with 2019 primarily due to lower spending at BCA and at Boeing NeXt on product development.
finding: BCA R&D fell from $1,956M to $1,385M in 2020 as Boeing cut product-development spending in the crisis.

quote: We are experiencing fewer new 737 MAX orders than we were receiving prior to the grounding. If 737 MAX aircraft remain grounded in certain jurisdictions for an extended period of time and/or if entry into service of the 777X, 737 MAX 7 and/or 737 MAX 10 is further delayed, we may experience additional reductions to backlog
finding: Boeing admitted that 737 MAX order intake fell after the grounding, putting backlog at risk.

quote: Aircraft order cancellations during the year ended December 31, 2020 totaled $34,618 million and primarily relate to 737 MAX aircraft. The ASC 606 adjustments for the year ended December 31, 2020 totaled $54,450 million and primarily relate to 737 MAX aircraft and 777X aircraft.
finding: BCA backlog fell from $376.6B to $281.6B in 2020, driven by $34.6B of mostly 737 MAX cancellations and $54.5B of ASC 606 removals.

quote: The grounding of the 737 MAX and the associated suspension of 737 MAX deliveries significantly reduced our market share with respect to deliveries of single aisle aircraft in 2019 and 2020 and may provide competitors with an opportunity to obtain more orders and increase market share.
finding: Boeing acknowledged the MAX grounding cost it single-aisle delivery share and opened the door for competitors to take more orders.

quote: We are focused on improving our products and services and continuing our business transformation efforts, which enhances our ability to compete and positions us for market recovery. We are also focused on taking actions to ensure that Boeing is not harmed by unfair subsidization of competitors.
finding: Boeing answers subsidized rivals with internal transformation plus trade and legal action against subsidies, not by matching on price.
trigger: Subsidized competitors (launch aid) and pricing pressure
response: Business transformation; actions against unfair subsidization

quote: BCA loss from operations was $13,847 million in 2020 compared with loss from operations of $6,657 million in 2019. The 2020 loss reflects the reach-forward loss on 777X of $6,493 million, lower deliveries and lower program margins resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic and 787 production issues and associated rework, $2,567 million of abnormal production costs related to 737 MAX
finding: BCA lost $13.8B in 2020 (-85.7% margin) on 777X charges, 787 rework and 737 MAX abnormal costs; deliveries fell to 157.
