quote: We reduced the program accounting quantity from 10,400 at December 31, 2019 to 10,000 at March 31, 2020. This reflects a slower than previously planned production rate ramp-up caused by commercial airline industry uncertainty due to the impact of COVID-19.
finding: Boeing slowed the planned 737 rate ramp-up because of COVID and cut the accounting quantity by 400 units.

quote: We are currently producing at a rate of 0.5 aircraft per month. We will complete production of the 747 in 2022. We believe that ending production of the 747 will not have a material impact on our financial position, results of operations or cash flows.
finding: Boeing chose to end the 747 program (at 0.5/month) and judged the cancellation immaterial financially.

quote: Pre-COVID-19, we were producing at a rate of 14 per month and had planned to adjust the 787 production rate to 12 per month in late 2020 and to 10 per month in early 2021. Due to the impacts of COVID-19 on customer demand, we now plan to reduce to 5 per month in 2021.
finding: Boeing cut the 787 rate from 14/month to a planned 5/month in 2021 in response to COVID demand, deeper than its pre-COVID plan of 10.
response: 787 rate 14 -> 5/month; accounting quantity cut by 100 units

quote: We launched the 737 MAX 7 in August 2011 and the 737 MAX 10 in June 2017. We launched the 777X in November 2013. We now anticipate that the first 737 MAX 10 and 777X delivery will occur in 2023.
finding: Boeing's derivative launches (MAX 7 in 2011, MAX 10 in 2017, 777X in 2013) had first-delivery dates slipping to 2023.

quote: Cash used to fund inventory was $12.4 billion during 2019 as we continued to produce aircraft while deliveries were suspended.
finding: In 2019 Boeing kept building 737s during the grounding, tying up $12.4B in inventory rather than stopping the line at once.
response: Continued production into inventory through 2019

quote: The increase for the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018 reflects a combination of higher purchases, an extension of payment terms with certain suppliers, and increased utilization of our supply chain financing programs.
finding: Boeing extended supplier payment terms and used supply-chain financing in 2018-2019, pushing working capital onto suppliers.

quote: Compensation payments to 737 MAX customers totaled $2.2 billion during 2020 and $1.2 billion during 2019.
finding: Boeing paid airlines $1.2B in 2019 and $2.2B in 2020 as cash compensation for the MAX grounding.

quote: Capital expenditures totaled $1.3 billion in 2020, compared with $1.8 billion in 2019 and $1.7 billion 2018. We expect capital expenditures in 2021 to be relatively consistent with 2020.
finding: Boeing cut capex to $1.3B in 2020 and planned to hold it flat in 2021.

quote: The increase in 2020 is primarily due to $29.9 billion of fixed rate senior notes issued in 2020 and $13.8 billion of new borrowings under a two-year delayed draw term loan agreement entered into in the first quarter of 2020.
finding: Boeing raised liquidity in 2020 through private markets ($29.9B of bonds plus a $13.8B term loan).

quote: During the year ended December 31, 2020, we did not repurchase any shares through our open market share repurchase program compared to repurchases of 6.9 million and 26.1 million shares in 2019 and 2018 totaling $2.7 billion and $9.0 billion. Share repurchases under this plan had been suspended since April 2019.
finding: Boeing went from $9.0B of buybacks in 2018 to none, halting repurchases in April 2019 right after the MAX grounding.
response: Buybacks suspended April 2019; authorization terminated March 2020

quote: During the twelve months ended December 31, 2020 we paid dividends of $1.2 billion compared with $4.6 billion and $3.9 billion in the same period in 2019 and 2018. In March 2020, the Company announced that our dividend will be suspended until further notice. In December 2018 we increased our quarterly dividend from $1.71 to $2.055
finding: Boeing raised the dividend 20% in December 2018, then suspended it in March 2020.

quote: In the fourth quarter of 2020, we contributed $3 billion of our common stock to our pension fund. ... we also began using our common stock in lieu of cash to fund Company contributions to our 401(k) plans for the foreseeable future, which we estimate will conserve approximately $1 billion of cash
finding: To save cash Boeing used its own stock instead of cash to fund pension and 401(k) contributions.

quote: We have approximately 425 airplanes in inventory as of December 31, 2020. A number of customers have requested to defer deliveries or to cancel orders for 737 MAX aircraft, and we are remarketing and/or delaying deliveries of certain aircraft included within inventory.
finding: About 425 737 MAX aircraft sat in inventory at end-2020, and Boeing was remarketing the ones customers declined.

quote: As we are producing at abnormally low production rates in 2020 and 2021, we expect to incur approximately $5.0 billion of abnormal production costs that are being expensed as incurred.
finding: Low 737 rates were expected to cost about $5.0B of abnormal production costs over 2020-2021.

quote: We currently expect to gradually increase the production rate to 31 per month by early 2022. We currently assume that we will implement further gradual production rate increases in subsequent periods based on market demand.
finding: Boeing planned a gradual 737 ramp to 31/month by early 2022, with later increases depending on demand.

quote: while any prolonged production suspension or delays in planned production rate increases could mitigate the impact on our liquidity, it could significantly increase the overall expected costs to produce aircraft included in the accounting quantity, which would reduce 737 program margins and/or increase abnormal production costs in the future.
finding: Boeing spells out the rate trade-off: slowing the ramp saves near-term cash but raises unit costs and hurts program margins.

quote: we entered into agreements with Embraer S.A. ... to establish joint ventures that included the commercial aircraft and services operations of Embraer, of which we were expected to acquire an 80 percent ownership stake for $ 4,200 ... In 2020, we exercised our contractual right to terminate these agreements based on Embraer’s failure to meet certain required closing conditions.
finding: Boeing walked away from the $4.2B, 80% Embraer commercial JV in 2020, citing unmet closing conditions during its cash crisis.
trigger: Embraer JV closing conditions unmet; 2020 liquidity crisis
response: Terminated JV agreements

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: I want to split that market ... I can't make up for the production gap that we created on our own right for that entire year. I can't make up to that. And so I'm not going to try to regain that ground.
finding: Boeing still wanted a 50/50 split in the long run, but would not chase back share lost to Airbus during the grounding. It would pace rate recovery instead.
trigger: Airbus narrowbody share gains during MAX grounding
response: Hold 'rightful share' going forward; stable rate ramp

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: There is no material change in our estimated for total 737 abnormal costs of $5 billion. During the first quarter, we expensed $568 million of abnormal production costs, which brought the cumulative abnormal cost expense to date to $3.1 billion.
finding: The MAX grounding cost Boeing about $5B in abnormal production costs.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Cumulatively, we've accrued a $9.3 billion liability for the estimated potential concessions and other considerations. To date, we've reduced the liability by $4.9 billion through cash payments to customers and other forms of compensation, including $1.2 billion we paid this quarter.
finding: Boeing accrued $9.3B of MAX customer compensation and was paying it down.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Once cash flow generation returns to more normal levels, reducing our debt level will be our top priority. We believe we currently have sufficient liquidity and are not planning to increase our debt levels.
finding: Boeing made debt reduction its top use of recovered cash and ruled out adding debt.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: as production rates begin to return to what we would consider ultimately normal and then above, we should get more leverage than we've ever gotten simply because of all the actions that we've taken with respect to the fixed and readiness to serve costs
finding: Boeing expected fixed-cost cuts to give record operating leverage when rates recover.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: I can't make up for the production gap that we created on our own right for that entire year. I can't make up to that. And so I'm not going to try to regain that ground. I'm simply, from this point forward, going to try to hold our own with respect to what I think is our rightful share.
finding: Boeing chose not to chase share lost to Airbus during the MAX grounding and aimed only to hold its share from then on.
trigger: Airbus delivering many A320neos and building backlog during the MAX grounding
response: No share-recapture push; hold share going forward, pace rates for stability

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: I want to split that market, let's put it that way. That's the way it's played out historically. They do better in some segments of that market, we do better in other parts
finding: Boeing's narrowbody share goal was an even split with Airbus.
trigger: Airbus's narrowbody share gains during the MAX grounding
response: Aim to split the narrowbody market with Airbus by segment

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: It's important that we get our share -- our fair share of that market, which historically has always been at 50%, a little more when you consider all the widebody activity.
finding: Boeing targeted restoring its historical 50%+ share of China.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: it is usually developed around a propulsion package that offers 15% to 20% improvement with respect to efficiency versus the one it's displacing. That's the way it's happened over a long period of time. I don't believe the next generation of engine can deliver that kind of performance.
finding: Boeing doubted the next engine generation would deliver the usual 15-20% gain, a view it repeated through 2021-22.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: But I am going to steer clear from blanket rate announcements that go out too far. I will always announce rate adjustments when I need to for the benefit of the supply chain, not in terms of signaling market shares.
finding: Boeing refused to match Airbus's long-range rate announcements, and criticised using forecast rates to signal share.
response: No long-range rate signalling

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: I'm only 1 player so I'm not going to comment on my competitors' rate announcements. ... The idea that we're going to compete on those forecasted rates, I think, creates trouble for our supply chain.
finding: Boeing refused to match Airbus's long-range rate announcements, arguing that competing on forecast rates destabilizes the supply chain.
trigger: Airbus signalled 64-75 per month A320 rates to suppliers
response: Declined to issue matching long-range 737 rate targets

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: I am going to steer clear from blanket rate announcements that go out too far. I will always announce rate adjustments when I need to for the benefit of the supply chain, not in terms of signaling market shares.
finding: Boeing explicitly rejected using rate announcements to signal market share against Airbus.
response: Announce rates only when suppliers need them

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: If we get it wrong, we pay a price for that. We don't satisfy demand that would otherwise be there. And/or we're getting crushed by too many inventory, and all of a sudden, we got to lay people off
finding: Boeing weighed the asymmetric costs of setting rates too low (lost demand) or too high (inventory, layoffs).

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: I do know that if it goes on for too long, I pay a price. I pay a price because they're the biggest part of the growth of the industry in the world. Roughly 25% over the next 10 years of the growth will come from China.
finding: Boeing saw loss of access to China, about 25% of industry growth, as a major strategic cost.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: are you not spending on some things you really would like to spend on? And the answer to that question is no. We have sustained what we think are all the important investments necessary to maintain leadership in our respective markets.
finding: Boeing claimed its debt had not forced cuts to investments it considered essential for market leadership.

speaker: analyst (Bernstein); David Calhoun, CEO
quote: Does that mean you can get all the way back in Charleston up to a 14 a month rate? ... Yes. The answer to that is yes. ... You don't go from 5 to that number overnight. You get there in increments.
finding: Boeing said the single Charleston 787 site could eventually reach about 14 per month, in increments.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: I don't want to ever repeat the mistake of us trying to pressure them to do things faster than they would otherwise do them and as diligently as they would otherwise do.
finding: After the MAX, Boeing committed not to pressure the FAA on timelines, accepting delivery instability.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: We'll stay on that clip. And I -- and we're still going to deliver the lion's share of the 100.
finding: In June 2021 Boeing still expected to deliver most of 100 787s in 2021, an expectation it later abandoned.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: I don't want to get past the 31 number until I have a real clarity around China. It's a real factor. It does affect the recovery trajectory. And if I try to run that number on the basis of an absolute win across the board in China at a certain moment and get it wrong, it's a big wrong.
finding: Boeing capped its 737 rate plan at 31 per month until China access was clear.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: if I had a clean slate of paper today and knowing -- and it wasn't a 777X loaded in my development pipeline, would you want to do it again? The answer is absolutely yes.
finding: Boeing reaffirmed the 777X despite delays, rejecting cancellation.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: it's another very important reason to do it because it will meet the standards. And so that's just another arrow in the quiver of wanting to do it. So it hadn't been announced, hasn't been approved by our Board. But I am confident that this one will move down that path.
finding: Boeing signalled a 777X freighter launch driven by coming ICAO emissions standards, before Board approval.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: I don't see that as a market-mover in that regard. And then it won't be all that long before we'll announce ours. And ours will not be predicated on replacing that because of what I just said.
finding: Boeing refused to launch a direct A321XLR response, saying its next airplane would target a bigger market.
trigger: Airbus A321XLR success in the middle of the market
response: No XLR-matching product; next airplane to target a larger market

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO
quote: we got lots of time because these are big bets that last from 30 to 50 years. So when we call out that next point design, we're not going to rush.
finding: Boeing believed it had time and would not rush its next new airplane.

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO

speaker: David Calhoun, CEO

quote: $3.5 billion of R&D and $2 billion of CapEx, very much in line with what the business historically done.

quote: The 3,7 in this forecast gets to about 50 a month, which we've done before. The 8,7 gets back to 10 -- gets to 10 a month, and the 777, 777 MAX gets to 4 a month.

quote: During 2022, as a result of the Russia Ukraine war, we suspended purchasing titanium from Russia. finding: Boeing dropped Russian titanium after the Ukraine invasion, covering the gap with inventory and alternative sources while keeping its sole-source suppliers.
response: Stopped buying Russian titanium; used inventory and alternative sources

quote: we have experienced production quality issues, including in our supply chain, which have contributed to lower 787 deliveries, including a suspension of 787 deliveries from May 2021 to August 2022.
finding: 787 quality problems, including in the supply chain, halted 787 deliveries for about 15 months (May 2021 to August 2022).

quote: The 737 program has experienced operational and supply chain challenges stabilizing production at 31 per month. We plan to gradually increase 737 production rates based on market demand and supply chain capacity.
finding: By FY2022 the 737 ramp was gated by supply-chain capacity as well as demand (FY2020 cited demand only), and the line was struggling to hold 31/month.

quote: We and our suppliers are experiencing supply chain disruptions as a result of the lingering impacts of COVID-19, global supply chain constraints, and labor instability. finding: In 2022 the binding limit on Boeing's ramp shifted from demand to supply-chain disruption, labor instability and inflation.

quote: Our Commercial Market Outlook forecast projects a 3.8% growth rate for passenger and cargo traffic over a 20-year period. quote: Research and development expense increased by $603 million in 2022 compared with 2021 primarily due to higher research and development expenditures on 777X, 737 MAX, as well as BCA and enterprise investments in product development.

quote: We have approximately 250 aircraft in inventory as of December 31, 2022, including approximately 140 aircraft in inventory that are designated for customers in China. We are remarketing some of these aircraft to other customers.

quote: We are following the lead of the FAA as we work through the certification process, and currently expect the 737-7 to be certified and delivered in 2023, and the 737-10 to begin FAA certification flight testing in 2023 with first delivery in in 2024.

finding: The 777X-9 slipped again, from late 2023 to 2025, because of certification requirements.

quote: In April 2022, we decided to pause production of the 777X-9 during 2022 and 2023. We implemented the production pause during the second quarter of 2022, and it is expected to result in abnormal production costs of approximately $1.5 billion that are being expensed as incurred until 777X-9 production resumes.
finding: Boeing paused 777X-9 production for two years rather than build uncertified jets into inventory, accepting about $1.5B of abnormal costs.
response: Production pause 2022-2023

quote: During the fourth quarter of 2022, we increased the accounting quantity for the 787 program by 100 units due to the program’s normal progress of obtaining additional orders and delivering aircraft. The increase in the accounting quantity improved the program’s profit margin.
finding: Boeing restored the 100 787 units it cut in 2020 (back to 1,600), a reversal that lifted program margin.

quote: In the third quarter of 2021, we determined that production rates below 5 per month represented abnormally low production rates and result in abnormal production costs.
finding: Boeing set 5/month as the 787's normal-rate floor; output below it is expensed as abnormal cost rather than carried in inventory.

quote: During the fourth quarter of 2022 we adjusted the total estimate of abnormal production costs up to $2.8 billion with most being incurred by the end of 2023. ... The increase was primarily driven by a decision in the fourth quarter of 2022 to slow down near-term production due to supply chain constraints and increased inspection and rework costs.
finding: In Q4 2022 Boeing slowed 787 production because of supply-chain constraints, raising expected abnormal costs to $2.8B.
response: Slowed 787 near-term production

quote: During the fourth quarter of 2021, we recorded a loss of $3.5 billion on the program primarily due to the additional rework, as well as other actions required to resume 787 deliveries, taking longer than expected.
finding: The 787 quality crisis produced a $3.5B reach-forward loss in Q4 2021.
Between FY2020 and FY2022, first-delivery dates slipped for all derivatives: 737-10 from 2023 to 2024, 777X-9 from 2023 to 2025, and 737-7 from 2021 to 2023.

quote: Non-cash items in 2021 include the $3.5 billion reach-forward loss on the 787 program which was recorded as a reduction to inventory, as well as $1.2 billion of treasury shares issued to fund Company contributions to the 401(k) plan and $0.8 billion of share-based plans expense reflecting a one-time stock grant to most employees in lieu of 2021 salary increases.
finding: To save cash, Boeing paid employees in stock (401(k) match in shares and a stock grant in place of 2021 raises).

quote: Capital expenditures totaled $1.2 billion in 2022, compared with $1.0 billion in 2021 and $1.3 billion in 2020. We expect capital expenditures in 2023 to be higher than in 2022.
finding: Capex bottomed at $1.0B in 2021 and Boeing guided it higher for 2023 as rates recovered.

quote: During 2021, debt repayments net of new borrowings were $5.6 billion, primarily due to $13.8 billion of repayments of our two-year delayed draw term loan credit agreement, partially offset by $9.8 billion of fixed rate senior notes issued in the first quarter of 2021.
finding: Boeing began deleveraging in 2021, repaying the $13.8B term loan partly with new bonds.

quote: During the years ended December 31, 2022, 2021 and 2020, we did not repurchase any shares through our open market share repurchase program. Share repurchases under this program have been suspended since April 2019. ... As a result, we did not pay any dividends in 2022 and 2021 compared with $1.2 billion paid in 2020.
finding: Through 2022 Boeing still paid no buybacks or dividends, keeping cash returns off while it repaired the balance sheet.

quote: We expect to be able to fund our cash requirements through cash and short-term investments and cash provided by operations, as well as continued access to capital markets. At December 31, 2022, we had $14.6 billion of cash, $2.6 billion of short-term investments, and $12.0 billion of unused borrowing capacity
finding: Boeing held $17.2B of cash and investments plus $12B of undrawn revolvers, and still relied on capital-market access.

quote: Net cumulative catch-up adjustments ... increased Loss from operations by $5,253 million, $880 million and $942 million in 2022, 2021 and 2020, respectively. The cumulative catch-up adjustments in 2022 were primarily due to losses recognized on the VC-25B, KC-46A Tanker, MQ-25, Commercial Crew and T-7A Red Hawk programs. These are all fixed-price development programs
finding: Aggressive fixed-price development bids (KC-46A, T-7A, MQ-25, VC-25B, Starliner) cost Boeing $5.25B in 2022, a warning against fixed-price development risk.

quote: The 767, 777X, and 787 programs had near break-even or single digit margins at December 31, 2022. Adverse changes to the revenue and/or cost estimates for these programs could result in earnings charges in future periods.
finding: At end-2022 all of Boeing's widebody programs were at near break-even or single-digit margins, leaving little cushion.

quote: Embraer has disputed our right to terminate the agreements, and the dispute is currently in arbitration. We cannot reasonably estimate a range of loss, if any, that may result from the arbitration, which we currently expect to be completed in late 2023 or early 2024.
finding: Walking away from the Embraer JV left an open arbitration liability into 2023-24.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: What's important is that, on that 38 for us, the factory space is there. The tooling is there, and the labor is there, right? So we wanted to make sure we were ready and ahead, and we are.
finding: Boeing positions factory space, tooling and labor ahead of each 737 rate break, so the supply chain becomes the only gate.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: it will start with handling the more complicated configuration airplanes so that Renton can be very predictable and very reliable. And then it's going to create that opportunity over time. to fulfill the demand of the skyline. I mean there's 3,600 737s that are in the order book.
finding: Boeing added a fourth 737 line in Everett (mid-2024) to take complex configurations off Renton and create future rate headroom for a 3,600-aircraft backlog.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we've had to take a little bit of a pause in that area in the near term to make an adjustment so that we can get the spirit fuselage in a spot where it was more predictable.
finding: Boeing paused 787 final assembly in early 2023 to let Spirit's fuselage deliveries stabilize, again showing supplier dependence.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We have a lot of resources that are deployed into Tier 1, Tier 2 supply houses, and it's lean manufacturing, it's engineering, it's quality.
finding: Boeing placed its own engineering, quality and lean staff inside Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers to stabilize them and spot problems early.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: In terms of vertical integration, it's not something that we're focused on. We're focused on stability, and that is job one.
finding: In March 2023 Boeing ruled out vertical integration; a year later it pursued reacquiring Spirit (reversal).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: On the Dash 7, while the regulator will dictate specific timing, we do expect certification and delivery this year.
finding: In March 2023 Boeing expected MAX 7 certification and delivery in 2023, which did not happen (later delayed by anti-ice issues).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the lesson learned is that there is a difference of expectations as it pertains to certification of airplanes. It is the new reality. We are going to resource it.
finding: Boeing accepted slower, stricter post-MAX certification as the new reality and resourced it rather than fighting it.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: I'm not sure I agree with all of that. But here's what I think about the narrow-body. So the MAX is sold firm through 2026, very good demand. ... think about the family across 7, 8, 9, 10, hold its own, right?
finding: Asked why it would not launch a new jet against Airbus's narrowbody lead, Boeing defended the MAX family (7-10) as competitive.
trigger: Airbus's ascension in the narrowbody segment
response: Stay with MAX family; no new jet

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we don't want to do thing niche. We want to do something that is step function changing of how our customers are going to be -- get more efficiency, and we'll be better. And right now, anything on that front is next decade, and we've been consistent with that.
finding: Boeing consistently placed any new airplane in the next decade and required a step-change product, not a niche entry.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: It turns out we beat our hiring goals last year, hired 15,000 people largely engineers and mechanics. 10,000 hires, right? It says something. I think it says that we are a technology company
finding: Boeing hired about 15,000 people in 2022, mostly engineers and mechanics, keeping engineering capability for future programs.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We're putting billions in R&D, and we'll spend more R&D money this year than last year, and we'll spend more R&D next year than this year.
finding: Boeing committed to rising R&D spending year after year during the recovery.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: if we deliver airplanes, we generate cash, we pay down debt, and that is going to naturally happen. ... In terms of what a return to capital discussion might look like, too early. But it'll be there someday.
finding: Boeing ranked debt paydown and reinvestment ahead of any dividend or buyback, which it called too early to discuss.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Deliveries and production will be lower near term, but we will recover over the coming months, and we plan to increase our rate to 38 per month later this year. As mentioned last week, we're also not changing the supplier master schedule to ensure that they can keep pace, and we're comfortable adding parts inventory.
finding: After the April 2023 Spirit fitting defect Boeing kept the supplier master schedule and the planned 38/month rate break, absorbing extra parts inventory.
response: Master schedule unchanged; rate 38 still planned

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: when you go from 2 to 1 and you optimize that 1 and you don't transport parts from one to another, you expect higher margins, and we do ... we don't see a big demand on investment to get us from what you noted as 7 to 10.
finding: Consolidating 787 final assembly in Charleston was expected to lift margins and reach 10/month with little new capital.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: So we will have a plan to get to 38. In terms of subsequent ramps to higher numbers, let's let that take care of itself. Let's focus on getting to 38. And we still believe that 50 is the number in '25, '26.
finding: Boeing declined to confirm reported interim 737 steps (42, 52), committing only to 38 next and 50 by 2025-26.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Nobody is sold-out. We're just all selling further out. So we still compete and then we -- the deliveries themselves are important competitive factor in everything that we go for and then pricing follows.
finding: Boeing treats delivery-slot timing as a key competitive weapon against Airbus, with price following availability.
trigger: Airbus narrowbody sold out for years
response: Compete on delivery slots, then price

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: I'm going to stick with sort of my posture, if you don't mind, that all of our guidance and all of our activities are going to assume that the best things don't happen.
finding: Calhoun built guidance on conservative assumptions that exclude upside scenarios such as China resuming deliveries.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we're perfectly comfortable keeping everyone at pace and hold a little buffer. We think that's a better alternative than keeping it a little bit too close to the wire. And we're going to keep having that posture, and that's going to help us get to 38 and then beyond.
finding: Boeing preferred keeping suppliers ahead of final assembly with buffer inventory over running lean, as the path to higher rates.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the current environment, it's pretty good for price realization. And why is that? Because you see the skyline, the deliveries keep moving to the right, which is a good dynamic. We will be disciplined on this topic.
finding: Boeing pledged pricing discipline while slots were scarce, using the sold-out skyline to improve price realization.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: But I also remind you that every campaign, we compete head to head, and that's the nature of our business. And the good news is if you look at our track record recently, we feel really good about the wins.
finding: Boeing competes with Airbus campaign by campaign and saw its recent win record as evidence that pricing discipline was not costing share.
response: Price discipline while competing

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Our rate projections, as you go forward, all the way up to 50, are lower than my competitor's rate projected. ... So if we can figure out a way to open up our constraints faster than the other guy, then so be it.
finding: Boeing accepted planning below Airbus's announced rates, and framed the race as who clears supply constraints faster.
response: Plan to 50/month; rise only as constraints clear

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Now I'm -- as you know, I'm heavily weighted to one of those suppliers, to one of those suppliers. And I have a lot of confidence in them to be able to get to where we need to get to.
finding: Boeing's sole-source engine position (CFM) tied its rate ceiling to one supplier, unlike Airbus's dual sourcing.
response: Rely on single engine supplier

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: with the targets we've put out there, I see us as still supply constrained. I'm not talking about my supply side, but the ability for the 2 airplane makers to meet the demands, I think, will still be constrained 5 years from now.
finding: Calhoun expected the Boeing-Airbus duopoly to stay supply-constrained for at least five years, so demand risk did not threaten targets.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We're all competing out there in '28, '29. And as you saw, some of our orders, of course, carry all the way into the early '30s.
finding: By mid-2023 both airframers were offering new narrowbody slots only in 2028-29, with some orders running into the early 2030s.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: with Ryan, and I give a lot of credit to Michael, we were patient with each other. We had some objectives we had to meet. He had some objectives he had to meet. We finally got to where we need to get.
finding: Boeing held out in long Ryanair negotiations until its own objectives were met, rather than conceding to close quickly.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Yes. And we'll just go up against that all day long, all day long. I believe this airplane will be just one of the most successful ever. It's hard for me to predict rate. I want to get certified first.
finding: Boeing dismissed the A350-1000 as a 777X rival and chose to compete head-on.
trigger: Airbus positioning the A350-1000 against the 777X
response: Stay the course on 777X

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: I've taken it out of all of our guidance, so our $10 billion in '25, '26 is -- has no China. And why did I do that? Because the rhetoric and discussion around all things geopolitical with China was beginning to confuse all of our investors
finding: Calhoun removed China from Boeing's $10B FCF underwriting case to insulate targets from geopolitical risk.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: If it gets better and better and better and better, our rate projections will get better and better and better and better, right? ... So if we can figure out a way to open up our constraints faster than the other guy, then so be it.
finding: Boeing's response to Airbus's higher rate targets was to compete on how fast it could unlock supply constraints, not to match announced rates.
trigger: Airbus announcing higher narrowbody rate targets
response: Raise rates only as supply constraints ease

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: the structural issues mostly were built around engines and then underneath them, forging, casting suppliers. ... I'm heavily weighted to one of those suppliers ... If I wanted to increase my rate projections, I mean 50 to 60 or whatever, that would be -- I'd go back to structural
finding: Boeing's 737 rate ceiling was set by engine makers (it relies heavily on one) and their forging and casting suppliers; going from 50 to 60 would need more structural engine capacity.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Seats is -- that was a perennial issue. As you know, we opened our own seat company, and it's doing incredibly well. And it's allowed us to, I think, overcome that constraint.
finding: Boeing vertically integrated into seat-making to remove a chronic supplier bottleneck.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: I think we would have started that fourth line under normal circumstances. In the world we used to know, we would have started that a year or 2 from now. We wanted to go early, start early, get ready, be prepared.
finding: Boeing built a fourth 737 line in Everett early, putting capacity ahead of demand to enable rates above 50.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: now we're in the tool up for the second line that allows us to get to 10, and we're confident we can do that, like you said, very limited capital. ... if we want to go over 10, and we believe we can, we will require some capital, we will require some footprint work.
finding: 787 rate 10 needed very limited capital, but rates above 10 would require extra capital and floor space.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: I think the Dash 10 will also have or play a big role in that one. More seats, more seats is a good move for us. It's both productive and it's price accretive.
finding: Boeing counted on the larger MAX 10 to restore pre-grounding 737 margins because extra seats are price-accretive.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: If they don't improve their performance for our customers, a minimum of 20%, a minimum of 20%, hopefully, something closer to 30%, and that performance now is both efficiency and emission. If you don't do that, it's really hard to justify a program for a new airplane.
finding: Boeing's new-airplane launch threshold is at least a 20% (ideally 30%) gain in efficiency and emissions.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: that investment will have to last a minimum of 50 years, it has to; and all the great airplane programs have, and the ones that weren't so great didn't, and the losses were massive.
finding: Boeing sees a new airplane as a 50-year bet with massive downside, which argues for waiting until technology is mature.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We have said -- I have said not before '35. Why? Because we know enough about our technology road map to know that they're not going to be mature enough
finding: Calhoun set 'not before 2035' for Boeing's next new airplane, tied to technology maturity.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: That is a very viable design. We have done a lot of test work. We're on step 2 of the maturity program. Step 2 is a joint program with NASA ... So that program is designed to prove its course by '28.
finding: Boeing's Transonic Truss-Braced Wing, run jointly with NASA, was meant to prove itself by 2028 as the basis for a future airplane.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: It can't be a niche. It can't be a niche. For me to design an airplane that sits on top of one of the other guy's airplanes, it makes no sense at all. It's -- there is no return. There is no return.
finding: Boeing refused to launch a new airplane that merely matches an Airbus product; it must target the largest market segment.
trigger: Airbus products occupying existing market segments
response: No me-too airplane; wait for a leap product

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: This includes engine technology, yes. The only way they're going to get to the kinds of numbers we need is a bigger bypass, so bigger fan.
finding: Boeing's next airplane depends on a higher-bypass, bigger-fan engine, which shapes airframe design and engine choice.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: I'm getting more and more confident they can do it, but it's not a short putt. ... at least one of these players has taken a big step forward on that front.
finding: Boeing was warming to open-rotor engines (the analyst cited CFM's RISE concept) but saw them as a long-horizon option with regulatory hurdles.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We have a couple of fixed-price development programs we have to just finish and never do them again. Never do them again. That fixed-price development world has to stop. It just doesn't work.
finding: Calhoun vowed never to take on fixed-price development contracts again after large defense losses.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: that target was way out of reach in many ways. And the out of reach cost us because capital was getting deployed for the sole purpose of achieving that number and without enough regard for the return on the capital we deployed.
finding: Calhoun rejected the earlier aspirational services revenue target because it drove return-blind capital deployment.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Supply chain stability takes it higher. Every step forward will take it higher because it will allow us to get a little more aggressive with rate, and more importantly, the productivity inherent is huge.
finding: Boeing saw supply-chain stability, which allows faster rate increases, as the main upside lever on its $10B FCF target.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we're going to run down the debt. So that will speak to most of the cash flow in those early years. ... I don't think we're going to want to move the balance sheet to a more conservative position than it was, say, in '17, '18, but we'll want to get close.
finding: Boeing planned to use most early free cash flow to cut debt toward, but not beyond, its 2017-18 balance-sheet posture before resuming shareholder returns.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: I don't view it as a meaningful competitor. There's nothing that I would want to do on the product development front to respond to it. It's not the world that we're interested in. ... The next airplane, in my view, with respect to development has to be a meaningful change, 25%, 30% better than what flies today.
finding: Boeing said it would not respond to a possible A220-500 stretch, and set a 25-30% improvement bar (transonic wing) for its next airplane.
response: No product response; focus on transonic wing

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We booked 460 net orders in the second quarter. And we're proud to announce or firm up key orders, I should say, 220 for Air India and we secured our commitment for up to 300 with Ryanair.
finding: Boeing won large 2023 narrowbody commitments (Air India 220, Ryanair up to 300 MAX 10s) while supply-constrained.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we are now transitioning production to 38 per month and still plan to increase to 50 per month in the '25, '26 time frame. As we move to the higher rate, we'll continue to prioritize stability, and it will take some time to consistently deliver at 38 per month off the line.
finding: In July 2023 Boeing began moving the 737 to 38/month, still targeting 50 by 2025-26 and prioritizing stability.
response: Rate break to 38

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We ended the quarter with approximately 228 MAX airplanes in inventory. This includes 85 for customers in China and 55 that have now been remarketed as part of the plan we've previously discussed.
finding: Boeing remarketed 55 China-destined MAX to other customers, cutting its China inventory to 85.
response: Remarketed 55 aircraft to other customers

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Abnormal costs were $136 million as expected, and we've lowered our total estimate from $1.5 billion to $1 billion, which reflects plans to resume production later this year rather than early 2024.
finding: Boeing pulled forward the 777X production restart to late 2023, cutting the estimated abnormal cost from $1.5B to $1B.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: In the quarter, we repaid $3.4 billion of maturing debt and provided a $180 million cash advance to Spirit as previously shared. Year-to-date, we've repaid $5.1 billion of debt, which is essentially all of our maturities for the year.
finding: Boeing repaid all its 2023 maturities from cash ($5.1B) and advanced $180M to Spirit to keep its key supplier stable.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: This is our desire to simply get ahead of the production curve. There's no -- yes, no breaks on the regulatory side. We still have margin in that.
finding: Boeing restarted 777X production early to get ahead of the production curve, not because certification had sped up.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We're heavily invested in this. We like what it could potentially deliver to this market, a level of performance that the industry is used to seeing with brand-new programs.
finding: Boeing was investing heavily in the Transonic Truss-Braced Wing as its candidate next narrowbody technology.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: You are right, we can use existing power, but we would prefer, frankly, to have a bigger fan diameter ultimately and maybe even open rotor someday. So those are all considerations without a doubt. I don't want to make choices too early.
finding: For its next narrowbody Boeing preferred a larger-fan or open-rotor engine over existing engines and deliberately delayed the engine choice.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: 38 has to come and has to come in a stable form so that we're not up and down every month. But maybe more important than that, we now have such good visibility into the supply chain. We know whether they're ready for the next -- for 40, 42, 44, et cetera.
finding: Boeing's rule for each 737 rate step (40/42/44) is stable output at the current rate plus supplier-by-supplier readiness.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Second half of '24 is a very important moment in time because I believe that's the step change for BCA in pretty much every way. And if we get through that well and we execute well, then we'll be talking to all of you about 60.
finding: Boeing made any move to 60/month conditional on winding down the shadow factories and stable execution in H2 2024.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: having a little too much capacity is not a problem for us right now when you're trying to knock down stability. So if we run something at a suboptimal level, it's not going to cost us much ... We want to have more capacity than we need so that we're ready for that next increment.
finding: Boeing deliberately carried surplus 737 capacity (such as the new Everett line) to protect stability and prepare for rate increases.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: The next airplane, in my view, with respect to development has to be a meaningful change, 25%, 30% better than what flies today. That's why we're focused on Transonic wings. That is -- that's just our game plan.
finding: Boeing's threshold for launching a new airplane is a 25-30% improvement, which is why it bet on Transonic Truss-Braced Wing technology rather than derivatives.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we still are committed to the long-term financial targets that we set out in November of last year at our Investor Day, $10 billion of free cash flow, 50 737 deliveries per month, 10 787 per month in the '25/'26 time frame. So that remains unchanged.
finding: In Sept 2023 Boeing reaffirmed its 2022 Investor Day targets ($10B FCF, 737 at 50/month, 787 at 10/month by 2025-26) despite supplier setbacks.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: It will impact about 75% of the 220 airplanes that were inventory -- that were in inventory as of the end of the second quarter. So it's large. In the near term, it will impact deliveries, but we have no intention of changing the master schedule.

response: Rework, master schedule unchanged

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We also expect us to have a drag from the 777X entry into service around 2025. As normal, when they start off, there's a bit of a drag.
finding: In 2023 Boeing planned 777X entry into service around 2025 and expected an early-production margin drag.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the biggest mover is going to be BCA productivity without a doubt. And it will come in the form of the higher rate ramps as we go from 38 to that 50 number over time, that's big. The dismantlement of these 2 dual factories, which are heavily resourced
finding: Boeing's bridge to $10B FCF depended mainly on 737 rate increases from 38 to 50 and closing the rework factories.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: I'm not quite there on the upside. I think that the $10 billion reflects a set of assumptions that we feel very confident in and we think are ones -- are numbers that we have ability to meet.

speaker: Brian West, CFO

quote: Our production system is poised for steady and efficient increases, but we won't push the system too fast, and we'll ensure the supply base is in lockstep with us.
finding: Boeing's rate-increase doctrine is to ramp only in lockstep with the supply base rather than push demand-driven rates.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We plan to complete the production transition to 38 per month by the end of the year and still plan to reach the key rate of 50 per month by that '25 and '26 time frame.
finding: Before Alaska 1282 Boeing planned 737 rate 38 by end-2023 and 50/month by 2025-26 (a plan later capped by the FAA).

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: given our year-to-date total, we now expect 737 deliveries for the year to be in the 375 to 400 range. While a setback, we'll regain our momentum as we progress through the issue. We are keeping our suppliers hot according to the master schedule.

quote: Important to note with respect to our supply chain, delivery shortfalls have been driven by nonconformances, not actual supply chain constraints.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we're pleased to have recently established a mutually beneficial agreement that will enhance stability of our production system and help us deliver on our customer commitments, a true win-win.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: in a fixed price environment, any unplanned hurdles can introduce unrecoverable cost. At the end of the day, we have 2 airplanes to build.
finding: Boeing's VC-25B losses showed the unrecoverable-cost risk of fixed-price development that shaped its later refusal of such contracts.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We have as clear and as transparent a relationship as we could possibly have with the GE and CFM teams. The rates that we have outlined in our guidance reflect those constraints. We all could go much higher, much faster if it was strictly a demand question
finding: Boeing sized its 737 rate plan to CFM engine supply and other supplier constraints, not demand.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: I am always tempted, based on demand, to tell you we can do more than 50 and get to 60. And we are physically capacitized to do it, you're correct in that. But I can't call it out until the supply chain constraints can make it
finding: Boeing had physical capacity for about 60/month 737s but would not announce rates beyond 50 until the supply chain could support them.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We've had, just in the last 30 days, as many interactions with Pat as we've had over the last year, even though we've had more than 100 people embedded at Spirit.
finding: Boeing embedded more than 100 staff at Spirit and stepped up engagement with its new CEO to fix fuselage conformance.
