speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We can't rush. We can't push the factory too hard or the system too hard because the payoff, if we do this right, is going to be big beyond 2025, and that's what we're aiming at.
finding: The 'don't rush the ramp' stance started under Calhoun and West in 2024, before Ortberg arrived.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: The CAAC has asked for additional validation on a lithium battery in that recorder. And because of that, we have not been delivering airplanes to China recently.
finding: Chinese regulatory actions repeatedly halted deliveries to China (2024 recorder battery, 2025 tariffs).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we expect the transaction to close mid-2025, subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions, including regulatory and Spirit shareholder approvals as well as the sale of Spirit operations related to certain Airbus commercial work packages.
finding: Boeing took its fuselage supply back in-house by buying Spirit, with Spirit's Airbus work packages split off to Airbus.
trigger: Spirit AeroSystems quality problems; shared supplier with Airbus
response: Acquire Spirit (~$4.7bn equity, $8.3bn EV)

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: We know that ASKs will be big. We know wage ASKs will be big. We're not afraid to treat our employees well in this process.
finding: Before the 2024 IAM talks Boeing said it would give sizeable wage increases to avoid a strike; members still rejected the offer and struck (p.156).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: if we are able to bump up against maturities we're going to do what it takes to protect that rating, period. And we've been consistent since April 2020 on that front and evidenced by the Spirit financing decision.
finding: Protecting the investment-grade rating has been Boeing's fixed financial priority since 2020.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: what you saw in the quarter that we had a pullback of about $1 billion on the advance balance. Those two things are both happening in that balance
finding: Customers reacted to Boeing's delivery problems by applying excess advances and holding back pre-delivery payments, a $1B cash hit.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: the third line, it also helps us with unforeseen issues because it gives us flexibility across three lines as opposed to having to close two if we end up the nonconformance somewhere. So we are simply trying to overcapacitize to accommodate things that appear and steady our production.
finding: Boeing builds spare final-assembly capacity (a third Renton line) to absorb disruptions.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: On cash and marketable securities, we ended the quarter at $12.6 billion, reflecting the $10 billion issuance of new debt in May ... The debt balance increased to $57.9 billion driven by the new debt issuance.
finding: Boeing issued $10B of new debt in May 2024, taking debt to $57.9B.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We'll continue to follow the lead of the FAA as we progress through the certification process and still expect first delivery in 2025.
finding: In July 2024 the 777X first delivery was still guided for 2025; it later moved to 2026 (October 2024) and 2027 (October 2025).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we announced a definitive agreement to acquire Spirit in an all-stock transaction worth approximately $4.7 billion with a total enterprise value of approximately $8.3 billion ... as well as the sale of Spirit operations related to certain Airbus commercial work packages.
finding: Boeing paid for Spirit in stock, and the deal required Spirit to sell its operations serving certain Airbus work packages.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: One of the most important actions we took was the transfer of our Renton fuselage inspection process to Wichita. On-site Boeing inspectors at Spirit increased by almost 3x the number that we had before January.
finding: Boeing moved fuselage inspection upstream to Spirit and tripled its inspectors there.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: we've identified an engineering solution for the engine anti-ice system for in-production aircraft that will be implemented and certified in 2025 to support the first delivery of our -7 and -10 in the MAX family.
finding: In July 2024 Boeing targeted 2025 certification of the 737-7/-10; it later slipped to 2026.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: Based on the lessons that we've learned in taking on these fixed-price development programs, we have maintained contracting discipline for all future opportunities.
finding: Calhoun had already sworn off risky fixed-price development bids, and Ortberg kept the stance.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: let me touch on the recently announced agreement to acquire Spirit AeroSystems. This is an important shift in strategic direction, and it would course correct the decision made decades ago.
finding: Calhoun called the Spirit AeroSystems buy-back a strategic shift that corrects Boeing's decades-old decision to outsource fuselage work.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, CEO
quote: The January accident obviously sharpened this focus, leading us to take multiple additional steps to improve the stability of our operations, including major elements of our supply chain. First, among our actions was to slow things down and control traveled work, allowing our supply chain to catch up
finding: Boeing responded to the January 2024 accident by deliberately slowing 737 production and controlling traveled work so suppliers could catch up.
trigger: January 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 door plug accident and FAA 38/month cap
response: Deliberately slow production, control traveled work, build supply-chain buffer

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: So we are perfectly comfortable to supplement our liquidity position to support these two objectives. And we're constantly evaluating our capital structure and liquidity levels to ensure that we could satisfy our debt maturities over the next 18 months while keeping confidence in our credit rating as investment grade.
finding: In September 2024 Boeing said it was ready to raise capital to protect its rating; it announced a $24B raise in October (p.120).
lag: about 1 month before the October 2024 capital raise

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: on the 37 cash margins, when we get to a point where we're more stable and hitting the rates you described, we are going to be approaching what those cash margins look like in the 2018 time frame. On the 787 program, similarly, as we move forward towards those rates we've described, we're going to be better than 2018.
finding: Boeing expects 737 unit cash margins to return to 2018 levels and 787 margins to beat them at target rates (50+ and 10).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: On the 777, we expect lower deliveries than last year, driven to a large extent by engine availability. That has been a constraint.
finding: Engine availability limited 777 deliveries in 2024.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: 787, there will be no change in the part supply chain expectations, right? That's just going to keep going. If there's a non-787 part that is behind, we're going to allow suppliers to catch up. If there are non-787 parts that are not behind and there's a safety stock, they are going to stop.
finding: Boeing's strike rule for suppliers: keep 787 parts flowing, let late suppliers catch up, and stop suppliers that are ahead.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: From a financial perspective, any impact is going to be dictated by the duration of the work stoppage ... strike will impact production and deliveries and operations and will jeopardize our recovery. So our immediate focus is to the laser-like focused on actions to conserve cash, and we will.
finding: The day after the IAM contract was rejected, Boeing switched to cash conservation.
trigger: IAM members rejected the tentative contract (96%) and began striking (Sep 2024)
response: Immediate cash-conservation actions; CEO on factory floor to reset union relationship

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: An example, just the 767 freighter. We looked at that and said, "Hey, look, there's an incoming on the 767 freighter. It's coming soon. Let's make the decision now and get that distraction out of the way.
finding: Boeing ended 767 Freighter production ahead of an approaching ('incoming') deadline to free resources.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I don't think we can walk away from these contracts. These are our core customers that need this capability. ... So walking away isn't an answer to this.
finding: Boeing will not cancel loss-making core contracts outright and renegotiates them instead.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: It is so much more important that we do this right than fast coming out of the chute. ... We've tried to manage that as best we could and keep folks like Spirit, for example, on fuselage, keep them funded and moving forward.
finding: Boeing kept funding critical suppliers such as Spirit through the strike and chose a slow restart.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: This is not a situation where we have to figure out what market opportunities are we going to go pursue. They're right in front of us. Our backlog is so strong.
finding: Ortberg ranks executing the existing backlog above pursuing new market opportunities.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: So we're going to really focus this workforce reduction in streamlining those overhead activities ... And I wouldn't think of it like we're going to take people off the production or out of the engineering labs.
finding: Boeing's layoffs targeted overhead and spared production and engineering staff.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Yes, it's too early for me to answer that. I would just say all the financial forecast, the long-term outlook are under review.
finding: In October 2024 Ortberg would not back the $10B free-cash-flow target; by mid-2025 he called it a question of when, not if.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I think that we're better off being -- doing less and doing it better than doing more and not doing it well.
finding: Ortberg prefers a narrower portfolio executed well to a broad one.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We're focused on maintaining $10 billion of cash in addition to our revolver capacity as we historically have.
finding: Boeing keeps a minimum cash balance of about $10B plus its revolver.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we have a plan to comprehensively address the balance sheet in the near term that could include an offering of equity and equity-linked securities.
finding: Boeing planned to repair its balance sheet with equity and equity-linked securities.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we ended the quarter at $10.5 billion, primarily reflecting the $2 billion use of free cash flow in the quarter. The debt balance remained stable, ending at $57.7 billion. Last week, we entered into a new $10 billion short-term credit facility
finding: Boeing's liquidity fell to $10.5B against $57.7B of debt, and it added a new $10B short-term credit line.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We've worked across our supply chain partners to significantly reduce expenditures while balancing the associated trade-offs. We shared plans to reduce our workforce to align with our financial reality and a more focused set of priorities. We're decisively implementing reductions to our discretionary spending across the company.
finding: In a liquidity crisis Boeing cut supplier spend, headcount and discretionary costs.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Revenue was $7.4 billion, and operating margin was minus 54%, primarily reflecting previously announced pre-tax charges of $3 billion on the 777X and 767 programs
finding: The strike and program charges drove commercial margins to -54% in Q3 2024.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Given the strike and our need to conserve cash, we've made near-term adjustments to broadly stop supplier shipments. We continue to manage supplier by supplier based on inventory levels and for certain suppliers, this will allow them to catch up.
finding: During the 2024 IAM strike Boeing stopped most supplier shipments to save cash, managing each supplier separately.
trigger: September 2024 IAM machinist strike halting Puget Sound production
response: Broadly stop supplier shipments; manage supplier by supplier; keep critical suppliers funded

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the $2.6 billion pretax charge primarily reflects our latest assessment of the certification time lines to address the delays in flight testing of the 777-9 as well as anticipated delays associated with the IAM work stoppage. ... now expect first delivery in 2026.
finding: The 777X slipped to 2026 with a $2.6B charge in 2024, the first of the Ortberg-era 777X resets (another followed in October 2025).

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: This include disciplined program and risk management in all phases of the project, including the bid phase.
finding: Boeing applies risk discipline from the bid phase of new programs.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Boeing's an airplane company. And at the right time in the future, we need to develop a new airplane but we have a lot of work to do before them. This includes stabilizing our business, improving the execution on the development programs, streamlining the portfolio to do what we do well and restoring the balance sheet
finding: From his first call Ortberg made a new airplane conditional on stabilisation, finished development programs, a streamlined portfolio and a restored balance sheet, and he held this position through 2025.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: First, we need a fundamental culture change in the company; second, we must stabilize the business; third, we need to improve our execution discipline on new platform commitments across the company; and fourth, while doing the first 3, we must build a new future for Boeing.
finding: Ortberg's 4-point plan puts culture, stabilisation and execution ahead of building the future (new products).

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we've got a backlog that is in place that has embedded escalation in it. That hasn't changed. That's good. And in terms of our supply contracts, they're vastly signed up until end of this decade.
finding: Escalation clauses in the backlog and supplier contracts locked to 2030 protect commercial margins from inflation.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we've got $87.5 billion worth of inventory in the company right now. That is too much. Now it's been an investment and stability
finding: Boeing held $87.5B of inventory, a deliberate stability buffer it expects to turn into cash.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I'm not putting a finer point on it, both externally nor internally. We're going to go to that rate when the KPIs say that we're going to go to that rate.
finding: Ortberg sets no rate-increase dates, even internally; KPIs decide the timing.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: they've got a big challenge with supporting our rate increases, our competitor rate increases and managing the aftermarket. And I work very closely with Larry and his team to make sure we stay aligned.
finding: Boeing competes with Airbus's ramps and the aftermarket for GE/CFM engine supply and manages this at CEO level.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the IAM agreement did put pressure. But keep in mind, we're talking about a cost that's less than 5% of the airplane.
finding: Boeing says the IAM wage settlement adds pressure but amounts to under 5% of airplane cost.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: it's an important technology development program. It's very challenging. ... And then we'll look at what comes out of that and how that factors into our next airplane. ... We've got some funding we're investing, but we've also got some funding there to support us.
finding: Boeing co-funds the X-66 NASA technology demonstrator as an input to its next airplane, sharing the cost of pre-launch R&D.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: because we've forecasted rates that the supply chain has built to and then we haven't met those rates. So I want to make sure that supply chain isn't making independent decisions on readiness for these out-year production rates and continuing to invest in the capacity that they need to supply us.
finding: Boeing admits suppliers lost faith after it missed forecast rates and is working to keep them investing in capacity.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: it's generally more in the commodities where there's long lead components like forgings, castings, that kind of stuff. I'm less worried about electronics. ... it's where you have to invest in that second and third tier supply chain that we want to make sure that they're making those investments and they haven't hedged their bets.
finding: Long-lead forgings and castings at lower supplier tiers are the rate-limiting part of the supply chain.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: We've been burned on that on the tanker program. And clearly, that's been a challenge for us on T-7A. So we've taken our medicine. We're not going to do that anymore.
finding: After KC-46 and T-7A losses, Boeing has sworn off fixed-price development with fixed-price production options.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we're building production airplanes while we're testing and certifying the design. And that's a disaster because every time you come up with a change that comes out of that, you've got to go ripple that change back through the production process
finding: Ortberg calls building production aircraft while the design is still being tested and certified a disaster because every change must ripple back through built aircraft.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we are getting the supply chain back to back in fixed price right now. Our goal is to get that 100% done. But as we're doing that, we're having to recognize the cost increases from the supply chain.
finding: Boeing is moving fixed-price risk onto suppliers with matching contracts and booking the cost of doing so.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: In some cases, you have potential that you could sell it and there are buyers. In some cases, that may not be a viable approach. We may want to just not continue with the next phase of the project or something like that. ... think of it as more pruning the portfolio, not cutting down the tree.
finding: Boeing will prune non-core activities by selling them or stopping further phases, but not restructure the core.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we ended the quarter at $26.3 billion, primarily reflecting the successful $24 billion capital raise in October, partially offset by the free cash flow usage and debt repayment. The debt balance ended at $53.9 billion, down $3.8 billion in the quarter, driven by the early repayment of a $3.5 billion bond
finding: Boeing raised $24B of capital in October 2024 and used part of it to repay a 2025 bond early.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Full year revenue was $66.5 billion, down 14% year-over-year ... The core loss per share was $20.38 ... Free cash flow was a $14.3 billion usage for the year
finding: 2024 was a crisis year: revenue down 14% and $14.3B of free cash flow burned.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: We are very focused on creating stability within the EACs, so we stop this quarterly drumbeat of cost growth. This means being more proactive and clear eyed on the risks and our estimates to complete the projects.
finding: Ortberg takes charges up front, with realistic estimates to complete, to stop repeated cost growth; he applied the same idea to the 777X in October 2025.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: They reported that they saw significant improvements, and I'm pleased that we have an agreed-upon path for rate increases beyond 38 per month. It's all about adhering to our safety management system and a stable factory as measured through agreed-upon key performance indicators or KPIs.
finding: By January 2025 Boeing had agreed with the FAA on a KPI-based path to lift the 38-per-month cap.

quote: As part of our plan to improve quality and safety and to address the issues identified, we slowed production rates and delayed planned production rate increases to reduce traveled work in our factory, as well as at our suppliers.
finding: After the January 2024 door-plug accident Boeing deliberately slowed 737 rates and deferred increases, putting quality ahead of volume and reversing its long rate-increase pattern.

quote: the FAA communicated it will not approve production rate increases beyond 38 per month or additional production lines until Boeing has complied with required quality and safety standards.
finding: From 2024 an external regulator, not Boeing, capped the 737 rate at 38 per month, a binding constraint on its production-rate lever.

quote: Prior to the Alaska Airlines accident, we were operating at a production rate of 38 per month. ... These actions also include conducting fuselage inspections at Spirit to improve quality prior to shipment to Boeing.
finding: Boeing moved its own inspectors upstream into Spirit's fuselage factory, taking direct control of supplier quality.

quote: We plan to gradually increase the production rate.
finding: Boeing's stated 737 posture after the accident and strike was a gradual rather than aggressive re-ramp.

quote: As a result of the strike, we paused production of our commercial aircraft (other than the 787 production in Charleston) and certain of our BDS products, adversely impacting our business and financial position. During the strike, we implemented hiring freezes and announced plans to reduce our overall workforce.
finding: Boeing answered the 2024 IAM strike with hiring freezes and workforce cuts; only non-union Charleston 787 production continued.

quote: On September 12, 2024, our contract with IAM 751, which represents over 30,000 Boeing manufacturing employees primarily located in Washington state, expired and 96% of IAM 751 members voted to initiate a strike.
finding: When the IAM 751 contract (extended in 2014 to 2024, p.2759) expired, 96% of members voted to strike.

quote: The introduction of new aircraft programs and/or derivatives, such as the 777X, 737-7 and 737-10, involves risks associated with meeting development, testing, certification and production schedules. We are following the lead of the FAA as we work through the certification process, and the FAA will ultimately determine the timing of certification and entry into service.
finding: By 2024 Boeing had ceded certification timing to the FAA and gave no entry-into-service dates for the 777X, 737-7 or 737-10.

quote: Delays on the 737, 777X and 787 programs have resulted in, and may continue to result in, customers having the right to terminate orders, be compensated for late deliveries and/or substitute orders for other Boeing aircraft.
finding: Boeing's delays across all three main programs gave customers termination and compensation rights, a risk of losing backlog.

quote: the anticipated first delivery of the 777-9 was delayed to 2026 and the 777-8 Freighter moved to 2028. First delivery of the 777-8 passenger aircraft is not expected to occur before 2030. In addition, we decided to slow the production rate ramp of 777X to address production challenges
finding: The 777X, launched in 2013 for 2020 delivery (p.2666), slipped to 2026 and the 777-8 passenger version to 2030 or later: a six-year delay on the widebody upgrade.

quote: As a result of these changes, as well as higher estimated labor and supplier costs, we recorded a $2,608 million reach-forward loss during the third quarter of 2024. During the fourth quarter of 2024, we recorded an additional reach-forward loss of $891 million on the 777X program
finding: The 777X became a loss-making program in 2024 ($3.5bn reach-forward loss), yet Boeing kept it going rather than cancel.

quote: During the third quarter of 2024, we decided to end production of the 767 freighter program in 2027 and, as a result of this decision, we reduced the accounting quantity for the 767 program by 9 units.
finding: Boeing ended the 767 freighter, as it had with the 747 (last delivered February 2023, p.2200), cancelling legacy lines once demand or regulation ran out.

quote: resulted in a reach-forward loss of $398 million during the third quarter of 2024. ... We recorded an additional reach-forward loss of $182 million as a result of the reduction in the accounting quantity and the new IAM 751 agreement.
finding: Ending the 767 freighter cost $580m in reach-forward losses in 2024.

quote: During 2024, we slowed production to below 5 per month due to supply chain constraints as well as other production issues. ... Delays associated with business class seats adversely impacted 2024 deliveries and will continue to impact deliveries in 2025.
finding: The 787 rate fell from 12-14 (2018-19 plans, p.2508) to below 5 in 2024, with seat suppliers a binding constraint.

quote: We are currently targeting a combined production rate of 4 per month for the 777/777X programs having resumed production in December 2024.
finding: Boeing targeted only 4 per month across 777 and 777X combined, far below the 8.3 per month 777 rate of 2013-14.

quote: We are continuing to work through the certification process of the 737-7 and 737-10 models, which have been delayed, while we work through the engineering solution for the engine anti-ice system for the 737-7 and 737-10 prior to certification of these minor models.
finding: The MAX 10, launched in 2017 for 2020 (p.2508), was still uncertified at end-2024 over an engine anti-ice issue, weakening Boeing's answer at the top of the single-aisle market.

quote: Approximate undelivered orders by minor model in 2024, 2023, and 2022, respectively: 737-7 (7%, 7%, 6%), 737-8 (63%, 65%, 70%), 737-9 (5%, 3%, 4%) and 737-10 (25%, 25%, 20%).
finding: A quarter of the 737 backlog (the -10) and 7% (the -7) were uncertified models, putting about 32% of 737 orders at certification risk.

quote: As of December 31, 2024, we had approximately 55 737-8 aircraft in inventory that were produced prior to 2023, including approximately 40 aircraft for customers in China.
finding: Boeing still held 737 MAX stored inventory tied to China deliveries five years after the grounding.
Boeing delivered only 348 airplanes in 2024 (265 737s, 18 767s, 14 777s, 51 787s), versus 806 in 2018.

quote: Revenues $22,861 $33,901 $26,026 % of total company revenues 34 % 44 % 39 % Loss from operations ($7,969) ($1,635) ($2,341) Operating margins (34.9)% (4.8)% (9.0)%
finding: BCA lost $8.0bn in 2024 (-34.9% margin) and has lost money every year since at least 2022.

quote: Aircraft order cancellations during the year ended December 31, 2024 totaled $11,311 million and primarily related to 737 aircraft. Net ASC 606 adjustments for the year ended December 31, 2024 totaled $16,553 million and primarily related to 777X aircraft.
finding: Customers cancelled $11.3bn of mostly 737 orders in 2024, and $16.6bn of mostly 777X orders came out of backlog under ASC 606.

quote: Program accounting quantities 11,600 1,263 1,822 500 1,800 Undelivered units under firm orders 4,303 * 109 68 358 719 (8)
finding: At end-2024 Boeing had 4,303 undelivered 737s, 358 777X and 719 787s; the 777X firm backlog fell from 416 to 358.

quote: Net cash (used)/provided by operating activities (12,080) 5,960 3,512
finding: Operating cash flow was -$12.1bn in 2024.

quote: Net cash used by operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2024 was $12.1 billion and we expect negative operating cash flows to continue in future quarters as we work to ramp up commercial airplanes production. As of December 31, 2024, our debt totaled $53.9 billion
finding: Boeing entered 2025 expecting continued cash burn, carrying $53.9bn of debt (vs $9-14bn in 2013-18).

quote: Cash provided by financing activities during 2024 was primarily driven by the issuance of common stock and Mandatory convertible preferred stock in the fourth quarter of 2024, which resulted in cash proceeds of $18.2 billion and $5.7 billion, net of issuance costs, as well as the issuance of $10.0 billion of fixed-rate senior notes
finding: Boeing raised about $24bn of equity plus $10bn of debt in 2024: the opposite of the $6-9bn a year of buybacks in 2014-2018.

quote: In 2020, we announced the suspension of our dividend to common shareholders until further notice. As a result, we did not pay any dividends to common shareholders in 2024, 2023 and 2022.
finding: Boeing's common dividend, raised every year from 2013 to 2018, has been suspended since 2020.

quote: Capital expenditures totaled $2.2 billion in 2024, compared with $1.5 billion in 2023 and $1.2 billion in 2022. We expect capital expenditures to grow in 2025 compared with 2024.
finding: Boeing kept raising capex through the 2024 crisis ($2.2bn), protecting investment while cash burned.

quote: We currently maintain investment grade credit ratings; however, Moody’s downgraded our short term and long term credit ratings to Baa3/P-3 in April 2024.
finding: Boeing's rating fell to the edge of junk (Baa3), and the equity raise defended investment grade.

quote: At December 31, 2024, we had $13.8 billion of cash, $12.5 billion of short-term investments, and $10.0 billion of unused borrowing capacity on revolving credit line agreements.
finding: Boeing ended 2024 with about $26bn of cash and investments plus $10bn of revolvers as a liquidity buffer.

quote: we have agreed to acquire Spirit AeroSystems Holdings, Inc. (Spirit) in an all-stock transaction at an equity value of approximately $ 4,700 , or $ 37.25 per share of Spirit Class A Common Stock. The transaction will include the assumption of Spirit's net debt at closing.
finding: Boeing chose to acquire its fuselage supplier Spirit and pay in stock rather than cash.

quote: During 2023 and 2024, Boeing reached agreements to provide Spirit up to $ 1,067 to support its liquidity, rate readiness, and 787 tooling and capital expenditures
finding: Boeing propped up its distressed key supplier with cash before buying it.

quote: additional losses on its five most significant fixed-price development programs (KC-46A Tanker, T-7A Red Hawk, Commercial Crew, VC-25B Presidential Aircraft, and MQ-25).
finding: Boeing's fixed-price defense development contracts (KC-46A, T-7A, Commercial Crew, VC-25B, MQ-25) produced further losses in 2024.

quote: the 737 program: deferred production costs of $ 9,679 and $ 6,011
finding: 737 deferred production costs rose from $6.0bn to $9.7bn in 2024, adding balance-sheet exposure to future 737 deliveries.

quote: the 787 program: deferred production costs of $ 13,178 and $ 12,384
finding: 787 deferred production costs rose again in 2024, to $13.2bn.

quote: Concessions paid to 737 MAX customers totaled $0.9 billion and $0.4 billion during 2024 and 2023.
finding: Boeing kept paying cash compensation to 737 MAX customers for delays and groundings.

quote: We face aggressive international competitors who are intent on increasing their market share, such as Airbus and entrants from China. We are focused on improving our products and processes and continuing cost reduction efforts.
finding: By 2024 Boeing named only Airbus and Chinese entrants as commercial competitors, and its stated response was unchanged since 2014: process and cost improvement.

quote: we project demand for approximately 43,975 new airplanes over the next 20 years.
finding: Boeing's 20-year demand forecast stayed high (about 44,000 airplanes) despite its own production crisis.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: there's great operational leverage in the ramp back up. So there's no question that, that will be a tailwind for us. We are going to have inflationary effects from the supply chain that we're going to see. So that's playing through. We have consideration to our customers for late deliveries
finding: Ortberg expects commercial margins to recover with volume, net of supplier inflation and customer compensation for late deliveries.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: there's a lot of productivity opportunities in the organization. I'm not really attacking that right now because I want to get stable, I want to get ramped back up. I don't want to get things confused.
finding: Ortberg sequences the turnaround: stability and ramp first, cost-cutting and productivity afterwards.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I think you've seen the criticality of Spirit's performance to our performance. It's hand in glove. And so having that a part of our organization is going to be a big uplift and strategic lift for us ... when I first started 6 months ago, that was probably the #1 concern that we had.
finding: Spirit was Boeing's biggest 737 constraint in 2024, and owning it is meant to remove that risk.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we'd want to see 2 to 3 months of stability at a rate. ... there's this thing called the Capstone review, which is usually done about 30 days before a rate increase with the FAA.
finding: Boeing's working rule is 2-3 months of KPI stability at a rate, then an FAA Capstone review about 30 days before a rate increase.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: So we've held off on rate increases on the 87 until we can get to the right level. Now that creates some challenges for our customers because it's fewer airplanes than if we went faster. But I think it's much more important that we'd be deliberate here
finding: Boeing accepts giving customers fewer aircraft to keep the 787 production system stable.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: So the first priority is to finish the certification deliveries of our current development programs. I got -7, -10, 777X, we have finished that, right? ... So that's job one, and we can't take our eye off that ball.
finding: Finishing the 737-7, -10 and 777X comes before any new airplane.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we're Boeing, we make airplanes. We're going to make an airplane someday. But he's also careful to say, yes, but it's not right now. ... Now it's a ways off, and there's been no timetable set.
finding: Boeing commits to a future new airplane in principle but has no timetable and says it is a long way off.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we just don't want to rush a decision for a product that's going to be out there for 50 years, right? It's a really important decision.
finding: Boeing treats a new-airplane launch as a 50-year bet that should not be rushed.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we have lots of engineers, thousands of engineers, who work on innovation, who work on capabilities that we're pretty sure are going to be important to whatever that next airplane is. ... It's not going to disrupt our financial profile. It's well within the envelope
finding: Boeing keeps funding pre-launch technology for its next airplane within its current R&D budget.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we understand that it's an investment, and it's an investment in things like long lead items, engines, fuselages that we have plenty of. But there will be a moment when we feel more stable, that we will deliberately begin to take those excess buffers down.
finding: Boeing treats excess inventory of engines and fuselages as a deliberate investment in stability, to be released later as cash.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: We are going to be able to take a much broader time horizon in terms of investments, right? We want to invest in quality, stability, innovation, and we'll do it in ways that perhaps they couldn't have done by themselves.
finding: Boeing is bringing Spirit AeroSystems back in-house to invest in fuselage quality and innovation over a longer horizon, trading capital for control of a key constraint.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: with that big backlog, we can move a lot around and still get them what they need and not disrupt our own business.
finding: Boeing answers tariff uncertainty by moving delivery slots around its large backlog instead of changing production.
trigger: 2025 tariff uncertainty affecting customers in different jurisdictions
response: Reshuffle deliveries within the backlog to accommodate customers while keeping production stable

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: It will be things like rework. It will be notice of escapes. It will be traveled work. It will be supplier shortages. It will be employee training, and it will be ticketing.
finding: The six FAA-agreed stability KPIs that gate Boeing's rates are rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training and ticketing.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we had implemented that process on 800 airplane moves, and we had stopped the airplanes 200 of those 800 times.
finding: The new travel-ready gate stopped 737 line moves a quarter of the time, trading short-term speed for quality.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: it's a combination of finding alternate source, requalifying, finding inventory and getting it in the right place. And it's not just us, as you know, it's some of our major suppliers as well who this impacts.
finding: Boeing answered a fastener-supplier fire (SPS) by finding alternate sources, requalifying parts and redistributing inventory.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: As you know, we've invested additional capital of $1 billion here in our Charleston facility. That's where we are today to expand our production capacity here. So we definitely want to get the 87 back up to double-digit production rates.
finding: Boeing put about $1B into Charleston capacity to take the 787 back to double-digit rates.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we don't see any pullback whatsoever in demand for the aircraft. So our rate increase plan is -- remains unchanged. ... our first rate increase will be from 38 to 42, and then we'll do 5 per month increments after that. So 42 to 47, 47 to 52.
finding: Boeing kept its 737 ramp plan (38, 42, 47, 52) despite the China tariff shock.
response: Keep rate increase plan unchanged; redeploy aircraft to other customers

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: the net annual impact of higher tariffs on our input costs is manageable and within our plan, it's less than $500 million annually. ... As it pertains to China specifically, we talk about 50 or so airplanes that's -- it could be north of $1 billion.
finding: Boeing put input tariffs below $500M a year and the China delivery risk above $1B, both covered by its conservative plan.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: The thing I'm really trying to make sure we're focused on is making sure that an argument over a 10% tariff, who's going to pay doesn't turn into a continuity of supply issue.
finding: Boeing will take on tariff costs rather than let pricing disputes with suppliers disrupt supply.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I don't think a day goes by where we aren't engaged with someone in the administration, including cabinet secretaries and up to POTUS himself. ... both Guillaume and I would welcome a nontariff fixed environment for both of us. This isn't good for either company to be in this situation or the industry.
finding: Boeing lobbies the US government heavily and says it shares Airbus's interest in tariff-free aircraft trade.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: we entered into an agreement to sell portions of our Digital Aviation Solutions business for $10.55 billion, which is an important component of our strategy to focus on our core businesses and strengthen the balance sheet.
finding: Boeing sold non-core digital assets for $10.55B to deleverage and refocus on core businesses.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: Specifically on China, it represents approximately 10% of our commercial backlog. And if we need to redirect supply to more stable demand, the strong market backdrop across the rest of the world still supports our planned production rate increases.
finding: China is about 10% of the backlog, and Boeing kept its rate plans because other customers could absorb the aircraft.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: We have approximately 50 China deliveries in our plan for the balance of the year. We're in close communication with our China customers, and we're actively assessing options for remarketing already built or in-process airplanes.
finding: When Chinese customers said they would not take deliveries because of tariffs, Boeing looked at remarketing built and in-process aircraft to other customers.
trigger: April 2025 China retaliatory tariffs; Chinese customers indicated they would not take delivery
response: Assess remarketing of built/in-process aircraft; reassign unbuilt positions to other customers

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we have many customers who want near-term deliveries, so we plan to redirect the supply to the stable demand. And we're not going to continue to build aircraft for customers who will not take them.
finding: Boeing will not build aircraft for a customer that refuses delivery and will move the slots to customers who want them.
trigger: Chinese airlines refusing deliveries due to tariffs
response: Redirect supply to other customers; stop building for customers that will not take aircraft

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I want to remind you that we planned the ramp-up conservatively so that we had some capacity to deal with unknown challenges.
finding: Boeing builds slack into its annual plans so shocks (such as China's tariffs) can be absorbed without cutting guidance.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: The equity raise at the end of last year was sized to provide us the ability to restore our production system to help.
finding: The late-2024 equity raise was sized to fund the production-system recovery.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I think we know cutting corners can't be an answer for our recovery. We've got to do this right.
finding: Ortberg rules out cost-cutting that weakens safety or quality, even under financial pressure.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: It's all around production rates. Moving the MAX production up is really the story. ... the cash performance for the company is very much driven by the MAX production rates.
finding: The 737 MAX production rate is the main driver of Boeing's cash flow.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: We invested in this area more than any investment we've ever made in our defense business and that investment paid off.
finding: Boeing will make large self-funded R&D bets in defense (F-47), and says it won.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: at the end of the year, I would expect we'd be doing the milestone review from 42 to 47, so that we can move with that, so we won't be outputting at 47, to be clear.
finding: Ortberg took back the implied promise of 47 per month by end-2025 and said only the 42-to-47 review would happen by then.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: But no real change to our forecast of getting that certification done so that we can start deliveries next year.
finding: In May 2025 Boeing still guided to 777-9 deliveries in 2026, later pushed to 2027 in October 2025.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: We'll wrap the 777, we call it the metal wing, the existing configuration. We'll wrap up that freighter configuration, expecting a Dash 9 freighter configuration the year after that.
finding: Boeing confirmed its current plan to wrap up the existing 777 Freighter and move to a 777X-based freighter the year after.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I look at that really kind of in 3 work streams. One is, when is the market ready? And two, when are we ready, both financially and from a capacity perspective? And third is, when is the technology ready? And I would say the answer is not now on all 3 of those work streams.
finding: Boeing's test for a next-generation airplane is market, financial and capacity readiness, and technology; in May 2025 all three failed.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: If you talk to our airline customers today, I think universally, they would say, we still have work to do and the durability of the existing newer engines that are there. And we'd like to make sure that we don't see the type of durability issues in the future.
finding: Poor durability of current-generation engines makes Boeing cautious about the engine technology for a new airplane.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I'll also say that the backlog is fantastic for our current product line and getting the Dash 10 into the market, I think, is going to be an important step for us as well. So there's no hurry here. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready.
finding: With a strong backlog and the 737-10 still to come, Boeing feels no urgency to launch a new airplane.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we're watching that real closely to make sure that we aren't overcommitting in terms of how many different seat configurations we can get certified in a certain period of time and the complexity.
finding: Seat certification delays are making Boeing limit how many custom seat configurations it commits to, including for the 737-10 and 777-9.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: both the 737-7 and 737-10 are slated to complete the certification this year. ... if there are any delays in getting the -- through the certification, which we're not anticipating right now, we will just continue to build the Dash 8.
finding: In May 2025 Boeing still targeted 2025 certification for the 737-7/-10 and would build -8s if it slipped; it slipped to 2026 by July.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: right now, the heat exchanger production output is meeting our demand and allowing us to go to 7 a month. If it wouldn't have been, we wouldn't have moved.
finding: The 787 went to 7 per month only after one supplier's output (heat exchangers) could support it.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we're not going to go to a 50 a month rate and have an unstable production system. We're just not going to do it.
finding: Ortberg flatly refuses to reach 50 per month on an unstable production system.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: So the next one would be to 47. I would not expect those to be any earlier than 6 months apart. And so that could get us to where we'd like to get to 47 here by the end of the calendar year.
finding: In May 2025 Boeing hoped to be at 47 per month by end-2025 (clarified on p.61 as the 42-to-47 review); in October it was just moving to 42.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we are essentially sold out through the end of the decade. We are going to increase production rates on virtually all of our aircraft.
finding: Being sold out to 2030 leads Boeing to raise rates on nearly every program.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: And we saw that in China where there was an increase in tariff. And sure enough, the Chinese airlines immediately said, I can't take delivery of the airplanes. And that's way more impactful to us. Now that's been reversed.
finding: Retaliatory tariffs, which can stop deliveries to a whole country, worry Boeing far more than input tariffs.
trigger: April 2025 China retaliatory tariffs; Chinese airlines refused deliveries
response: Worked through the stoppage until China reversed; deliveries set to resume the following month

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I'm not in a position where I want to announce any decision dates at this particular time. ... I don't think the market is ready yet for a new airplane.
finding: In 2025 Boeing declined to match Airbus's NGSA timeline. New-airplane timing depended on market readiness, Boeing's cash recovery and technology maturity.
response: No launch date; three gating work streams

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I see nothing structural that says we can't get back -- get to that $10 billion. So I think you framed it perfectly. It's not if, but when. And I'm not ready yet to say when.
finding: Ortberg keeps the $10B free-cash-flow target in principle but gives no date.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: I'm not in a position where I want to announce any decision dates at this particular time. ... we've got 3 work streams here that we've got to mature. One is the readiness of the market for the new airplane, and that needs more work. I don't think the market is ready yet for a new airplane.
finding: Asked about Airbus's NGSA timing, Boeing would not set a launch date and said the market was not ready for a new airplane.
trigger: Airbus expected to make NGSA architecture/engine decisions by ~2027 (analyst question)
response: No new-airplane decision date; wait for market, company-readiness and technology work streams to converge

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: When are we ready and this whole discussion around turning the company around and generating cash flow is really important to when we're ready to launch it as well as when is the technology ready? ... we'll do that when those 3 work streams all kind of converge. That's not today and probably not tomorrow.
finding: Boeing will launch a new single-aisle only when market readiness, its own cash recovery and technology all line up, and that is not near term.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: it's about 3,200 employees. They build the fighters mechanics. They build the fighters in our munitions business in St. Louis and St. Charles. So the order of magnitude of this is much, much less than what we saw last fall. That was roughly 30,000 machinists.
finding: Boeing played down the 2025 St. Louis strike (about 3,200 workers) compared with the 2024 Puget Sound machinist strike (about 30,000).

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: these recent big wins we have, the development parts of those programs have all been cost plus. So we're not making the errors of the past and signing up for fixed price development, high-risk programs.
finding: Boeing now refuses fixed-price development risk and calls its earlier fixed-price bids a mistake.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: predominantly, that will be focused at the Dash 10 variant. The Dash 10 variant is -- has the most change from all the other variants. So it will naturally flow through the factory at a slower pace. So by isolating or providing that fourth line in Everett will allow us to let the 3 lines in Renton flow faster.
finding: Boeing added a fourth 737 line in Everett for the -10 so the three Renton lines can reach higher rates.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Now keep in mind, we generally have them at a higher rate than we are at. And so we'll be able to see where those supply chain constraints are in advance, and we go work them and beat them down.
finding: Boeing sets supplier rates above its own rate so it can find bottlenecks early.

speaker: Brian West, CFO
quote: BCA booked 455 net orders in the quarter, including 120 787 and 30 777-9 airplanes for Qatar Airways and 32 787-10 airplanes for British Airways. Backlog in the quarter ended at $522 billion, which was up more than $60 billion sequentially.
finding: Large widebody orders (787 and 777-9) drove Q2 2025 order intake.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Production of the first 777X-8 Freighter is underway with the first hole drilled in the wing spar this month
finding: Boeing is building the 777-8 Freighter while 777-9 certification is still unfinished.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Work on the solution is taking longer than expected, and we now are expecting certification in 2026. As we previously said, we don't expect a material impact to our production plans, and we're prepared to build other 737 models for our customers.
finding: When a variant's certification slips, Boeing keeps the line rate by moving customers to certified MAX models.
response: Build other 737 models for affected customers; hold planned production rates

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Hey, we almost -- we are almost at parity on deliveries with Airbus this last month.
finding: By August 2025 Boeing measured its recovery by near-parity with Airbus monthly deliveries.
response: Rate increases

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Thinking about the certification process, it's way too slow. We've got to work with the FAA in swinging the pendulum back and making that process that will work. I can't imagine that we can do a new airplane without having that process refined.
finding: Reform of the FAA certification process is another precondition Ortberg sets for a new airplane.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: as we get these development programs done, that will also free up a lot of capital for us to focus on what's next.
finding: Finishing the 777X and MAX 7/10 would free the capital Boeing needs for its next program, so a new-airplane launch comes after those.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Far and away, our priority is debt. Through this crisis we've been through, we've taken on way too much debt. And so as we come back and we start generating cash, we want to be solidly investment grade. And we need to be there for the next-generation airplane as we start to think about that.
finding: Boeing will pay down debt to be solidly investment grade before it launches a next-generation airplane.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: We're targeting that facility investment completion in the '28 time frame. So that gives you a feel for where we are today and where we could go. Strong demand for the airplane. There's no question about that. So it's selling quite well. If we could build more, we could sell more.
finding: Capacity, not demand, limits 787 sales, so Boeing is building capacity for rates above 10, due around 2028.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: We're flying a lot of sorties and there are no new technical issues on the airplane or the engine. ... we are falling behind on the certification.
finding: In September 2025 Boeing was already flagging the 777X certification slip that it charged for in October.
lag: about 7 weeks before the Q3 2025 $4.9B charge

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: We've kept those suppliers that were either concerned about their ability to meet our demand or they need financial support. We've kept those higher and many of our suppliers are at a higher rate than 38 a month. So they're already at the 42 in many cases.
finding: Boeing keeps fragile or financially weak suppliers producing above its own rate to protect the ramp, and lets stronger suppliers burn down inventory.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Pricing, I would say, is almost independent of the trade demand activity right now. We've been in this, a supply-constrained environment for quite a while. We do have inflationary pressure coming from the supply chain. And certainly, we're taking that into account in how we're pricing the new product.
finding: Boeing prices new orders for supply scarcity and supplier inflation, not for trade-deal demand.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: in many cases, we're seeing upgauging of demand, so like a 787 moving to a larger variant or a MAX moving to a larger variant, which also gives us some opportunity for higher pricing.
finding: Boeing uses customers' moves to larger variants (787, MAX) to raise prices.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: There's no better way to correct the balance of trade than to buy a large number of aircraft. And certainly, we're the beneficiary of that. The administration has been very helpful. I would say that in many of these announcements, they aren't yet contracts, they're intention to buy aircraft.
finding: Boeing benefits from orders announced in US trade deals but notes many are only intentions to buy, not yet contracts.
trigger: 2025 US tariff/trade negotiations producing government-announced aircraft purchase intentions (Qatar, British Airways, Korean Air)
response: Accept the orders as announced intentions and work to firm them up through the normal contracting process

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we have to watch the continued demand on the engines in both the forward fit and the aftermarket and the durability upgrades that are going on in the market. So that'll be an area that we'll continue to work with GE and CFM on.
finding: Boeing sees engine supply from GE and CFM, split between new aircraft and aftermarket durability fixes, as a risk to watch.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: people also are gaining confidence in our ability to meet our production output. So the fear of people discounting our production in the supply chain, I think, is diminishing
finding: Suppliers had been discounting Boeing's rate plans; Boeing thinks its credibility with them is recovering.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: if we thought capping at 10 was as far as we go, we would not be investing in expanding Charleston. So we're going to have a formal groundbreaking. But essentially, what you're going to see, if you've been to Charleston, we're going to double the footprint, the manufacturing footprint.
finding: Boeing commits capital to double the Charleston 787 footprint so it can ramp beyond 10 per month.

speaker: Jay Malave, CFO
quote: it's really a little early for me to comment on a specific long-term framework, but I'm confident in the underlying cash generation capability for us to return historical levels that you've seen before.
finding: The new CFO would not endorse the old $10B free-cash-flow target and did not give a timeline for a return to historical cash levels.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: our next rate increase will be from this 8, which we should be at 8 by the end of the year, and then we'll move to 10 next year. I do think on 787, the move from 8 to 10 will be more challenging for us with the supply chain, particularly seats.
finding: The 787 plan is 8 per month by end-2025 and 10 in 2026, with seat certification the main constraint.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: it's way more impactful for us to move when we're not ready than to hold off and wait till we're ready. And we will not go to the next rate until we show the maturity in the system. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early in this process.
finding: Ortberg repeats (he says it since the campaign began a year earlier) that the cost of ramping too early outweighs the cost of waiting.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we've got significant inventory right now, and that's clearly boosting us from going from 38 to 42, will also still help us when we go 42 to 47. But at that point, I think we start to get more, I'll say, aligned with the supply chain
finding: Boeing's buffer of supplier inventory allows early 737 steps; beyond 47 the supply chain becomes the constraint.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we just have to flow the new revised schedule out to our suppliers. And then we're going to have to negotiate ... the impact that has to the various suppliers. ... the revised estimate and the charge here contemplated the impact to the supply chain as well.
finding: Boeing handles the 777X delay's supplier effects by pushing out the schedule and negotiating supplier compensation, provisioned in the charge.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: the philosophy I want here is, I don't want this to be a continuous quarterly issue for us to make sure we have a solid financial estimate here, that we have a high level of confidence that we can get this certification work done.
finding: Ortberg's stated philosophy is to take one conservative, high-confidence reset of program estimates rather than repeated quarterly charges.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: We very much underestimated how much work it was going to take for us to get the TIA approvals and for the FAA to have the opportunity to review all the data submissions that are required.
finding: Boeing admits the 777X delay comes from underestimating the certification paperwork and FAA review under the new TIA process.

speaker: Jay Malave, CFO
quote: So next year will be a heavy use year. The year after that will be better in 2027. And then we would expect ourselves to get closer to neutral in 2028.
finding: The 777X will keep using cash until about 2028 and turn cash-positive from 2029.

speaker: Jay Malave, CFO
quote: Cash and marketable securities ended at $23 billion, and the debt balance ended at $53.4 billion. The company also maintains access to $10 billion of revolving credit facilities, all of which remain undrawn. We remain committed to strengthening the balance sheet and supporting our investment-grade rating.
finding: Boeing puts deleveraging and keeping its investment-grade rating first, with $53.4B of debt against $23B of cash.

speaker: Jay Malave, CFO
quote: This outlook continues to assume significant capital expenditures for future products and growth, particularly in St. Louis and Charleston. This ramp-up was seen in our third quarter CapEx spend, which we now expect to be closer to $3 billion for the year.
finding: Boeing is raising capex for growth and future products even while burning cash.

speaker: Jay Malave, CFO
quote: Importantly, this was the first positive free cash flow quarter since the fourth quarter of 2023 and serves as an important progress point in our company's recovery.
finding: Boeing returned to positive quarterly free cash flow in Q3 2025 for the first time since Q4 2023.

speaker: Jay Malave, CFO
quote: Backlog in the quarter ended at $535 billion and includes more than 5,900 airplanes, with the 737 and 787 both sold firm into the next decade.
finding: Commercial backlog is large enough that 737 and 787 slots are sold out into the 2030s.

speaker: Jay Malave, CFO
quote: The charge amount includes additional customer concessions, the cost of incremental rework on built aircraft, learning curve adjustments and the carrying cost of production operations spread out over a longer period of time.
finding: The 777X charge covers customer concessions, rework, learning-curve losses and carrying costs, so a delay costs money all along the program.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: We are building JDAMs without IAM workforce at about the same production rate as before the work stoppage
finding: During the St. Louis IAM strike Boeing kept building JDAMs at about pre-strike rates without union workers.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we expect rate increases beyond 42 per month will go in increments of 5. And while rate increase breaks won't be earlier than 6 months apart, we will remain disciplined, and we won't move to higher rates until we achieve stability and readiness.
finding: Boeing sets a rule for 737 ramps: steps of 5 per month, at least 6 months apart, and only once KPIs show stability.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: now we anticipate first delivery of the 777-9 will occur in 2027.
finding: Boeing now expects 777-9 first delivery in 2027 (the prior expectation was 2026, p.7).

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: we now have a final set of design changes to permanently address the engine anti-ice issue. This effort remains on the critical path
finding: The engine anti-ice fix is still the critical path for certifying the 737-7 and -10, now targeted for 2026.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, CEO
quote: Once we were satisfied with the sustained health and stability of the production system, we then presented our disciplined plan to the FAA to increase production to 42 airplanes a month.
finding: Boeing only asked the FAA for the 737 rate increase from 38 to 42 after demonstrating a stable production system at 38.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I will say that it seems they are trying to cover two of our airplane families with one airplane, which is a tough putt.
finding: Boeing read Airbus's 2006 A350 relaunch as a single product aimed at both the 787 and the low end of the 777.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: will they aggressively price old technology to bridge some customers? I would be tempted to do that, and that is the A330 story.
finding: Boeing expected Airbus to discount its older A330 aggressively to hold customers until the A350 arrived.
trigger: A350 arriving 2-3 years after the 787; Airbus pricing A330 aggressively

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have seen very aggressive pricing from our competition, in part because old technology is fighting new technology.
finding: Boeing attributed Airbus's aggressive pricing in 2006 to older Airbus products competing against newer Boeing technology.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: if they seek launch aid on the same terms that they have had it historically, I think our government would view that as a step backwards, a significant step backwards in the negotiating process.
finding: Boeing treated Airbus's expected A350 launch aid as a trade-dispute issue to be fought through government channels.
trigger: Airbus likely to seek launch aid for the A350

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: it seems they are trying to cover two of our airplane families with one airplane, which is a tough putt. ... it has some elements of competitiveness with the low-end of the 777 line ... We do not see it as a plane that can compete very well with our 787 line.
finding: Boeing read the relaunched A350 as a threat mainly to the low end of the 777, not the 787, which shaped its later wait-and-see stance on the 777.
trigger: Airbus relaunched A350 (XWB) at Farnborough, July 2006

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think if they seek launch aid on the same terms that they have had it historically, I think our government would view that as a step backwards, a significant step backwards in the negotiating process.
finding: Boeing treated Airbus launch aid for the A350 as a trade-dispute issue and signalled US government pushback.
trigger: Airbus expected to seek launch aid for A350

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We don't have the complexity on our airplane that the A380 is, we have a fifth of the electrical wiring in it. So I think if some of the concern is being driven by what you see out there in other places, then I think you have to understand there's some distinct differences
finding: Boeing pointed to the A380's wiring problems as a rival failure that it claimed the 787 would avoid.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have competitors that aren’t going to sit still and let us take easily as much of the market forever as we are taking now. ... we are determined to be ready to make any necessary competitive responses, any kinds of investments we need to making customers
finding: Boeing expected Airbus to fight back for share and would give up some margin gains to fund competitive responses.

speaker: analyst (Lehman Brothers)
quote: our aircrafts seems like firmly on the weight of 40 narrow-body a month and with somewhere between 250 and 300 on the FWB pushing forward on that aircraft, targeted against the 777, I guess with delivery in 2013 but Boeing thus far has narrow-body only to 31 a month
finding: Analysts pressed Boeing that the rival was heading to about 40 narrowbodies a month and building A350 orders against the 777, while Boeing held at 31 a month.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Your major competitor talked about price increases the other day. Have you seen that realized in the market in any fashion? Jim McNerney No.
finding: Boeing said Airbus's announced price increases in 2008 had not shown up in the market.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: So it's more of a geographic deployment. They've announced similar things in China, US. They've got lots of dispersed production in Europe. It will not be an in complicated supply chain for them to manage
finding: Boeing saw Airbus spreading final assembly to China and the US (a dollar-cost base), which it judged would make Airbus's supply chain harder to manage.
trigger: EADS tanker win and Airbus plans for US and China production sites

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
